Posterior transverse collateral sulcus.note: A short transverse sulcus on the basal occipital surface, at the posterior end of the Sulcus collateralis, between the Gyrus lingualis and the Gyrus occipitotemporalis lateralis, lying just above the Tentorium cerebelli. Pitfall: on axial CT, partial volume of the tentorium and the cerebellar folia beneath it can mimic or hide this sulcus.

????????.note: Coronary sinus tributary (name missing in source) on the diaphragmatic surface of the heart, next to the A. coronaria dextra between the Atrium dextrum and the Ventriculus dexter, lying on the Diaphragma above the liver. Pitfall: on non-gated CT, this vein next to the RCA can be mistaken for the artery or for a pericardial recess.

?x.note: Unlabelled small branch in the arterial tree of the Arteria canalis pterygoidei. It runs in the septal mucosa along the vomer and the posterior nasal septum toward the nasopharynx. Pitfall: CT cannot resolve it. Do not read septal mucosal enhancement or a vomerine groove as a lesion.
passing: Posterior lateral nasal branches of sphenopalatine artery.
Septal branches of posterior ethmoidal artery
Anterior septal branches of anterior ethmoidal artery

Abdominal aorta.note: Begins at the hiatus aorticus at about T12. It runs on the lumbar vertebral bodies left of the Vena cava inferior and bifurcates near L4. Pitfall: a retro-aortic or circumaortic Vena renalis sinistra, or retro-aortic nodes, can mimic a periaortic mass or a dissection flap.

Abducens nerve (VI).note: It exits at the pontomedullary junction, climbs the clivus through Dorello canal over the petrous apex, and runs inside the Sinus cavernosus lateral to the ICA. It then passes through the anulus tendineus to the lateral rectus. Pitfall: a VI palsy can be a false localising sign of raised ICP; also look for clival fracture or petrous apicitis.
landmarks: lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipital bone

Abductor digiti minimi of foot.note: Runs along the lateral plantar border from the calcaneal tuberosity to the base of the fifth proximal phalanx, superficial to the flexor digiti minimi. Pitfall: fatty atrophy of this muscle alone suggests entrapment of Baxter's nerve (the first branch of the nervus plantaris lateralis). It is not an age-related change.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of foot

Abductor digiti minimi of hand.note: The most medial (ulnar) and superficial hypothenar muscle. It runs from the pisiform and FCU tendon to the ulnar base of the little finger's proximal phalanx. Pitfall: an accessory ADM slip crossing the Guyon canal is a common variant that can compress the ulnar nerve; do not report it as a ganglion or tumour.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand
Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Abductor hallucis.note: Forms the medial plantar border, from the processus medialis tuberis calcanei to the medial base of the hallux proximal phalanx. The plantar nerves and vessels leave the tarsal tunnel deep to it. Pitfall: a hypertrophied or accessory muscle belly at the tarsal tunnel exit can mimic a soft-tissue mass.
neighbours: Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis
Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot

Abductor pollicis brevis.note: The most superficial and lateral (radial) thenar muscle. It runs from the flexor retinaculum and the scaphoid and trapezium tubercles to the radial base of the thumb's proximal phalanx. Pitfall: in median neuropathy it atrophies first; do not mistake fatty atrophy of the thenar eminence for a lipoma.
neighbours: Superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis
Deep head of flexor pollicis brevis
Tendon sheath of flexor carpi radialis

Abductor pollicis longus.note: Starts on the posterior ulna, radius and membrana interossea, crosses over ECRL/ECRB in the distal forearm and runs in the first extensor compartment over the processus styloideus radii to the base of the first metacarpal. Pitfall: APL often has several tendon slips, which can be mistaken for a longitudinal tear. Also, the oblique crossing (intersection) is proximal to de Quervain territory.

Accessory branch of middle meningeal art.key: Accessory branch of middle meningeal artery
Accessory branch of middle meningeal art.note: Arises from the Arteria maxillaris or the middle meningeal artery in the infratemporal fossa, passes the lateral pterygoid muscle and enters the skull through the foramen ovale. Pitfall: an emissary foramen of Vesalius or a foramen spinosum next to the foramen ovale can be mistaken for its route on skull-base CT.
neighbours: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Accessory hemi-azygos vein.note: This vein runs left paravertebrally behind the descending aorta from about T4 to T8. It then crosses the midline behind the aorta and oesophagus to reach the azygos. Pitfall: a contrast-filled or dilated vein can mimic a periaortic or paraoesophageal node, or a periaortic haematoma. Follow it on consecutive slices.

Accessory nerve (XI).note: The spinal root ascends through the foramen magnum and exits with the vagus via the foramen jugulare, posterior to the intrajugular process. It then crosses the internal jugular vein, passes deep to the sternocleidomastoid and crosses the posterior triangle to the trapezius. Pitfall: after neck dissection, sternocleidomastoid and trapezius denervation atrophy can make the normal contralateral side look like a mass.
landmarks: lm:Intrajugular process of occipital bone|Occipital bone
lm:Styloid process of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Accessory nucleus of oculomotor nerve.note: The Edinger–Westphal nucleus lies dorsal to the oculomotor nucleus, ventral to the aqueduct, at the level of the superior colliculus. Pitfall: its pupillary fibres run on the surface of CN III. A dilated pupil with III palsy suggests compression (PComm aneurysm, uncal herniation), not a nuclear or ischaemic lesion.

Accessory pancreatic duct.note: Drains the anterosuperior pancreatic head into the minor duodenal papilla, which lies cranial and ventral to the major papilla. Pitfall: in pancreas divisum the dominant dorsal duct crosses anterior to the Ductus biliaris without joining it. A periampullary duodenal diverticulum can mimic a dilated duct.

Acetabular labrum.note: A fibrocartilage ring on the margo acetabuli that joins the transverse acetabular ligament across the incisura acetabuli. It is not separately visible on non-arthrographic CT. Pitfall: an os acetabuli or ossified labrum (common with FAI) looks like an acetabular rim fracture. On CT arthrography, a sublabral sulcus mimics a tear.

Acromial part of deltoid muscle.note: The middle part arises from the lateral acromion, covers the tuberculum majus and the subacromial–subdeltoid bursa, and inserts on the deltoid tuberosity. Pitfall: the subacromial and subdeltoid bursae normally communicate, so fluid under the deltoid is one compartment. An unfused os acromiale at its origin can be mistaken for an acromial fracture.
neighbours: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

Acromioclavicular ligament.note: Capsular thickening across the joint between the Extremitas acromialis of the clavicle and the acromion. It provides horizontal stability and blends with the trapezius and deltoid fascia. Pitfall: joint width and step-off vary between people, and supine CT underestimates displacement. Compare with the other side and look at the coracoclavicular distance.

Adductor brevis.note: Arises from the body and inferior ramus of the pubis and inserts on the upper linea aspera. It lies between the adductor longus and pectineus anteriorly and the adductor magnus posteriorly. Pitfall: without fat planes it merges with the longus. Its planes are marked by the anterior obturator nerve branch in front and the posterior branch behind.

Adductor longus.note: Arises by a tendon from the pubic body below the tubercle and forms the medial border of the femoral triangle and floor of the adductor canal. Pitfall: in athletic pubalgia, an injury at the shared aponeurosis with the rectus abdominis looks subtle on CT. Origin enthesophytes or a small avulsion can be mistaken for symphyseal degeneration.

Adductor magnus.note: Arises from the Ramus ischiopubicus and ischial tuberosity and inserts along the linea aspera and the Tuberculum adductorium. The adductor hiatus carries the femoral vessels into the popliteal fossa. Pitfall: cortical irregularity at the posteromedial distal femoral metaphysis is a benign traction lesion (cortical desmoid) and should not be called a tumour.

Adenohypophysis.note: The anterior lobe fills most of the hypophysial fossa, with the Sinus cavernosus on each side and the Chiasma opticum above. Normal height is up to about 8–10 mm, with a convex upper margin in adolescents and in pregnancy. Pitfall: enhancing intercavernous sinuses can mimic or mask a microadenoma, and CT sensitivity for microadenoma is low.

Ampulla of lacrimal canaliculus.note: A short vertical dilatation just beyond each punctum, before the canaliculus turns horizontally. It sits in the medial lid margin, medial to the tarsus, surrounded by palpebral orbicularis fibres. Pitfall: it is not seen on routine CT. Punctal plugs or concretions here can mimic a periorbital foreign body.

Amygdaloid body.note: Grey-matter mass in the medial temporal lobe under the uncus. It lies just in front of and above the tip of the temporal horn, in front of the hippocampal head, with the Tractus opticus above. The amygdala sits in front of the temporal horn tip and the hippocampus behind and below it. Do not mix them up.

Anconeus muscle.note: A small triangular muscle on the posterolateral side, running from the posterior lateral epicondyle to the lateral olecranon and proximal ulna. It covers the posterolateral elbow capsule. Pitfall: it is lateral. Do not confuse it with the medial accessory anconeus epitrochlearis over the cubital tunnel, which can compress the ulnar nerve.
neighbours: Humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris
Subtendinous bursa of triceps brachii muscle

Angular artery.note: Terminal part of the facial artery. It runs along the lateral nose to the medial canthus and anastomoses with ophthalmic branches. Pitfall: the adjacent Vena angularis is the valveless route to the cavernous sinus. In medial-canthal cellulitis, don't mistake the artery for a thrombosed or engorged vein.
landmarks: lm:Nasal margin of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Angular gyrus.note: Inferior parietal lobule gyrus that caps the posterior end of the Superior temporal sulcus, behind the Supramarginal gyrus and below the Intraparietal sulcus. Pitfall: it lies in the posterior MCA–PCA watershed, and subtle early hypodensity here is often missed. On the dominant side, an infarct here causes Gerstmann syndrome and may be mistaken clinically for confusion.
passing: Parietal branches of middle cerebral artery

Angular vein.note: The Vena angularis runs along the side of the nose, over the frontal process of the maxilla, up to the medial canthus. It continues below as the Vena facialis and joins the Vena ophthalmica superior, which has no valves. Pitfall: an enhancing angular vein next to the lacrimal sac can be mistaken for dacryocystitis or a preseptal abscess.

Annular ligament of radius.note: Fibro-osseous ring that encircles the caput and collum radii and attaches to the anterior and posterior margins of the incisura radialis ulnae. The ramus profundus nervi radialis passes nearby at the supinator. Pitfall: in children, check the radiocapitellar line; a subtle radial head dislocation (Monteggia) is easily missed.

Anserine bursa.note: Lies between the pes anserinus tendons (Musculi sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus) and the superficial Ligamentum collaterale tibiale on the proximal medial tibia. It is only visible on CT when distended. Pitfall: anserine bursitis can be mistaken for a parameniscal cyst or semimembranosus bursa; it lies more distal and anterior, superficial to the MCL.
neighbours: Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament

Antebrachial fascia.note: Deep fascia of the forearm. It fuses with the Margo posterior ulnae and thickens distally into the wrist retinacula. Pitfall: the cephalic, basilic and median cubital veins lie above the fascia, while the median and ulnar nerves lie beneath it. Separate superficial infiltration or collections from deep compartment involvement.
neighbours: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Anterior axillary nodes.note: These pectoral nodes lie along the lateral thoracic vessels, at the lower border of the Musculus pectoralis minor and on the Serratus anterior over ribs 3–4, and count as level I. Pitfall: breast tissue in the axillary tail or an accessory breast can mimic nodes. Assign level I, II or III strictly by the borders of the pectoralis minor.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Anterior basal segmental artery of left.key: Anterior basal segmental artery of left lung
Anterior basal segmental artery of left.note: Supplies segment VIII and runs with the anterior basal segmental bronchus (BVIII) toward the anterior diaphragmatic surface of the lower lobe. Pitfall: on the left, the anterior and medial basal arteries often share a common trunk (anteromedial). Do not mistake an intrapulmonary node beside the vessel for a filling defect.
neighbours: Lateral basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BIX)
Posterior basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BX)

Anterior basal segmental artery of right.key: Anterior basal segmental artery of right lung
Anterior basal segmental artery of right.note: A8 runs anterolaterally with BVIII into the anterior basal segment, behind the oblique fissure and above the diaphragmatic dome. Pitfall: the basal veins run between segments toward the inferior pulmonary vein. When reporting subsegmental emboli, trace the vessel back to the hilum to tell artery from vein.
passing: Inferior lobar artery of right lung
Posterior basal segmental artery of right lung
Superior basal vein of right lung
neighbours: Lateral basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BIX)

Anterior basal segmental bronchus of lef.key: Anterior basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BVIII)
Anterior basal segmental bronchus of lef.note: BVIII arises from the basal trunk, often as a common anteromedial stem with BVII. It runs anteroinferiorly toward the diaphragm, just behind the oblique fissure. Pitfall: the lingula lies across that fissure. Use the fissure on sagittal views to assign basal lesions to the lower lobe rather than the upper lobe.
passing: Lateral basal segmental artery of left lung
neighbours: Lateral basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BIX)

Anterior basal segmental bronchus of rig.key: Anterior basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BVIII)
Anterior basal segmental bronchus of rig.note: Runs anterolaterally and inferiorly from the basal trunk toward the anterior hemidiaphragm, directly behind the oblique fissure. Pitfall: opacity next to the fissure may lie in the middle lobe rather than BVIII, so assign the lobe using the fissure on sagittal reformats.
passing: Inferior lobar artery of right lung
Lateral basal segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Medial basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BVII)
Lateral basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BIX)

Anterior belly of digastric muscle.note: Runs from the digastric fossa of the mandible to the intermediate tendon, superficial to the mylohyoid. The paired bellies bound the submental triangle (level IA). Pitfall: after V3 denervation the affected belly atrophies and fills with fat. The normal opposite side can then be wrongly read as a mass. Accessory bellies are a normal variant.

Anterior branch of medial antebrachial c.key: Anterior branch of medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve
Anterior branch of medial antebrachial c.note: Runs in the subcutis over the anteromedial forearm, superficial to fascia antebrachii, next to the vena mediana antebrachii. CT cannot resolve it. Pitfall: it often crosses the cubital veins, so it is easily injured during venipuncture or a hand-made line; do not mistake a small subcutaneous vein for it.
passing: Posterior branch of medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Anterior branch of obturator nerve.note: Leaves the canalis obturatorius above the obturator externus and descends anterior to the adductor brevis, deep to the pectineus and adductor longus, to supply the gracilis. Pitfall: the adductor brevis separates the anterior from the posterior branch, so use it, not the adductor longus, to assign the branch.

Anterior branch of renal artery.note: The anterior division of the right renal artery passes in front of the renal pelvis in the sinus renalis and supplies most of the kidney. Pitfall: the avascular plane between the anterior and posterior divisions (Brödel line) is used for access. Accessory or polar arteries arising directly from the aorta are common and must be reported.

Anterior cells of ethmoid bone.note: Cellulae anteriores ossis ethmoidei lie behind the Os lacrimale and medial to the lamina orbitalis, with the Pars orbitalis ossis frontalis as the roof, and drain to the middle meatus. Pitfall: a low or asymmetric lateral lamella of the cribriform plate (Keros III) is easy to miss on axial images; check coronal reconstructions.
landmarks: lm:Orbital part of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Anterior cerebral artery.note: A1 runs medially above the optic chiasm and nerve to the anterior communicating artery, then A2 rises in the interhemispheric fissure in front of the lamina terminalis. Pitfall: A1 hypoplasia or aplasia is a common variant. Do not mistake asymmetry for occlusion. An AComm aneurysm can mimic a suprasellar mass.
passing: Orbitofrontal branches of anterior cerebral artery

Anterior chamber of eyeball.note: The anterior chamber is the fluid-density space between the Cornea and the Iris/Lens. Pitfall: always compare chamber depth with the other side. A shallow chamber suggests corneal laceration or anterior lens displacement. A deepened chamber suggests occult posterior globe rupture.

Anterior circumflex humeral artery.note: Arises from the third part of the axillary artery. It passes laterally in front of the collum chirurgicum, deep to coracobrachialis and biceps, and its ascending branch runs in the sulcus intertubercularis beside the long head of biceps tendon. Pitfall: in four-part and anatomical-neck fractures, loss of this branch predicts humeral head avascular necrosis. Do not mistake its vessels for tendon-sheath fluid.

Anterior circumflex humeral vein.note: This vein winds around the front of the surgical neck of the humerus, deep to coracobrachialis and the biceps heads, and drains into the Vena axillaris. Its ascending branch runs in the intertubercular sulcus. Pitfall: the vessel in the bicipital groove can be mistaken for fluid in the tendon sheath of the long head of biceps.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle
Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Anterior cochlear nucleus.note: It lies at the pontomedullary junction on the inferior cerebellar peduncle, where the cochlear nerve enters from the cerebellopontine angle. It cannot be resolved on CT, so localise it via the cerebellopontine angle and the porus acusticus internus. Pitfall: a normal CT does not exclude a retrocochlear lesion; small vestibular schwannomas need MRI.

Anterior commissure.note: Commissura anterior crosses the midline in the lamina terminalis, in front of the columns of the fornix, forming the anterior wall of the third ventricle. Laterally it runs below the lentiform nucleus. It is the anterior reference point of the AC–PC line. Pitfall: on axial slices, do not mistake it for the posterior commissure or the columns of the fornix.

Anterior communicating artery.note: It joins both A1 segments in the lamina terminalis cistern. It lies above the Chiasma opticum and below and between the Gyri recti. Pitfall: this is the most common aneurysm site, and a gyrus rectus or interhemispheric haematoma points to it. Fenestration, duplication or a dominant A1 can mimic a small aneurysm on CTA.

Anterior corticospinal tract.note: Uncrossed motor tract beside the Fissura mediana anterior, medial to the Cornu anterius. It usually ends in the mid-thoracic cord. CT cannot resolve it. Pitfall: the enhancing Arteria spinalis anterior in the fissure on CTA is not an intramedullary lesion; an infarct in its territory involves this tract bilaterally.

Anterior cruciate ligament.note: Runs from the medial surface of the lateral femoral condyle in the fossa intercondylaris to the area intercondylaris anterior, in front of the PCL. Pitfall: CT rarely shows the ligament itself. Look for indirect signs: a tibial eminence avulsion or a Segond fragment at the lateral tibial rim, which should not be dismissed as an ossicle.

Anterior cutaneous branches of femoral n.key: Anterior cutaneous branches of femoral nerve
Anterior cutaneous branches of femoral n.note: Arise in the femoral triangle and pierce the sartorius and fascia lata to supply the anterior and medial thigh skin. Pitfall: do not confuse them with the saphenous nerve, the only femoral branch that continues with the femoral artery into the canalis adductorius.

Anterior deep temporal artery.note: Branch of the maxillary artery that ascends deep to the Musculus temporalis on the temporal surface of the greater wing. It is extracranial. Pitfall: its shallow groove on the outer table must not be confused with the intracranial middle meningeal groove. Only an inner-table fracture crossing the MMA groove raises concern for epidural hematoma.
landmarks: lm:Temporal surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone

Anterior division of inferior trunk of b.key: Anterior division of inferior trunk of brachial plexus
Anterior division of inferior trunk of b.note: Lies behind the clavicle and continues alone as the medial cord, which runs medial to the A. axillaris and gives off the ulnar, medial cutaneous and medial pectoral nerves. Pitfall: the divisions are retroclavicular, so displaced clavicle fractures and subclavian or axillary vessel injury can involve them. The medial cord lies between the axillary artery and vein.
passing: Posterior division of inferior trunk of brachial plexus

Anterior division of internal iliac arte.key: Anterior division of internal iliac artery
Anterior division of internal iliac arte.note: Continues anteroinferiorly along the lateral pelvic wall. It gives visceral branches plus the obturator, internal pudendal and inferior gluteal arteries, which leave below the piriformis. Pitfall: the branching pattern varies widely, and the superior gluteal artery can arise from it. Name branches by where they exit (supra- or infrapiriform), not by order of origin.
passing: Posterior division of internal iliac artery

Anterior division of mandibular nerve.note: The smaller, mainly motor trunk of V3 leaves the nerve just below the foramen ovale, in the upper fossa infratemporalis deep to the musculus pterygoideus lateralis. It is not seen on CT, so localise it from the foramen ovale. Pitfall: do not mistake the foramen spinosum (posterolateral, carries the arteria meningea media) for the foramen ovale when looking for perineural spread.
neighbours: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Anterior division of middle trunk of bra.key: Anterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus
Anterior division of middle trunk of bra.note: Lies behind the middle third of the clavicula, above the first rib, and joins the anterior division of the superior trunk to form the lateral cord. Pitfall: on contrast CT, the suprascapular artery and vein crossing just above can look like plexus elements, or hide them.
passing: Anterior division of superior trunk of brachial plexus
Posterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus

Anterior division of retromandibular vei.note: Leaves the lower pole of the parotid behind the mandibular angle and joins the facial vein to form the common facial vein, superficial to the posterior digastric belly. Pitfall: an enhancing vessel at the parotid tail can look like a tail lesion or a level II node. Trace it back to the retromandibular vein.
landmarks: lm:Styloid process of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Anterior division of superior trunk of b.key: Anterior division of superior trunk of brachial plexus
Anterior division of superior trunk of b.note: The most superolateral division. It lies behind the clavicula near the conoid tubercle and helps form the lateral cord. Pitfall: in a clavicle fracture or callus, describe the relation to this division, and do not confuse it with the suprascapular nerve, which leaves the superior trunk more proximally and runs toward the scapular notch.
passing: Anterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus
Posterior division of superior trunk of brachial plexus

Anterior ethmoidal artery.note: Leaves the orbit through the anterior ethmoidal canal at the frontoethmoidal suture and crosses the ethmoid roof to the lamina cribrosa. On coronal CT it shows as a notch ('beak') in the medial orbital wall. Pitfall: a canal hanging below the skull base on a mesentery is at risk in FESS. Do not confuse it with the posterior ethmoidal canal.
passing: Anterior septal branches of anterior ethmoidal artery

Anterior fasciculus proprius.note: Short intersegmental fibres that hug the grey matter of the Cornu anterius, deep in the anterior funiculus. CT cannot see them. Pitfall: CT shows only canal dimensions and cord contour. Do not infer which tract is injured from ventral cord flattening caused by a disc–osteophyte complex.

Anterior horn of spinal cord.note: The ventral grey column, enlarged at the cervical and lumbar enlargements, from which the anterior roots exit through the anterolateral sulcus. Pitfall: CT cannot separate grey from white matter in the cord. Cord segments lie higher than the vertebrae of the same number, so do not assign the level from the vertebral body.

Anterior inferior cerebellar artery.note: It arises from the lower A. basilaris, crosses the N. abducens, and runs into the cerebellopontine angle towards the Flocculus. Its meatal loop often enters the internal acoustic meatus next to CN VII/VIII. Pitfall: this vascular loop can mimic a small intracanalicular lesion. AICA and PICA have a reciprocal size balance and may share a common trunk.
landmarks: lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipital bone

Anterior inferior jugular nodes.note: These nodes lie in front of the lower internal jugular vein, deep to the Musculus sternocleidomastoideus and behind the strap muscles. The jugulo-omohyoid node sits where the Omohyoid crosses the vein. Pitfall: in early arterial-phase scans, an unopacified or partly flow-mixed Vena jugularis interna can mimic a low-density node.

Anterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal ar.note: Runs along the anterior surface of the pancreatic head, in the groove next to the descending duodenum, and joins the anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery to form an arcade. Pitfall: it can be mistaken for the nearby gastrocolic trunk or right gastro-omental vein. Check the arterial phase, and look for arcade aneurysms with coeliac stenosis.

Anterior intercavernous sinus.note: Runs across the front of the hypophysial fossa within the diaphragma sellae and links the two cavernous sinuses. It lies below the optic chiasm. Pitfall: on contrast CT its enhancement can mimic an enhancing pituitary lesion edge. A large sinus is a bleeding risk in transsphenoidal surgery.

Anterior intermuscular septum of leg.note: Thin septum running from the Fascia cruris to the anterior border of the fibula, separating the extensor compartment from the fibular compartment. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the Membrana interossea cruris, which lies deeper between the tibia and fibula. The deep fibular nerve runs anterior to the membrane, not inside this septum.

Anterior interosseous nerve of forearm.note: Leaves the N. medianus between the heads of pronator teres and descends on the volar Membrana interossea between FDP and FPL, ending in pronator quadratus. It is purely motor (Kiloh–Nevin syndrome). Pitfall: isolated fatty atrophy of pronator quadratus points to this nerve, not to carpal tunnel syndrome. Do not confuse it with the posterior interosseous nerve.
neighbours: Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Anterior interventricular artery.note: The LAD runs in the anterior interventricular groove between the left and right ventricles toward the apex. It gives off septal and diagonal branches, and the Vena magna cordis runs alongside. Pitfall: an intramyocardial (bridged) mid-LAD segment appears narrowed in systole. Do not report it as fixed stenosis or occlusion.
passing: Septal branches of anterior interventricular artery

Anterior jugular vein.note: This paramedian superficial vein lies anterior to the infrahyoid strap muscles. The paired veins are joined by the arcus venosus juguli in the suprasternal space before draining into the v. jugularis externa. Pitfall: the two veins are often asymmetric or single. Unopacified, they can mimic anterior cervical nodes, and they are a bleeding hazard at cricothyrotomy.

Anterior lateral segment of liver (VI).note: Segment VI lies below the right portal plane and lateral to the right hepatic vein. It borders the right kidney at the hepatorenal recess and the hepatic flexure. Pitfall: a Riedel lobe (an elongated segment VI) can look like hepatomegaly or a right-sided abdominal mass.

Anterior layer of thoracolumbar fascia.note: Lamina anterior fasciae thoracolumbaris covers the front of quadratus lumborum. It attaches medially to the lumbar transverse processes, above to the 12th rib, and below to the iliolumbar ligament and iliac crest. Pitfall: it blends laterally with fascia transversalis, so do not confuse it with the psoas fascia when tracing retroperitoneal collections.

Anterior ligament of fibular head.note: Reinforces the anterior aspect of the superior tibiofibular joint, running obliquely from the fibular head to the lateral tibial condyle. Pitfall: in anterolateral dislocation of the fibular head the joint is widened only subtly. Always compare with the contralateral side.
neighbours: Articular capsule of superior tibiofibular joint

Anterior longitudinal ligament.note: Runs along the anterior vertebral bodies and discs from the Tuberculum anterius atlantis to the Os sacrum, behind the aorta, oesophagus and diaphragmatic crura. It is visible on CT only when ossified. Pitfall: flowing ossification in DISH (four or more levels, disc spaces preserved) is mistaken for the thin marginal syndesmophytes of ankylosing spondylitis.

Anterior medial segment of liver (V).note: Segment V lies below the portal plane, between the right hepatic vein and Cantlie's line (gallbladder fossa to middle hepatic vein). The gallbladder fossa marks its medial edge. Pitfall: focal fatty sparing or infiltration next to the gallbladder fossa, caused by aberrant cystic venous drainage, mimics a lesion.

Anterior meniscotibial ligament (Lateral.note: Anterior root of the lateral meniscus: attaches in the area intercondylaris anterior just in front of the lateral intercondylar tubercle. Its fibres blend with the ACL tibial footprint. Pitfall: ACL tibial avulsions and reconstruction tunnels can involve this root. Do not attribute an eminence fragment solely to the ACL.

Anterior meniscotibial ligament (Medial.note: Anterior root of the medial meniscus: the most anterior attachment in the area intercondylaris anterior, in front of the ACL footprint. Pitfall: the junction with the ligamentum transversum genus mimics an anterior horn tear (pseudotear) on CT arthrography. The attachment also varies (it may insert on the ACL or transverse ligament without a bony footprint).

Anterior occipital sulcus*.note: A variable vertical sulcus on the lateral convexity that marks the boundary between the temporal and occipital lobes. It separates the Gyrus temporalis medius and inferior in front from the lateral occipital gyri behind. Pitfall: it is often discontinuous and easily confused with the end of the Sulcus temporalis superior, so do not rely on it alone to assign lobes.

Anterior papillary muscle of right ventr.key: Anterior papillary muscle of right ventricle
Anterior papillary muscle of right ventr.note: This is the largest papillary muscle of the Ventriculus dexter. It arises from the anterior wall, where the moderator band connects it to the septum, and anchors tricuspid chordae. Pitfall: on axial CT it and the moderator band mimic RV thrombus or tumour, so check continuity on reformats.
passing: Inferior papillary muscle of right ventricle

Anterior quadrangular lobule.note: Upper anterior part of the cerebellar hemisphere, under the Tentorium cerebelli and lateral to the Culmen. The fissura prima separates it from the posterior quadrangular lobule. Pitfall: on axial CT, temporo-occipital cortex overlaps it at the tentorium. Use coronal or sagittal images to tell an SCA infarct from a PCA infarct.

Anterior root of posterior femoral cutan.key: Anterior root of posterior femoral cutaneous nerve
Anterior root of posterior femoral cutan.note: This root comes from the anterior divisions of the sacral plexus (S2–S3). It lies on the anterior surface of the musculus piriformis, lateral to the anterior sacral foramina. CT cannot separate it from the sciatic trunk. Pitfall: piriformis asymmetry or a split sciatic nerve variant can look like a mass at the greater sciatic foramen.
passing: Posterior root of posterior femoral cutaneous nerve

Anterior root of spinal nerve.note: It leaves the anterolateral sulcus of the cord, runs through the subarachnoid space and joins the posterior root just beyond the ganglion in the foramen. Pitfall: cervical roots exit above the vertebra of the same number, and from C8 down they exit below. A pseudomeningocele on CT myelography means root avulsion, not a cyst.

Anterior sacro-iliac ligament.note: A thin thickening of the ventral capsule over the anterior Articulatio sacroiliaca, beneath psoas and iliacus. It is the only sacroiliac ligament torn in an APC-II open-book injury, which shows as anterior-only widening. Pitfall: anterior bridging osteophytes (DISH) can mimic ankylosis. True sacroiliitis ankylosis is intra-articular.

Anterior segment of eyeball.note: Extends from the cornea to the lens and zonules and includes the anterior and posterior chambers. It is bounded by the iris and the sclera at the limbus. Pitfall in trauma: compare anterior chamber depth with the other side. A shallow chamber suggests a corneal laceration, a deepened one suggests occult posterior rupture, and also check for lens dislocation.

Anterior segmental artery of left lung.key: Anterior segmental artery of left lung
Anterior segmental artery of left lung.note: Arises from the left pulmonary artery arch to supply segment III, running alongside bronchus BIII in the left upper lobe. Pitfall: left upper lobe arterial branching is very variable, with one to several branches. The apicoposterior vein runs close by, so do not confuse vein and artery or call a variant a filling defect.
passing: Apical segmental artery of left lung
Posterior segmental artery of left lung
Superior lingular artery of left lung
neighbours: Anterior segmental bronchus of left lung (BIII)

Anterior segmental artery of right lung.key: Anterior segmental artery of right lung
Anterior segmental artery of right lung.note: A3 branches from the truncus anterior and runs anteriorly with BIII into the anterior segment, which is bounded below by the horizontal fissure. Pitfall: the central Vena apicalis runs between the apical and anterior bronchi and can be mistaken for the artery. The artery lies alongside its bronchus, inside the bronchovascular bundle.
passing: Superior lobar artery of right lung
Apical segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Anterior segmental bronchus of right lung (BIII)

Anterior segmental bronchus of left lung.key: Anterior segmental bronchus of left lung (BIII)
Anterior segmental bronchus of left lung.note: Arises from the upper division of the Bronchus lobaris superior sinister and runs anteriorly, almost in the axial plane, with its segmental artery beside it. Pitfall: the left side has a common BI+BII trunk, so do not apply right-sided three-branch upper lobe nomenclature.
passing: Anterior segmental artery of left lung
neighbours: Apicoposterior segmental bronchus of left lung (BI+BII)

Anterior segmental bronchus of right lun.key: Anterior segmental bronchus of right lung (BIII)
Anterior segmental bronchus of right lun.note: Runs anteriorly, almost in the axial plane, from the right upper lobe bronchus, with its segmental artery beside it. The anterior segment rests on the horizontal fissure. Pitfall: an opacity above the horizontal fissure belongs to BIII territory, not the middle lobe, so locate the fissure on sagittal images.
passing: Anterior segmental artery of right lung
Apical segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Apical segmental bronchus of right lung (BI)
Posterior segmental bronchus of right lung (BII)

Anterior semilunar leaflet of pulmonary.key: Anterior semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valve
Anterior semilunar leaflet of pulmonary.note: Anterior cusp of the pulmonary valve at the top of the infundibulum of the Ventriculus dexter, directly behind the anterior mediastinum and thymus. Pitfall: the pulmonary valve sits higher and further forward than the aortic valve. Do not mix up their cusps, or mistake thymic tissue for a mass touching the valve.
passing: Left semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valve
Right semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valve

Anterior septal branches of anterior eth.key: Anterior septal branches of anterior ethmoidal artery
Anterior septal branches of anterior eth.note: Run in the anterosuperior septal mucosa over the lamina perpendicularis ossis ethmoidalis and contribute to Kiesselbach's area. They are below CT resolution. Pitfall: these are internal carotid artery (ophthalmic) branches, so anterosuperior epistaxis may continue after sphenopalatine (external carotid artery) embolisation. Do not assign all septal bleeding to the sphenopalatine artery.
passing: Posterior lateral nasal branches of sphenopalatine artery.

Anterior spinal artery.note: It forms from paired branches of both Arteriae vertebrales on the ventral Medulla oblongata. It then runs in the anterior median fissure along the cord, inside the Dura spinalis. Pitfall: on thoracolumbar CTA, the larger anterior median spinal vein can mimic the hairpin-shaped arteria radicularis magna (Adamkiewicz). Check that the vessel connects to an intercostal or lumbar artery.

Anterior spinocerebellar tract.note: Superficial tract along the ventrolateral margin of the lateral funiculus, anterior to the Tractus spinocerebellaris posterior and near the dentate ligament. CT does not show it. Pitfall: on CT myelography, the dentate ligament and the spinal root of the Nervus accessorius along the lateral cord surface can look like an intradural lesion.

Anterior spinothalamic tract.note: Crossed tract for crude touch in the anterolateral funiculus, ventral to the Cornu anterius, at the exit zone of the ventral rootlets. CT cannot resolve it. Pitfall: because the fibres cross, a deficit is contralateral and starts a few segments below the lesion, so do not assign the side or level from the deficit alone.

Anterior sternoclavicular ligament.note: Ligamentum sternoclaviculare anterius thickens the front of the capsule between the medial clavicle and the Incisura clavicularis of the manubrium. The sternal head of sternocleidomastoid covers it. Pitfall: anterior dislocation is subtle on axial slices; compare clavicular head position with the other side on coronal/3D reformats.
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Anterior talocalcaneal ligament.note: A short band from the talar neck to the dorsal calcaneus at the front of the talocalcanean joint, at the anterior edge of the sinus tarsi. Pitfall: within the sinus tarsi fat it is easily confused with the interosseous talocalcaneal ligament and the cervical ligament. Name it only at the anterior subtalar margin.

Anterior talofibular ligament.note: A thin band inside the capsule. It runs from the anterior margin of the lateral malleolus to the lateral talar neck and is the first lateral ligament to tear. Pitfall: an os subfibulare can look like an acute avulsion. A rounded, well-corticated ossicle points to a chronic or accessory ossicle rather than a fresh fracture.

Anterior temporal branch.note: Often arises early from M1 and runs over the temporal pole and the lateral temporal gyri beneath the squamous temporal bone. Pitfall: an early temporal branch can be mistaken for an M1 bifurcation, which leads to wrong M1/M2 occlusion staging. The squamous temporal bone also causes artefact over the temporal pole.
passing: Insular branches of middle cerebral artery (M2)
landmarks: lm:Squamous part of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Anterior tibial artery.note: It arises at the lower border of the popliteus and passes over the Membrana interossea cruris into the anterior compartment. It descends on the membrane between the tibialis anterior and the extensor hallucis/digitorum longus and becomes the Arteria dorsalis pedis at the ankle. Pitfall: a high origin anterior to the popliteus is at risk during tibial osteotomy and knee arthroplasty.

Anterior tibial veins.note: A pair of veins running with the anterior tibial artery and the deep fibular nerve on the front of the interosseous membrane, between the tibialis anterior and the EDL/EHL. Pitfall: in the anterior compartment, the two veins beside the artery can mimic a three-vessel bundle or a fibular branch.

Anterior tibiofibular ligament.note: Runs obliquely downward and lateral from the anterolateral tibial tubercle (Chaput) to the anterior fibula (Wagstaffe), just above the talar dome. Pitfall: a small anterior tibial or fibular avulsion fleck (Tillaux–Chaput) is easy to miss. Judge syndesmotic widening at the incisura fibularis against the other ankle.
passing: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

Anterior vein of left lung.note: Vena anterior pulmonis sinistri drains segment S3 of the left upper lobe and joins the Vena pulmonalis sinistra superior anterior to the left upper lobe bronchus. Pitfall: it lies close to the anterior segmental and lingular arteries. Follow it to the left atrium before calling a filling defect, because arterial-phase mixing can mimic a clot.
passing: Superior lingular artery of left lung

Anterior vein of right lung.note: Vena anterior pulmonis dextri drains segment S3 of the right upper lobe and runs to the anterior Vena pulmonalis dextra superior, anterior to the hilum. Pitfall: veins run between segments, away from bronchus BIII. Do not confuse this vein with the Arteria segmentalis anterior, which runs next to the bronchus.

Aortic arch.note: Lies in the superior mediastinum at T4, left of the Trachea and in front of and left of the Oesophagus, and gives off the supra-aortic branches. Pitfall: the Vena intercostalis superior sinistra ('aortic nipple') or a ductus diverticulum can mimic an ulcer or a dissection.

Apical axillary nodes.note: These level III nodes lie at the apex of the axilla, medial to the Musculus pectoralis minor and below the clavicle, along the axillary and subclavian vein. Pitfall: a cross-section of the axillary vein or its tributaries can mimic an apical node, especially on non-contrast CT. Because these nodes drain toward the subclavian trunk, involvement means a higher stage.

Apical segmental artery of left lung.key: Apical segmental artery of left lung
Apical segmental artery of left lung.note: The apical artery rises from the arch of the Arteria pulmonalis sinistra and runs alongside BI+BII into the apex of Lobus superior pulmonis sinistri, under the pleural cupula. Pitfall: the left apical and posterior arteries often share one trunk. Do not mistake the Vena apicoposterior or the extrapleural left subclavian artery for this artery.
passing: Posterior segmental artery of left lung
Anterior segmental artery of left lung
neighbours: Apicoposterior segmental bronchus of left lung (BI+BII)

Apical segmental artery of right lung.key: Apical segmental artery of right lung
Apical segmental artery of right lung.note: A1 rises from the truncus anterior, medial to BI, into the lung apex beneath the pleural cupula. Pitfall: the Arteria subclavia dextra and the Arteria thoracica interna lie just outside the pleura at the apex. Do not confuse these systemic vessels with branches of the pulmonary artery.
passing: Superior lobar artery of right lung
Anterior segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Apical segmental bronchus of right lung (BI)
Posterior segmental bronchus of right lung (BII)
Anterior segmental bronchus of right lung (BIII)

Apical segmental bronchus of right lung.key: Apical segmental bronchus of right lung (BI)
Apical segmental bronchus of right lung.note: Runs vertically to the lung apex and appears as a round lumen on axial images. Pitfall: an apical pleural cap, first costochondral calcification or the Vena subclavia dextra in partial volume can mimic an apical nodule or Pancoast tumour.
passing: Apical segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Anterior segmental bronchus of right lung (BIII)
Posterior segmental bronchus of right lung (BII)

Apical vein of right lung.note: Vena apicalis pulmonis dextri drains segment S1 and descends anterolateral to the right upper lobe arteries (truncus anterior) to the Vena pulmonalis dextra superior. Pitfall: at the upper hilum it lies against the branches of the Arteria pulmonalis dextra. Partial anomalous drainage into the superior vena cava must not be overlooked.
passing: Apical segmental artery of right lung
Anterior segmental artery of right lung
Posterior segmental artery of right lung

Apicoposterior segmental bronchus of lef.key: Apicoposterior segmental bronchus of left lung (BI+BII)
Apicoposterior segmental bronchus of lef.note: Common trunk that runs cranially from the upper division toward the apex, so it appears in cross-section on axial images. Pitfall: an apical pleural cap, a first costochondral junction or the Arteria subclavia sinistra seen in partial volume can mimic an apical nodule or a Pancoast mass.
passing: Apical segmental artery of left lung
Posterior segmental artery of left lung
neighbours: Anterior segmental bronchus of left lung (BIII)

Apicoposterior vein of left lung.note: Vena apicoposterior pulmonis sinistri drains segments S1+2 and runs medially and inferiorly to the Vena pulmonalis sinistra superior. Pitfall: in the apex it runs parallel to the apical segmental artery and bronchus BI+BII, so on single slices vein and artery are easily swapped. Confirm by tracing it to the left atrium versus the Arteria pulmonalis sinistra.
passing: Apical segmental artery of left lung
Anterior segmental artery of left lung
neighbours: Apicoposterior segmental bronchus of left lung (BI+BII)

Appendicular artery.note: Runs in the free edge of the mesoappendix behind the terminal ileum to the vermiform appendix. A pelvic appendix may lie next to the psoas and iliac vessels. Pitfall: an enhancing vessel or the right gonadal vein in the right iliac fossa can mimic the appendix. Follow the blind-ending tube from the caecum.

Appendicular nodes.note: Nodi appendiculares lie in the mesoappendix along the appendicular artery, near the caecum and anterior to the right psoas major. Pitfall: small reactive nodes are common and nonspecific; do not confuse a node with the appendix itself. The appendix is blind-ending and tubular, usually with a wall or contained gas.

Aqueduct of midbrain.note: Narrow channel from the Ventriculus tertius to the Ventriculus quartus, with the tectum behind and the tegmentum in front. Pitfall: dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal-sized fourth ventricle mean aqueductal obstruction. Look for a tectal glioma, which can be isodense, or a pineal mass.

Arcuate artery.note: Runs laterally from the a. dorsalis pedis across the bases of metatarsals 2–4 at the tarsometatarsal level, deep to the EDB and EDL tendons, and gives off dorsal metatarsal arteries 2–4. Pitfall: it is often hypoplastic or absent, with the lateral tarsal artery or the perforators taking over; this is not occlusion.

Arcuate popliteal ligament.note: Y-shaped thickening of the posterolateral capsule running from the apex capitis fibulae over the popliteus tendon. It is not resolvable on CT. Do not mistake an avulsed fragment at the fibular apex (arcuate sign) for a normal fabella or os; it indicates posterolateral corner injury.

Artery of central sulcus.note: Rolandic artery. It runs in the sulcus centralis between the gyrus precentralis and gyrus postcentralis and supplies the sensorimotor face and arm cortex. Pitfall: the central sulcus is easy to mislabel on axial CT. Find it with the 'hand knob' (omega) sign and the pars marginalis rather than counting sulci.
passing: Insular branches of middle cerebral artery (M2)
neighbours: Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus
Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci*)

Artery of precentral sulcus.note: Cortical MCA branch from the superior trunk. It ascends in the sulcus precentralis between the pars opercularis/gyrus frontalis medius in front and the gyrus precentralis behind. Pitfall: a hyperdense dot in a convexity sulcus can be a thrombosed branch, a small subarachnoid bleed or partial volume of the calvaria; compare with the other side and use thin slices.
passing: Insular branches of middle cerebral artery (M2)
neighbours: Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus
Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Artery of pterygoid canal.note: The vidian artery runs in the pterygoid canal at the base of the medial pterygoid plate, from the pterygopalatine fossa to the foramen lacerum region. Pitfall: on coronal CT, the pterygoid canal lies inferomedial and the foramen rotundum lies superolateral. Don't swap them when reporting perineural spread or juvenile angiofibroma extension.

Articular capsule of acromioclavicular j.note: Capsula articularis acromioclavicularis encloses the gap between the Facies articularis acromialis of the clavicle and the Facies articularis clavicularis of the acromion. The Ligamentum acromioclaviculare reinforces it from above, and the Bursa subacromialis and supraspinatus lie below. Pitfall: normal joint width and clavicular step vary, so compare with the other side before calling subluxation.

Articular capsule of elbow joint.note: Encloses the humero-ulnar, humeroradial and proximal radio-ulnar joints. Anteriorly it lies deep to brachialis, posteriorly deep to triceps and anconeus, and it includes the fossa coronoidea and fossa olecrani. Pitfall: an elevated fat pad with no visible fracture suggests an occult radial head or supracondylar fracture, so look for cortical step-offs.

Articular capsule of glenohumeral joint.note: Attaches around the collum scapulae and labrum and to the anatomical neck of the humerus. It is lax inferiorly, forming the axillary recess, which is close to the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery. Pitfall: on CT arthrography, contrast in the subacromial bursa means a full-thickness cuff tear, not a capsular leak.

Articular capsule of hip joint.note: Attaches to the acetabular rim and transverse ligament. On the femur it reaches the intertrochanteric line in front but only about the mid-neck behind. Pitfall: posterior basicervical fractures can be partly extracapsular. A distended iliopsoas bursa that communicates with the joint can mimic a cystic groin mass.

Articular capsule of interphalangeal joi.key: Articular capsule of interphalangeal joint of great toe
Articular capsule of interphalangeal joi.note: Encloses the single hallux interphalangeal joint between the proximal and distal phalanges. The flexor hallucis longus tendon lies plantar to it and the extensor hallucis longus tendon dorsal. Pitfall: an interphalangeal sesamoid of the hallux sits plantar to the joint. Do not mistake it for an avulsion fragment or loose body.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of deep fibular nerve
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot
Distal phalanx of first finger of foot

Articular capsule of knee joint.note: Encloses the femorotibial and femoropatellar compartments and communicates with the bursa suprapatellaris. On CT, look for a fat-fluid level (lipohaemarthrosis) on a horizontal-beam scan, because it signals an occult intra-articular fracture. Do not confuse a joint effusion extending into a popliteal (Baker) cyst with a vascular lesion.

Articular capsule of radiocarpal joint.note: Encloses the joint between the Facies articularis carpea of the radius plus the TFCC and the proximal carpal row (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum). Palmar and dorsal extrinsic ligaments thicken it. Pitfall: on CT arthrography, contrast reaching the DRUJ or midcarpal joint suggests a tear. In older patients, degenerative TFCC and lunotriquetral perforations are common.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus

Articular capsule of sternoclavicular jo.note: Capsula articularis sternoclavicularis encloses the medial clavicle, the Incisura clavicularis and the first costal cartilage. Sternohyoid and sternothyroid lie behind it, with the brachiocephalic veins just beyond. Pitfall: the medial clavicular epiphysis fuses last, up to about age 25; an unfused ossification centre can mimic a fracture fragment.

Articular capsule of superior tibiofibul.key: Articular capsule of superior tibiofibular joint
Articular capsule of superior tibiofibul.note: Plane synovial joint between the facies articularis capitis fibulae and the posterolateral tibial condyle. Its orientation varies (horizontal or oblique), and in about 10% it communicates with the knee joint. Pitfall: a ganglion cyst arising here can track along the nervus fibularis communis.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of fibula|Fibula

Articular capsule of temporomandibular j.note: Attaches from the rim of the mandibular fossa and the Tuberculum articulare to the condylar neck. The lateral pterygoid inserts anteromedially and the tympanic plate lies behind. Pitfall: on an open-mouth scan the condyle normally sits under or in front of the articular tubercle (physiological translation). Do not call this a dislocation without a closed-mouth comparison.
neighbours: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Articular capsules of distal interphalan.key: Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints
Articular capsules of distal interphalan.note: Encloses the joint between the head of the middle phalanx and the base of the distal phalanx. The terminal extensor tendon reinforces it dorsally and the volar plate plus the FDP insertion reinforce it on the palmar side. Pitfall: a dorsal base fragment means a mallet avulsion and a palmar one means an FDP avulsion. Do not dismiss either as a Heberden osteophyte.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Distal phalanx of third finger of hand
Middle phalanx of third finger of hand
Distal phalanx of second finger of hand
Middle phalanx of second finger of hand

Articular capsules of distal interphalan.key: Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints of foot
Articular capsules of distal interphalan.note: These capsules enclose the joints between the middle and distal phalanges of toes 2–5. The flexor digitorum longus tendon inserts plantar to them and the extensor expansion lies dorsal. Pitfall: fusion of the middle and distal phalanges of the fifth (sometimes fourth) toe is a common normal variant. It should not be called ankylosis or a missing joint.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
neighbours: Middle phalanx of second finger of foot
Distal phalanx of second finger of foot
Middle phalanx of third finger of foot
Distal phalanx of third finger of foot
Middle phalanx of fifth finger of foot
Distal phalanx of fifth finger of foot

Articular capsules of metacarpophalangea.note: Encloses the metacarpal head and the base of the proximal phalanx. The extensor hood lies dorsally, the volar plate lies on the palmar side and is linked to its neighbours by the deep transverse metacarpal ligament. Pitfall: normal sesamoids on the palmar side of MCP I, II and V can be mistaken for avulsion fragments. Sesamoids are smooth and fully corticated.
passing: Common palmar digital branches of median nerve
Common palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand

Articular capsules of metatarsophalangea.note: Enclose each caput ossis metatarsi and the base of the proximal phalanx. They are reinforced plantarly by the plantar plates and on the sides by the collateral ligaments. Pitfall: at the 1st MTP joint a bipartite sesamoid (smooth, corticated, often bilateral) is often mistaken for a sesamoid fracture.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Common plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
landmarks: lm:Head of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone
lm:Base of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot

Articular capsules of proximal interphal.key: Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints
Articular capsules of proximal interphal.note: Encloses the joint between the Trochlea phalangis of the proximal phalanx and the base of the middle phalanx. The central slip lies dorsally, the volar plate lies on the palmar side and the collateral ligaments lie at the sides. Pitfall: a tiny fleck at the palmar base of the middle phalanx is a volar plate avulsion. It is easily missed on axial images, so check sagittal reformats.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
landmarks: lm:Trochlea of phalanx of hand|Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
Middle phalanx of third finger of hand
Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Middle phalanx of second finger of hand

Articular capsules of proximal interphal.key: Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints of foot
Articular capsules of proximal interphal.note: These capsules enclose the joint between the trochlea of the proximal phalanx and the base of the middle phalanx. The flexor digitorum brevis slips lie plantar and the extensor expansion dorsal. Pitfall: in hammer-toe flexion the joint is cut obliquely and can look narrowed or subluxed. Assess it on reformats aligned to the toe axis.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve
landmarks: lm:Head of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
lm:Trochlea of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of second finger of foot
Middle phalanx of second finger of foot
Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
Middle phalanx of third finger of foot
Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of foot

Articular disc of acromioclavicular join.note: Discus articulationis acromioclavicularis is a small, often incomplete wedge between the facets. On CT it has the same density as the capsule and cannot be seen separately. Pitfall: age-related disc degeneration with vacuum phenomenon or chondrocalcinosis in the AC gap is common; do not read it as fracture or septic arthritis.

Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joi.key: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint
Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joi.note: The triangular disc runs from the margin of the Incisura ulnaris of the radius to the ulnar fovea and styloid base, between the ulnar head and the lunate/triquetrum. Pitfall: the disc is invisible on plain CT, and calcification in it suggests CPPD. A fracture at the ulnar styloid base suggests foveal TFCC avulsion, unlike a tip fracture. Report ulnar variance.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris

Articular disc of sternoclavicular joint.note: Discus articulationis sternoclavicularis divides the joint into two compartments. It attaches to the upper clavicular head above and the first costal cartilage below. Pitfall: vacuum phenomenon and degenerative sclerosis are common in older patients; do not mistake them for septic arthritis, which shows erosions and soft-tissue swelling.

Articular disc of temporomandibular join.note: A biconcave disc between the Caput mandibulae and the mandibular fossa/articular tubercle, attached anteriorly to the lateral pterygoid. Only the thin fossa roof separates it from the middle cranial fossa. Pitfall: CT does not show the disc. A normal joint space does not exclude disc displacement, which needs MRI. Check the fossa roof for intrusion of the condyle.
neighbours: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid.key: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle
Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid.note: Lies within the aryepiglottic fold, running from the Apex cartilaginis arytenoideae to the lateral epiglottis. The fold separates the laryngeal vestibule medially from the piriform sinus laterally. Pitfall: apparent fold thickening from head rotation or a collapsed piriform sinus can mimic a supraglottic tumour.

Arytenoid cartilage.note: Cartilago arytenoidea sits on the upper border of the Lamina cartilaginis cricoideae. Its Processus vocalis marks the level of the true vocal cord. Pitfall: asymmetric ossification or sclerosis is normal and must not be read as tumour invasion. Head rotation can also simulate arytenoid dislocation; compare cricoarytenoid joint congruence.
landmarks: lm:Articular surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage

Ascending aorta.note: Starts at the valva aortae, lies right of the Truncus pulmonalis and left of the Vena cava superior, and ends at the origin of the brachiocephalic trunk. Pitfall: pulsation artefact at the aortic root mimics a dissection flap, and the superior pericardial recess can mimic a dissection or nodes. ECG gating resolves the artefact.

Ascending branch of left colic artery.key: Ascending branch of left colic artery
Ascending branch of left colic artery.note: Runs cranially in the left retroperitoneum toward the splenic flexure, where it anastomoses with the middle colic artery through the marginal artery. Pitfall: the splenic flexure is a watershed zone (Griffiths point) for ischaemic colitis. The nearby left testicular vein should not be mistaken for this artery.
passing: Descending branch of left colic artery

Ascending colon.note: It is secondarily retroperitoneal and runs from the caecum in the iliac fossa up to the hepatic flexure under segment VI. It lies in front of the right kidney, with the right paracolic gutter on its lateral side. Pitfall: a fatty, lipomatous ileocaecal valve or a collapsed caecum can look like a mass or wall thickening.

Ascending part of trapezius muscle.note: This mesh runs from the occipital bone and Ligamentum nuchae to the lateral clavicle, over the Musculus splenius capitis. In TA, those upper fibres are the pars descendens. Pitfall: the TA pars ascendens is the lower thoracic part (T4–T12 to the Spina scapulae), so check which part you mean before reporting; after N. accessorius injury the upper part atrophies.

Ascending pharyngeal artery.note: Smallest ECA branch. It arises near the bifurcation and ascends between the ICA and the pharyngeal wall toward the skull base. Pitfall: it is rarely resolved on CT. A pulsatile retropharyngeal tubular structure is usually a medially displaced ICA ('kissing carotids'), which matters before tonsillectomy or biopsy.

Atlas (C1).note: The atlas is a ring of anterior and posterior arches around paired Massae laterales. It articulates with the Condyli occipitales above and C2 below, with the dens behind the Arcus anterior. Pitfall: congenital clefts of either arch have smooth, corticated edges and must not be reported as a Jefferson fracture.

Auditory tube.note: The bony part leaves the anterior tympanic wall and runs anteromedially along the carotid canal. The cartilaginous part opens at the torus tubarius in the nasopharynx, above the superior constrictor. Pitfall: only a thin plate separates it from the Arteria carotis interna. Look for dehiscence or an aberrant artery, and do not confuse it with the semicanal for tensor tympani directly above.
landmarks: lm:Internal opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone

Axillary artery.note: Runs from the lateral border of the first rib to the inferior border of teres major. Pectoralis minor divides it into three parts, and the axillary vein lies anteromedial. Pitfall: the subclavian–axillary boundary is the first rib, not the clavicle. Dense contrast streak artefact from an arm injection in the adjacent vein can hide or mimic arterial pathology.

Axillary nerve.note: Arises from the posterior cord, crosses the front of subscapularis below the capsula articularis, and passes through the quadrangular space around the surgical neck. Pitfall: do not confuse the quadrangular space with the triangular space, which carries the circumflex scapular vessels. Anterior or inferior dislocation and surgical neck fractures put the nerve at risk.
passing: Posterior division of inferior trunk of brachial plexus

Axillary vein.note: The Vena axillaris begins at the lower border of teres major, where the basilic and brachial veins join. It runs deep to Musculus pectoralis minor and becomes the subclavian vein at the outer border of the first rib. Pitfall: on the injection side, dense contrast and mixing of opacified and unopacified blood can mimic thrombus. Check the delayed phase.
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Axis (C2).note: The Dens axis rises behind the Arcus anterior atlantis and is held by the transverse ligament. The body joins C3 through the C2-C3 disc. Pitfall: os odontoideum or a leftover subdental synchondrosis can mimic a type II dens fracture; rounded, corticated edges point to a variant.
landmarks: lm:Posterior articular facet of dens axis|Axis (C2)

Azygos vein.note: This vein ascends right prevertebrally, beside the oesophagus and behind the right crus, then arches over the right main bronchus at T4–T5 into the SVC. Pitfall: an unopacified or dilated arcus venae azygos can mimic a right tracheobronchial node. In azygos continuation of the IVC, the enlarged vein can be mistaken for a mass.
neighbours: Node of arch of azygos vein

Base of peduncle.note: Anterolateral crus of the Mesencephalon. The interpeduncular fossa is medial and the ambient cistern and parahippocampal uncus are lateral. CN III and the PCA wrap around it. Pitfall: a Kernohan notch (opposite peduncle pressed against the tentorium) gives hemiparesis on the same side as the mass, a false localising sign.

Basilar artery.note: Formed by both Aa. vertebrales at the pontomedullary junction, it lies in the prepontine cistern between the Clivus and the Pons, and divides into the Aa. cerebri posteriores at the Dorsum sellae. Pitfall: normal dense blood or calcification can be read as a hyperdense basilar sign; compare its density with other vessels and the haematocrit.
landmarks: lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipital bone

Basilar venous plexus.note: A venous network between the dural layers on the back of the clivus. It connects the intercavernous and inferior petrosal sinuses with the epidural plexus around the foramen magnum, and CN VI crosses it. Pitfall: the enhancing plexus behind the clivus can mimic an epidural haematoma, a chordoma or a meningioma.

Basilic vein.note: The Vena basilica starts on the ulnar side of the dorsal venous network and runs up the subcutaneous fat of the ulnar forearm. It pierces the brachial fascia in the middle of the arm and joins the brachial veins at teres major to form the axillary vein. Pitfall: the deep segment in the upper arm can be confused with the brachial veins.
neighbours: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Bicipitoradial bursa.note: Sits between the distal biceps tendon and the anterior Tuberositas radii, deep in the cubital fossa beside the supinator. Pitfall: when distended, this bursa looks like a cystic mass or ganglion in the antecubital fossa. It can also compress nearby nerves; check that it sits right next to the biceps tendon.

Bifurcation of pulmonary trunk.note: The bifurcation lies to the left of the ascending aorta, below the aortic arch, at about the level of the carina. The right pulmonary artery passes behind the aorta, and the left pulmonary artery arches over the left main bronchus. Pitfall: the fluid-filled superior pericardial recess can mimic a node or a dissection. Measure the trunk perpendicular to its axis; more than 29 mm suggests pulmonary hypertension.

Bile duct.note: Ductus biliaris runs in the free edge of the Omentum minus, anterolateral to the portal vein. It then passes behind the duodenum and through the pancreas to the major duodenal papilla, where it joins the Ductus pancreaticus. Pitfall: in the pancreatic head, the non-enhancing duct can be confused with the enhancing gastroduodenal artery. Non-calcified stones may be isodense to bile.

Biventral lobule.note: The Lobulus biventer lies on the inferior hemispheric surface. The Tonsilla cerebelli is medial, the flocculus anterior and the occipital squama inferolateral. Pitfall: the interpetrous beam-hardening band (Hounsfield bar) crosses this level and can mimic hypodense infarct or oedema. Confirm on other slices or on MRI.
landmarks: lm:Posterior surface of petrous part|Temporal bone
lm:Occipital margin of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Body of sternum.note: Corpus sterni runs from the manubriosternal junction at the Angulus sterni (second costal cartilage) down to the xiphisternal junction. Its Incisurae costales receive cartilages 2–7. Pitfall: unfused ossification centres or a sternal foramen (normal variant) can look like a fracture or a lytic lesion, so check the sagittal reformats.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Brachial artery.note: Starts at the inferior border of teres major and runs in the sulcus bicipitalis medialis on brachialis with the median nerve. It bifurcates in the cubital fossa at the level of the radial neck. Pitfall: a high bifurcation (superficial brachial artery, about 15%) gives two arterial channels in the arm. Do not report them as an occluded segment or as brachial veins.

Brachial fascia.note: Fascia brachii is the thin investing layer of the arm deep to subcutaneous fat. It continues into fascia deltoidea proximally and fascia antebrachii distally, and sends the medial and lateral intermuscular septa to the humerus. Pitfall: vena basilica pierces it mid-arm while vena cephalica stays superficial, so do not mistake either vein for a node or a subfascial collection.

Brachial nodes.note: These are the lateral axillary/humeral nodes, lying along the axillary vein and the upper-arm veins and bounded by the pectoralis major and deltoid. Pitfall: the Vena cephalica in the deltopectoral groove, seen in cross-section, mimics a small node; trace it on consecutive slices.
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle
Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Brachial veins.note: The Venae brachiales are paired veins that run alongside the brachial artery in the medial bicipital groove, beside the median nerve. They form from the radial and ulnar veins in the cubital fossa and drain into the axillary vein. Pitfall: the paired veins wrapped around the artery can look like a periarterial collection or haematoma.

Brachialis muscle.note: Arises from the distal anterior humerus, covers the anterior elbow capsule deep to the biceps, and inserts on the Processus coronoideus and Tuberositas ulnae. Pitfall: after elbow trauma, myositis ossificans in the brachialis can mimic a coronoid fracture fragment. Separately, look for small coronoid tip fractures.

Brachiocephalic nodes.note: These are prevascular superior mediastinal nodes (station 3a) along the brachiocephalic veins, behind the manubrium and sternoclavicular joints. Pitfall: residual thymus, or a partially volumed left brachiocephalic vein or internal thoracic vein, mimics a node, especially without IV contrast.

Brachiocephalic trunk.note: The first branch of the Arcus aortae. It ascends to the right, posterior to the Vena brachiocephalica sinistra, and divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the Arteria subclavia dextra and Carotis communis dextra. Pitfall: a shared origin with the left common carotid (bovine arch) can be mistaken for a long trunk. Also, an aberrant right subclavian artery means there is no trunk at all.

Brachioradialis muscle.note: Arises from the lateral supracondylar ridge, forms the lateral border of the cubital fossa and inserts on the crista suprastyloidea of the radius. The radial nerve runs in the groove between it and brachialis, and the superficial branch runs under it in the forearm. Pitfall: distally, APL/EPB cross over its tendon, so do not count it as a first-compartment tendon.

Branch to angular gyrus.note: Terminal MCA branch to the gyrus angularis at the end of the sulcus temporalis superior. Pitfall: the gyrus angularis sits in the triple ACA–MCA–PCA watershed. Isolated hypodensity there after hypotension suggests a border-zone infarct rather than an embolus.

Buccal artery.note: Arises from the maxillary artery in the infratemporal fossa and runs anteroinferiorly with the buccal nerve on the Bucinator, then anastomoses with the facial artery. Pitfall: vessels crossing the buccal fat pad can mimic an enhancing buccal-space lesion. Look for continuity with the facial or maxillary branches.

Buccal nerve.note: It passes between the two heads of the musculus pterygoideus lateralis, then along the front edge of the ramus to the outer surface of the bucinator. It carries sensation to the cheek and buccal gingiva. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the buccal branches of the facial nerve, which are the motor supply to the bucinator.
landmarks: lm:Infratemporal surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
neighbours: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Bucinator.note: Forms the cheek wall from the alveolar processes and pterygomandibular raphe to the modiolus, with buccal fat and masseter lateral and the oral vestibule medial. The parotid duct pierces it. Pitfall: a Bucinator node in the buccal fat can mimic a dental abscess or a duct stone.
landmarks: lm:Vestibular surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

Bucinator node.note: Lies in the buccal fat on the outer surface of the M. buccinator, next to the V. facialis. Pitfall: in a dental infection it can look like a buccal-space abscess. The facial vein seen in cross-section also looks like a node. Check the premolar roots for a dental source.

Bursa of piriformis muscle.note: Small bursa between the Musculus piriformis tendon and the superior border of the greater trochanter, next to the Musculus gluteus minimus insertion. Pitfall: when distended it is easily mistaken for trochanteric (gluteus maximus) bursitis or a hip-joint recess; check its relation to the piriformis tendon.

Calcaneal branches of fibular artery.note: Lateral calcaneal branches arise from the a. fibularis behind the lateral malleolus and supply the lateral heel, joining the medial calcaneal branches of the a. tibialis posterior. Pitfall: these supply the lateral heel. Do not confuse them with the medial branches. They matter for the blood supply of extensile lateral calcaneal approaches.

Calcaneal branches of posterior tibial a.key: Calcaneal branches of posterior tibial artery
Calcaneal branches of posterior tibial a.note: Arise from the a. tibialis posterior in the tarsal tunnel, pierce the retinaculum flexorum and supply the medial heel and tuber calcanei, together with the medial calcaneal nerves. Pitfall: these supply the medial heel. Do not confuse them with the calcaneal branches of the a. fibularis on the lateral side.

Calcaneal tendon.note: Inserts on the posterior tuber calcanei, with Kager fat anterior to it and the bursa subtendinea calcanea between the tendon and the posterosuperior calcaneus. Pitfall: an intact plantaris tendon running medially can look like preserved fibres in a complete rupture.

Calcaneocuboid ligament.note: The lateral limb of the bifurcate ligament, running from the anterior process of the calcaneus to the dorsomedial cuboid. Pitfall: an avulsion of the anterior process of the calcaneus at its origin is often missed or mistaken for an os calcaneus secundarius. Acute fragments have sharp, uncorticated edges.

Calcaneofibular ligament.note: Runs from the tip of the fibula downward and backward to the lateral calcaneal wall, deep to the fibular tendons, and spans both the ankle and subtalar joints. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the superior fibular retinaculum. Fluid between the ligament and the fibular tendons is normal tendon-sheath fluid.

Calcaneonavicular ligament.note: The medial limb of the bifurcate ligament, running from the anterior process of the calcaneus to the lateral navicular. Do not confuse it with the plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament. Pitfall: a calcaneonavicular coalition follows the same course. An osseous or fibrous bar with irregular facing cortices is a coalition, not a normal ligament.

Calcaneus.note: Articulates with the talus at the posterior, middle and anterior subtalar facets, which are separated by the sinus tarsi. It meets the cuboid anteriorly, and the tendo calcaneus inserts on the tuber calcanei. The flexor hallucis longus runs under the sustentaculum tali. Pitfall: the normal trabecular-poor neutral triangle mimics a cyst or lipoma. Also, anterior process fractures are easily missed.
passing: Calcaneal branches of posterior tibial artery
landmarks: lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of calcaneus|Calcaneus

Calcarine sulcus.note: A horizontal medial occipital sulcus between the Cuneus above and the Gyrus lingualis below, running from the Polus occipitalis to its junction with the Sulcus parietooccipitalis. It indents the occipital horn as the calcar avis. Pitfall: the calcar avis can mimic a mass in the occipital horn, and the calcarine sulcus is easily confused with the parieto-occipital sulcus.

Callosomarginal artery.note: Runs in the sulcus cinguli, parallel to and above the pericallosal artery, on the medial hemisphere next to the falx cerebri. Pitfall: it is often absent or hypoplastic, so a missing vessel is not an occlusion. Do not confuse it with the pericallosal artery on sagittal CTA.

Capitate bone.note: The largest carpal bone. Its head sits in the lunate concavity, it lies between the trapezoid and hamate, and it bears the third metacarpal base. Pitfall: an os styloideum (carpal boss) at the dorsal second/third CMC joint mimics a fracture. Also exclude a scaphocapitate fracture-dislocation, where the capitate head is rotated.
