Capitohamate interosseous ligament.note: Strong intra-articular ligament between the opposing distal surfaces of the os capitatum and os hamatum. It is a key stabiliser of the distal carpal row. Pitfall: a widened capitohamate interval is easily dismissed as normal joint space; it suggests an axial carpal disruption, usually with metacarpal base injuries.

Cauda equina.note: The lumbosacral roots run inside the dural sac from the conus medullaris (about L1–L2) to the end of the sac at about S2. Pitfall: without myelography CT cannot show the individual roots, so judge canal stenosis from the area of the dural sac. Clumped roots seen on CT myelography suggest arachnoiditis, not tumour.

Caudate nucleus.note: The head bulges into the lateral wall of the frontal horn. The anterior limb of the internal capsule separates it from the Nucleus lentiformis. The body and tail curve along the ventricle. A caudate-head bleed often ruptures into the ventricle. Atrophy of the caudate head (a large bicaudate ratio) should not be mistaken for plain ventricular enlargement.

Cavernous sinus.note: Lies beside the sella and sphenoid body, from the superior orbital fissure to the petrous apex. CN III, IV, V1 and V2 run in its lateral wall; the ICA and CN VI run through it. Pitfall: normal fat and uneven enhancement can look abnormal. A bulging outer wall with an enlarged V. ophthalmica superior suggests a carotid–cavernous fistula or thrombosis.

Central axillary nodes.note: These nodes lie in the axillary fat behind the Musculus pectoralis minor (level II), between the Serratus anterior on the inner wall and the Teres major and subscapularis behind. Pitfall: normal nodes with a fatty hilum can be long. Judge by short axis and cortical thickness (more than about 3 mm is suspicious), not by long axis.

Central canal.note: Canalis centralis runs through the grey commissure. It is continuous with the fourth ventricle at the obex and widens into the terminal ventricle in the conus medullaris. It is not visible on CT. Pitfall: a slightly dilated canal or ventriculus terminalis is a normal variant, not syringomyelia.

Central lobule.note: The Lobulus centralis is the anterior vermian lobule between the lingula below and the culmen above. It lies behind the Colliculi inferiores and roofs the upper fourth ventricle. Pitfall: CT cannot resolve it separately, and the hyperdense tentorial apex or Sinus rectus nearby can mimic vermian or subarachnoid haemorrhage.

Central retinal artery.note: Enters the nervus opticus about 1 cm behind the globe and runs inside it to the optic disc. Not resolved on CT. Pitfall: a punctate calcification at the disc is usually optic disc drusen, not a calcified vessel or foreign body. Central retinal artery occlusion shows no CT sign.

Central sulcus.note: Separates the Gyrus precentralis (frontal lobe) from the Gyrus postcentralis (parietal lobe). It runs from the Lobulus paracentralis at the vertex down to just above the Sulcus lateralis. Pitfall: it is easily confused with the Sulcus pre- or postcentralis. Use the superior frontal sulcus–precentral sulcus junction, the pars marginalis 'bracket' sign and the thicker precentral cortex to identify it.
neighbours: Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci*)

Central superior mesenteric nodes.note: Nodi mesenterici superiores centrales lie around the SMA and SMV at the mesenteric root, below the pancreas and anterior to the third duodenal part. Pitfall: jejunal and middle colic branches seen in cross-section mimic nodes. Also, a misty mesentery with small nodes is a common incidental finding, not lymphadenopathy.

Cephalic vein.note: The Vena cephalica runs subcutaneously along the radial forearm and the lateral bicipital groove. It then runs in the deltopectoral groove and pierces the clavipectoral fascia to join the axillary vein below the clavicle. Pitfall: dense contrast injected through this vein causes streak artefact and inflow effects that can mimic thrombus or stenosis where it ends.
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Chorda tympani.note: It branches from the mastoid segment of VII and crosses the tympanic cavity between the manubrium mallei and the long limb of the incus. It leaves through the petrotympanic fissure and joins the lingual nerve medial to the lateral pterygoid. Pitfall: on high-resolution CT its bony canaliculi look like a fine lucent line that can be misread as a temporal bone fracture.

Choroid plexus.note: Largest at the glomus in the trigone. It runs along the floor of the ventricle body through the foramen of Monro to the roof of the third ventricle, and into the temporal horn through the choroid fissure. Pitfall: calcification of the glomus is physiological in adults and should not be read as haemorrhage. Head tilt can make it look asymmetric.

Cingulate gyrus (Posteroventral part*).note: The isthmus of the Gyrus cinguli wraps behind the splenium of the Corpus callosum and continues into the Gyrus parahippocampalis. The Precuneus lies above it and the calcarine junction below. Pitfall: a calcified or dense Falx cerebri and the Inferior sagittal sinus nearby can mimic interhemispheric subdural or subarachnoid blood.
neighbours: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Posterior dorsal part)

Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle anter.key: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle anterior part)
Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle anter.note: Arches over the body of the Corpus callosum, separated from it by the Sulcus corporis callosi. Above it, the Sulcus cinguli separates it from the medial Gyrus frontalis superior. Pitfall: in subfalcine herniation, the cingulate gyrus shifts under the Falx cerebri, which can compress the Pericallosal artery (ACA infarct).
neighbours: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle posterior part)

Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle poste.key: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle posterior part)
Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle poste.note: The midportion of the Gyrus cinguli lies above the Corpus callosum and below the Lobulus paracentralis, close to where the pars marginalis arises. Pitfall: the hyperdense Pericallosal artery and the Falx cerebri next to it can be mistaken for interhemispheric blood.
neighbours: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle anterior part)
Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Posterior dorsal part)

Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Posterior do.key: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Posterior dorsal part)
Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Posterior do.note: The posterior cingulate lies above the posterior body and splenium of the Corpus callosum. The Sulcus subparietalis separates it from the Precuneus. Pitfall: the Inferior sagittal sinus along the free edge of the falx can be mistaken for a thin interhemispheric hematoma.

Cingulate sulcus (Marginal part*).note: The pars marginalis turns up to the vertex and separates the Lobulus paracentralis in front from the Precuneus behind. On axial CT it forms the paired 'bracket' sign. Pitfall: it is easily confused with the Sulcus centralis. The central sulcus lies just in front of the bracket.
neighbours: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Posterior dorsal part)

Circular sulcus of insula.note: Outlines the Insula and separates it from the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula. The Putamen lies deep to it, beyond the capsula extrema and externa. Pitfall: in early MCA infarction, loss of the insular ribbon is a subtle sign. Do not mistake asymmetric opercular partial volume or patient tilt for this sign.
neighbours: Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci*)
Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus
Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Circumflex artery of heart.note: The circumflex artery runs in the left atrioventricular groove between the Atrium sinistrum and Ventriculus sinister. The Vena magna cordis and coronary sinus lie alongside. Pitfall: mitral annular calcification lies right next to the circumflex. Do not count it as coronary calcium or mistake the vein for the artery.

Circumflex scapular artery.note: Passes through the triangular space (teres minor above, teres major below, long head of triceps laterally) around the lateral scapular border into the infraspinous fossa, where it joins the suprascapular artery. Pitfall: do not confuse the triangular space with the quadrilateral space, which carries the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery.

Circumflex scapular vein.note: This vein runs with the a. circumflexa scapulae through the triangular space. The space is bounded by teres minor above, teres major below and the long head of triceps laterally. The vessels then wind around the lateral border of the scapula. Pitfall: do not confuse the triangular space with the quadrangular space, which carries the n. axillaris and the a. circumflexa posterior humeri.

Clavicle.note: The sternal end articulates with the clavicular notch of the manubrium and the acromial end with the acromion. The coracoclavicular ligaments attach to the inferior surface, and the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus lie beneath. Pitfall: the medial epiphysis stays unfused until about age 25 and can look like a fracture or a physeal separation.
passing: Anterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus

Clavicular head of pectoralis major musc.key: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle
Clavicular head of pectoralis major musc.note: It runs from the medial half of the clavicle to the crista tuberculi majoris of the humerus, superficial to pectoralis minor and subclavius. The deltopectoral groove and the clavicular part of the deltoid lie laterally. Pitfall: in the deltopectoral triangle, the cephalic vein seen in cross-section can mimic an infraclavicular node.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Clavicular part of deltoid muscle.note: The anterior part arises from the lateral third of the clavicle and covers the coracoid tip, the biceps sulcus and the humeral head anteriorly. The deltopectoral groove with the v. cephalica separates it from the clavicular head of pectoralis major. Pitfall: the enhancing cephalic vein in the groove can be mistaken for a lymph node or a vascular lesion.
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Clavipectoral fascia.note: Runs from the clavicle and encloses subclavius and pectoralis minor before joining the axillary fascia. Its costocoracoid membrane is pierced by the cephalic vein, the thoraco-acromial vessels and the lateral pectoral nerve. Pitfall: interpectoral (Rotter) nodes lie between pectoralis major and minor, so do not report them as level I axillary nodes.
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle
Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Coccygeus muscle.note: This triangular muscle runs from the spina ischiadica to the lateral lower sacrum and coccyx, fused with the pelvic surface of the ligamentum sacrospinale. Pitfall: on CT it cannot be separated from the ligament, and side-to-side asymmetry can mimic a presacral or pelvic sidewall mass.

Coccyx.note: The base of the Os coccygis meets the Apex ossis sacri at the Symphysis sacrococcygea. Musculus coccygeus and the iliococcygeus and pubococcygeus muscles attach along its sides and front. Pitfall: normal forward angulation, unfused segments or a sacrococcygeal step can mimic fracture, so look for a true cortical break and soft-tissue oedema.

Cochlea.note: Has 2.5 turns in the Pars petrosa, anterior to the vestibule. Its basal turn forms the promontory, and the labyrinthine facial canal arches above it. Pitfall: the normal pericochlear lucency (cochlear cleft) can mimic otospongiosis. Check bilaterality and look for a fissula ante fenestram focus.
landmarks: lm:Fundus of internal acoustic meatus (approx.)|Temporal bone
lm:Geniculum of facial nerve (geniculate ganglion)|Temporal bone

Cochlear nerve.note: It runs in the anteroinferior quadrant of the meatus acusticus internus, below the facial nerve, and enters the modiolus through the cochlear aperture. Pitfall: a narrow cochlear aperture (under about 1.4 mm) or a stenotic meatus suggests a hypoplastic nerve. This matters before cochlear implantation.
passing: Lateral pontine branches of basilar artery
landmarks: lm:Fundus of internal acoustic meatus (approx.)|Temporal bone
lm:Internal acoustic opening (porus of internal acoustic meatus)|Temporal bone

Coeliac nodes.note: Nodi coeliaci surround the origin of the coeliac trunk anterior to the aorta abdominalis, between the diaphragmatic crura, above the pancreatic body. Pitfall: the thick crura diaphragmatis and the coeliac ganglia look like small nodes; ganglia are flat, symmetric and lie lateral to the trunk.

Coeliac trunk.note: Short anterior trunk from the Aorta abdominalis at T12–L1. It sits just below the median arcuate ligament of the Diaphragma and above the Pancreas, and divides into hepatic, splenic and left gastric arteries. Pitfall: narrowing by the median arcuate ligament on expiration mimics atherosclerotic stenosis. A hooked indentation on the upper wall is typical.

Colic branch of ileocolic artery.note: Ascends from the ileocolic artery to the caecum and lower ascending colon and anastomoses with the right colic artery through the marginal artery. Pitfall: when the right colic artery is absent, this branch takes over its territory. Do not mislabel it as the right colic artery.

Collateral interphalangeal ligaments of.note: These ligaments thicken the medial and lateral sides of each interphalangeal capsule, running from the phalangeal head to the base of the next phalanx. The digital neurovascular bundles run alongside. Pitfall: a tiny corticated ossicle beside a joint (old ossification) mimics an acute collateral avulsion. Acute fragments have sharp, uncorticated edges and a matching donor site.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve

Articular capsule of interphalangeal joint of great toe

Distal phalanx of first finger of foot

Collateral interphalangeal ligaments of.note: Run from the lateral recesses of the phalangeal head (trochlea) obliquely to the palmar-lateral base of the next phalanx, alongside the proper digital neurovascular bundles. Pitfall: avulsion flakes at the lateral base and unicondylar fractures of the trochlea are subtle. In a pronated hand, label the side as radial or ulnar, not left or right.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
landmarks: lm:Trochlea of phalanx of hand|Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand

Middle phalanx of third finger of hand
Distal phalanx of third finger of hand
Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints

Collateral metacarpophalangeal ligaments.note: Run from the dorsal tubercles of the metacarpal head obliquely to the palmar-lateral base of the proximal phalanx, with the interossei lying alongside. Pitfall: in the thumb, a fragment at the ulnar base of the proximal phalanx is a UCL avulsion (skier's thumb). CT cannot exclude a Stener lesion.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand
Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand

Collateral metatarsophalangeal ligaments.note: Run from the dorsal tubercles on the sides of each caput ossis metatarsi obliquely to the plantar base of the proximal phalanx. Interossei and lumbricals lie alongside. Pitfall: avulsion flakes at the phalangeal base corners are easily overlooked or mistaken for sesamoids/ossicles. Check for joint deviation, such as hallux valgus or a crossover toe.
landmarks: lm:Head of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone
lm:Base of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot
Proximal phalanx of second finger of foot

Collateral sulcus.note: A basal temporo-occipital sulcus separating the Gyrus parahippocampalis and Gyrus lingualis (medially) from the Gyrus occipitotemporalis lateralis. It indents the temporal horn as the eminentia collateralis. Pitfall: the eminentia collateralis is easily confused with the Hippocampus in the floor of the temporal horn. A widened sulcus can be a normal age-related finding, so do not read it alone as focal atrophy.

Common facial vein.note: Formed below the mandibular angle by the facial vein and the anterior division of the retromandibular vein. It crosses below the posterior digastric belly and drains into the vena jugularis interna near the hyoid. Pitfall: in axial section it can look like a level II node. Follow it across slices: the vein is tubular and enhances like the IJV.

Common fibular nerve.note: The nerve follows the medial border of the biceps femoris and passes behind the lateral head of gastrocnemius. It winds around the collum fibulae within the musculus fibularis longus. Pitfall: fibular neck fractures and ganglia from the proximal tibiofibular joint are the classic causes of injury. Check the fibular neck closely in knee CT.
passing: Sural communicating branch of common fibular nerve

Common flexor tendon sheath.note: This ulnar bursa wraps the flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus tendons inside the carpal tunnel, deep to the retinaculum flexorium. It continues into the digital sheath of the little finger. Pitfall: it often communicates with the radial bursa of the flexor pollicis longus, so infection can spread as a horseshoe abscess. The median nerve lies radial and volar.
passing: Common palmar digital branches of median nerve
Common palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand

Common hepatic artery.note: Runs to the right from the Truncus coeliacus along the upper border of the Pancreas and divides into the Arteria gastroduodenalis and the Arteria hepatica propria. Pitfall: it may arise from the SMA or directly from the aorta, and an enlarged station-8 node along it can mimic the artery.

Common iliac artery.note: Runs from the aortic bifurcation (about L4) along the medial Psoas major to its own bifurcation in front of the sacro-iliac joint, where the Ureter crosses. Pitfall: the right common iliac artery crosses the left Vena iliaca communis. Compression there (May–Thurner) or inflow mixing can mimic venous thrombosis.

Common iliac vein.note: The common iliac veins join at about L5, right of midline, posterior to the arteries. The left vein crosses posterior to the right Arteria iliaca communis, anterior to L5. Pitfall: do not dismiss marked compression of the left vein there as normal flattening. It may be May-Thurner syndrome, so look for DVT and collaterals.

Common interosseous artery.note: Short trunk from the Arteria ulnaris just distal to the radial tuberosity, deep to the flexor digitorum superficialis. It divides at the proximal border of the interosseous membrane into the anterior and posterior interosseous arteries. Pitfall: a persistent median artery or a high-origin radial/ulnar artery can be misnamed as this trunk.
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Common palmar digital arteries.note: Three arteries from the superficial arch that run distally over the lumbricals between the flexor tendons, deep to the palmar aponeurosis. Each divides at the web space after receiving a palmar metacarpal artery. Pitfall: do not confuse them with the deeper palmar metacarpal arteries, which lie on the interossei.
passing: Common palmar digital branches of median nerve
Common palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Common palmar digital branches of median.key: Common palmar digital branches of median nerve
Common palmar digital branches of median.note: Lie deep to the Aponeurosis palmaris and the Arcus palmaris superficialis, superficial to the flexor tendons and lumbricals, and divide proximal to the deep transverse metacarpal ligament. Pitfall: in the palm the arterial arch is superficial to the nerves. In the fingers this reverses, and the nerves lie palmar to the arteries.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Common palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Common palmar digital branches of ulnar.key: Common palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
Common palmar digital branches of ulnar.note: Runs from distal to the hamulus ossis hamati, deep to the palmar aponeurosis and superficial to the flexor tendons, to the fourth web space. It divides there, palmar to the ligamentum metacarpeum transversum profundum. Pitfall: a common communicating branch to the median nerve (Berrettini) is a normal variant that confuses sensory mapping.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
Common palmar digital branches of median nerve
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Common plantar digital arteries.note: Lie between the metatarsal heads, plantar to the lig. metatarseum transversum profundum, beside the common digital nerves, and divide into proper digital arteries at the web spaces. Pitfall: an intermetatarsal bursa or Morton neuroma, typically in the third space, sits in the same place. Do not mistake the enhancing vessel for a lesion.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Perforating branches of plantar metatarsal arteries
landmarks: lm:Head of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone

Common plantar digital branches of later.key: Common plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
Common plantar digital branches of later.note: Come from the superficial branch of the Nervus plantaris lateralis. They run plantar to the interossei toward the fourth intermetatarsal space at the metatarsal heads. Pitfall: a Morton neuroma typically lies in the third space, where a communicating branch joins the medial plantar nerve, not the fourth. Count the intermetatarsal spaces carefully.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
Perforating branches of plantar metatarsal arteries

Common plantar digital branches of media.key: Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Common plantar digital branches of media.note: Three branches run between the flexor digitorum brevis and the lumbricals to the first, second and third intermetatarsal spaces. They pass plantar to the Ligamentum metatarseum transversum profundum at the metatarsal heads. Pitfall: soft tissue between the third and fourth metatarsal heads may be a Morton neuroma. Do not dismiss it as an intermetatarsal bursa.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
landmarks: lm:Head of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone
neighbours: Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis
Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis

Common tendinous ring.note: Fibrous ring at the orbital apex that encircles the optic canal and the medial superior orbital fissure. It is the origin of the four recti. It encloses the optic nerve, ophthalmic artery, oculomotor nerve, abducens nerve and nasociliary nerve. Pitfall: the trochlear, frontal and lacrimal nerves and the superior ophthalmic vein pass above and outside the ring. Apical crowding compresses the optic nerve here.

Common tendon sheath of fibularis muscle.key: Common tendon sheath of fibularis muscles
Common tendon sheath of fibularis muscle.note: Lies in the sulcus malleolaris fibulae under the superior fibular retinaculum, with the brevis anteromedial to the longus, and splits at the fibular trochlea of the calcaneus. Pitfall: a thin cortical flake at the lateral malleolar rim is a retinacular avulsion showing tendon dislocation, not a lateral ligament fracture.

Conoid ligament.note: Ligamentum conoideum runs from the base of the coracoid process up to the Tuberculum conoideum of the clavicle, posteromedial to the Ligamentum trapezoideum. Pitfall: ossified coracoclavicular ligaments or a coracoclavicular joint (normal variant) can mimic an avulsion fragment. A widened coracoclavicular distance is the sign of rupture.

Coraco-acromial ligament.note: Triangular band from the lateral coracoid process to the anterior acromion. It forms the roof of the coracoacromial arch above the subacromial bursa and supraspinatus. Pitfall: an enthesophyte at its acromial attachment (subacromial spur) narrows the outlet. Do not confuse it with an os acromiale, an unfused ossification centre seen best on axial images.

Coracobrachial bursa.note: Lies below the coracoid process, between the conjoint tendon (coracobrachialis and short head of biceps) in front and the subscapularis behind. Pitfall: on CT arthrography, contrast here is easily confused with the subscapular recess of the glenohumeral joint, which it may connect with.

Coracobrachialis muscle.note: Arises from the tip of the coracoid process together with the short head of biceps (the conjoint tendon) and inserts on the medial mid-shaft of the humerus, lateral to the brachial bundle. Pitfall: on CT the two muscles of the conjoint tendon cannot be separated. Do not report the conjoint tendon as one muscle.

Coracohumeral ligament.note: Runs from the lateral base of the processus coracoideus to both tubercles, roofing the rotator interval between the supraspinatus and subscapularis tendons. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the more superior ligamentum coracoacromiale. Thickening and loss of rotator-interval fat suggest adhesive capsulitis.

Cornea.note: A thin, curved anterior rim of the globe that is continuous with the sclera at the limbus. The anterior chamber lies behind it and the eyelids in front. Pitfall: a contact lens or eyelid makeup shows as a thin hyperdense curve on the cornea. Do not report it as a corneal foreign body or calcification.

Corniculate cartilage.note: Cartilago corniculata sits on the Apex cartilaginis arytenoideae within the posterior aryepiglottic fold, next to the piriform recess of the laryngopharynx. Pitfall: when calcified, this small dense focus is easily mistaken for an ingested foreign body or a calcified node. Its paired, symmetric position on the arytenoid apex identifies it.
neighbours: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle

Coronary sinus.note: It runs in the posterior atrioventricular groove between the Atrium sinistrum and the Ventriculus sinister and opens into the Atrium dextrum next to the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve. Pitfall: a dilated coronary sinus usually points to a persistent left superior vena cava; do not misread it as a pericardial cyst or a left atrial diverticulum.

Corpus callosum.note: The rostrum, genu, body and splenium form the roof of the lateral ventricles below the free edge of the falx, separated from the cingulate gyrus by the callosal sulcus. Pitfall: a pericallosal lipoma (fat density, often with rim calcification) should not be called falx calcification. Parallel lateral ventricles with colpocephaly suggest callosal agenesis.

Corpus cavernosum of penis.note: Paired dorsal erectile bodies inside the tunica albuginea, separated by the septum penis. Their crura attach to the ischiopubic rami of the Os coxae. Pitfall: heterogeneous or asymmetric enhancement in early phases is normal and can mimic thrombosis or a fracture. A penile fracture is defined by a defect in the tunica albuginea.

Corpus spongiosum of penis.note: A ventral midline erectile body around the spongy urethra. Proximally it widens into the bulb at the perineal membrane and distally it expands into the Glans penis. Pitfall: the bulb of the penis in the perineum can be mistaken for a mass or haematoma, and urethral injury is easy to miss without retrograde urethrography.

Corrugator supercilii.note: Small muscle from the medial superciliary arch running laterally into the eyebrow skin, deep to frontalis and orbicularis oculi. Pitfall: the supratrochlear and supra-orbital neurovascular bundles pass through it. Do not mistake the supra-orbital notch or foramen for a fracture of the orbital rim.

Costal cartilage of eighth rib.note: This cartilage joins the seventh costal cartilage to form the costal margin and does not reach the sternum. It lies in front of the diaphragm and liver. Pitfall: patchy cartilage calcification can mimic a rib fracture, or a liver or gallbladder stone, on partial-volume axial slices.

Costal cartilage of fifth rib.note: This cartilage joins the fifth rib to its Incisura costalis on the Corpus sterni. Musculus transversus thoracis and the pleura lie deep to it, pectoralis major superficial. Pitfall: costochondral calcification or a prominent cartilage can mimic a parasternal mass, so compare with the other side.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Costal cartilage of first rib.note: This short, broad cartilage joins the first rib to the manubrium just below the sternoclavicular joint, deep to the Ligamentum costoclaviculare and Musculus subclavius. Pitfall: it calcifies first and often asymmetrically, which can look like an apical lung nodule or an osteochondroma on axial CT.

Costal cartilage of fourth rib.note: This cartilage links the fourth rib to the Corpus sterni. The Arteria thoracica interna and Nodi parasternales run just deep to its sternal end, in front of Musculus transversus thoracis. Pitfall: enlarged parasternal nodes sit between cartilage and pleura, so do not dismiss soft tissue here as partial volume of cartilage.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Costal cartilage of ninth rib.note: This cartilage joins the eighth cartilage in the costal margin and lies between the abdominal wall muscles and the diaphragm. Pitfall: slipping rib (interchondral subluxation of ribs 8–10) is easy to miss, so inspect the interchondral junctions on coronal reformats.

Costal cartilage of second rib.note: This cartilage meets both the manubrium and the Corpus sterni at the Angulus sterni, the reference point for counting ribs. Pitfall: mistaking it for the first cartilage shifts every rib level in the report, so confirm the sternal angle on sagittal reformats.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Costal cartilage of seventh rib.note: This is the last cartilage to reach the sternum, attaching at the xiphisternal junction. Behind it the internal thoracic vessels divide into the Arteria epigastrica superior and Arteria musculophrenica. Pitfall: lumpy calcification next to the xiphoid can mimic a fractured or bifid xiphoid, so trace continuity on oblique reformats.

Costal cartilage of sixth rib.note: This cartilage joins the sixth rib to the lower Corpus sterni. Musculus rectus abdominis arises from its front and Musculus transversus thoracis lies deep. Pitfall: the internal thoracic vessels divide nearby, and dilated or collateral vessels can mimic parasternal nodes on non-contrast CT.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Costal cartilage of tenth rib.note: This is the lowest cartilage of the costal margin, joining the ninth cartilage within the lateral abdominal wall muscles. Pitfall: the tenth rib is sometimes free-floating (normal variant), and its free cartilage tip should not be reported as a displaced fracture fragment.

Costal cartilage of third rib.note: The costal cartilage runs from the anterior end of the third rib to the sternocostal joint at the corpus sterni. Musculus pectoralis major lies in front of it, and musculus transversus thoracis and the vasa thoracica interna lie behind it. Pitfall: patchy cartilage calcification can mimic a fracture, a parasternal node or a pulmonary nodule. Use the bone window and compare with the other side.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Costocervical trunk.note: Arises from the posterior subclavian artery (second part on the right, behind scalenus anterior). It arches back over the cupula pleurae to the neck of the first rib, then divides into the supreme intercostal and deep cervical arteries. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the thyrocervical trunk (anterior, at the medial edge of scalenus anterior) or with the vertebral artery.

Costoclavicular ligament.note: Ligamentum costoclaviculare runs from the first rib and its costal cartilage up to the Impressio ligamenti costoclavicularis on the underside of the medial clavicle. It lies lateral to the sternoclavicular joint, with subclavius further lateral. Pitfall: the impression is often a deep rhomboid fossa (normal variant) that mimics an osteolytic lesion or erosion.
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Costotransverse ligament.note: Joins the neck of the rib to the transverse process of the same-numbered vertebra, filling the costotransverse foramen medial to the costotransverse joint. Pitfall: wrong level counting. Rib N articulates with transverse process TN, so count from the first rib. Vacuum or arthrosis of the costotransverse joint is not a lytic lesion.
neighbours: Intra-articular ligament of head of rib

Cricoid cartilage.note: Cartilago cricoidea is the only complete ring of the airway, at C6 level. It has an anterior Arcus and a tall posterior Lamina that carries the arytenoids, with the trachea below and the oesophageal inlet behind. Pitfall: patchy, asymmetric ossification mimics fracture or tumour invasion. Compare with the contralateral side and the adjacent soft tissue.

Cricopharyngeal ligament.note: Runs from the corniculate cartilages and cricoid lamina to the posterior pharyngeal mucosa. It lies in the postcricoid region where the laryngopharynx becomes the oesophagus. Pitfall: a collapsed postcricoid hypopharynx and its venous plexus can mimic a postcricoid mass. Reassess on a phonation or modified Valsalva scan.

Cruciform part of fibrous sheath of digi.key: Cruciform part of fibrous sheath of digit of hand
Cruciform part of fibrous sheath of digi.note: Thin criss-crossing fibres (C1–C3) lie between the annular pulleys over the interphalangeal joints and are not resolvable on CT. Pitfall: a pulley injury shows only indirectly, as flexor tendon bowstringing with increased tendon-to-bone distance. A normal-looking sheath does not exclude rupture.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
landmarks: lm:Trochlea of phalanx of hand|Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
neighbours: Synovial sheaths of digits of hand
Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints
Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
Middle phalanx of third finger of hand

Crural fascia.note: Deep investing fascia of the leg. It fuses with the medial surface of the tibia and thickens at the ankle into the retinacula, then continues as the foot fasciae. Pitfall: separate epifascial (subcutaneous) oedema or collections from subfascial ones. CT cannot rule out compartment syndrome.
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve

Cubital nodes.note: These epitrochlear nodes lie in the subcutaneous fat of the medial elbow above the medial epicondyle, along the basilic vein and superficial to the antebrachial fascia and the flexor–pronator group. Pitfall: superficial veins such as the Vena mediana cubiti, varices or small lipomas can mimic a node; check for a fatty hilum and whether the structure is tubular.
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Cuboid bone.note: Lateral column bone between the calcaneus and the bases of the fourth/fifth metatarsals. It articulates medially with the lateral cuneiform and sometimes the navicular. The fibularis longus tendon grooves its plantar surface. Pitfall: an os peroneum next to the tuberositas ossis cuboidei mimics an avulsion fragment. Also look for a subtle compressive 'nutcracker' fracture.
passing: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

Culmen.note: The culmen is the highest point of the vermis, lying just under the tentorial apex. The Fissura prima separates it from the declive behind it, and the Lobulus quadrangularis anterior lies on each side. Pitfall: on axial CT, partial volume from the tentorial apex and the superior vermian cistern can mimic tentorial subdural haematoma or SAH. Check coronal reformats.

Cuneate fasciculus.note: Lateral part of the posterior funiculus, found only above about T6. It lies between the Fasciculus gracilis medially and the Cornu posterius laterally, and ends at the tuberculum cuneatum of the medulla. CT cannot resolve it. Pitfall: buckled Ligamenta flava compress the cord from behind at C5–C6 on extension CT; judge this on sagittal reformats.

Cuneocuboid interosseous ligament.note: A strong interosseous band filling the non-articular part of the space between the lateral cuneiform and the medial cuboid. Pitfall: the narrow cuneocuboid space and the partial volume of this ligament can mimic a coalition. It can also hide diastasis in a midfoot injury that extends laterally, so compare with the intercuneiform spaces.

Cuneometatarsal interosseous ligaments.note: Include the Lisfranc ligament, which runs from the lateral os cuneiforme mediale to the medial base of the 2nd metatarsal, plus bands to the 3rd metatarsal base. Pitfall: the fleck sign (avulsion between the medial cuneiform and 2nd MT base) is easily missed. Subtle C1–M2 widening on non-weight-bearing CT should not be called normal.
landmarks: lm:Base of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone

Cuneus.note: A wedge-shaped medial occipital gyrus between the Sulcus parietooccipitalis in front and the Sulcus calcarinus below, against the Falx cerebri. Pitfall: in posterior circulation (PCA) infarction it is involved together with the Gyrus lingualis. Beam hardening from the occipital bone can mimic or mask hypodensity here.

Cystic node.note: Nodus cysticus lies at the gallbladder neck in the Calot triangle, next to the cystic duct and the bile duct. Pitfall: an impacted cystic duct stone, a folded gallbladder neck or reactive enlargement in cholecystitis can mimic a pathological node.

Declive.note: The declive is the posterior slope of the superior vermis, behind the Fissura prima and above the folium. It continues laterally into the Lobulus quadrangularis posterior beneath the tentorium. Pitfall: the obliquely sectioned tentorium can mimic a vermian hyperdensity on axial slices. Use coronal or sagittal reformats.

Deep artery of penis.note: Runs centrally within each Corpus cavernosum penis, from the crus to the distal shaft. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the Arteria dorsalis penis, which lies on the dorsal surface of the corpora under Buck fascia. Only the central (cavernosal) artery is relevant in priapism and in assessing erectile flow.

Deep brachial artery.note: Arises from the proximal brachial artery and follows the radial nerve in the sulcus nervi radialis between the medial and lateral heads of triceps. It ends as the middle and radial collateral arteries. Pitfall: fractures of the mid-to-distal third of the humeral shaft (Holstein–Lewis) threaten this bundle. Do not dismiss soft-tissue haematoma in the groove as simple bleeding from the fracture.

Deep branch of radial nerve.note: Arises at the radiocapitellar level, enters the supinator under the arcade of Frohse, and winds around the radial neck. It continues as the posterior interosseous nerve, deep to the extensors, to the dorsal wrist capsule. Pitfall: radial head and neck fractures, Monteggia injuries and dorsal proximal radius screws put it at risk. Radial nerve lesions often leave the wrist extensors working (ECRL is supplied above this level).

Deep branch of ulnar nerve.note: Leaves Guyon canal between the os pisiforme and the hamulus ossis hamati. It curves around the hook through opponens digiti minimi and runs with the arcus palmaris profundus to adductor pollicis. Pitfall: a hamulus fracture can injure it, so check the axial CT; a bipartite hamulus or os hamuli proprium can mimic a fracture.
neighbours: Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand

Deep cervical artery.note: Arises from the Truncus costocervicalis and passes backward between the C7 transverse process and the neck of the first rib. It then ascends among the deep posterior neck muscles. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the vertebral artery, which usually enters the C6 transverse foramen and stays inside the foramina.

Deep dorsal vein of penis.note: A single midline vein in the dorsal groove between the corpora cavernosa, deep to Buck fascia and between the paired dorsal arteries. It passes under the pubic symphysis to the prostatic venous plexus. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the venae dorsales superficiales penis, which lie superficial to Buck fascia and drain to the external pudendal veins.

Deep external pudendal artery.note: It arises from the medial side of the Arteria femoralis and runs medially deep to the fascia lata, across the Musculus pectineus and Adductor longus, to the scrotum or labia. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the superficial external pudendal artery, which lies superficial to the fascia lata near the saphenofemoral junction. It crosses the Vena femoralis, so it can bleed after a groin puncture.

Deep femoral artery.note: It arises posterolaterally from the Arteria femoralis about 3–5 cm below the inguinal ligament. It descends close to the Os femoris, behind the Adductor longus and in front of the Adductor brevis and magnus. Pitfall: the profunda vein lies between it and the femoral artery. Do not call the femoral artery beyond this origin the deep femoral artery; it is the femoral artery (often called the superficial femoral artery).

Deep femoral vein.note: Lies in front of the adductors and behind the arteria profunda femoris, and joins the vena femoralis a few centimetres below the inguinal ligament. Pitfall: the vessel called the 'superficial femoral vein' is actually a deep vein. Also, a duplicated femoral vein can look like the deep femoral vein where they join.

Deep fibular nerve.note: The nerve runs in the anterior compartment on the membrana interossea cruris with the anterior tibial vessels, between the tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus. It passes beneath the extensor retinacula alongside the arteria dorsalis pedis to reach the first web space. Pitfall: dorsal talonavicular or tarsometatarsal osteophytes can compress it (anterior tarsal tunnel syndrome).
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Dorsal digital branches of deep fibular nerve

Deep head of flexor pollicis brevis.key: Deep head of flexor pollicis brevis
Deep head of flexor pollicis brevis.note: Lies deep to the FPL tendon. It arises from the trapezoid and capitate region and inserts with the superficial head on the radial sesamoid and the base of the thumb's proximal phalanx. Pitfall: on CT it cannot be separated from the oblique head of adductor pollicis; the radial sesamoid at the MCP joint is normal, not a fracture fragment.
neighbours: Superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis
Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus

Deep head of pronator teres.note: Arises from the medial side of the ulnar coronoid process and joins the superficial head to insert on the lateral mid-shaft of the radius. The median nerve passes between the two heads, and the ulnar artery runs deep to the deep head. Pitfall: the deep head is often small or absent, which shifts the median nerve's usual position.
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Deep infrapatellar bursa.note: Lies between the distal Ligamentum patellae and the anterior tibia, just proximal to the Tuberositas tibiae. The Corpus adiposum infrapatellare lies above and behind it. Pitfall: a small amount of fluid here is physiological; do not mistake it for joint effusion or Hoffa fat-pad pathology, as it does not communicate with the joint.

Deep palmar arch.note: Lies on the bases of metacarpals 2–5 and the interossei, deep to the flexor tendons, about 1 cm proximal to the superficial arch. It is formed mainly by the Arteria radialis and travels with the Ramus profundus nervi ulnaris. Pitfall: an incomplete arch is a normal variant and should not be reported as occlusion on CTA.

Deep part of masseter.note: Arises from the deep surface of the zygomatic arch and inserts on the lateral ramus up to the coronoid base. It lies deep to the superficial part and in front of the TMJ capsule. Pitfall: one-sided masseteric hypertrophy, or atrophy after V3 denervation, can mimic a mass. Compare both sides and check that fat planes are preserved.

Deep part of tibial collateral ligament.key: Deep part of tibial collateral ligament
Deep part of tibial collateral ligament.note: Capsular layer made up of the meniscofemoral and meniscotibial bands, firmly attached to the medial meniscus deep to the pars superficialis. CT cannot reliably separate it from the superficial layer. Do not mistake a fat plane or bursa between the two layers for a tear.
neighbours: Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament

Deep plantar artery.note: Dives from the dorsum through the proximal first intermetatarsal space, between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous next to the base of MT2, and completes the arcus plantaris. Pitfall: it sits right at the Lisfranc region. Fracture-dislocation of the MT2 base can tear it, so check for active extravasation there.

Deep popliteal nodes.note: Lie in the popliteal fat around the A./V. poplitea, between the heads of the gastrocnemius and deep to the popliteal fascia. Pitfall: a popliteal aneurysm, a Baker cyst or the popliteal vein in cross-section can look like a node. Use contrast and check the semimembranosus–gastrocnemius bursa.

Deep transverse metacarpal ligament.note: Joins the volar plates of MCP joints II–V. The lumbricals and digital neurovascular bundles pass palmar to it and the interossei pass dorsal to it. Pitfall: it does not reach the thumb. Do not confuse it with the Ligamentum metacarpeum transversum superficiale, which belongs to the palmar aponeurosis and lies more superficially.
passing: Common palmar digital branches of median nerve
Common palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve

Deep transverse metatarsal ligament.note: Links the plantar plates of the five MTP joints across the metatarsal heads. The interossei lie dorsal to it; the lumbricals and the common digital nerves/vessels lie plantar to it. Pitfall: an intermetatarsal (Morton) neuroma lies plantar to this ligament and is essentially invisible on CT. Do not exclude it on CT.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve

Deep venous palmar arch.note: The Arcus venosus palmaris profundus lies at the level of the metacarpal bases, on the interossei and deep to the long flexor tendons, alongside the deep palmar arterial arch and the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. Pitfall: it can be confused with the superficial arch, which lies more distal and superficial to the flexor tendons.

Deltoid fascia.note: Fascia deltoidea encloses the musculus deltoideus and is continuous with fascia pectoralis anteriorly and fascia brachii distally. The bursa subdeltoidea lies deep to the muscle, over the rotator cuff. Pitfall: subdeltoid bursal fluid is deep to the muscle, not in the fascial plane, so do not report it as a subcutaneous or intramuscular collection.
neighbours: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

Depressor anguli oris.note: Triangular muscle from the oblique line of the mandible to the modiolus. It lies over the depressor labii inferioris and is continuous with the platysma. Pitfall: the mental foramen beneath it, at premolar level, can mimic a lytic lesion or fracture line on CT.

Depressor labii inferioris.note: Runs from the mandibular oblique line, between symphysis and mental foramen, to the lower lip. It lies deep to depressor anguli oris and lateral to mentalis. Pitfall: the mental nerve exits beneath it, and perineural spread of lip carcinoma along it is easily missed. Look for widening of the Foramen mentale.
passing: Mental branch of inferior alveolar artery

Depressor septi nasi.note: Small muscle from the incisive fossa of the maxilla, above the central incisors, to the columella and septal cartilage, deep to orbicularis oris. Pitfall: on CT it blends with orbicularis oris. Swelling near the incisor root tips should be checked for a periapical abscess rather than called muscle.

Descending branch of lateral circumflex.key: Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery
Descending branch of lateral circumflex.note: It descends along the anterior border of the Musculus vastus lateralis, deep to the rectus femoris, to the Rete patellare. It is the pedicle of the anterolateral thigh flap. Pitfall: when the femoral artery is occluded it becomes a large collateral. Do not mistake it for a patent femoral artery or for reconstitution.

Descending branch of left colic artery.key: Descending branch of left colic artery
Descending branch of left colic artery.note: Runs caudally along the descending colon toward the sigmoid and anastomoses with the sigmoid arteries through the marginal artery. Pitfall: it lies alongside the left gonadal vein and the ureter on the psoas. Confirm arterial enhancement and continuity with the inferior mesenteric artery.
passing: Ascending branch of left colic artery

Descending colon.note: It is retroperitoneal and runs from the splenic flexure down the left paracolic gutter, lateral to the left kidney and over the musculus quadratus lumborum and iliacus, to the sigmoid at the pelvic brim. Pitfall: a retrorenal colon variant puts the colon behind the kidney. Report it before a percutaneous nephrostomy.

Descending palatine artery.note: Arises in the pterygopalatine fossa and descends in the greater palatine canal, between the maxilla and the palatine bone, to exit at the greater palatine foramen as the Arteria palatina major. Pitfall: the vertical greater palatine canal should not be confused with the pterygoid canal. It is also a perineural spread route and a bleeding risk in Le Fort I osteotomy.

Descending part of iliofemoral ligament.note: The medial limb of the Y ligament. It runs from below the anterior inferior iliac spine to the lower intertrochanteric line and thickens the anterior capsule. Pitfall: heterotopic ossification here after arthroplasty, and an avulsion at the rectus femoris origin, can look like a fracture of the anterior acetabular rim.

Descending part of trapezius muscle.note: This mesh runs from the thoracic spinous processes down to about T10, converging on the medial Spina scapulae. It lies superficial to the Musculi rhomboidei and overlaps the upper Musculus latissimus dorsi. Pitfall: in TA these lower fibres are the pars ascendens, not the descendens, so avoid swapping the terms in reports.

Diaphragm.note: The crura attach to the L1–L3 bodies and the anterior longitudinal ligament. The arcuate ligaments arch over psoas major and quadratus lumborum, and the costal slips attach to ribs 7–12. Pitfall: thick, nodular crura can mimic retrocrural lymphadenopathy, and muscle slips indenting the liver can mimic peripheral liver lesions.

Diaphragmatic fascia.note: This fascia lines the abdominal surface of the Diaphragma and continues into the transversalis and psoas fascia. It is not seen on CT apart from the diaphragm itself. Pitfall: thick or nodular diaphragmatic crura and muscle slips can mimic retrocrural nodes, adrenal masses or liver lesions. Follow them across adjacent slices.

Distal lateral striate branches.note: Lenticulostriate end arteries leave lateral M1 and pass through the substantia perforata anterior into the lateral putamen and capsula externa. Pitfall: these are the typical sites of hypertensive bleeds and lacunes. Do not confuse dilated perivascular spaces at the perforated substance with lacunes.

Distal phalanx of fifth finger of foot.key: Distal phalanx of fifth finger of foot
Distal phalanx of fifth finger of foot.note: The distal phalanx articulates with the middle phalanx at the DIP joint, where flexor digitorum longus inserts on the plantar side and the extensor digitorum longus tendon dorsally. Pitfall: fusion of the middle and distal phalanges of the fifth toe (biphalangeal toe) is a common variant, not ankylosis or a missing bone.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
neighbours: Middle phalanx of fifth finger of foot
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints of foot

Distal phalanx of fifth finger of hand.key: Distal phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Distal phalanx of fifth finger of hand.note: Lies distal to the DIP joint. The flexor digitorum profundus inserts on the palmar base and the terminal extensor tendon on the dorsal base, and the tuft lies under the nail bed. Pitfall: Kirner deformity (palmar-radial curving of the fifth distal phalanx) and normal tuft irregularity mimic a fracture. Look for cortical breaks and soft-tissue swelling.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Middle phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints

Distal phalanx of first finger of foot.key: Distal phalanx of first finger of foot
Distal phalanx of first finger of foot.note: The great toe has only two phalanges. The distal phalanx articulates with the proximal phalanx at the single interphalangeal joint, and flexor hallucis longus inserts on its plantar base. Pitfall: an interphalangeal sesamoid on the plantar side of the joint mimics an avulsion fragment. Its smooth corticated outline tells them apart.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of deep fibular nerve
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot
Articular capsule of interphalangeal joint of great toe

Distal phalanx of first finger of hand.key: Distal phalanx of first finger of hand
Distal phalanx of first finger of hand.note: The thumb has only two phalanges, so this phalanx articulates directly with the proximal phalanx at the IP joint. The flexor pollicis longus inserts palmar and the extensor pollicis longus dorsal. Pitfall: a sesamoid at the palmar IP joint can be taken for an avulsion fragment. Also avoid calling this joint a 'DIP' in reports.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints

Distal phalanx of fourth finger of foot.key: Distal phalanx of fourth finger of foot
Distal phalanx of fourth finger of foot.note: The distal phalanx articulates with the middle phalanx at the DIP joint and receives flexor digitorum longus on the plantar side and the extensor digitorum longus tendon dorsally. Pitfall: a fused middle and distal phalanx is a normal variant. A tuft fracture from crush injury is easily missed without thin reformats.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve
neighbours: Middle phalanx of fourth finger of foot
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints of foot

Distal phalanx of fourth finger of hand.key: Distal phalanx of fourth finger of hand
Distal phalanx of fourth finger of hand.note: Lies distal to the DIP joint, with the flexor digitorum profundus inserting at the palmar base and the terminal extensor dorsal. Pitfall: the ring finger is the classic site of FDP avulsion (jersey finger). A small palmar basal fragment may have retracted proximally along the flexor sheath, so look beyond the joint.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Dorsal digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Middle phalanx of fourth finger of hand
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints

Distal phalanx of second finger of foot.key: Distal phalanx of second finger of foot
Distal phalanx of second finger of foot.note: The distal phalanx articulates with the middle phalanx at the DIP joint and receives flexor digitorum longus on the plantar side and the extensor digitorum longus tendon dorsally. Pitfall: in a flexed or clawed toe, oblique slices make the DIP joint look subluxed. Judge alignment on reformats along the axis of the ray.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of deep fibular nerve
neighbours: Middle phalanx of second finger of foot
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints of foot

Distal phalanx of second finger of hand.key: Distal phalanx of second finger of hand
Distal phalanx of second finger of hand.note: Lies distal to the DIP joint. The terminal extensor tendon inserts on the dorsal base and the flexor digitorum profundus on the palmar base. Pitfall: a dorsal basal avulsion (bony mallet) can be tiny and is easily missed on axial slices. Check sagittal reformats for the fragment and for palmar subluxation of the phalanx.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
neighbours: Middle phalanx of second finger of hand
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints

Distal phalanx of third finger of foot.key: Distal phalanx of third finger of foot
Distal phalanx of third finger of foot.note: The distal phalanx runs from its base at the DIP joint, with flexor digitorum longus inserting on the plantar side, to the tuberositas phalangis distalis at the tip. Pitfall: the irregular tuft normally looks frayed or pointed and should not be read as erosion or acro-osteolysis.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
landmarks: lm:Tuberosity of distal phalanx of foot|Distal phalanx of third finger of foot
neighbours: Middle phalanx of third finger of foot
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints of foot

Distal phalanx of third finger of hand.key: Distal phalanx of third finger of hand
Distal phalanx of third finger of hand.note: Base articulates with the middle phalanx at the DIP joint; flexor digitorum profundus inserts palmar, the terminal extensor tendon dorsal at the base, distally the tuberositas phalangis distalis. Pitfall: a small dorsal-base avulsion (bony mallet) is easily missed on axial slices; use sagittal reformats and do not confuse normal tuft irregularity with a fracture.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
landmarks: lm:Tuberosity of distal phalanx of hand|Distal phalanx of third finger of hand
neighbours: Middle phalanx of third finger of hand
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints

Dorsal artery of penis.note: A terminal branch of the Arteria pudendalis interna. It passes beneath the pubic symphysis and runs on the dorsum of the Corpus cavernosum penis under Buck fascia, between the deep dorsal vein (medial) and the dorsal nerve (lateral). Pitfall: do not mistake it for the central deep artery or for superficial external pudendal branches.

Dorsal branch of ulnar nerve.note: Arises about 5 cm above the wrist and passes deep to flexor carpi ulnaris. It winds dorsally around the ulna, distal to the caput ulnae, superficial to the extensor carpi ulnaris sheath. Pitfall: ulnar styloid fractures and K-wires put it at risk. It is spared in Guyon canal lesions, so dorsal ulnar hand numbness points to a more proximal lesion.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
Dorsal digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris
Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Dorsal calcaneocuboid ligament.note: Thickens the dorsolateral capsule of the calcaneocuboid joint, deep to the origin of the extensor digitorum brevis. Pitfall: a dorsal capsular avulsion fleck of the cuboid or calcaneus is easily mislabelled as an anterior process fracture. Localise the fragment on sagittal reformats.

Dorsal carpal anastomosis.note: A fine network on the dorsal carpal ligaments over the capitate and proximal row, deep to the extensor tendons. It is fed by radial and ulnar dorsal carpal branches. Pitfall: the much larger, superficial Rete venosum dorsale manus and Vena cephalica lie above the extensor tendons and should not be mistaken for this rete.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery

Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery.key: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery.note: Arises just proximal to the pisiform and winds dorsally around the ulnar side of the wrist, deep to the ECU tendon, to reach the Rete dorsale carpi over the triquetrum. Pitfall: it runs beside the Ramus dorsalis nervi ulnaris and Vena basilica tributaries, so trace it from the ulnar artery before naming it.
neighbours: Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint
Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris

Dorsal carpometacarpal ligaments.note: Join the dorsal surfaces of the distal carpal row to the metacarpal bases, deep to the extensor tendons (ECRL/ECRB inserting on MC2/MC3). Pitfall: dorsal fracture-dislocation at the 4th/5th CMC joint is easily missed, so check the hamate–MC articulation on sagittal images. A carpal boss (os styloideum) at the 2nd/3rd CMC is a normal variant, not a fracture.

Dorsal cuboideonavicular ligament.note: Runs obliquely between the dorsal navicular and the dorsal cuboid, just distal to the bifurcate ligament. Pitfall: the cuboideonavicular contact is often fibrous rather than synovial. A narrow, irregular gap is normal and should not be over-called as a coalition, though true cuboideonavicular coalition exists.

Dorsal cuneocuboid ligament.note: Bridges the dorsal lateral cuneiform and cuboid, deep to the extensor digitorum brevis, with the arteria arcuata nearby. Pitfall: tiny dorsal flecks here belong to the cuneocuboid joint, not the fourth tarsometatarsal joint. Check the level on sagittal reformats.
passing: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

Dorsal cuneonavicular ligaments.note: Bands from the dorsal navicular to each of the three cuneiforms. The arteria dorsalis pedis and the nervus fibularis profundus run directly over them. Pitfall: a dorsal navicular fleck at the naviculocuneiform joint is easily attributed to the talonavicular joint, so name the joint by its level on sagittal reformats.

Dorsal digital arteries of foot.note: Paired small vessels along the dorsomedial and dorsolateral margins of the phalanges, beside the extensor tendons. CT rarely resolves them beyond the proximal phalanx. Pitfall: the plantar digital arteries are the main toe supply. Calcified dorsal digital vessels in diabetics should not be mistaken for foreign bodies or periosteal reaction.
passing: Dorsal digital branches of deep fibular nerve
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve

Dorsal digital arteries of hand.note: Tiny vessels on the dorsolateral sides of the proximal phalanges, which usually end around the PIP joint. The distal dorsum is supplied by the proper palmar digital arteries. Pitfall: when they are not seen distal to the proximal phalanx on CTA, this is normal and not occlusion.

Dorsal digital branches of deep fibular.key: Dorsal digital branches of deep fibular nerve
Dorsal digital branches of deep fibular.note: These branches supply only the adjacent sides of the hallux and second toe in the first web space. They run with the first dorsal metatarsal artery over the dorsal interossei. Pitfall: do not attribute sensation in other web spaces to the deep fibular nerve, because those are superficial fibular territory. Dorsal first MTP osteophytes (hallux rigidus) can irritate these branches.
passing: Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve

Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve.key: Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve.note: Subcutaneous branches over the dorsum of the thumb, index, middle and radial ring finger, superficial to the extensor tendons, reaching about the PIP joints. Pitfall: the dorsal skin of the distal phalanges belongs to the proper palmar digital nerves of the median nerve, not to the radial nerve.
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand
Proximal phalanx of second finger of hand

Dorsal digital branches of superficial f.key: Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve
Dorsal digital branches of superficial f.note: These subcutaneous branches run over the extensor tendons and metatarsals to the dorsal toes. They spare the first web space, which belongs to the deep fibular nerve, and the lateral fifth toe, which belongs to the sural nerve. Pitfall: CT cannot show them. Do not mistake dorsal digital veins or tight shoe-related soft-tissue thickening for neuromas.
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

Dorsal digital branches of ulnar nerve.key: Dorsal digital branches of ulnar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of ulnar nerve.note: Run in the dorsal subcutis of the fifth finger and the ulnar side of the fourth, usually only to about the PIP joint. Pitfall: the dorsal skin over the middle and distal phalanges is supplied by the palmar digital nerves, so numbness there does not mean a dorsal branch injury.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand

Dorsal digital veins of foot.note: Small subcutaneous veins along the dorsal margins of the toes, superficial to the extensor expansion, draining into the dorsal metatarsal veins. They are not resolved on CT. Pitfall: dorsal soft-tissue swelling of a toe is not venous anatomy. Check the phalanx beneath for fracture or erosion.

Dorsal digital veins of hand.note: Thin subcutaneous veins run along the dorsum of the phalanges, superficial to the extensor hood. They join to form the dorsal metacarpal veins and the rete venosum dorsale. Pitfall: these veins are tiny and usually invisible on CT. A focal dorsal digital density is more likely a foreign body, gouty tophus or soft-tissue swelling than a vessel.

Dorsal fascia of hand.note: Fascia dorsalis manus covers the extensor tendons on the back of the hand and continues proximally into the retinaculum extensorium. The rete venosum dorsale manus lies superficial to it. Pitfall: these thin planes sit close together, so do not mistake prominent dorsal veins or fluid in a tendon sheath for a soft-tissue mass.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensor digiti minimi manus
Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand

Dorsal intercarpal ligaments.note: Run from the dorsal triquetrum across the lunate to the scaphoid and trapezium/trapezoid, forming a lateral V with the ligamentum radiocarpeum dorsale under the extensor tendons. Pitfall: a dorsal flake on sagittal CT usually comes from the triquetrum (avulsion), so do not assign it to the lunate or hamate.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery

Dorsal intercuneiform ligaments.note: Short transverse bands across the dorsal medial–intermediate and intermediate–lateral cuneiform joints. The arteria dorsalis pedis runs over them. Pitfall: diastasis between the medial and intermediate cuneiforms is a proximal extension of a Lisfranc injury. Do not dismiss it as normal joint width.
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

Dorsal interossei muscles of foot.note: Four bipennate muscles that fill the dorsal intermetatarsal spaces 1–4 and insert on the sides of the proximal phalanges of toes 2–4. Pitfall: on CT they merge with the plantar interossei. The deep plantar artery passes through the first space, so enhancement there is normal and not a lesion.
passing: Perforating branches of plantar metatarsal arteries

lm:Base of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot

Dorsal interossei muscles of hand.note: Four bipennate muscles that fill the dorsal intermetacarpal spaces and insert on the proximal phalanges and extensor hoods of digits 2–4; the middle finger receives two. Pitfall: on axial CT do not mix them up with the palmar interossei, which lie on the volar side of the same spaces; the radial artery enters the palm between the heads of the first.

Dorsal metacarpal arteries.note: Run on the dorsal interossei in the intermetacarpal spaces, deep to the extensor tendons, from the Rete dorsale carpi to the MCP level. Pitfall: the larger, superficial dorsal venous network lies in the subcutis above the extensor tendons and should not be called arterial.

Dorsal metacarpal ligaments.note: Transverse dorsal bands joining the bases of metacarpals II–V, deep to the extensor tendons and just distal to the CMC joints. Pitfall: dorsal fracture-dislocations of the fourth and fifth CMC joints are often missed. Check CMC alignment on sagittal reconstructions.

Dorsal metatarsal arteries.note: Run distally on the dorsal interossei in each intermetatarsal space, link to the plantar metatarsal arteries through perforating branches, and divide into dorsal digital arteries near the MTP joints. Pitfall: the first one comes from the a. dorsalis pedis and the 2nd–4th from the a. arcuata. If the arcuate artery is absent, perforators fill them.
passing: Perforating branches of plantar metatarsal arteries
Dorsal digital branches of deep fibular nerve

Dorsal metatarsal ligaments.note: Short transverse bands joining the dorsal bases of metatarsals 2–5. There is no such ligament between the bases of metatarsals 1 and 2; that gap is bridged by the Lisfranc ligament from the medial cuneiform. Pitfall: fleck fractures at the bases or a widened gap between metatarsals 1 and 2 mean a Lisfranc injury, not a minor sprain.
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

Dorsal metatarsal veins.note: Run dorsally in the intermetatarsal spaces over the Musculi interossei dorsales. They receive the dorsal digital and intercapitular veins and drain into the Arcus venosus dorsalis pedis. Pitfall: these vessels lie dorsal to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament, whereas a Morton neuroma lies plantar to it, so do not report dorsal intermetatarsal vessels as neuroma.

Dorsal parts of lateral intertransversar.key: Dorsal parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles
Dorsal parts of lateral intertransversar.note: Small slips between adjacent lumbar costal processes, lying dorsal to the ventral parts and lateral to the intervertebral foramen. The dorsal ramus passes between the two parts. Pitfall: an extraforaminal disc herniation or a swollen exiting root can mimic muscle here. Also, an undisplaced costal-process fracture can be mistaken for a muscle gap, or the reverse.

lm:Lateral part of transverse process|Vertebra L3

Dorsal radio-ulnar ligament.note: Dorsal limb of the TFCC. It runs from the dorsal rim of the incisura ulnaris radii to the ulnar fovea and styloid base, deep to the extensor digiti minimi compartment. CT does not resolve it, so infer injury from DRUJ subluxation. Pitfall: dorsal subluxation is only valid if both wrists are scanned in the same forearm rotation.
neighbours: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint

Dorsal radiocarpal ligament.note: Runs obliquely from the dorsal rim of the distal radius to the dorsal triquetrum. With the dorsal intercarpal ligaments it forms a lateral V, deep to the extensor compartments. Pitfall: a dorsal flake beside the triquetrum on sagittal images is an avulsion of this ligament. Do not mistake it for an osteophyte or a lunate fragment.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum and extensor indicis

Dorsal scaphotriquetral ligament.note: Dorsal intercarpal ligament running from the triquetrum to the scaphoid and trapezium, forming a lateral 'V' with the dorsal radiocarpal ligament under the fourth extensor compartment. Pitfall: a dorsal triquetral flake is an avulsion at these ligament attachments. Look for it on sagittal images and do not dismiss it as an osteophyte or os triquetrum secundarium.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum and extensor indicis

Dorsal scapular nerve.note: Arises from the C5 root, pierces scalenus medius and descends deep to levator scapulae and the rhomboids along the medial scapular border. Pitfall: it is easily confused with the long thoracic nerve, which also pierces scalenus medius but turns anterolaterally onto serratus anterior. Look for fatty atrophy of the rhomboids, not serratus anterior.

Dorsal tarsometatarsal ligaments.note: Thin bands on the dorsum of the Lisfranc joint, from the cuneiforms and cuboid to the metatarsal bases, deep to the extensor tendons. These are the weakest TMT ligaments, so metatarsal bases displace dorsally. Pitfall: the dorsalis pedis artery dives between the 1st and 2nd metatarsal bases, so displaced fragments there carry vascular risk.
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

Dorsal ulnocarpal ligament.note: Thin dorsal capsular band from the ulnar head and TFCC to the triquetrum and lunate, lying next to the ECU tendon sheath. Pitfall: an ossicle at the processus styloideus ulnae may be an os triangulare or lunula variant rather than an acute avulsion; check whether it is corticated.
neighbours: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint
Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint
Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris

Dorsal venous arch of foot.note: Subcutaneous arch over the metatarsal shafts, superficial to the extensor tendons, draining medially into the Vena saphena magna and laterally into the Vena saphena parva. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the Arteria dorsalis pedis, which lies deep to the extensor tendons between EHL and EDL over the first intermetatarsal space.
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

Dorsal venous network of hand.note: The rete venosum dorsale manus lies in the subcutaneous fat over the metacarpals, superficial to the extensor tendons. It drains radially into the vena cephalica and ulnarly into the vena basilica. Pitfall: an IV cannula here can leave gas or contrast in the soft tissue. Do not mistake this for soft-tissue emphysema or an abscess.
passing: Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve

Dorsalis pedis artery.note: Continues the a. tibialis anterior below the ankle. It runs over the talus, os naviculare and intermediate cuneiform, lateral to the EHL tendon, and passes deep to EHB to reach the first intermetatarsal space. Pitfall: it is absent or comes from the perforating fibular branch in a minority of people, so do not report occlusion automatically.

Ductus deferens.note: Runs from the Epididymis in the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal and hooks around the inferior epigastric vessels at the deep ring. It then crosses the external iliac vessels and the ureter to reach the posterior bladder wall next to the Glandula seminalis. Pitfall: wall calcification, for example in diabetes, can be mistaken for ureteric stones or vascular calcification.

Duodenum.note: The bulb is intraperitoneal. D2–D4 are retroperitoneal in the anterior pararenal space: D2 wraps around the pancreatic head, and D3 crosses between the Aorta abdominalis and the SMA. Pitfall: a collapsed, unopacified duodenum or a periampullary diverticulum can look like a pancreatic head mass or a fluid collection.

Eighth rib.note: False rib. Its head articulates with T7 and T8 at the T7–T8 disc, and its costal cartilage joins the cartilage of the seventh rib, not the sternum. Pitfall: fractures of ribs 8–11 call for a search for liver or spleen injury and pneumothorax. Count ribs from the first rib, not from the costal margin.

Ejaculatory duct.note: Formed where the ampulla of the Ductus deferens joins the duct of the Glandula seminalis. It runs obliquely through the central zone of the Prostata to open beside the colliculus seminalis. Pitfall: a paramedian ejaculatory duct cyst can be confused with a midline prostatic utricle cyst, and duct calcifications can mimic urethral stones.

Eleventh rib.note: Floating rib with a single facet for T11, no costotransverse articulation and a free tapered tip within the abdominal wall muscles. Pitfall: the free tip can be mistaken for a fracture fragment or a calcified abdominal wall lesion. Fractures here call for a check of the kidney, spleen and liver.

Epicranial aponeurosis.note: Fibrous scalp layer joining frontalis and occipitalis, separated from the pericranium by loose areolar tissue. Pitfall: a subgaleal haematoma crosses sutures, whereas a cephalohaematoma (under the periosteum) stops at them. Do not mistake a parietal foramen for a fracture.
landmarks: lm:External surface of parietal bone|Parietal bone
lm:Sagittal border of parietal bone|Parietal bone

Epididymis.note: The Epididymis lies along the posterolateral Testis: the caput sits at the upper pole and the cauda continues into the Ductus deferens. On CT it is iso- to slightly hyperdense to the testis. Pitfall: an enlarged caput or a spermatocele can mimic a testicular mass. Ultrasound decides whether a lesion is intra- or extratesticular.

Epiglottis.note: The free tip of the Epiglottis projects behind the tongue base, with the valleculae in front of it. Below, the pre-epiglottic fat separates it from the Ligamentum thyreohyoideum medianum and Cartilago thyreoidea. Pitfall: a slice through an obliquely angled tip can make it look thickened and mimic epiglottitis. Check the pre-epiglottic fat for tumour spread.
neighbours: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle

Ethmoid bone.note: The cribriform plate sits in the Incisura ethmoidea of the frontal bone. The lamina orbitalis (papyracea) forms the medial orbital wall, and the posterior cells border the sphenoid sinus. Pitfall: the lateral lamella of the cribriform plate is the thinnest part of the skull base. Report Keros depth, and do not read a thin or dehiscent lamina papyracea as a fracture.
landmarks: lm:Orbital part of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Extensor carpi radialis brevis.note: Arises from the common extensor origin on the lateral epicondyle, where it is the main site of epicondylitis. It runs in the second compartment on the ulnar side of ECRL and inserts on the dorsal base of the third metacarpal. Pitfall: an os styloideum or carpal boss at the second/third CMC joint near its insertion can be mistaken for an osteophyte or fracture fragment.

Extensor carpi radialis longus.note: Arises from the lateral supracondylar ridge, proximal to the common extensor origin and just below brachioradialis. It runs in the second compartment on the radial side of ECRB and inserts on the base of the second metacarpal. Pitfall: just proximal to the retinaculum, the oblique crossing of APL/EPB over ECRL/ECRB is the site of intersection syndrome. Do not label this de Quervain.

Extensor digiti minimi.note: Arises from the common extensor origin and runs in the fifth compartment over the dorsal distal radioulnar joint to the little finger extensor hood. Pitfall: it often has a double tendon, which is a normal variant. With dorsal ulnar head prominence or DRUJ arthropathy it is the first tendon to rupture (Vaughan-Jackson), so do not overlook a gap.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
neighbours: Humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris
Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand

Extensor digitorum.note: Arises from the common extensor origin and runs in the fourth compartment with extensor indicis over the dorsal carpus. Its tendons to fingers 2–5 are linked by juncturae tendinum and insert through the extensor hoods on the middle and distal phalanges. Pitfall: the slip to the little finger is often absent or replaced by a junctura, so do not misread it as a rupture.
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
