Extensor digitorum brevis.note: A muscle belly on the dorsolateral foot, from the dorsolateral calcaneus near the sinus tarsi to the extensor tendons of toes 2–4, lying deep to the EDL tendons. Pitfall: its belly can mimic a ganglion or mass. A small dorsolateral calcaneal flake from its origin is an EDB avulsion, not an anterior process (bifurcate ligament) fracture.
passing: Muscular branches of deep fibular nerve
Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

Extensor digitorum longus.note: This is the most lateral muscle of the anterior compartment. It arises from the lateral tibial condyle, the Margo anterior fibulae and the interosseous membrane, and the anterior intermuscular septum separates it from the fibular muscles. Pitfall: the fibularis tertius is a distal, fused part of the EDL, so do not call it a separate mass or a tear.

Extensor hallucis brevis.note: The medial slip of the EDB complex. Its tendon inserts on the dorsal base of the hallux proximal phalanx and crosses over the dorsalis pedis artery and deep fibular nerve. Pitfall: do not confuse its thin tendon with the extensor hallucis longus tendon, which lies medial and inserts on the distal phalanx.
passing: Dorsal digital branches of deep fibular nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot

Extensor hallucis longus.note: Arises from the mid-fibula and interosseous membrane between the tibialis anterior and the EDL, and its tendon inserts on the base of the distal phalanx of the hallux. Pitfall: at the ankle the tendon crosses over the anterior tibial vessels and deep fibular nerve. Below the ankle the A. dorsalis pedis lies just lateral to the tendon, so do not confuse the two.
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot

Extensor indicis.note: Arises from the distal posterior ulna and membrana interossea and runs deep in the fourth extensor compartment with extensor digitorum. It joins the extensor hood of the index finger on the ulnar side of the ED index tendon. Pitfall: two extensor tendons to the index finger at the MCP joint are normal and should not be called a split tear.
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of second finger of hand

Extensor pollicis brevis.note: Arises from the distal posterior radius and membrana interossea, distal to APL. It runs with APL in the first extensor compartment and inserts on the base of the thumb's proximal phalanx. Pitfall: an intracompartmental septum that separates EPB from APL is a common variant and matters for de Quervain release. Do not mistake it for tendon splitting.
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand

Extensor pollicis longus.note: Arises from the posterior ulna and membrana interossea and passes in the third compartment on the ulnar side of the tuberculum dorsale radii (Lister). It then crosses over ECRL/ECRB and inserts on the distal phalanx of the thumb. Pitfall: after distal radius fractures, rupture can happen at the Lister tubercle, even when the fracture is nondisplaced, and a dorsal screw can irritate it.
neighbours: Distal phalanx of first finger of hand

Extensor retinaculum of wrist.note: Retinaculum extensorium carpi runs from the dorsal distal radius to the triquetrum and pisiform. Septa to the radius divide it into six extensor compartments. Pitfall: the tuberculum dorsale radii (Lister's tubercle) separates compartment 2 (ECRL/ECRB) from compartment 3 (EPL), so do not miscount compartments; fragments at the tubercle put EPL at risk.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensors carpi radialis
Tendon sheath of extensor pollicis longus
Tendon sheath - abd. pollicis longus - ext. pollicis brevis
Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum and extensor indicis
Tendon sheath of extensor digiti minimi manus
Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris

External abdominal oblique muscle.note: Musculus obliquus externus abdominis is the outermost flank muscle. It arises from ribs 5–12, interdigitating with serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi, and inserts on the outer lip of the iliac crest and, via its aponeurosis, the linea alba and ligamentum inguinale. Pitfall: lumbar (Petit) hernias pass between its free posterior border, latissimus dorsi and the iliac crest.
landmarks: lm:Outer lip of iliac crest|Hip bone

External anal sphincter.note: Sphincter externus ani encircles the anal canal below the levator ani, with the ischio-anal fossa fat lateral and the perineal body anterior. Pitfall: at the anorectal junction, partial volume with the puborectal sling and a collapsed anal canal can look like focal wall thickening or a mass.

External carotid artery.note: Arises at the carotid bifurcation, runs anteromedial to the Carotis interna, then passes deep to the posterior digastric belly into the Glandula parotidea, medial to the Vena retromandibularis. Pitfall: only the ECA gives cervical branches. Use branching, not position, to tell it from the ICA, because a laterally placed ICA is a common variant.
landmarks: lm:Styloid process of temporal bone|Temporal bone

External iliac artery.note: Runs from the common iliac bifurcation along the medial border of the Psoas major to the inguinal ligament, where it becomes the Arteria femoralis. The vein lies medial to it. Pitfall: use the origin of the Arteria epigastrica inferior, not an arbitrary slice, to mark the external iliac–femoral transition. Do not mistake a pelvic appendix lying on the vessel for a node.

External iliac vein.note: Runs along the pelvic brim medial to psoas major and posteromedial to the arteria iliaca externa, from the vena iliaca communis to the inguinal ligament, where it becomes the femoral vein. Pitfall: inflow mixing artefact in early-phase CT can look like thrombus. The medial external iliac nodes sit right against the vein and can be mistaken for it.

External intercostal membrane.note: Replaces the musculi intercostales externi anteriorly, between the costal cartilages up to the sternum, superficial to the internal intercostals. Pitfall: irregular costal cartilage calcification can mimic fractures or lesions, while fractures of non-calcified cartilage are often invisible on CT.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

External intercostal muscles.note: Musculi intercostales externi form the outermost intercostal layer, running from the tubercles to the costochondral junctions. Further forward they continue as the membrana intercostalis externa. Pitfall: CT cannot separate the three layers, and the neurovascular bundle runs deep to this layer in the sulcus costae, not within it.

External jugular vein.note: The Vena iugularis externa forms from the posterior division of the retromandibular vein. It descends across the surface of the sternocleidomastoid, deep to the platysma, then pierces the fascia above the clavicle and drains into the subclavian vein. Pitfall: an asymmetric or ectatic EJV seen in cross-section can mimic a supraclavicular node or mass.

External part of thyro-arytenoid muscle.note: Forms the muscular bulk of the true vocal fold, running from the inner thyroid lamina to the arytenoid, with paraglottic fat laterally. Pitfall: the true fold is the level of the Processus vocalis and is muscle-dense, while the false fold above contains fat; do not confuse the two levels on axial slices.
landmarks: lm:Anterolateral surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage
neighbours: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle

External pudendal veins.note: Run medially in the subcutaneous fat over the pectineus and adductor longus, from the scrotum or labia and the penis to the great saphenous vein close to the saphenofemoral junction. Pitfall: do not confuse them with the internal pudendal veins in Alcock's canal. When enlarged, they feed recurrent groin varices.

Facial artery.note: Arises from the ECA and grooves the posterior and deep surface of the Glandula submandibularis. It crosses the lower mandibular border at the anterior edge of the masseter, then runs a tortuous course to the medial canthus. Pitfall: the Vena facialis lies posterior and runs straighter. In cross-section a tortuous loop can mimic a level IB node.

Facial nerve (VII).note: Course through the canal: labyrinthine segment above the cochlea, geniculate ganglion, tympanic segment above the oval window and stapes, then mastoid segment to the stylomastoid foramen. In the parotid it lies lateral to the retromandibular vein. Pitfall: a dehiscent tympanic segment, which is common, looks like soft tissue on the stapes and can be mistaken for cholesteatoma.

Facial vein.note: Starts as the angular vein at the medial canthus and runs down behind the tortuous facial artery. It crosses the mandible at the anterior border of masseter and passes superficial to the submandibular gland. Pitfall: it has no valves and connects through the ophthalmic veins to the cavernous sinus (the danger triangle). The vein is straighter and lies behind the artery.

Falx cerebri.note: A sickle-shaped dural fold in the interhemispheric fissure, running from the crista galli and frontal crest to the internal occipital protuberance. It joins the tentorium at the straight sinus, and its free edge lies above the corpus callosum. Pitfall: physiological falx calcification or a dense falx can mimic an interhemispheric subdural haematoma, which is thicker, tapers and runs along the tentorium.
landmarks: lm:Sagittal border of parietal bone|Parietal bone

Fascia lata.note: Deep fascia of the thigh. It thickens laterally into the Tractus iliotibialis, and its hiatus saphenus lets the great saphenous vein through. Pitfall: a fluid collection between the subcutaneous fat and the Fascia lata (Morel-Lavallée lesion) lies above the fascia and should not be called an intramuscular haematoma.
passing: Anterior cutaneous branches of femoral nerve

Femoral artery.note: The femoral artery starts behind the Ligamentum inguinale, in the vascular compartment. In the femoral triangle it lies lateral to the femoral vein and medial to the femoral nerve. It then passes under the sartorius through the adductor canal to the adductor hiatus. Pitfall: if the Arteria profunda femoris arises high, do not mislabel the branches. A puncture site above the femoral head risks retroperitoneal haemorrhage.

Femoral branch of genitofemoral nerve.note: Runs lateral to the external iliac artery, passes under the inguinal ligament inside the femoral sheath beside the femoral artery, then pierces the fascia lata to supply skin over the femoral triangle. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the femoral nerve, which lies lateral to the sheath in the lacuna musculorum.

Femoral nerve.note: Forms within the psoas major, descends in the iliopsoas groove under the iliopsoas fascia, and passes under the inguinal ligament through the lacuna musculorum. The iliopectineal arch separates it from the femoral sheath, and it lies lateral to the femoral artery. Pitfall: an iliacus or psoas haematoma (anticoagulation) compresses it; it lies outside the femoral sheath.
passing: Anterior cutaneous branches of femoral nerve

Femoral vein.note: In the femoral triangle it lies medial to the A. femoralis. In the adductor canal under the M. sartorius it moves behind the artery, then becomes the V. poplitea at the adductor hiatus. Pitfall: the 'superficial femoral vein' is a deep vein. Also, a duplicated vein or mixing of unenhanced blood can look like or hide a thrombus.

Femur.note: Os femoris runs from caput ossis femoris in the acetabulum through the collum and trochanters to the corpus and the condyles, which articulate with tibia and patella. Pitfall: the fovea capitis is a normal central notch, not erosion or osteonecrosis. A small herniation pit in the anterosuperior neck is also benign.
landmarks: lm:Fovea for ligament of head of femur|Femur

Fibula.note: Caput fibulae articulates with the tibia at the superior tibiofibular joint, and the common fibular nerve winds around the neck. Distally, malleolus lateralis sits in the incisura fibularis and against the talus. Pitfall: a syndesmotic ankle injury may come with a proximal fibular (Maisonneuve) fracture, so check the whole bone. An os subfibulare mimics avulsion.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of fibula|Fibula

Fibular artery.note: Arises from the tibiofibular trunk and descends in the deep posterior compartment, posteromedial to the fibula and within or under the FHL, ending behind the lateral malleolus. Pitfall: on runoff CTA it is often the last patent vessel in diabetics. Before calling occlusion or planning a fibula flap, check for a peronea magna variant.

Fibular collateral ligament.note: Extracapsular cord running from the lateral femoral epicondyle to the fibular head, where it forms a conjoint insertion with the biceps femoris tendon. Pitfall: the popliteus tendon passes deep to it in the sulcus popliteus, so do not mistake that tendon for the ligament. A fibular head avulsion means posterolateral corner injury.
neighbours: Articular capsule of superior tibiofibular joint

Fibular veins.note: A pair of veins running with the fibular artery along the posteromedial fibula, within or deep to the flexor hallucis longus. They join the posterior tibial veins to form the tibioperoneal trunk. Pitfall: isolated calf DVT often sits here and is easily missed. Do not confuse these veins with the soleal venous sinuses.

Fibularis brevis muscle.note: In the Sulcus malleolaris fibulae the brevis tendon lies directly against the fibula, anterior to the longus. It passes above the fibular trochlea of the calcaneus and inserts on the fifth metatarsal tuberosity. Pitfall: a tuberosity avulsion is not a Jones fracture, and an os vesalianum or unfused apophysis should not be called a fracture.

Fibularis longus muscle.note: Arises from the fibular head next to the common fibular nerve and runs behind the lateral malleolus, posterior to the brevis. It turns in the cuboid groove to insert on the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base. Pitfall: the os peroneum at the cuboid is a normal sesamoid. Fracture or proximal migration of the os peroneum indicates a tendon tear.

Fibularis tertius muscle.note: This is the distal lateral slip of the EDL in the anterior compartment. Its tendon runs under the extensor retinacula to the dorsal base of the fifth metatarsal. Pitfall: it is often absent, which is a normal variant. Do not confuse it with the fibularis brevis, which inserts on the tuberosity at the base of the fifth metatarsal (the site of avulsion fractures).
passing: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

Fifth metacarpal bone.note: Base articulates with Os hamatum and the fourth metacarpal base, where extensor carpi ulnaris inserts; the head forms the fifth MCP joint. Pitfall: in a boxer's neck fracture, check for an associated 4th/5th carpometacarpal dorsal dislocation, which is easily overlooked on axial images; confirm hamate–metacarpal congruity on sagittal reformats.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand
Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris

Fifth metatarsal bone.note: The basis articulates with the os cuboideum and MT IV, and fibularis brevis inserts on the tuberositas. The caput articulates with the proximal phalanx. Pitfall: the longitudinal tuberosity apophysis in adolescents, or an os vesalianum, mimics avulsion. Also tell a zone-1 avulsion from a Jones fracture at the metadiaphyseal junction.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of foot

Fifth rib.note: True rib that articulates with T4 and T5 and connects to the sternum through its costal cartilage. Laterally it lies deep to serratus anterior, and posteriorly it lies under the scapula. Pitfall: irregular calcification at the costochondral junction mimics a fracture or a destructive lesion. Compare it with the opposite side.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

First metacarpal bone.note: Base forms the saddle joint with Os trapezium; abductor pollicis longus inserts radially, the head forms the thumb MCP joint. Pitfall: distinguish Bennett (two-part intra-articular, volar-ulnar fragment stays, shaft subluxes radially/dorsally) from Rolando (comminuted) and extra-articular base fractures; always state CMC subluxation.
passing: Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand

First metatarsal bone.note: The basis articulates with the os cuneiforme mediale and receives the tibialis anterior and fibularis longus. The caput articulates with the proximal phalanx and the sesamoids. Pitfall: there is no interosseous ligament between MT I and MT II. Widening between their bases, or between the medial cuneiform and MT II, indicates a Lisfranc injury.
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot
Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis

First posterior intercostal artery.note: Runs in the first intercostal space below the first rib, just outside the apical parietal pleura, and joins anteriorly with the internal thoracic artery branches. Pitfall: it arises from the supreme intercostal artery (costocervical trunk), not from the aorta, so look for it there rather than as an aortic branch.

First rib.note: Short, broad, flat rib that articulates only with T1. The tuberculum musculi scaleni anterioris separates the groove for the vena subclavia (anterior) from the groove for the arteria subclavia and plexus (posterior), and the pleural cupula lies beneath. Pitfall: a cervical rib or long C7 transverse process can be miscounted as the first rib. Confirm by its T1 articulation.

Flexor carpi radialis.note: Arises from the common flexor origin between pronator teres and palmaris longus. Its tendon runs in its own canal in the trapezium groove, outside the carpal tunnel, and inserts on the base of the second metacarpal. Pitfall: do not count the FCR tendon as a carpal tunnel structure, and do not mistake it for the median nerve.
neighbours: Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Tendon sheath of flexor carpi radialis

Flexor digiti minimi of foot.note: Runs from the base of the fifth metatarsal and the fibularis longus sheath to the base of the fifth proximal phalanx, deep and medial to the abductor digiti minimi. Pitfall: on CT it cannot be reliably separated from the abductor digiti minimi, so describe them together as the lateral plantar (hypothenar) muscle group.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of foot

Flexor digiti minimi of hand.note: Runs from the hamulus ossis hamati and flexor retinaculum to the ulnar base of the little finger's proximal phalanx, between ADM and opponens. The deep ulnar branch passes between FDM and ADM. Pitfall: FDM is often small or absent, which is a normal variant; check the hamulus for fracture, which is easy to miss on CT.
passing: Common palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand
Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Flexor digitorum brevis.note: The central superficial plantar muscle. It arises from the processus medialis tuberis calcanei directly deep to the aponeurosis plantaris and inserts on the middle phalanges of toes 2–5. Pitfall: do not mistake the FDB origin for a thickened plantar fascia (plantar fasciitis). Measure only the aponeurosis.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Common plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
landmarks: lm:Head of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
neighbours: Middle phalanx of third finger of foot

Flexor digitorum longus.note: Arises from the posterior tibia. Behind the medial malleolus its tendon lies between the tibialis posterior (anterior) and the posterior tibial vessels and tibial nerve. It crosses superficial to the FHL at the knot of Henry and inserts on distal phalanges 2–5. Pitfall: do not swap it with the tibialis posterior tendon, which is the larger tendon closest to the malleolus.
landmarks: lm:Tuberosity of distal phalanx of foot|Distal phalanx of third finger of foot
neighbours: Distal phalanx of second finger of foot

Flexor digitorum profundus.note: Arises from the anteromedial ulna and interosseous membrane. Its tendons pass through the carpal tunnel deep to the FDS, go through the FDS split and insert on the volar bases of the distal phalanges. Pitfall: a small volar fragment at the distal phalanx base, often in the ring finger, is a jersey-finger avulsion, not an incidental ossicle.
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Synovial sheaths of digits of hand
Distal phalanx of fourth finger of hand
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints
Middle phalanx of third finger of hand

Flexor hallucis longus.note: Arises from the posterior fibula. Its tendon runs in the groove between the medial and lateral talar tubercles, then under the sustentaculum tali, and passes between the sesamoids to the distal phalanx of the hallux. Pitfall: an os trigonum (smooth, corticated) is not a fracture of the processus posterior tali, though it can cause FHL tenosynovitis.
landmarks: lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of talus|Talus
lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of calcaneus|Calcaneus
neighbours: Distal phalanx of first finger of foot

Flexor pollicis longus.note: Arises from the anterior radius and interosseous membrane. It is the most radial tendon in the carpal tunnel, passes near the trapezium and inserts on the base of the thumb's distal phalanx. Pitfall: volar plate screws or a distal radius spur sticking out past the watershed line can cause attrition rupture of this tendon.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Palmar carpal branch of radial artery
neighbours: Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus
Distal phalanx of first finger of hand

Flexor retinaculum of ankle.note: Runs from the medial malleolus to the medial calcaneus and forms the roof of the tarsal tunnel. From anterior to posterior the contents are tibialis posterior, FDL, the posterior tibial vessels, the tibial nerve and FHL. Pitfall: accessory muscles (e.g. flexor digitorum accessorius longus) or varicose veins can look like a mass in the tunnel.
passing: Calcaneal branches of posterior tibial artery
neighbours: Tendon sheath of tibialis posterior muscle
Tendon sheath of flexor digitorum longus
Tendon sheath of flexor hallucis longus

Flexor retinaculum of wrist.note: Retinaculum flexorium carpi spans from the pisiform and hamulus ossis hamati to the scaphoid tubercle and trapezium. It forms the roof of the canalis carpi, which holds the flexor tendons and median nerve. Pitfall: the ligament itself is faint on CT, so define it by its bony attachments, and do not confuse the carpal tunnel with Guyon's canal, which lies superficial and ulnar.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus
Tendon sheath of flexor carpi radialis

Flocculus.note: The flocculus projects into the cerebellopontine angle cistern next to the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle. It lies behind the CN VII/VIII complex and in front of the Facies posterior partis petrosae. Pitfall: the flocculus, or calcified choroid plexus coming out of the foramen of Luschka, can mimic a CPA mass such as a vestibular schwannoma.
landmarks: lm:Posterior surface of petrous part|Temporal bone

Folium of vermis.note: The Folium vermis is a small posterior vermian lamina between the declive and the tuber. It lies at the horizontal fissure in the posterior cerebellar notch, and the semilunar lobules sit on either side. Pitfall: CT cannot resolve it. The CSF and dura in the posterior cerebellar notch can mimic a midline vermian cleft or lesion.

Fornix.note: The fornix arches from the fimbria of the hippocampus under the splenium. Its body runs along the lower edge of the septum pellucidum, and its columns curve in front of the interventricular foramen down to the mamillary bodies. Pitfall: a hyperdense colloid cyst sits between the columns of the fornix at the foramen of Monro. Do not dismiss it as normal fornix or choroid plexus.

Fourth metacarpal bone.note: Base articulates mainly with Os hamatum, variably with Os capitatum, and with the third and fifth metacarpal bases; the head forms the fourth MCP joint. Pitfall: the thin shaft's oblique nutrient canal mimics a nondisplaced fracture; a true fracture breaches both cortices or shows a step.
passing: Common palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fourth finger of hand

Fourth metatarsal bone.note: The basis articulates with the os cuboideum, the lateral cuneiform, MT III and MT V. The caput articulates with proximal phalanx IV. Pitfall: diaphyseal stress fractures may show only subtle periosteal reaction. Also check that the medial cortex of the MT IV base lines up with the medial edge of the cuboid; malalignment points to a tarsometatarsal injury.
passing: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Common plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fourth finger of foot

Fourth rib.note: True rib that articulates with T3 and T4. Anteriorly it lies under pectoralis major and minor, laterally under serratus anterior, and posteriorly under the scapula. Pitfall: posterior fractures are hidden by the overlying scapula and run nearly parallel to the axial plane. Review curved reformats or 3D reconstructions.

Fourth ventricle.note: The pons and upper medulla form its floor (rhomboid fossa), and the medullary vela and nodulus form its roof. It connects upward to the aquaeductus mesencephali and drains through the median and lateral apertures. Pitfall: beam-hardening streaks between the petrous bones can obscure or mimic effacement, and a Blake pouch or mega cisterna magna can be mistaken for Dandy-Walker malformation.

Free taenia.note: One of the three taeniae coli. It runs on the anterior surface of the ascending, descending and sigmoid colon and the inferior surface of the transverse colon, and all three taeniae meet at the base of the appendix. Pitfall: in collapsed colon, the taeniae and haustral folds look like focal wall thickening.

Frenula capsulae.note: Synovial folds (retinacula) that run up the femoral neck from the capsular attachment toward the head and carry the retinacular vessels. Pitfall: on CT arthrography these folds can look like plicae or loose bodies. Their vessels explain the risk of avascular necrosis after displaced intracapsular neck fractures.

Frontal bone.note: The squama meets the parietal bones at the coronal suture. The orbital parts form the orbital roofs around the Incisura ethmoidea, and the frontal sinus lies between the anterior and posterior tables. Pitfall: hyperostosis frontalis interna (symmetric, spares the midline) is a normal variant. Do not mistake it for meningioma or Paget disease.
landmarks: lm:Foramen caecum of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Frontal branch of superficial temporal a.key: Frontal branch of superficial temporal artery
Frontal branch of superficial temporal a.note: Runs tortuously forward in the subcutaneous scalp superficial to the temporal fascia and anastomoses with the Arteria supraorbitalis. Pitfall: an enhancing tortuous branch mimics a scalp lesion. In giant cell arteritis or post-traumatic pseudoaneurysm, compare with the other side.

Frontal branches of callosomarginal arte.note: Medial frontal branches climb over the superior frontal gyrus toward the convexity next to the falx. Pitfall: ACA-territory infarcts are parasagittal and easily missed next to the hyperdense falx. Compare the medial frontal cortex on both sides.

Frontalis muscle.note: Thin forehead muscle from the galea to the eyebrow skin, interlacing with procerus, corrugator and orbicularis oculi over the Arcus superciliaris. Pitfall: the thin soft tissue here hides little swelling, so a fracture of the anterior frontal sinus wall underneath is easy to miss. Always check the bone window.
passing: Frontal branch of superficial temporal artery

Gallbladder.note: It lies in the gallbladder fossa between segments IVb and V, on the Cantlie line. The neck points toward the porta hepatis, and the fundus touches the duodenum and hepatic flexure. Pitfall: many gallstones are isodense to bile, so a normal CT does not exclude cholelithiasis. Use ultrasound.

Ganglia of sympathetic trunk.note: Segmental swellings of the trunk. The cervicothoracic (stellate) ganglion sits in front of the neck of the first rib at C7–T1, and the thoracic ganglia lie over the costal heads. Pitfall: a normal ganglion, especially the superior cervical ganglion behind the ICA at C2–C3, can be mistaken for a retropharyngeal or intercostal lymph node.
neighbours: Radiate ligament of head of rib

Gastroduodenal artery.note: Descends from the Arteria hepatica communis behind the duodenal bulb and in front of the pancreatic head, then divides into gastro-omental and superior pancreaticoduodenal branches. Pitfall: after Whipple surgery, a pseudoaneurysm of the GDA stump can be mistaken for a fluid collection. The artery is also the classic source of bleeding from posterior duodenal ulcers.

Genicular veins.note: Run with the genicular arteries around the femoral condyles and the tibial plateau, close to the knee capsule, and drain into the vena poplitea. Pitfall: their vascular channels and nutrient foramina in the condyles can mimic non-displaced fracture lines on bone-window CT.

Genioglossus muscle.note: Paired fan-shaped muscle from the superior mental spine into the tongue, with the midline lingual septum between the two sides. The geniohyoid lies below it; the hyoglossus and sublingual space lie lateral. Pitfall: in XII palsy the affected side undergoes fatty atrophy, so the normal side can be mistaken for a mass.

Geniohyoid muscle.note: Paired strap muscle running from the inferior mental spine to the body of the os hyoideum. It lies above the mylohyoid and below the genioglossus. Pitfall: the thin fatty midline septum between the paired geniohyoid and genioglossus muscles is normal and should not be reported as a lesion or abscess.

Genital branch of genitofemoral nerve.note: Enters the deep inguinal ring and runs within the spermatic cord (with the round ligament in females) to the cremaster and scrotal or labial skin, ending near the pubic tubercle. Pitfall: it lies inside the cord, whereas the ilio-inguinal nerve lies on its anterior surface; mixing them up matters in post-herniorrhaphy pain.

Genitofemoral nerve.note: Pierces the anterior surface of the psoas major at about L3–L4 and descends on it, posterior to the ureter and gonadal vessels, before dividing above the inguinal ligament. Pitfall: on CT, the thin linear density on the anterior psoas is more often the ureter or gonadal vein, so trace it before labelling.

Gingiva.note: The gingiva is mucosa covering the alveolar processes up to the tooth necks. On CT it cannot be separated from the buccal or lingual mucosa. Look for underlying cortical erosion of the Mandibula. Pitfall: the Foramen mentale below the premolar roots can be mistaken for a periapical lucency or a lytic lesion. Dental streak artefact hides small changes.
landmarks: lm:Neck of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

Glans penis.note: The distal expansion of the Corpus spongiosum penis, which caps the blunt tips of the corpora cavernosa and holds the external urethral orifice. Pitfall: partial volume with the foreskin, or a catheter balloon or contrast at the meatus, can mimic a glans lesion. Penile carcinoma is staged by MRI, not CT.

Glenoid labrum.note: Fibrocartilaginous rim on the fossa glenoidea that anchors the biceps long head superiorly and the glenohumeral ligaments. On plain CT, look for a bony Bankart fragment at the anteroinferior rim. Pitfall: on CT arthrography, a sublabral foramen or Buford complex at the anterosuperior rim mimics a labral tear.

Globus pallidus.note: Medial part of the Nucleus lentiformis. The putamen lies lateral (separated by the lateral medullary lamina) and the internal capsule lies medial, separating it from the thalamus and caudate. Small symmetric pallidal calcification is common and normal with age. Do not report it as bleeding or Fahr disease.

Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).note: It leaves the postolivary sulcus and passes through the anteromedial pars nervosa of the Foramen jugulare with the inferior petrosal sinus. The intrajugular process separates it from X and XI. It then runs between the ICA and IJV. Pitfall: an asymmetric jugular foramen or a high jugular bulb is a normal variant, not a mass or erosion.
landmarks: lm:Intrajugular process of occipital bone|Occipital bone

Gluteus maximus muscle.note: Arises from the posterior ilium behind the linea glutea posterior, the sacrum, coccyx and ligamentum sacrotuberale, and inserts on the tuberositas glutea and iliotibial tract. Pitfall: calcified injection granulomas in its superficial fibres are common and should not be called tumour calcification.
neighbours: Trochanteric bursa of gluteus maximus muscle

Gluteus medius muscle.note: Arises from the outer ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines, deep to the gluteus maximus and superficial to the minimus. It inserts on the lateral and superoposterior facets of the greater trochanter. Pitfall: calcific tendinopathy at the trochanter can mimic an avulsion fragment; check for the cortical donor site.
neighbours: Trochanteric bursa of gluteus medius muscle

Gluteus minimus muscle.note: The deepest gluteal muscle, arising between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines above the hip capsule and inserting on the anterior facet of the greater trochanter. Pitfall: its thin belly blends with the gluteus medius on partial volume; follow the fat plane to tell isolated atrophy apart.
neighbours: Trochanteric bursa of gluteus minimus muscle

Gracile fasciculus.note: Medial part of the posterior funiculus, next to the sulcus medianus posterior, found at all cord levels. It ends at the tuberculum gracile. CT does not show it. Pitfall: dorsal dural or ligamentous compression and arachnoid webs can be subtle on CT myelography, and a midline dorsal septum can be mistaken for a web.

Gracile lobule.note: The Lobulus gracilis is the hemispheric part next to the pyramis and tuber. It lies between the Lobulus semilunaris inferior and the Lobulus biventer, on the inner surface of the occipital squama. Pitfall: streak artefact and partial volume from the squama can mimic a thin subdural collection or cortical hyperdensity.

Gracilis muscle.note: The most superficial medial thigh muscle. It runs from the inferior pubic ramus next to the symphysis to the pes anserinus on the medial proximal tibia, where its tendon lies between the sartorius and semitendinosus tendons. Pitfall: fluid in the bursa anserina can mimic a meniscal cyst or a semimembranosus bursa.

Great cardiac vein.note: It rises in the anterior interventricular sulcus with the R. interventricularis anterior, then turns into the left atrioventricular groove next to the A. circumflexa and continues as the Sinus coronarius. Pitfall: in the AV groove it lies superficial to the circumflex artery and can be mistaken for it, or mimic a stenosis where it crosses.
passing: Superior lingular vein of left lung

Great saphenous vein.note: Runs up in front of the medial malleolus, along the medial tibia and the posteromedial knee in the subcutaneous saphenous compartment, then pierces the fascia lata at the saphenous opening to join the vena femoralis. Pitfall: accessory or duplicated saphenous veins mimic the main trunk. Report how close a thrombus is to the saphenofemoral junction.
passing: Medial crural cutaneous branches of saphenous nerve

Greater omentum.note: A fatty apron hangs from the greater curvature of the stomach, in front of the transverse colon and small bowel and just behind the anterior abdominal wall. It carries the vasa gastroomentalia. Pitfall: normal omentum is thin fat with fine vessels. Nodular soft-tissue density or caking suggests peritoneal carcinomatosis, and a focal fat-stranding mass suggests omental infarction.

Greater palatine artery.note: Continues the Arteria palatina descendens through the canalis palatinus major and exits at the foramen palatinum majus, medial to the third molar. It then runs forward in the hard-palate mucosa toward the canalis incisivus. Pitfall: do not confuse the greater palatine foramen with the more posterior foramina palatina minora.
passing: Posterior septal branches of sphenopalatine artery

Habenula.note: The habenula sits in the epithalamus at the posteromedial thalamus. It lies just in front of the pineal gland and above the Commissura posterior, at the back of the third ventricle. Pitfall: normal curvilinear calcification of the habenular commissure lies a few mm in front of pineal calcification. Do not mistake it for pineal or thalamic pathology.

Hamate bone.note: Distal-row carpal between Os capitatum (radial) and Os triquetrum (proximal-ulnar), bearing the 4th/5th metacarpals; the hamulus forms the ulnar wall of the carpal tunnel and the radial wall of Guyon's canal. Pitfall: hook fracture versus os hamuli proprium—an accessory ossicle has smooth corticated margins; assess on axial carpal-tunnel slices.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
neighbours: Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand

Hemi-azygos vein.note: This vein ascends left prevertebrally through the left crus, posterior to the descending aorta. It crosses behind the aorta at about T8–T9 to join the azygos. Pitfall: when dilated, as in hemiazygos continuation of a left IVC, it mimics retrocrural or paraaortic lymphadenopathy. Trace it to the crossing level.

Hepatic portal vein.note: Formed behind the pancreatic neck where the V. mesenterica superior meets the V. splenica. It runs in the hepatoduodenal ligament to the porta hepatis, in front of the IVC and the caudate lobe (segment I). Pitfall: in the arterial phase, mixing of opacified and unopacified blood can mimic a portal vein thrombus. Check the portal venous phase.

Hepatic veins.note: The right, middle and left Venae hepaticae run between liver segments and converge on the suprahepatic IVC just below the diaphragm. Segment I drains separately and directly into the IVC. Pitfall: in early phases, unopacified hepatic veins mimic Budd-Chiari syndrome. Also, hepatic veins lie between segments, whereas portal branches run within segments.

Hip bone.note: Formed by the ilium, ischium and pubis, which meet at the acetabulum. It meets the sacrum at the facies auricularis and the opposite side at the symphysis. The superior gluteal vessels exit through the greater sciatic notch. Pitfall: an unfused triradiate cartilage, an os acetabuli or apophyses (AIIS, ischial) in young patients mimic fractures or avulsions.

Hippocampal commissure.note: A thin sheet of fibres between the crura of the fornix, just under the splenium, forming the roof of the velum interpositum. It is not separately visible on CT. Pitfall: a CSF space below it is a cavum velum interpositum or cavum vergae, both normal variants. Do not call it a cyst or a dilated third ventricle.

Hippocampus.note: Lies in the floor and medial wall of the temporal horn. The Corpus amygdaloideum is anterosuperior, the Gyrus parahippocampalis inferomedial and the Fimbria/Fornix posterosuperior. Pitfall: a widened temporal horn in hydrocephalus can mimic hippocampal atrophy. Calcified Choroid plexus or hippocampal sulcus remnant cysts are normal findings, not lesions.

Humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris.key: Humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris
Humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris.note: Arises from the common extensor origin on the lateral epicondyle, merges with the ulnar head and forms the tendon of the sixth compartment. That tendon lies in the groove dorsal to the processus styloideus ulnae and inserts on the base of the fifth metacarpal. Pitfall: in supination the tendon normally sits partly outside the groove, so do not call isolated positional subluxation on a single CT pathologic.
neighbours: Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris

Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris.key: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris.note: Arises from the epicondylus medialis. Together with the ulnar head it forms the cubital tunnel arch, where the ulnar nerve enters the forearm. Its tendon inserts on the pisiform and continues as the pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments. Pitfall: the pisiform is a sesamoid bone inside the FCU tendon; do not report it as an avulsion fragment or loose body.
neighbours: Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum su.key: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum su.note: Arises from the medial epicondyle and coronoid process. The median nerve and ulnar artery pass deep to the arch between its heads. Its tendons cross the carpal tunnel superficial to FDP and insert on the middle phalanges. Pitfall: in the finger each FDS tendon normally splits around FDP (Camper chiasm); do not read this split as a tear.
passing: Common palmar digital branches of median nerve
neighbours: Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Middle phalanx of third finger of hand

Humerus.note: Caput humeri articulates with the glenoid; the distal condylus humeri articulates with radius and ulna, flanked by the epicondyles. Pitfall: mid-to-distal shaft fractures involving the sulcus nervi radialis threaten the radial nerve, and the surgical-neck/greater-tubercle region the axillary nerve—name the fracture's relation to these grooves.
neighbours: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

Hyoglossus muscle.note: Flat sheet from the greater horn and body of the hyoid to the side of the tongue. The submandibular duct and the lingual and XII nerves run lateral to it; the lingual artery runs medial. Pitfall: it is the key divider of the sublingual space. Do not mistake the lingual vessels medial to it for duct stones or nodes.

Hyoid bone.note: Os hyoideum lies at C3 level. Suprahyoid muscles insert above it and the Membrana thyrohyoidea connects it to the thyroid cartilage below. The Cornu majus points backward toward the pharyngeal wall. Pitfall: an unfused synchondrosis between the body and Cornu majus, often asymmetric, mimics a fracture. Look for corticated margins and the absence of soft-tissue swelling.
landmarks: lm:Greater horn of hyoid bone|Hyoid bone
lm:Lesser horn of hyoid bone|Hyoid bone

Hypoglossal nerve (XII).note: It leaves the preolivary sulcus and passes through the Canalis nervi hypoglossi above the occipital condyle. It descends between the ICA and IJV, then runs on the lateral surface of the hyoglossus. Pitfall: do not confuse the hypoglossal canal with the more lateral jugular foramen. In a XII palsy the atrophic, fatty half-tongue is the abnormal side; the normal side is not a mass.

Hypothalamus.note: Forms the floor and lower lateral walls of the Ventriculus tertius below the thalamus. The chiasm and lamina terminalis lie in front, the Corpora mammillaria behind and the infundibulum below. CT cannot show it as a separate structure. Before you call a suprasellar mass hypothalamic, separate it from the chiasm and the pituitary and check whether the sella is enlarged.

Ileal branch of ileocolic artery.note: Supplies the terminal ileum and anastomoses with the end of the superior mesenteric artery. It runs in the ileocaecal mesentery. Pitfall: in Crohn disease, engorged vasa recta here (comb sign) reflect active inflammation. Do not dismiss them as normal mesenteric vessels.

Ileocolic artery.note: Terminal right-sided branch of the SMA. It runs in the root of the mesentery, crosses the third part of the duodenum, and continues toward the ileocaecal region. Pitfall: it lies right next to the ileocolic and superior mesenteric veins. Lymph node station and right-hemicolectomy planning depend on correct artery–vein identification.

Ileocolic nodes.note: Nodi ileocolici lie along the ileocolic vessels in the mesentery, running from the SMA/SMV root towards the ileocaecal junction in the right lower quadrant. Pitfall: reactive ileocolic nodes in mesenteric adenitis can mimic appendicitis; confirm a normal appendix before reporting adenitis.

Iliacus branch of iliolumbar artery.note: Runs laterally across the iliac fossa between the bone and the Musculus iliacus, supplying the muscle and the main nutrient artery of the ilium. Pitfall: in CT bone windows, its nutrient canal in the iliac fossa can be mistaken for a non-displaced iliac wing fracture.

Iliacus muscle.note: Fills the Fossa iliaca and joins the psoas over the iliopubic eminence to insert on the lesser trochanter. The femoral nerve lies in the groove between the iliacus and psoas. Pitfall: an iliacus haematoma in an anticoagulated patient compresses the femoral nerve. A fluid-filled iliopsoas bursa connecting with the hip joint mimics a cystic mass.

Ilio-inguinal nerve.note: An L1 branch that crosses the quadratus lumborum and iliacus, pierces the transversus near the iliac crest and runs between the internal oblique and transversus. It enters the inguinal canal, where it runs anterior to the spermatic cord. Pitfall: it lies outside the cord, so do not confuse it with the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve; mesh or tack entrapment happens here.

Iliococcygeus muscle.note: Arises from the arcus tendineus levatoris ani and the spina ischiadica and inserts on the anococcygeal body and coccyx. It separates the pelvis above from the ischioanal fossa below. Pitfall: this thin, sloping sheet blurs into the obturator internus by partial volume. The pudendal canal lies below it, in the wall of the ischioanal fossa.

Iliocostalis colli muscle.note: Most lateral column of the erector spinae in the neck; it runs from the angles of ribs 3–6 to the posterior tubercles of the C4–C6 transverse processes, lateral to longissimus colli. Pitfall: near the posterior tubercles it lies close to the scalenes and brachial plexus roots, so the posterior and anterior tubercles should not be mixed up.

Iliocostalis lumborum muscle.note: Lateral erector spinae column, running from the iliac crest, sacrum and thoracolumbar aponeurosis to the angles of the lower 6–8 ribs, lateral to longissimus and posterior to quadratus lumborum. Pitfall: normal fatty atrophy or asymmetry in older patients should not be called denervation or a mass. Compare the paraspinal muscles of both sides at the same level.

Iliocostalis thoracis muscle.note: Runs from the angles of the lower six ribs to the angles of the upper six ribs and the C7 transverse process, lying over the rib angles lateral to longissimus thoracis. Pitfall: rib-angle fractures beneath it are easy to miss on axial images, so use oblique or curved reformats. Also check rib counting before reporting a level.

Iliohypogastric nerve.note: An L1 nerve that emerges at the lateral border of the psoas major, below the twelfth rib, and crosses posterior to the kidney on the quadratus lumborum. It runs between the transversus and internal oblique and pierces the external oblique aponeurosis above the superficial ring. Pitfall: it is cranial to and parallel with the ilio-inguinal nerve and easily mislabelled.

Iliolumbar artery.note: Ascends from the posterior division behind the psoas, anterior to the sacral ala and sacro-iliac joint, then splits into lumbar, iliacus and spinal branches. Pitfall: in sacral or alar fractures it is an overlooked bleeding source. The adjacent Vena iliolumbalis at L5 is the main vascular hazard in anterior or lateral lumbar access.
passing: Posterior division of internal iliac artery

Iliolumbar ligament.note: Runs from the L5 (sometimes L4) transverse process tip to the posterior iliac crest, between quadratus lumborum and psoas. Pitfall: an L5 transverse process avulsion is a marker of posterior pelvic ring instability. Ossification of this ligament should not be mistaken for a transitional-vertebra pseudarthrosis, so number the vertebrae carefully.

Iliolumbar vein.note: Runs from the iliac fossa medially, deep to psoas, near the L5 transverse process and the ligamentum iliolumbale, and drains into the internal or common iliac vein. Pitfall: it often drains directly into the vena iliaca communis and is easily missed. That matters for anterior L4–S1 approaches, and in cross-section it can look like a node.

Iliopectineal arch.note: A thickening of the Fascia iliopsoae running from the inguinal ligament to the iliopubic eminence. It divides the lacuna musculorum (iliopsoas, femoral nerve) from the lacuna vasorum (femoral artery and vein). Pitfall: the femoral nerve lies lateral to the arch, outside the femoral sheath, so do not place it with the vessels.

Iliopsoas fascia.note: This fascia wraps the psoas major and iliacus from the lumbar spine down to the lesser trochanter. The Arcus iliopectineus divides the muscular lacuna (containing the N. femoralis) from the vascular lacuna. Pitfall: a psoas abscess or haematoma can track inside this sheath to the groin or lesser trochanter. It can be mistaken for an inguinal mass or a hip effusion.
landmarks: lm:Costal part of transverse process|Vertebra L3

Iliotibial tract.note: A lateral fascial band from the tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus that crosses the lateral femoral epicondyle and inserts on Gerdy's tubercle of the anterolateral tibia. Pitfall: a Gerdy's tubercle avulsion is more anterior than a Segond fracture of the lateral tibial rim, so do not confuse them.

Incus.note: Corpus incudis lies in the epitympanic recess behind caput mallei, forming the axial 'ice-cream cone'. Crus longum descends parallel to manubrium mallei to the processus lenticularis, which articulates with stapes. Pitfall: the thin crus longum and processus lenticularis often show partial-volume loss, which mimics erosion or incudostapedial discontinuity.

Inferior alveolar artery.note: Enters the Foramen mandibulae medial to the ramus and runs in the mandibular canal beneath the molar roots to the Foramen mentale. Pitfall: the corticated canal, including bifid-canal variants, should not be read as a lucent lesion or fracture. Always report the canal's relation to the third-molar roots.
passing: Mental branch of inferior alveolar artery
Mylohyoid branch of inferior alveolar artery

Inferior alveolar nerve.note: It enters the foramen mandibulae at the lingula and runs in the canalis mandibulae below the molar roots to the foramen mentale. Report the canal's distance from the root apices. Pitfall: a bifid canal, or the anterior loop and incisive canal, can be mistaken for fracture lines or lesions. A canal touching the roots of an impacted third molar matters before surgery.
passing: Mylohyoid branch of inferior alveolar artery
landmarks: lm:Root of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

Inferior basal vein of left lung.key: Inferior basal vein of left lung
Inferior basal vein of left lung.note: Vena basalis inferior pulmonis sinistri drains the posterior and lateral basal segments just above the Diaphragma and joins the Vena pulmonalis sinistra inferior. Pitfall: veins run intersegmentally, away from the bronchi, whereas the basal segmental arteries run alongside the bronchi. Do not read a basal vein as an embolised artery.
passing: Superior basal vein of left lung
neighbours: Medial basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BVII)

Inferior basal vein of right lung.key: Inferior basal vein of right lung
Inferior basal vein of right lung.note: Vena basalis inferior pulmonis dextri drains the posterior basal segments of the right lower lobe and joins the Vena pulmonalis dextra inferior. Pitfall: in the posterior costophrenic recess, dependent atelectasis and breathing motion around this vein can mimic consolidation or emboli. Veins run between segments; arteries run with the bronchi.
passing: Superior basal vein of right lung
neighbours: Posterior basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BX)

Inferior colliculus.note: Lower part of the tectum. The quadrigeminal cistern is behind it, the superior medullary velum and Lingula are below, and CN IV exits just caudal to it. Pitfall: tectal glioma thickening is subtle on CT, so compare collicular contour. A quadrigeminal arachnoid cyst can mimic tectal compression.

Inferior deep lateral cervical nodes.note: Level IV nodes lie along the lower Vena jugularis interna, from the cricoid level down to the clavicle, in front of the Musculus scalenus anterior and above the pleural dome. Pitfall: asymmetric jugular veins, the vertebral vein or, on the left, the thoracic duct terminus can mimic a node; check contrast phase and tubular continuity.

Inferior diaphragmatic nodes.note: Lie on the abdominal surface of the diaphragm along the inferior phrenic vessels, near the caval and oesophageal hiatus, next to liver segments IV and VIII. Pitfall: they are easily confused with supradiaphragmatic (paracardiac) nodes on axial slices. Use coronal or sagittal reformats to place the node relative to the diaphragm.

Inferior epigastric artery.note: Arises from the Arteria iliaca externa just above the inguinal ligament. It ascends medial to the deep inguinal ring, deep to the Musculus rectus abdominis, and anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery. Pitfall: it separates direct hernias (medial) from indirect hernias (lateral). Check for an aberrant obturator branch (corona mortis) and for a source of rectus sheath haematoma.

Inferior epigastric nodes.note: Small nodes along the inferior epigastric vessels, deep to the rectus abdominis on the fascia transversalis, just medial to the deep inguinal ring. Pitfall: they can be confused with superficial inguinal nodes along the superficial epigastric vessels, which lie superficial to the external oblique aponeurosis.

Inferior epigastric vein.note: Arises from the vena iliaca externa just above the inguinal ligament, runs up medial to the deep inguinal ring, and enters the rectus sheath behind rectus abdominis. Pitfall: these vessels are the landmark for telling hernias apart. Indirect inguinal hernias lie lateral to them and direct hernias medial, so mislabelling the vessels gives the wrong hernia type.

Inferior extensor retinaculum of ankle.note: Y-shaped band. Its stem starts on the lateral calcaneus at the sinus tarsi and its limbs reach the medial malleolus and the medial plantar fascia. It forms the roof of the anterior tarsal tunnel. Pitfall: the stem in the sinus tarsi should not be mistaken for the interosseous talocalcaneal or cervical ligament.
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensor hallucis longus
Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum longus

Inferior fibular retinaculum.note: Attaches to the lateral calcaneus around the trochlea fibularis. It holds fibularis brevis above the trochlea and fibularis longus below it. Pitfall: an os peroneum or a hypertrophic trochlea fibularis can look like a fracture fragment, and swapping brevis and longus is a common laterality error.

Inferior frontal sulcus.note: The sulcus frontalis inferior separates the middle frontal gyrus from the inferior frontal gyrus and usually joins the inferior precentral sulcus at its back end. Pitfall: do not mistake it for the ascending or horizontal rami of the lateral sulcus. Those rami lie below it and split the inferior frontal gyrus into the pars triangularis and pars opercularis.
neighbours: Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus
Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Inferior gemellus muscle.note: Arises from the upper ischial tuberosity, joins the lower border of the Obturator internus tendon and inserts in the Fossa trochanterica. The sciatic nerve runs posterior to it. Pitfall: on CT it cannot be separated from the obturator internus tendon. Do not confuse it with the Quadratus femoris just below.

Inferior glenohumeral ligament.note: Hammock of anterior band, axillary pouch and posterior band running from the anteroinferior labrum to the humeral anatomical neck. It is the main anterior stabiliser in abduction. Pitfall: a humeral avulsion (HAGL) is missed if you only check the glenoid side; look for contrast extravasation or a flake at the humeral neck.

Inferior gluteal artery.note: Leaves the pelvis through the infrapiriform part of the greater sciatic foramen, posteromedial to the Nervus ischiadicus, and enters the gluteus maximus. Pitfall: the Musculus piriformis is the divider. Vessels below it are inferior gluteal or internal pudendal, and vessels above it are superior gluteal. Do not mix them up when reporting active bleeding.
passing: Anterior division of internal iliac artery

Inferior gluteal nodes.note: These nodes run along the inferior gluteal vessels through the infrapiriform part of the greater sciatic foramen, with the internal pudendal vessels nearby. Pitfall: the sciatic nerve and the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve in the infrapiriform foramen look like soft-tissue nodules, so do not report them as nodes.

Inferior gluteal veins.note: Pass with the arteria glutea inferior through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis (infrapiriform), medial to the sciatic nerve. Pitfall: dilated gluteal varices, for example in pelvic congestion, can look like a thickened sciatic nerve or a soft-tissue mass. Also keep these apart from the superior gluteal vessels, which run above piriformis.

Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscl.key: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscl.note: Runs from the lateral pterygoid plate to the pterygoid fovea of the condylar neck. The medial pterygoid lies inferomedially and the temporalis laterally. Pitfall: the maxillary artery loops lateral or medial to this head, so a tortuous enhancing vessel here is normal and not a vascular malformation.
passing: Accessory branch of middle meningeal artery
landmarks: lm:Infratemporal surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
neighbours: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Inferior labial artery.note: Arises from the facial artery near the oral commissure and runs in the lower lip between the Musculus orbicularis oris and the mucosa. Pitfall: dental-restoration streak artifact and normal labial vascular enhancement can mimic a lip lesion. Correlate with the opposite side.
passing: Mental branch of inferior alveolar artery

Inferior labial veins.note: The Venae labiales inferiores lie in the lower lip, deep to Musculus orbicularis oris and in front of the mandibular dental arch. They drain laterally into the Vena facialis. Pitfall: streak artefact from dental work can hide or mimic them, and the nearby mental neurovascular bundle should not be mistaken for a lip vessel.

Inferior lateral brachial cutaneous nerv.note: Arises from the radial nerve in the spiral groove and pierces the lateral head of triceps below the deltoid insertion to reach the skin of the lower lateral arm. Pitfall: the posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve leaves at almost the same point, and the two are easily confused. Both are at risk in lateral humeral plating.

Inferior lateral genicular artery.note: It leaves the Arteria poplitea and runs laterally above the fibular head, deep to the lateral gastrocnemius and the Ligamentum collaterale fibulare, along the lateral meniscus margin to the Rete patellare. Pitfall: it runs at joint-line level, higher than the inferior medial genicular artery. It is a common source of pseudoaneurysm or haemarthrosis after knee arthroplasty or posterolateral corner surgery.

Inferior leaflet of right atrioventricul.key: Inferior leaflet of right atrioventricular valve
Inferior leaflet of right atrioventricul.note: Inferior (posterior) tricuspid cusp at the diaphragmatic part of the annulus, close to the ostium of the Sinus coronarius. Pitfall: on non-gated CT the thin leaflets are mostly invisible. Mixing artefact from IVC and coronary sinus inflow near the annulus can mimic a leaflet mass or thrombus.
passing: Inferior papillary muscle of right ventricle
Septal leaflet of right atrioventricular valve

Inferior lingular artery of left lung.key: Inferior lingular artery of left lung
Inferior lingular artery of left lung.note: A5 runs with BV into the anteroinferior lingula, between the oblique fissure and the left heart border. Pitfall: the lingula belongs to Lobus superior pulmonis sinistri and is not a left "middle lobe". The two lingular arteries often come off a common trunk from the interlobar left pulmonary artery.
passing: Superior lingular artery of left lung
neighbours: Inferior lingular segmental bronchus of left lung (BV)
Superior lingular segmental bronchus of left lung (BIV)

Inferior lingular segmental bronchus of.key: Inferior lingular segmental bronchus of left lung (BV)
Inferior lingular segmental bronchus of.note: Lower branch of the lingular bronchus. It runs anteroinferiorly toward the left heart border and lies in front of the oblique fissure. Pitfall: the lingula belongs to the upper lobe and is not a left middle lobe; lingular disease erases the left heart border.
passing: Inferior lingular artery of left lung
Inferior lingular vein of left lung
Superior lingular artery of left lung
neighbours: Superior lingular segmental bronchus of left lung (BIV)

Inferior lingular vein of left lung.key: Inferior lingular vein of left lung
Inferior lingular vein of left lung.note: Vena lingularis inferior pulmonis sinistri drains segment S5 next to the left heart border and joins the Vena lingularis. Pitfall: the lingula lies close to the Ventriculus sinister, so cardiac motion and partial volume of the heart border can mimic lingular consolidation or a nodule along this vein.
passing: Superior lingular vein of left lung
neighbours: Inferior lingular segmental bronchus of left lung (BV)

Inferior lobar artery of right lung.key: Inferior lobar artery of right lung
Inferior lobar artery of right lung.note: The interlobar artery runs lateral to the intermediate and inferior lobar bronchi, within the oblique fissure. It gives off the middle lobar artery and A6, then continues as the basal trunk. Pitfall: interlobar lymph nodes between the artery and the bronchus can mimic a filling defect. A normal width is about 16 mm or less.
passing: Superior segmental artery of right lung
Middle lobar artery of right lung
Anterior basal segmental artery of right lung
Lateral basal segmental artery of right lung
Posterior basal segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Lateral basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BIX)
Anterior basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BVIII)

Inferior lobe of left lung.note: The oblique fissure separates this lobe from the upper lobe and lingula. Medially it lies against the descending Aorta thoracica and paravertebral gutter, and below it is the left hemidiaphragm. Pitfall: in supine scans, dependent atelectasis in the posterior basal segments mimics consolidation or a nodule. Rescan prone if unsure.
passing: Inferior basal vein of left lung
Posterior basal segmental artery of left lung

Inferior lobe of right lung.note: The oblique fissure separates this lobe from the upper and middle lobes. Medially it fills the azygo-oesophageal recess next to the Oesophagus and Vena azyga. The posterior basal segment reaches into the costophrenic recess above the liver. Pitfall: the liver dome, partly included in a slice, can mimic a basal mass or consolidation.
passing: Inferior basal vein of right lung
Superior basal vein of right lung
Posterior basal segmental artery of right lung
Medial basal segmental artery of right lung

Inferior medial genicular artery.note: It runs medially below the medial tibial condyle, deep to the Ligamentum collaterale tibiale and pes anserinus tendons, to the Rete patellare. Pitfall: it lies a little below the joint line, lower than its lateral counterpart. Asymmetric levels are normal, and a vessel there is not a meniscal-level lesion. It is a typical bleeding source after arthroplasty.
neighbours: Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament
Deep part of tibial collateral ligament

Inferior mesenteric artery.note: Arises from the front-left of the Aorta abdominalis at L3, a few centimetres above the bifurcation. It descends to the left, giving the Arteria colica sinistra, sigmoid and superior anorectal branches. Pitfall: the Vena mesenterica inferior runs further left and is separate. Do not confuse the two on venous-phase CT.

Inferior mesenteric vein.note: Ascends retroperitoneally left of the duodenojejunal flexure and lateral to the Arteria mesenterica inferior, then passes behind the pancreatic body to join the splenic vein, SMV or confluence. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the left gonadal vein, which lies more laterally on the psoas and drains into the left renal vein.

Inferior nasal concha bone.note: This separate bone attaches to the medial wall of the maxilla and the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone. It roofs the inferior meatus, where the Ductus nasolacrimalis opens. Pitfall: the nasal cycle swells one side's turbinate mucosa, and this asymmetry should not be reported as a mass or polyp.
passing: Posterior lateral nasal branches of sphenopalatine artery.

Inferior oblique muscle.note: The only extra-ocular muscle that does not arise from the orbital apex. It arises from the anteromedial orbital floor lateral to the nasolacrimal canal and runs posterolaterally beneath the inferior rectus to the globe. Pitfall: its oblique course along the anterior floor can look like floor hematoma or a mass on axial images. Coronal images show it best in floor fractures.

Inferior occipital gyrus and sulcus*.note: The inferolateral occipital convexity lies on the Tentorium cerebelli above the Sinus transversus. It continues forward into the Gyrus temporalis inferior. Pitfall: next to the tentorium and transverse sinus, a hyperdense sinus or tentorial partial volume can mimic subdural or subarachnoid blood, or sinus thrombosis.

Inferior ophthalmic vein.note: Runs on the orbital floor above the musculus rectus inferior and drains back through the inferior orbital fissure to the pterygoid plexus or into the sinus cavernosus. It is small and usually not resolved on CT. Pitfall: do not mistake it for the inferior rectus margin or for fat herniating through an orbital-floor fracture.

Inferior pancreatic nodes.note: Nodi pancreatici inferiores lie along the inferior border of the pancreatic head and body, at the root of the mesocolon transversum. Pitfall: the first jejunal loops, the duodenojejunal flexure and a lobulated uncinate process can mimic these nodes.

Inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery.note: Arises from the SMA, or a common trunk with the first jejunal artery, behind the pancreatic head and uncinate process. It forms the pancreaticoduodenal arcades. Pitfall: with coeliac stenosis these arcades enlarge and can form aneurysms. Do not mistake them for peripancreatic varices or nodes.

Inferior papillary muscle of left ventri.key: Inferior papillary muscle of left ventricle
Inferior papillary muscle of left ventri.note: The inferior (posteromedial) papillary muscle arises from the inferior Ventriculus sinister wall and sends chordae to the mitral leaflets. It usually has a single blood supply, so it is prone to ischaemic rupture. Pitfall: in cross-section it mimics an intraventricular thrombus or mass, so trace it on multiplanar reformats.
passing: Posterior leaflet of left atrioventricular valve

Inferior papillary muscle of right ventr.key: Inferior papillary muscle of right ventricle
Inferior papillary muscle of right ventr.note: Arises from the inferior (diaphragmatic) wall of the Ventriculus dexter and anchors chordae of the Cuspis inferior valvae atrioventricularis dextrae; the Diaphragma lies just below. Pitfall: on contrast CT it shows up as a filling defect inside the opacified RV and can be mistaken for thrombus or a mass. Check for continuity with the wall and the chordae.
passing: Inferior leaflet of right atrioventricular valve
Anterior papillary muscle of right ventricle

Inferior parathyroid gland.note: Usually lies at or just below the inferior pole of the thyroid lobe, anterolateral to the Oesophagus. Its position varies because it can descend along the thyrothymic tract into the anterior mediastinum. Pitfall: a thyroid nodule, a level VI lymph node or tortuous inferior thyroid vessels can mimic an adenoma, so use multiphase enhancement.

Inferior petrosal sinus.note: Runs in a groove along the petro-occipital fissure, from the back of the cavernous sinus to the front-inner part of the jugular foramen next to CN IX, then drains into the V. jugularis interna. Pitfall: do not report the petro-occipital fissure or this groove as a fracture of the skull base.
landmarks: lm:Occipital margin of temporal bone|Temporal bone
lm:Intrajugular process of occipital bone|Occipital bone

Inferior pharyngeal constrictor.note: Arises from the linea obliqua of the thyroid cartilage and the side of the cricoid. Its cricopharyngeal part forms the upper oesophageal sphincter at about C5–C6, with the retropharyngeal space and longus colli behind it. Pitfall: a contracted cricopharyngeus can look like a mass. Zenker diverticulum arises posteriorly through Killian's dehiscence.
landmarks: lm:Oblique line of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage
lm:Inferior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage
lm:Superior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

Inferior phrenic artery.note: Arises from the Aorta abdominalis or the coeliac trunk just below the hiatus aorticus and runs along the crura and the underside of the Diaphragma. Pitfall: its origin varies (coeliac or renal artery), and the thin vessel is easily missed as a source of bleeding or of extrahepatic supply to hepatocellular carcinoma.

Inferior pubic ligament.note: Arcuate band beneath the Symphysis pubica, joining the inferior pubic rami and forming the rounded apex of the subpubic angle. It is not seen as a separate structure on CT. Pitfall: inferior marginal osteophytes or calcification here can look like an avulsion fragment from the adductor longus/gracilis enthesis.

Inferior rectus muscle.note: Runs along the orbital floor (maxilla) from the anulus tendineus communis to the globe, with the infraorbital canal beneath it. Pitfall: on axial images partial volume with the floor mimics thickening, so judge it on coronal. A rounded belly or herniation into a floor fracture means entrapment risk. In thyroid eye disease it is usually the first muscle to enlarge.

Inferior sagittal sinus.note: Runs in the free lower edge of the falx cerebri, above the corpus callosum. It joins the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus at the falcotentorial junction. Pitfall: it is usually not visible on CT. A dense falx or falx calcification should not be mistaken for an interhemispheric subdural haematoma.
neighbours: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Posterior dorsal part)

Inferior salivatory nucleus.note: This parasympathetic nucleus of the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) lies in the upper medulla, just below the superior salivatory nucleus. It supplies the parotid gland via the otic ganglion. Pitfall: it is easily confused with the superior salivatory nucleus, which belongs to the facial nerve (VII) and supplies the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands. Neither is visible on CT.

Inferior semilunar lobule.note: The Lobulus semilunaris inferior lies below the horizontal fissure on the posteroinferior surface. It rests on the occipital squama below the Sulcus sinus transversi. Pitfall: a normally dense or dominant Sinus transversus can mimic a subdural haematoma. Arachnoid granulations in the groove can look like lytic lesions on bone windows.

Inferior subscapular nerve.note: Arises from the posterior cord and runs down on the anterior surface of musculus subscapularis to its lower part and to teres major. Pitfall: it lies right next to the thoracodorsal nerve and vessels on the posterior axillary wall. Teres major atrophy without latissimus dorsi atrophy points to this nerve, not the thoracodorsal nerve.

Inferior subtendinous bursa of biceps fe.key: Inferior subtendinous bursa of biceps femoris muscle
Inferior subtendinous bursa of biceps fe.note: Lies between the distal Musculus biceps femoris tendon and the Ligamentum collaterale fibulare at the fibular head. Pitfall: when distended it mimics a ganglion of the Articulatio tibiofibularis superior or a fibular-head lesion; check its tendon–ligament interface location.
neighbours: Articular capsule of superior tibiofibular joint

Inferior superficial inguinal nodes.note: Vertical chain along the great saphenous vein near the saphenous opening, superficial to the Fascia lata and in front of the femoral vessels. Pitfall: the saphenofemoral junction or a varix seen in cross-section looks like a node. A femoral hernia also lies here. Check that a fatty hilum is present.

Inferior suprarenal artery.note: Arises from the right renal artery and ascends to the lower part of the right suprarenal gland, behind the bare area of the liver and the IVC. Pitfall: it is a small vessel near the adrenal limbs. Do not mistake its cross-section for a small adrenal nodule.

Inferior tarsus.note: Dense fibrous plate of the lower eyelid, lying deep to the palpebral orbicularis oculi and in front of the globe. It is connective tissue, not muscle. Pitfall: CT does not show it separately from the eyelid soft tissue. The orbital septum attached to it is the key preseptal versus postseptal boundary in orbital cellulitis.

Inferior temporal gyrus.note: Inferolateral temporal gyrus below the Inferior temporal sulcus, lying on the floor of the middle cranial fossa and on the petrous ridge, Tegmen tympani and Tentorium cerebelli. Pitfall: streak and beam-hardening artefact from the Pars petrosa mimics or hides basal temporal contusion. A dense transverse or sigmoid sinus may be mistaken for an extra-axial haematoma.
passing: Temporal branches of middle cerebral artery

Inferior temporal sulcus.note: Inferolateral temporal sulcus between the middle and inferior temporal gyri. It curves onto the basal surface above the Tegmen tympani and petrous ridge. Pitfall: near the skull base it is easily confused with the Occipitotemporal sulcus. Petrous beam-hardening also hides adjacent contusions.

Inferior thyroid artery.note: It rises from the Truncus thyrocervicalis along the medial border of the M. scalenus anterior, then loops medially behind the carotid sheath to reach the posterior thyroid lobe. Pitfall: its tortuous loop next to the thyroid can look like a parathyroid adenoma or a node; on arterial phase, look for continuity with the trunk.

Inferior tracheobronchial nodes.note: These are the subcarinal nodes (station 7), below the carina between the right and left main bronchi and anterior to the oesophagus. Pitfall: the superior pericardial recess, a fluid-filled oesophagus or the azygo-oesophageal recess can mimic a subcarinal node. Water density and shape tell them apart.
neighbours: Node of arch of azygos vein

Inferior transverse scapular ligament.note: Spinoglenoid ligament. It bridges the Incisura spinoglenoidea from the lateral scapular spine to the posterior glenoid neck, over the suprascapular nerve. Pitfall: a paralabral cyst or ganglion here compresses the nerve and causes isolated infraspinatus atrophy. Do not attribute this to a rotator cuff tear.

Inferior trunk of brachial plexus.note: Formed by the C8 and T1 roots behind scalenus anterior. It lies on the first rib posterior to the A. subclavia, the lowest element of the plexus. Pitfall: look for a cervical rib or an elongated C7 transverse process, which compresses this trunk (thoracic outlet), and for an apical Pancoast tumour invading T1/C8.
passing: Anterior division of inferior trunk of brachial plexus
Posterior division of inferior trunk of brachial plexus

Inferior ulnar collateral artery.note: Arises from the brachial artery about 5 cm above the elbow, crosses medially on brachialis in front of the epicondylus medialis, and joins the elbow anastomosis. Pitfall: in supracondylar fractures, a patent collateral network can keep distal pulses despite brachial artery injury. Do not take distal opacification as proof that the brachial artery is intact.
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Inferior vein of left ventricle.note: It runs on the inferior/posterior wall of the Ventriculus sinister and drains into the Sinus coronarius to the left of the middle cardiac vein. It is a key target for CRT lead placement. Pitfall: it lies parallel to inferolateral arterial branches; on non-gated or venous-phase CT, use opacification timing to tell vein from artery.
passing: Right inferolateral branch of right coronary artery

Inferior vein of left ventricle (//Poste.note: This is the same vessel as the posterior vein of the left ventricle, shown as a duplicate segment. It runs on the diaphragmatic surface of the Ventriculus sinister over the Diaphragma and opens into the Sinus coronarius. Pitfall: next to the diaphragm, partial volume with the dome and liver can hide or mimic this vessel.
passing: Right inferolateral branch of right coronary artery

Inferior vena cava (abdominal part).note: Formed at L5 by the common iliac veins. It ascends right of the aorta, anterior to the vertebral bodies, behind the duodenum, pancreatic head and caudate lobe. Pitfall: in the portal venous phase, infrarenal mixing of unopacified blood from the legs with opacified renal return mimics thrombus.

Inferior vena cava (thoracic part).note: A short segment from the caval opening in the central tendon of the diaphragm (about T8) to the right atrium. It receives the Venae hepaticae just below the diaphragm. Pitfall: contrast injected in the arm can reflux into the IVC and hepatic veins. Unopacified blood flowing in from below can also mimic a thrombus.

Infra-auricular nodes.note: Lie at the lower pole of the Glandula parotidea, below the earlobe and above the angle of the mandible. Pitfall: these nodes look like a mass in the parotid tail or an upper level II node. The N. facialis runs close by. Place the node relative to the retromandibular vein.

Infra-orbital artery.note: Runs from the pterygopalatine fossa through the infraorbital groove and canal in the orbital floor. It exits at the infraorbital foramen below the rim. Pitfall: the infraorbital canal can mimic an orbital-floor blowout fracture. It may also protrude into the maxillary sinus on a septum, a variant to report before sinus surgery.

Infraclavicular nodes.note: These deltopectoral nodes lie below the Clavicula and Musculus subclavius, along the cephalic vein in the deltopectoral triangle, in front of the axillary vessels. Pitfall: the anatomical deltopectoral nodes are not the same as oncological 'infraclavicular' level III axillary nodes, which lie medial to the pectoralis minor. State which one you mean.
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Infrapatellar branch of saphenous nerve.note: Pierces the sartorius and crural fascia at the medial knee and curves anteroinferiorly below the patella to the infrapatellar skin.
