Pitfall: it is injured at medial arthroscopy portals and hamstring graft harvest, and CT cannot resolve it, so do not label small subcutaneous vessels here as the nerve.

Infrapatellar fat pad.note: Intracapsular but extrasynovial fat (Hoffa) that lies behind the ligamentum patellae and in front of the femoral condyles and tibia. On CT, a fat-fluid level or haemarthrosis can outline it. Pitfall: do not mistake normal fibrous septa or vessels for loose bodies, and do not mistake Hoffa fat for a lipoma.

Infraspinatus muscle.note: Fills the fossa infraspinata under the spina scapulae, with teres minor along its inferolateral edge, and inserts on the middle facet of the tuberculum majus. The suprascapular nerve reaches it through the incisura spinoglenoidea. Pitfall: fatty atrophy of infraspinatus only, with normal supraspinatus, points to nerve compression at the spinoglenoid notch (paralabral cyst), not a cuff tear.
neighbours: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

Inguinal ligament.note: Ligamentum inguinale is the rolled-under lower edge of the external oblique aponeurosis. It runs from the anterior superior iliac spine to the tuberculum pubicum and forms the floor of the inguinal canal. Pitfall: inguinal hernias lie above and medial to the pubic tubercle, while femoral hernias lie below and lateral to it, just medial to the femoral vein.

Innermost intercostal muscles.note: Musculi intercostales intimi form the deepest layer, lying on the endothoracic fascia and parietal pleura. The intercostal neurovascular bundle runs between this layer and the internal intercostals. Pitfall: this thin muscle line next to extrapleural fat can be mistaken for pleural thickening or plaques, especially in the paravertebral region.

Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and po.key: Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci*)
Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and po.note: The subcentral gyrus (central operculum) joins the pre- and postcentral gyri below the lower end of the central sulcus. It roofs the posterior insula above the lateral sulcus. Pitfall: this is opercular cortex, not the insular ribbon. In early MCA infarction, the 'insular ribbon sign' refers to the cortex deep to the sulcus circularis insulae.
passing: Temporal branches of middle cerebral artery
neighbours: Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Insular branches of middle cerebral arte.key: Insular branches of middle cerebral artery (M2-segment)
Insular branches of middle cerebral arte.note: Starts at the genu at the limen insulae and runs over the insular cortex in the deep sulcus lateralis, beneath the opercula, up to the circular sulcus. Pitfall: an M2 'dot sign' in the Sylvian fissure has to be told apart from calcification and from a symmetric high hematocrit. Also, an early anterior temporal branch arising from M1 is not M2.
neighbours: Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Insular branches of middle cerebral arte.key: Insular branches of middle cerebral artery (M2)
Insular branches of middle cerebral arte.note: Superior and inferior trunks run over the insula in the Sylvian fissure, from the limen insulae to the circular sulcus, deep to the opercula. Pitfall: the Sylvian dot sign. A partial-volume hyperdense M2 can mimic a clot, so check density and the other side. Early temporal branches are not M2.
neighbours: Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Intercapitular veins of foot.note: Short communicating veins that pass between the metatarsal heads and connect the plantar and dorsal venous systems. Pitfall: on contrast CT, an enhancing tubular structure in the intermetatarsal space is vascular. Do not mistake it for a Morton neuroma or an intermetatarsal bursa, which are plantar to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament.
passing: Perforating branches of plantar metatarsal arteries
landmarks: lm:Body of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone

Interclavicular ligament.note: Ligamentum interclaviculare bridges the two medial clavicles across the upper border of the manubrium (jugular notch) and blends with both sternoclavicular capsules. Pitfall: suprasternal ossicles (normal variant) or calcified fibres at the jugular notch can mimic fracture fragments; check that they are symmetric and well corticated.

Intercornual ligament.note: Joins the Cornua sacralia to the Cornua coccygea on each side, completing the opening for the fifth sacral nerve behind the sacrococcygeal symphysis. It is not visible on CT. Pitfall: the normal gap between the sacral and coccygeal cornua can be mistaken for a fracture or a widened sacral hiatus.

Intercostal nerves.note: Run in the Sulcus costae between the internal and innermost intercostals, lowest in the vein–artery–nerve order. The lower nerves continue between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis. Pitfall: the nerve lies below the rib and is the least protected by the groove. Plan needle and drain tracks along the upper border of the rib below.

Intercostal nodes.note: These nodes lie in the extrapleural paravertebral fat next to the rib heads and costovertebral joints, outside the parietal Pleura. Pitfall: sympathetic trunk ganglia, tortuous intercostal veins and rib-head osteophytes can all mimic small posterior intercostal nodes.
neighbours: Radiate ligament of head of rib

Intercuneiform interosseous ligaments.note: Strong interosseous bands in the non-articular parts of the spaces between the cuneiforms. They stabilise the recessed mortise for the second metatarsal base. Pitfall: medial–intermediate cuneiform widening is easy to miss on axial images alone. Coronal reformats show intercuneiform instability that accompanies Lisfranc injury.

Intermediate bronchus.note: Runs from the origin of the right upper lobe bronchus down to the origins of the middle lobe bronchus and BVI. Its posterior wall faces the aerated azygo-oesophageal recess. Pitfall: this posterior wall is normally ≤3 mm, so thickening suggests oedema, tumour or subcarinal nodes rather than normal anatomy.
passing: Middle lobar artery of right lung
Superior lobar artery of right lung
neighbours: Superior segmental bronchus of right lung (BVI)

Intermediate common iliac nodes.note: These nodes lie posterior to the common iliac vessels, in the lumbosacral fossa between psoas major and the vertebral body. The obturator nerve and lumbosacral trunk run close by. Pitfall: an unopacified or partially volumed common iliac vein behind the artery mimics a node, so use a venous phase.

Intermediate cuneiform bone.note: The smallest cuneiform. It lies between the medial and lateral cuneiforms, the navicular proximally and the second metatarsal base distally. Because it is short, the second metatarsal base is recessed into a mortise. Pitfall: subtle Lisfranc injury. Look for widening between the medial and intermediate cuneiforms, or medial cuneiform–second metatarsal diastasis, and small avulsion flecks.
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of f.key: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of f.note: The nerve crosses the anterolateral ankle in the subcutaneous fat, superficial to the inferior extensor retinaculum and lateral to the extensor digitorum longus and fibularis tertius tendons. It then runs toward the third to fifth metatarsals. Pitfall: it is at risk from the anterolateral arthroscopy portal and lateral malleolar fixation. Do not confuse it with the sural nerve, which lies further posterolateral.
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve

Intermediate external iliac nodes.note: These nodes lie between and behind the external iliac artery and vein, medial to psoas major on the pelvic brim. Pitfall: on the right, a pelvic-lying appendix or small bowel loop next to the vessels mimics a node. Postoperative lymphoceles also lie here.

Intermediate lumbar nodes.note: Nodi lumbales intermedii lie in the aortocaval groove between the aorta abdominalis and inferior vena cava, posterior to the left renal vein and third duodenal part. Pitfall: the left renal vein, right gonadal/testicular artery or unopacified duodenum can mimic an aortocaval node; follow vessels on contiguous slices.

Intermediate tendon of digastric muscle.note: Held to the body and greater horn of the os hyoideum by a fibrous sling, and passes through the split stylohyoid. It lies superficial to the hyoglossus, where the hypoglossal nerve and lingual vein run. Pitfall: on a single axial slice it can look like a small level IB/II node. Follow it in coronal reformats.

Intermediolateral nucleus.note: Forms the lateral horn (sympathetic) from T1 to L2 in the intermediate zone, with sacral parasympathetic neurons at S2–S4. It is not visible on CT. Pitfall: a lateral horn exists only at thoracolumbar levels. A Horner syndrome localises to C8–T2, not to the mid-cervical cord.

Intermediomedial nucleus.note: Medial intermediate zone (lamina VII) just lateral to the central canal, relaying visceral afferent signals. It is not visible on CT. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the thoracic nucleus (Clarke) at the base of the posterior horn, or with the intermediolateral nucleus of the lateral horn.

Intermuscular gluteal bursae.note: Small bursae between the Musculus gluteus maximus tendon and the proximal femur near the gluteal tuberosity, next to the Musculus vastus lateralis origin. Pitfall: do not mistake them for the more cranial trochanteric bursa over the greater trochanter or for a fluid collection in the lateral thigh.

Internal abdominal oblique muscle.note: Musculus obliquus internus abdominis is the middle flank layer, between external oblique and transversus abdominis. It arises from the linea intermedia of the iliac crest, the thoracolumbar fascia and the lateral inguinal ligament, and inserts on ribs 10–12 and the rectus sheath. Pitfall: Spigelian hernias at the linea semilunaris can hide beneath an intact external oblique aponeurosis.

Internal carotid artery.note: Cervical segment lies in the carotid sheath with the Vena jugularis interna posterolateral and the vagus between them. It enters the petrous carotid canal, then the Sinus cavernosus lateral to the sphenoid sinus. Pitfall: a dehiscent canal or aberrant ICA in the tympanic cavity can look like a middle-ear mass. Always trace the vessel.
landmarks: lm:External opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone
lm:Internal opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone

Internal iliac artery.note: Descends into the pelvis in front of the sacro-iliac joint. The Ureter lies anterior and the Vena iliaca interna posteromedial. It divides near the upper edge of the greater sciatic foramen. Pitfall: in unenhanced or late-phase CT, a tortuous or partial-volume vessel can be mistaken for an internal iliac node. Follow it across slices.
passing: Anterior division of internal iliac artery
Posterior division of internal iliac artery

Internal iliac vein.note: Lies posteromedial to the arteria iliaca interna, anterior to the sacral ala and sacroiliac joint, and joins the external iliac vein at the sacroiliac level. Pitfall: normal variants such as duplication or a left vein draining into the right common iliac vein can be mistaken for internal iliac nodes or a mass.

Internal intercostal membrane.note: Replaces the musculi intercostales interni posteriorly, from the costal angle to the vertebrae, just outside the pleura. Pitfall: the paravertebral intercostal neurovascular bundle in the sulcus costae can mimic pleural plaques, nodules or small lymph nodes. Follow it across adjacent slices.
landmarks: lm:Crest of neck of rib|Sixth rib

Internal intercostal muscles.note: Musculi intercostales interni form the middle layer, running from the sternum and costal cartilages back to the costal angles. Behind the angles they continue as the membrana intercostalis interna. Pitfall: medial to the costal angle the intercostal artery runs tortuously within the mid-space, so planning needle or drain paths 'just above the rib' is unsafe paravertebrally.

Internal jugular vein.note: Leaves the posterior (venous) part of the jugular foramen and runs in the carotid sheath, lateral to the ICA and CCA, with the vagus nerve behind and between them. It joins the subclavian vein at the venous angle. Pitfall: the two sides are often unequal, usually larger on the right. A small or poorly opacified vein is not automatically a thrombus.
landmarks: lm:Intrajugular process of occipital bone|Occipital bone

Internal pudendal artery.note: Exits through the infrapiriform greater sciatic foramen and hooks around the Spina ischiadica and Ligamentum sacrospinale. It re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen into the pudendal canal on the medial Obturator internus. Pitfall: at the foramen it runs beside the inferior gluteal artery. Trace the hook around the ischial spine to tell them apart.
passing: Anterior division of internal iliac artery

Internal pudendal vein.note: Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, crosses the spina ischiadica and sacrospinous ligament, then re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen into the pudendal (Alcock) canal on obturator internus. Pitfall: do not mix up the greater and lesser sciatic foramina along this route.

Internal thoracic artery.note: Descends about 1 cm lateral to the sternal border, behind the costal cartilages and in front of the pleura and transversus thoracis. It divides at the sixth intercostal space into the musculophrenic and superior epigastric arteries. Pitfall: in cross-section the artery and its paired veins look like parasternal nodes. Check continuity on adjacent slices before reporting adenopathy.

Internal thoracic veins.note: Paired veins run about 1–2 cm lateral to the sternal margin, behind the costal cartilages and in front of the musculus transversus thoracis and parietal pleura. They drain into the venae brachiocephalicae. Pitfall: an enlarged parasternal node can look like a dilated vein or an SVC-obstruction collateral. Follow it across slices to see whether it is tubular.

Interosseous membrane of forearm.note: Spans the interosseous borders of the radius and ulna and separates the flexor from the extensor compartment. Pitfall: in an Essex-Lopresti injury a radial head fracture comes with a membrane tear and distal radio-ulnar joint (DRUJ) disruption. Always assess both radio-ulnar joints. Ossification along the membrane may represent post-traumatic radio-ulnar synostosis.

Interosseous membrane of leg.note: The interosseous membrane spans the interosseous borders of the tibia and fibula and separates the anterior and posterior compartments. The anterior tibial vessels pass through its upper opening. Pitfall: it is barely visible on CT, so a syndesmotic injury with a high fibular (Maisonneuve) fracture is easy to miss; widened tibiofibular clear space is the clue.
neighbours: Articular capsule of superior tibiofibular joint

Interosseous metacarpal ligaments.note: Short ligaments bridging the opposed bases of metacarpals II–V, just distal to the small intermetacarpal joints that communicate with the CMC joints. Pitfall: these intermetacarpal joint clefts are normal. Do not mistake them for longitudinal base fractures; real fractures are not covered by cartilage-lined facets.

Interosseous sacro-iliac ligament.note: Fills the dorsal retroarticular space between the sacral and iliac tuberosities, behind the synovial sacroiliac joint, and is its strongest stabiliser. Pitfall: this dorsal fibrous part normally has an irregular bony outline. Do not call erosions or sacroiliitis there; judge only the anteroinferior synovial part. Widening here means a posterior ring disruption.

Interpectoral nodes.note: These Rotter nodes lie in the thin fat plane between the Musculus pectoralis major and the Musculus pectoralis minor. Pitfall: they are easily missed on axial slices or mistaken for pectoral branches of the thoraco-acromial vessels. Check for a nodular shape in sagittal reconstructions.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle
Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Interpeduncular fossa.note: CSF cistern between the crura cerebri, with the Corpora mammillaria in front and the posterior perforated substance as its floor. CN III emerges here. Pitfall: a small amount of subarachnoid blood here is easily missed. Perimesencephalic haemorrhage still needs a basilar-tip aneurysm excluded.

Interpubic disc.note: Fibrocartilage between the medial articular surfaces of both Os pubis, capped by the superior and inferior pubic ligaments, with the bladder/retropubic space behind it. Pitfall: vacuum gas and subchondral irregularity are common degenerative findings and do not mean osteitis or infection. Judge diastasis by width (>10 mm) and vertical step-off.

Intersesamoid ligament.note: Spans the medial (tibial) and lateral (fibular) sesamoids plantar to the first metatarsal head and floors the groove for the flexor hallucis longus tendon. Pitfall: a bipartite sesamoid, usually the medial one, has smooth corticated margins and should not be called a fracture. Compare with the other side.
neighbours: Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis
Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis

Interspinales colli muscles.note: Paired slips running between the bifid cervical spinous processes from C2 to T1, on either side of the Ligamentum nuchae. The atlas has only a posterior tubercle. Pitfall: on CT they blend with the Ligamenta interspinalia. The sign of posterior ligamentous injury is a widened interspinous distance (fanning), not the soft-tissue density.

Interspinales lumborum muscles.note: Paired short muscles between adjacent lumbar spinous processes, beside the Ligamenta interspinalia and deep to the Ligamentum supraspinale. Pitfall: when spinous processes touch (Baastrup, kissing spines), interspinous bursitis or cystic change can mimic a mass or infection. Check for neoarthrosis and sclerosis of the adjacent processes.

Interspinales thoracis muscles.note: Present only at the cervicothoracic (T1–T3) and thoracolumbar junctions, between the spinous processes beside the Ligamenta interspinalia. Pitfall: they are normally missing in the mid-thoracic spine. Do not report their absence as atrophy or post-operative change.

Interspinous ligaments.note: Fill the space between adjacent Processus spinosi, with the Ligamenta flava in front and the Ligamentum supraspinale behind. They are not seen directly on CT. Pitfall: a widened interspinous distance in trauma indicates posterior ligamentous complex disruption. Do not dismiss it as a normal variant, and do not confuse it with Baastrup kissing spinous processes.

Intertransverse ligaments.note: Thin bands joining adjacent processus transversi, strongest in the lumbar spine. Musculus quadratus lumborum and psoas major lie ventrally and the erector spinae dorsally. Pitfall: an ossified ligament or a transitional L5–sacrum pseudarthrosis can be mistaken for a transverse process fracture or a bone fragment.
landmarks: lm:Lateral part of transverse process|Vertebra L3
lm:Costal part of transverse process|Vertebra L3
neighbours: Dorsal parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles

Intertubercular tendon sheath.note: This synovial extension of the glenohumeral joint surrounds the caput longum tendon in the intertubercular groove, under the ligamentum transversum humeri. Pitfall: because the sheath communicates with the joint, fluid in it usually reflects a joint effusion rather than isolated tenosynovitis. An empty groove points to medial dislocation of the tendon.

Intervertebral disc C2-C3.note: Discus intervertebralis C2-C3 is the first true disc, between the lower endplate of the axis and C3. The anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments cover its front and back, and longus colli lies anterolaterally. Pitfall: in children, physiological C2-C3 pseudosubluxation can mimic ligamentous injury; check the spinolaminar line.

Intervertebral disc C3-C4.note: Discus C3-C4 lies between the C3 and C4 bodies. The Processus uncinati (uncovertebral joints) bound it laterally, and the posterior longitudinal ligament and dura lie behind. Pitfall: uncovertebral osteophytes narrow the foramen of the exiting C4 root and are easily missed on axial slices; check oblique or sagittal reformats.

Intervertebral disc C4-C5.note: Discus C4-C5 lies between the C4 and C5 bodies at the level of the thyroid cartilage. Longus colli and the laryngopharynx lie in front, the posterior longitudinal ligament and dural sac behind. Pitfall: partly calcified laryngeal cartilages project at this level and can mimic prevertebral calcification or an osteophyte fragment.

Intervertebral disc C5-C6.note: Discus C5-C6 is the most common level of cervical degeneration. The oesophagus and thyroid lie in front, the posterior longitudinal ligament and dura behind. Pitfall: cervical roots exit above the vertebra with the same number, so a foraminal lesion at C5-C6 affects the C6 root, not C5.

Intervertebral disc C6-C7.note: Discus C6-C7 lies between the C6 and C7 bodies, with the oesophagus in front and the dural sac behind; the C7 root exits here. Pitfall: beam-hardening streaks from the shoulders can mimic or hide a disc herniation. Count levels down from C2 to avoid mislabelling.

Intervertebral disc C7-T1.note: Discus C7-T1 marks the cervicothoracic junction, between the C7 and T1 bodies; the first rib head articulates with T1 laterally and the C8 root exits here. Pitfall: identify T1 by its first rib. A cervical rib or long C7 transverse process can mimic it and lead to miscounting.

Intervertebral disc L1-L2.note: Discus L1-L2 lies between the L1 and L2 bodies. The diaphragmatic crura and psoas origins lie anterolaterally, the aorta in front, and the conus medullaris usually ends at about this level. Pitfall: transitional vertebrae or hypoplastic 12th ribs shift lumbar numbering; count from C2 or state which vertebra carries the last rib.

Intervertebral disc L2-L3.note: Discus L2-L3 sits between the L2 and L3 bodies. Psoas lies laterally, the diaphragmatic crura taper out in front, the IVC and aorta lie anterior, and the cauda equina is behind. Pitfall: on non-contrast CT, prominent ascending lumbar veins or retrocaval nodes can mimic a lateral disc herniation.

Intervertebral disc L3-L4.note: Discus L3-L4 lies between the L3 and L4 bodies, with psoas major laterally, the IVC and aortic bifurcation region in front and the cauda equina behind. Pitfall: a far-lateral herniation compresses the exiting L3 root, while a paracentral one affects L4. Check the foramina, not just the canal.
neighbours: Ventral parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles

Intervertebral disc L4-L5.note: Discus L4-L5 lies between the L4 and L5 bodies, behind the iliac bifurcation and common iliac veins, with psoas laterally and the cauda equina behind. Pitfall: with lumbosacral transitional anatomy the level may be mislabelled. Always state how you numbered the levels, because surgical level depends on it.

Intervertebral disc L5-S1.note: Wedge-shaped disc between the inferior endplate of L5 and the Basis ossis sacri, with the Promontorium at its anterior margin. Ligamentum longitudinale anterius lies in front and Ligamentum longitudinale posterius behind. Pitfall: a lumbosacral transitional vertebra (sacralisation or lumbarisation) mislabels the level, so count down from C2 or from the last rib-bearing vertebra.

Intervertebral disc T1-T2.note: Lies between the T1 and T2 bodies. Musculus longus colli and the oesophagus are in front, and the dural sac is behind. The head of the second rib articulates at this disc level. Pitfall: beam-hardening from the shoulders hides the cervicothoracic junction, which leads to miscounting. Confirm the level on the sagittal view, counting from C2 and using the first rib.

Intervertebral disc T10-T11.note: Lies between T10 and T11, at the posterior costophrenic recesses. The diaphragmatic crura are beginning anterolaterally. Pitfall: the eleventh rib articulates only with the T11 body, not with this disc. Do not take the missing demifacet for erosion. A thick crus or the azygos vein can also mimic a paravertebral mass.

Intervertebral disc T11-T12.note: Lies between T11 and T12 inside the retrocrural space. The aorta and the azygos and hemiazygos veins lie anterior to it, between the crura diaphragmatis. Pitfall: unopacified azygos or hemiazygos veins look like retrocrural lymph nodes. Follow them on contiguous slices before calling nodes enlarged, which here means a short axis over 6 mm.

Intervertebral disc T12-L1.note: Disc at the thoracolumbar junction. The crura diaphragmatis are anterior and the origins of musculus psoas major are lateral. The conus medullaris lies behind it. Pitfall: a hypoplastic twelfth rib or a lumbar rib causes T12/L1 mislabelling. Correlate with the rib count, because this is the most common level for fractures.

Intervertebral disc T2-T3.note: Lies between T2 and T3. Musculus longus colli and the oesophagus are anterior, and the head of the third rib articulates posterolaterally. Pitfall: costovertebral joint surfaces partial-volumed at the disc margin mimic osteophytes or a fracture fragment. Check them in the coronal plane.

Intervertebral disc T3-T4.note: Lies between T3 and T4. The head of the fourth rib articulates laterally and the oesophagus lies in front. Pitfall: the vena intercostalis superior sinistra and paravertebral intercostal vessels look like small paravertebral nodules on non-contrast CT.

Intervertebral disc T4-T5.note: Lies between T4 and T5, around the level of the aortic arch and the azygos arch. The oesophagus is anterior and the head of the fifth rib is lateral. Pitfall: the aortic arch causes pulsation and streak artefact across the anterior disc margin, which can mimic an endplate defect.

Intervertebral disc T5-T6.note: Lies between T5 and T6. The oesophagus is directly anterior, the aorta thoracica is left anterolateral and the vena azyga is on the right. Pitfall: aortic pulsation suppresses left-sided bridging in DISH, so predominantly right-sided flowing ossification is typical and is not a sign of asymmetric disease.
landmarks: lm:Crest of head of rib|Sixth rib

Intervertebral disc T6-T7.note: Lies between T6 and T7. The oesophagus and the juxta-oesophageal and prevertebral nodes are anterior, the aorta is on the left and the azygos vein on the right. Pitfall: a prevertebral node or the azygos vein at the disc margin can mimic a paravertebral abscess or a disc extrusion beyond the anterior longitudinal ligament.

Intervertebral disc T7-T8.note: Lies between T7 and T8. The aorta, azygos vein and oesophagus are anterior, and the dural sac is posterior. Pitfall: calcified thoracic disc herniations are common at mid-to-lower thoracic levels and look like posterior osteophytes or an ossified Ligamentum longitudinale posterius. Use bone and soft-tissue windows to assess compromise of the spinal canal.

Intervertebral disc T8-T9.note: Lies between T8 and T9. The aorta thoracica is left anterolateral, the vena azyga is right anterior, and the lower lobes contact it laterally. Pitfall: dependent atelectasis in the lower lobe next to the disc mimics a paravertebral soft-tissue mass. Check in lung windows.

Intervertebral disc T9-T10.note: Lies between T9 and T10. The aorta is anterior to it, with the azygos vein on the right and the hemiazygos vein on the left, and the lower lobes and pleura are lateral. Pitfall: when the hemiazygos vein crosses behind the aorta near this level it can mimic a retro-aortic node or a paravertebral collection.

Intra-articular ligament of head of rib.key: Intra-articular ligament of head of rib
Intra-articular ligament of head of rib.note: Joins the crista capitis costae to the intervertebral disc and divides the joint of the head of the rib into two cavities, in ribs 2–9. Pitfall: ribs 1 and 10–12 have a single facet and no intra-articular ligament. Rib N's head sits at disc T(N−1)–TN, which matters when assigning levels.
landmarks: lm:Crest of head of rib|Sixth rib
neighbours: Radiate ligament of head of rib

Intraglandular parotid nodes.note: Lie inside the parotid tissue, mostly in the superficial lobe above the masseter. Pitfall: normal intraparotid nodes are common and can look like small Warthin tumours or metastases, e.g. from scalp skin cancer. Use the retromandibular vein to separate superficial from deep lobe.

Intraparietal sulcus.note: Oblique sulcus that separates the Superior parietal lobule from the inferior parietal lobule (Supramarginal and Angular gyri). It usually joins the Postcentral sulcus anteriorly. Pitfall: because of this junction, the intraparietal–postcentral sulcus complex is often mistaken for the central sulcus on high axial CT slices.

Intrapulmonary nodes.note: These nodes lie along the lobar and segmental bronchi inside the lung (stations 12–14). They sit in the bronchovascular bundles next to the segmental arteries. Pitfall: vessels cut in cross-section can mimic nodes. Small triangular perifissural or subpleural nodes are also easily mistaken for pulmonary nodules.
passing: Inferior lobar artery of right lung
Middle lobar artery of right lung
Inferior basal vein of right lung
Superior lingular artery of left lung
neighbours: Superior segmental bronchus of right lung (BVI)
Superior segmental bronchus of left lung (BVI)

Intrarenal arteries of left kidney.note: The segmental, interlobar and arcuate arteries of the left kidney branch within the sinus renalis around the renal pelvis and run through the columns into the cortex. Pitfall: these are end arteries, so occlusion causes wedge-shaped perfusion defects. Do not confuse these defects with pyelonephritis or the normal corticomedullary phase.

Intrarenal arteries of right kidney.note: Segmental, interlobar and arcuate branches of the right renal artery within the sinus renalis and the parenchyma. Pitfall: sinus vessels next to the renal pelvis can look like calculi or urothelial thickening. Compare unenhanced, arterial and excretory phases.

Intrarenal veins of left kidney.note: Interlobar veins run between the pyramids and join in the sinus renalis, mostly in front of the pelvis renalis, to form the left renal vein. Pitfall: unopacified sinus veins on unenhanced or arterial-phase CT can look like a dilated collecting system or hydronephrosis. Check them on the excretory phase.

Intrarenal veins of right kidney.note: Interlobar veins join in the sinus renalis in front of the pelvis renalis to form the short right renal vein, which drains straight into the IVC. Pitfall: unenhanced sinus veins can look like caliectasis or a parapelvic cyst. Confirm with the nephrographic or excretory phase.

Investing abdominal fascia.note: This thin deep fascia covers the M. obliquus externus abdominis. It continues into the fascia lata at the Lig. inguinale and attaches to the iliac crest and pubis. It cannot be separated from the muscle on CT. Pitfall: do not confuse it with Scarpa's membranous subcutaneous layer, the plane in which superficial fluid collections spread.

Iris.note: The Iris is a thin soft-tissue diaphragm between the Camera anterior bulbi oculi and the Lens. Routine CT does not show it separately from the ciliary body. Pitfall: a pseudophakic intraocular lens shows up as a thin hyperdense line at the iris–lens plane. Do not report it as a foreign body.

Ischiofemoral ligament.note: Thickens the posterior capsule. It spirals from the ischium behind the acetabulum up and laterally to the base of the greater trochanter, and the posterior capsule here is the weakest part. Pitfall: posterior dislocation fragments can endanger the nearby deep branch of the medial circumflex femoral artery. Ischiofemoral impingement involves quadratus femoris, not this ligament.

Jejunum.note: The jejunum starts at the duodenojejunal flexure, left of the Inferior mesenteric vein. Its loops sit mainly in the left upper abdomen, with a feathery fold pattern and stronger mucosal enhancement than the ileum. Pitfall: collapsed, unopacified loops can look like a mesenteric mass or enlarged lymph nodes.

Jugulodigastric node.note: This level IIA node lies where the posterior belly of the digastric crosses the Vena jugularis interna, deep to the Musculus sternocleidomastoideus. Pitfall: it is normally the largest neck node, and a short axis up to about 15 mm can be benign. Do not overcall it on size alone; look for necrosis or a rounded shape.

Juxta-intestinal mesenteric nodes.note: Small nodes in the mesentery next to the bowel wall, between jejunal loops and the vasa recta, under the Omentum maius. Pitfall: unopacified jejunal loops or vessels seen in cross-section can look like nodes. Follow them across slices and use oral contrast. Small oval mesenteric nodes are normal.

Juxta-oesophageal nodes.note: Nodi juxtaoesophagei (station 8) lie beside the Oesophagus below the carina. The Aorta thoracica is on the left and the azygo-oesophageal recess on the right. Pitfall: a fluid-filled or collapsed oesophageal lumen, or a small hiatal hernia, can look like an enlarged node. Look for intraluminal air or oral contrast before calling a node.

Kidney.note: The Ren lies in the perirenal space: Psoas major is posteromedial, the Diaphragma posterosuperior, the Hepar and Glandula suprarenalis superior, and the Duodenum (descending part) and Colon ascendens anterior. Pitfall: a prominent column of Bertin or a dromedary hump can mimic a renal mass. Its enhancement matches normal parenchyma in every phase.

Lacrimal artery.note: Runs along the upper border of the musculus rectus lateralis to the glandula lacrimalis in the superolateral orbit. Pitfall: its recurrent meningeal branch may pass through a meningo-orbital (Hyrtl) foramen in the ala major. That foramen is a normal variant, not a fracture, and is relevant in embolisation.

Lacrimal bone.note: This bone forms the posterior half of the lacrimal fossa (posterior lacrimal crest), with the frontal process of the maxilla in front and the lamina orbitalis of the ethmoid behind. The lacrimal sac sits in the fossa. Pitfall: the bone is paper-thin, so partial volume can make it look dehiscent or fractured. Check the agger nasi cell, which lies medial to it.
landmarks: lm:Orbital part of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Lacrimal canaliculus.note: The upper and lower canaliculi run from the puncta along the medial lid margins within the palpebral orbicularis. They join as a common canaliculus entering the Saccus lacrimalis behind the medial palpebral ligament. Pitfall: they are invisible on routine CT. Small calcifications there are usually canaliculitis concretions or punctal plugs, not foreign bodies.

Lacrimal gland.note: Lies extraconally in the superolateral anterior orbit, in the Fossa glandulae lacrimalis. The levator aponeurosis divides it into orbital and palpebral lobes. Pitfall: compare both sides. Smooth bone remodelling suggests a pleomorphic adenoma, a gland moulding to the globe without bone change suggests lymphoma or inflammation, and erosion suggests carcinoma.

Lacrimal sac.note: Lies in the lacrimal fossa between the anterior lacrimal crest (maxilla) and the posterior lacrimal crest (Os lacrimale), anterior to the orbital septum. It continues downward as the Ductus nasolacrimalis. Pitfall: air in the sac is normal. A fluid-filled dacryocystocele must not be mistaken for an anterior ethmoid (agger nasi) mucocele lying medially.

Laryngopharynx.note: Extends from the level of the hyoid and pharyngoepiglottic folds down to the lower border of the Cartilago cricoidea, where it continues as the Oesophagus. Its subsites are the piriform sinus, the postcricoid region and the posterior wall. Pitfall: a collapsed piriform sinus looks like an asymmetric mass, so repeat with modified Valsalva.

Lat_Fis-ant-Horizont.note: Anterior horizontal branch of the Sulcus lateralis. It runs forward and separates the pars orbitalis below from the pars triangularis above. It is the lower border of Broca's area. Do not confuse it with the anterior ascending branch. Both start from the same point, and together they outline the triangular pars triangularis.
neighbours: Orbital part of  inferior frontal gyrus
Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Lat_Fis-ant-Vertical.note: Anterior ascending branch of the Sulcus lateralis. It runs upward and separates the pars triangularis in front from the pars opercularis behind (Broca's area). On axial slices it is easily confused with the inferior precentral sulcus, which marks the back edge of the pars opercularis.
neighbours: Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus
Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Lat_Fis-post.note: The posterior ramus of the Sulcus lateralis, with the Planum temporale and Gyri temporales transversi below it and the Gyrus supramarginalis capping its end. Pitfall: it is normally longer and more horizontal on the left. Do not read this physiological asymmetry as atrophy or mass effect.
neighbours: Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci*)

Lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve.note: It emerges lateral to the biceps tendon at the elbow, between the biceps and brachialis, and runs deep to the vena cephalica along the radial forearm. Pitfall: near the wrist it overlaps the superficial branch of the radial nerve. Do not confuse the two when reporting injury from cannulas or venepuncture.

Lateral aortic nodes.note: Nodi aortici laterales lie along the left side of the aorta abdominalis, anterior to the left psoas major and medial to the left ureter, from the diaphragmatic crus to the aortic bifurcation. Pitfall: the left gonadal vein, left ureter or an unopacified duodenojejunal flexure can look like a node; trace them across contiguous slices.

Lateral axillary nodes.note: The nodi humerales lie along the medial and posterior side of the axillary vein. They sit medial to coracobrachialis and anterior to the tendons of latissimus dorsi and teres major (level I). Pitfall: in non-contrast CT, an oblique section through the axillary vein or a brachial vein can look like an enlarged node.

Lateral basal segmental artery of left l.key: Lateral basal segmental artery of left lung
Lateral basal segmental artery of left l.note: Supplies segment IX and runs with the lateral basal segmental bronchus (BIX), between the anterior and posterior basal arteries. Pitfall: in the dependent lung base, basal veins run close by and partial volume blurs them. Trace each vessel to the hilum (artery) or to the left atrium (vein) before calling an embolus.
passing: Posterior basal segmental artery of left lung
Medial basal segmental artery of left lung
Superior segmental artery of left lung
neighbours: Anterior basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BVIII)

Lateral basal segmental artery of right.key: Lateral basal segmental artery of right lung
Lateral basal segmental artery of right.note: A9 runs laterally with BIX in the lateral basal segment, behind the oblique fissure that separates it from the middle lobe. Pitfall: A8 and A9 often share a trunk. Partial volume at the fissure can make a lesion look like it is in the middle lobe when it is in the lower lobe.
passing: Inferior lobar artery of right lung
Superior basal vein of right lung
neighbours: Anterior basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BVIII)

Lateral basal segmental bronchus of left.key: Lateral basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BIX)
Lateral basal segmental bronchus of left.note: BIX arises from the basal trunk, often as a common stem with BX, and runs laterally toward the costophrenic recess above the left hemidiaphragm. Pitfall: the spleen or splenic flexure beneath the dome, partly included in a slice, can mimic consolidation or a mass in the lateral basal segment.
passing: Anterior basal segmental artery of left lung
Superior basal vein of left lung
neighbours: Posterior basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BX)
Anterior basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BVIII)

Lateral basal segmental bronchus of righ.key: Lateral basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BIX)
Lateral basal segmental bronchus of righ.note: Runs laterally and inferiorly from the basal trunk toward the lateral costophrenic recess, often sharing a short trunk with BX. Pitfall: partial volume of the liver dome and diaphragm at the lung base mimics consolidation or nodules, so check on coronal images.
passing: Inferior lobar artery of right lung
Anterior basal segmental artery of right lung
Posterior basal segmental artery of right lung
Superior basal vein of right lung
neighbours: Anterior basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BVIII)

Lateral caval nodes.note: Nodi cavales laterales lie along the right lateral border of the inferior vena cava, anterior to the right psoas major and diaphragmatic crus, medial to the right ureter. Pitfall: the right gonadal vein, right ureter or the duodenal C-loop can look like a lateral caval node; follow tubular structures through slices.

Lateral circumflex femoral artery.note: It arises laterally from the Arteria profunda femoris and runs laterally deep to the rectus femoris, in front of the hip capsule and iliopsoas, near the Linea intertrochanterica. It divides into ascending, transverse and descending branches. Pitfall: in about 15–20% it arises directly from the femoral artery. Do not then mistake it for a high profunda origin.
passing: Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery

Lateral circumflex femoral veins.note: Run laterally with the arteria circumflexa lateralis femoris, deep to the musculus rectus femoris, in front of the hip capsule and the linea intertrochanterica, towards the musculus vastus lateralis. Pitfall: they often drain directly into the vena femoralis. Do not mistake them for the deep femoral vein or for an inguinal lymph node.
passing: Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery

Lateral common iliac nodes.note: These nodes lie lateral to the common iliac artery and medial to psoas major, where the ureter crosses the iliac bifurcation. Pitfall: the unopacified ureter at the pelvic brim looks just like a small round node. Follow it on contiguous slices or check an excretory phase.

Lateral corticospinal tract.note: Main crossed motor tract in the posterior lateral funiculus, lateral to the Cornu posterius and deep to the Tractus spinocerebellaris posterior. CT cannot resolve it. Pitfall: the fibres cross in the medulla, so a cord lesion causes weakness on the same side (Brown-Séquard pattern). Report the side of the lesion, not the side of the symptoms.

Lateral crico-arytenoid muscle.note: Runs from the upper lateral cricoid arch to the Processus muscularis, in the lower paraglottic space deep to the thyroid lamina. Pitfall: in recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy the paralysed fold is atrophic and the ventricle and piriform sinus are dilated; do not call the normal contralateral fold a mass.
landmarks: lm:Inferior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

Lateral cuneiform bone.note: Lies between the intermediate cuneiform and the cuboid, with the navicular proximally. Distally it meets mainly the third metatarsal base and touches the second and fourth. Pitfall: the many overlapping tarsometatarsal joint lines on oblique slices can hide or mimic fracture lines. Check intermediate column alignment in Lisfranc injuries on reformats.
passing: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
landmarks: lm:Base of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone

Lateral fasciculus proprius.note: Intersegmental fibres that line the lateral edge of the grey matter between the Cornu anterius and the Cornu posterius. CT does not show them. Pitfall: CT cannot tell grey from white matter in the cord, so a hypodensity next to the grey matter is usually streak or partial-volume artifact, not a lesion of this tract.

Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.note: An L2–L3 nerve that emerges lateral to the psoas, crosses behind the kidney and over the iliacus, then passes under or through the lateral inguinal ligament just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine into the thigh. Pitfall: its course varies (over the spine or through the sartorius), so look for anterior superior iliac spine avulsion or a bone graft site in meralgia paraesthetica.

Lateral femoral intermuscular septum.note: Runs from the Tractus iliotibialis to the Labium laterale lineae asperae and separates vastus lateralis (anterior) from biceps femoris short head (posterior). Pitfall: the irregular cortex where it inserts on the linea aspera is normal and should not be read as periosteal reaction. Perforating vessels pierce the septum.

Lateral frontobasal artery.note: Lateral orbitofrontal artery, arising from M1/M2. It supplies the pars orbitalis and lateral gyri orbitales above the orbital roof and the ala major. Pitfall: partial volume and beam hardening from the orbital roof make false basal frontal hypodensity, which can be mistaken for infarct or contusion. Check on coronal reformats.
passing: Insular branches of middle cerebral artery (M2)
neighbours: Orbital part of  inferior frontal gyrus
Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Lateral geniculate body.note: Small swelling on the posterolateral underside of the pulvinar thalami. The Tractus opticus ends here, the Corpus geniculatum mediale lies medial to it and the ambient cistern and hippocampus lie lateral and below. CT cannot show it. In the ambient cistern, do not confuse the Arteria cerebri posterior with an abnormality of this region.

Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis.key: Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis
Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis.note: Runs from the cuneiforms and cuboid along the plantar first metatarsal. It inserts through the lateral (fibular) sesamoid together with the adductor hallucis, lateral to the FHL tendon. Pitfall: in hallux valgus the fibular sesamoid drifts into the first intermetatarsal space. Report its position relative to the metatarsal head, not as a fragment.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
neighbours: Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis
Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot

Lateral head of gastrocnemius.note: Arises from the posterior lateral femoral condyle, lies deep to the biceps femoris and superficial to the plantaris and popliteus. Pitfall: a fabella in its proximal tendon, round and corticated behind the lateral condyle, is a normal sesamoid and not a loose body or osteophyte.
passing: Sural communicating branch of common fibular nerve
neighbours: Lateral subtendinous bursa of gastrocnemius muscle

Lateral head of triceps brachii.note: Arises from the posterior humerus above the radial groove and joins the common triceps tendon to the olecranon. The radial nerve and its collateral arteries run in the groove deep to it. Pitfall: the medial head arises below the groove; check the radial nerve in midshaft humeral fractures (Holstein–Lewis fracture).

Lateral intermediate substance.note: Grey matter of the intermediate zone between the anterior and posterior horns, bordered laterally by the lateral funiculus and the lateral corticospinal tract. It is not resolvable on CT. Pitfall: it is not the same as the lateral horn, which is a bulge only at T1–L2. Cord segments lie higher than their vertebrae.

Lateral intermuscular septum of arm.note: Septum intermusculare laterale brachii runs from the lateral supracondylar ridge to fascia brachii. It separates the anterior compartment (brachialis, brachioradialis) from the posterior compartment (triceps). Pitfall: the nervus radialis pierces it in the distal third, so with a distal-third humeral shaft fracture, check how close the fragments are to the nerve.

Lateral meniscus.note: C-shaped fibrocartilage that is more circular than the medial meniscus, with its horns attached close to the ACL insertion. It has no attachment to the fibular collateral ligament. Pitfall: the popliteus tendon passing through the popliteal hiatus mimics a posterior horn tear. Chondrocalcinosis can mimic a meniscal fragment on CT.

Lateral occipital artery.note: PCA branch that runs above the Tentorium cerebelli and supplies the inferior temporal and occipital surface, including the Gyrus occipitotemporalis lateralis. Pitfall: an inferotemporal infarct next to the tentorium can be mistaken for cerebellar hypodensity on axial CT; use coronal reformats to show which side of the tentorium it is on.

Lateral occipital gyrus (Middle occipita.note: Forms the middle of the lateral occipital convexity, between the superior and inferior occipital gyri, continuing forward into the Gyrus angularis and Gyrus temporalis medius. Pitfall: it lies in a watershed (MCA–PCA border zone) area. Beam hardening from the calvaria can mimic cortical hypodensity.

Lateral occipitotemporal gyrus.note: Fusiform gyrus on the basal temporo-occipital surface, between the Occipitotemporal sulcus laterally and the Collateral sulcus medially, resting on the Tentorium cerebelli and petrous ridge. Pitfall: basal hypodensity here from a PCA infarct is easily dismissed as petrous beam-hardening artefact. Use thin slices and coronal reformats.
landmarks: lm:Petrous part of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Lateral patellar retinaculum.note: A thin band running from the lateral patellar margin to the lateral femoral epicondyle and the Tractus iliotibialis, superficial to the capsule. Pitfall: it merges with iliotibial tract fibres. A thickened, tight lateral retinaculum goes with lateral patellar tilt, while transient dislocation tears the medial side.

Lateral pectoral nerve.note: It comes from the lateral cord, pierces the fascia clavipectoralis with the arteria thoracoacromialis, and supplies the deep surface of the pectoralis major. Pitfall: the names follow the cords, not position. The lateral pectoral nerve lies medial to the medial pectoral nerve, so its laterality is easy to get wrong in reports.
passing: Anterior division of superior trunk of brachial plexus
Anterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle
Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Lateral pericardial nodes.note: These nodes lie in the cardiophrenic angle, lateral to the pericardium and on the Diaphragma, next to the middle lobe. Pitfall: the pericardial fat pad, a pericardial cyst (fluid density) or a Morgagni hernia can mimic nodes. Report a node only if it is soft-tissue density and larger than about 5 mm in short axis.

Lateral plantar artery.note: The larger terminal branch of the a. tibialis posterior. It enters the sole deep to the abductor hallucis and runs anterolaterally between the FDB and quadratus plantae toward the base of MT5, then turns medially as the arcus plantaris. Pitfall: it is larger than the medial plantar artery, so do not swap the two labels.

Lateral plantar nerve.note: The nerve branches from the tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel and passes deep to the abductor hallucis. It then runs laterally between the flexor digitorum brevis and the quadratus plantae. Pitfall: its first branch (Baxter's nerve) can be trapped near a plantar calcaneal spur. Isolated fatty atrophy of abductor digiti minimi is the clue, so do not dismiss it as age-related.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve

Lateral plantar veins.note: Run obliquely laterally with the lateral plantar artery and nerve, between the flexor digitorum brevis and the quadratus plantae, and continue as the plantar venous arch. Pitfall: the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve (Baxter nerve) runs alongside near the calcaneal tubercle. Its entrapment is a cause of heel pain that is easy to overlook.

Lateral pontine branches of basilar arte.key: Lateral pontine branches of basilar artery
Lateral pontine branches of basilar arte.note: Short circumferential branches that wrap around the anterolateral Pons to its lateral tegmentum, passing near the root exit zones of CN V–VIII. They are too small to see on CT; occlusion shows as lateral pontine hypodensity. Pitfall: beam-hardening streaks between the petrous apices produce false pontine hypodensities.
passing: Medial pontine branches of basilar artery
landmarks: lm:Internal acoustic opening (porus of internal acoustic meatus)|Temporal bone

Lateral process of nasal septal cartilag.key: Lateral process of nasal septal cartilage
Lateral process of nasal septal cartilag.note: Processus lateralis cartilaginis septi nasi (the upper lateral cartilage) lies under the caudal edge of the Os nasale and merges with the septal cartilage. It forms the internal nasal valve. Pitfall: the bone–cartilage junction (keystone area) has an irregular, non-ossified edge that must not be reported as a nasal bone fracture. It is not visible in bone window.

Lateral rectus muscle.note: Runs along the lateral orbital wall (zygomatic bone, greater wing of sphenoid) from the anulus to the globe, with the lacrimal gland superolateral. Pitfall: thyroid eye disease thickens the belly and spares the tendon. Orbital myositis involves the tendon insertion. Do not confuse the lacrimal gland with the muscle belly on axial slices.
landmarks: lm:Orbital surface of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Lateral reticulospinal tract.note: Medullary reticulospinal fibres in the deep lateral funiculus, next to the Substantia intermedia lateralis. CT cannot resolve them. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the Tractus reticulospinalis medialis, which is pontine in origin and lies in the anterior funiculus.

Lateral sacral nodes.note: These nodes lie on the anterior surface of the sacrum, along the lateral sacral vessels near the anterior sacral foramina and the piriformis origin. Pitfall: sacral ventral rami leaving the foramina, perineural (Tarlov) cysts and the presacral veins mimic nodes. Check that a node is not continuous with a foramen.

Lateral sacral veins.note: Run on the pelvic surface of the sacrum next to the anterior sacral foramina, join the sacral venous plexus, and drain to the internal iliac vein. Pitfall: dilated presacral veins can look like a presacral mass or nodes. They also connect to the internal vertebral venous plexus, so they are a source of bleeding in sacral surgery.

Lateral segmental artery of right lung.key: Lateral segmental artery of right lung
Lateral segmental artery of right lung.note: A4 runs laterally with BIV in the middle lobe, with the horizontal fissure above and the oblique fissure behind and below. Pitfall: on the right, segment IV is the lateral middle lobe segment, whereas on the left IV is the superior lingula. The Vena lateralis runs right next to the artery.
passing: Middle lobar artery of right lung
Inferior lobar artery of right lung
neighbours: Lateral segmental bronchus of right lung (BIV)
Medial segmental bronchus of right lung (BV)

Lateral segmental bronchus of right lung.key: Lateral segmental bronchus of right lung (BIV)
Lateral segmental bronchus of right lung.note: Lateral branch of the middle lobe bronchus. It runs anterolaterally toward the lateral pleura, bounded by the horizontal fissure above and the oblique fissure behind. Pitfall: a right BIV is a lateral middle lobe segment, not the equivalent of the left superior lingular BIV.
passing: Lateral segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Medial segmental bronchus of right lung (BV)

Lateral spinothalamic tract.note: Crossed pain and temperature tract in the anterolateral funiculus. It is somatotopic, with sacral fibres lying most superficially. CT cannot see it. Pitfall: the deficit is on the side opposite the lesion. Also, the spinal root of the Nervus accessorius runs outside the cord along its lateral surface and is not an intramedullary structure.

Lateral subtendinous bursa of gastrocnem.key: Lateral subtendinous bursa of gastrocnemius muscle
Lateral subtendinous bursa of gastrocnem.note: Lies deep to the origin of the Caput laterale musculi gastrocnemii on the posterolateral femoral condyle, next to the knee capsule. It may communicate with the joint. Pitfall: when distended it can be mistaken for a Baker cyst, which arises medially between the Caput mediale and Musculus semimembranosus; a fabella nearby is a normal variant, not a loose body.

Lateral superior jugular node.note: This node lies along the upper Vena jugularis interna, deep to the Musculus sternocleidomastoideus and below the posterior belly of the digastric, close to the carotid bifurcation. Pitfall: a carotid body paraganglioma that splays the internal and external carotid arteries and enhances avidly can mimic a node. Also, level IIA and IIB are separated by the posterior margin of the jugular vein.

Lateral talocalcaneal ligament.note: A short band from the lateral process of the talus to the lateral calcaneus. It runs deep and roughly parallel to the calcaneofibular ligament, just anterior to it, with the fibularis tendons lateral. Pitfall: a fracture of the lateral talar process (snowboarder's fracture) is often missed or called a ligament avulsion. Check coronal reformats.

Lateral tarsal artery.note: Arises from the a. dorsalis pedis at the talar head or navicular level and runs laterally deep to the EDB over the cuboid, joining the arcuate and perforating fibular branches. Pitfall: the EDB muscle belly over the lateral midfoot can look like a soft-tissue mass. This artery runs beneath it.

Lateral temporomandibular ligament.note: A thickening of the lateral capsule from the articular tubercle/zygomatic root to the posterolateral condylar neck, deep to the parotid. Pitfall: CT cannot separate it from the capsule. The superficial temporal vessels and facial nerve branches lie just superficial to it, so a preauricular soft-tissue mass is parotid, not joint, until proven otherwise.

Lateral thoracic artery.note: Arises from the second part of the axillary artery behind pectoralis minor. It descends along the lateral border of pectoralis minor on serratus anterior and supplies the lateral breast. Pitfall: the pectoral (anterior axillary) nodes lie along it. A vessel seen in cross-section can be miscounted as a node, so follow it on adjacent slices.

Lateral thoracic vein.note: The Vena thoracica lateralis runs down the surface of Musculus serratus anterior on the lateral chest wall and drains into the axillary vein. Through the superficial epigastric vein it forms the thoraco-epigastric collateral pathway. Pitfall: a dilated vessel here suggests SVC or IVC obstruction and should not be dismissed as axillary nodes or normal chest-wall vessels.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Lateral thyrohyoid ligament.note: Cord-like posterior free edge of the thyrohyoid membrane. It joins the superior horn of the thyroid cartilage to the tip of the greater hyoid horn, lateral to the piriform sinus. Pitfall: a calcified triticeous cartilage inside it mimics a foreign body, a calcified carotid plaque or a fractured superior horn.

Lateral vein of right lung.note: Vena lateralis pulmonis dextri drains middle lobe segment S4 and usually joins the Vena pulmonalis dextra superior together with the medial vein. Pitfall: the middle lobe vein drains separately into the left atrium as a third right ostium in a substantial minority of patients. Do not call this a duplicated or anomalous vein.
passing: Lateral segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Lateral segmental bronchus of right lung (BIV)

Lateral ventricle.note: C-shaped CSF space. The Corpus callosum forms its roof, the septum pellucidum its medial wall at the front, and the caudate and thalamus its floor and lateral wall. The temporal horn is bordered by the hippocampus. Mild asymmetry and a cavum septi pellucidi are normal variants. Calcified choroid plexus in the atrium is normal and should not be called a bleed.

Lateral vesical nodes.note: These nodes lie in the paravesical fat lateral to the bladder, above the arcus tendineus levatoris ani, along the vesical vessels. Pitfall: the distal ureter, a bladder diverticulum or a vesical venous plexus with phleboliths can mimic a node. Calcified phleboliths must not be mistaken for distal ureteric stones.

Lateral vestibulospinal tract.note: Ipsilateral tract in the anterior funiculus, ventral to the Cornu anterius, at the exit zone of the ventral rootlets. It runs the full length of the cord. CT cannot resolve it. Pitfall: ventral rootlets crossing the subarachnoid space on CT myelography look like intradural filling defects.

Latissimus dorsi muscle.note: Arises from the T7–T12 spinous processes, the thoracolumbar fascia, the iliac crest and the lower ribs, and inserts on the floor of the intertubercular sulcus. Together with the teres major it forms the posterior axillary fold. Pitfall: elastofibroma dorsi, deep to latissimus and serratus at the scapular tip and often bilateral, mimics a soft-tissue tumour.

Left anterior lateral segment of liver (.key: Left anterior lateral segment of liver (III)
Left anterior lateral segment of liver (.note: Segment III lies left of the umbilical fissure (ligamentum teres) and below the left portal vein plane. It sits anterior to the stomach, under the xiphoid. Pitfall: fat in the fissure for the ligamentum teres can look like a hypodense lesion. A replaced left hepatic artery from the Arteria gastrica sinistra runs in the Omentum minus.
neighbours: Left posterior lateral segment of liver (II)

Left ascending lumbar vein.note: This vein ascends from the common iliac vein in the groove between the lumbar vertebral bodies and the psoas. It joins the left subcostal vein to form the v. hemiazyga. Pitfall: it often connects with a retroaortic left renal vein. When dilated, it mimics left paraaortic lymphadenopathy, a psoas lesion or a nerve-root tumour.

Left atrium.note: The Atrium sinistrum is the most posterior chamber. It sits below the carina, in front of the Oesophagus and descending aorta, and receives the pulmonary veins. Pitfall: incomplete contrast mixing in the left auricle on single-phase CT mimics thrombus. A delayed-phase acquisition resolves it.

Left brachiocephalic vein.note: This vein starts behind the left sternoclavicular joint and crosses obliquely behind the manubrium, anterior to the arch branches, to join the right vein and form the SVC. Pitfall: a dense contrast bolus causes streak artifact here that can mimic dissection or thrombus. A retroaortic course or a persistent left SVC must not be mistaken for a mediastinal mass.

Left colic artery.note: First branch of the inferior mesenteric artery. It runs retroperitoneally to the left, across the left psoas and ureter, toward the descending colon and splenic flexure. Pitfall: it runs next to the inferior mesenteric vein, which lies more lateral and continues cranially behind the pancreas. Do not swap artery and vein in the portal-venous phase.
passing: Ascending branch of left colic artery
Descending branch of left colic artery

Left colic nodes.note: Nodi colici sinistri lie along the left colic artery in the left retroperitoneum, medial to the descending colon and anterior to the left psoas major. Pitfall: unopacified jejunal loops and the inferior mesenteric vein next to them can look like nodes; use oral contrast and follow structures across slices.
passing: Ascending branch of left colic artery

Left common carotid artery.note: This artery arises directly from the Arcus aortae, to the left of the trachea. In the carotid sheath it lies medial to the internal jugular vein, with the vagus nerve behind and between them. It divides at about C3–C4. Pitfall: in a bovine arch it shares an origin with the brachiocephalic trunk, so do not report it as absent.

Left coronary artery.note: The left main coronary artery arises from the left aortic sinus. It runs between the pulmonary trunk and the Atrium sinistrum or left auricle, then divides into the LAD and the circumflex artery. Pitfall: look for a malignant interarterial course between the aorta and pulmonary trunk. A trifurcation with a ramus intermedius is a normal variant.

Left coronary leaflet.note: Left posterior aortic cusp below the left sinus, which gives off the left main coronary artery; the Atrium sinistrum lies behind it. Pitfall: the anatomically left cusp lies posterior-left on axial CT. Avoid mislabelling cusps, and assess the commissures before calling the valve bicuspid.

Left gastric artery.note: Smallest coeliac branch. It ascends to the cardia and then runs along the lesser curvature within the Omentum minus. Pitfall: a replaced or accessory left hepatic artery may arise from it and run in the fissure for the ligamentum venosum. Do not mistake that vessel for a node or the left gastric vein.

Left gastro-omental vein.note: Runs along the greater curvature of the stomach within the gastrocolic ligament and drains into the Vena splenica near the splenic hilum. Pitfall: dilated gastro-omental and gastric collaterals with a normal liver suggest sinistral (left-sided) portal hypertension from splenic vein thrombosis, not cirrhosis.

Left inferior lobar bronchus.note: This bronchus continues the left main bronchus after the upper lobe takeoff. It first gives BVI posteriorly, then the basal trunk, with the descending left pulmonary artery posterolateral to it. Pitfall: on the left, BVII and BVIII usually share an anteromedial basal stem. A missing separate BVII is normal, not an occlusion.
passing: Lateral basal segmental artery of left lung
neighbours: Superior segmental bronchus of left lung (BVI)
Medial basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BVII)
Anterior basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BVIII)
Lateral basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BIX)

Left inferior pulmonary vein.note: Vena pulmonalis sinistra inferior drains the Lobus inferior and enters the posterolateral Atrium sinistrum below the left hilum, inside the ligamentum pulmonale region. Pitfall: a common left trunk shared with the superior vein is a normal variant. Unopacified veins in arterial phase can mimic a filling defect or hilar node.
passing: Superior basal vein of left lung
Inferior basal vein of left lung

Left lobe of thymus.note: Prevascular anterior mediastinal tissue behind the manubrium, in front of the arcus aortae, ascending aorta and truncus pulmonalis, bordered laterally by the pleura. Pitfall: normal thymus in young patients, or rebound hyperplasia after chemotherapy, mimics an anterior mediastinal mass. Look for a triangular shape and fatty involution.

Left main bronchus.note: The left main bronchus is longer and more horizontal than the right. It runs under the aortic arch, with the Arteria pulmonalis sinistra arching over it, the Oesophagus and descending aorta behind it, and the Atrium sinistrum below. Pitfall: without contrast, the Arteria pulmonalis sinistra or the left atrial appendage at the hilum is easily mistaken for hilar or subcarinal nodes.

Left medial segment of liver (IV).note: Segment IV lies between the middle hepatic vein and the umbilical fissure. The portal plane divides it into IVa (upper) and IVb (lower), and IVb borders the gallbladder fossa and porta hepatis. Pitfall: pseudolesions from focal fat or fatty sparing next to the ligamentum teres and porta hepatis, caused by aberrant venous inflow.
neighbours: Left anterior lateral segment of liver (III)
Left posterior lateral segment of liver (II)

Left posterior lateral segment of liver.key: Left posterior lateral segment of liver (II)
Left posterior lateral segment of liver.note: Segment II lies posterosuperior to the left portal vein plane and is drained by the left hepatic vein. It sits under the left hemidiaphragm, anterior to the stomach fundus. Pitfall: a long lateral segment wrapping around the spleen ('beaver tail' liver) mimics a perisplenic haematoma or a splenic lesion.
neighbours: Left anterior lateral segment of liver (III)

Left pulmonary artery.note: Arches over the Bronchus principalis sinister and the upper lobe bronchus, then runs down behind them as the interlobar artery. Pitfall: the left hilum is higher than the right because the artery arches over the bronchus. Do not misread a variable upper lobe branching pattern, or a partial-volume averaged hilar artery, as lymphadenopathy.
passing: Apical segmental artery of left lung
Anterior segmental artery of left lung
Superior segmental artery of left lung
Superior lingular artery of left lung
neighbours: Superior segmental bronchus of left lung (BVI)

Left renal artery.note: Arises from the left side of the Aorta abdominalis at L1–L2, just below the Arteria mesenterica superior. It runs behind the Vena renalis sinistra to the renal hilum. Pitfall: accessory and polar renal arteries are common, so trace every lateral aortic branch before reporting a single supply.

Left renal vein.note: Crosses anterior to the aorta just below the origin of the Arteria mesenterica superior to reach the IVC, and receives the left gonadal vein. Pitfall: a retroaortic or circumaortic left renal vein can mimic a retroperitoneal lymph node. Nutcracker narrowing between the SMA and aorta should not be overcalled without collaterals.

Left semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valv.key: Left semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valve
Left semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valv.note: Left cusp of the pulmonary valve at the junction of the RV outflow tract and the Truncus pulmonalis, next to the left atrial appendage. Pitfall: the thin cusps are usually invisible without gating, so a leaflet-like line may be pulsation artefact. Do not misread it as a pulmonary embolus at the valve level.
passing: Anterior semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valve
Right semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valve

Left subclavian artery.note: Third branch of the Arcus aortae. It climbs over the pleural cupula and passes between Musculus scalenus anterior and medius across Costa prima, then becomes the Arteria axillaris. Pitfall: a vertebral artery arising directly from the arch changes the expected branching pattern and can be mistaken for an extra arch branch.

Left subclavian vein.note: Continues from the V. axillaris at the outer edge of the first rib. It passes in front of the M. scalenus anterior (the artery lies behind it) and under the clavicle and M. subclavius to the left venous angle. Pitfall: dense undiluted contrast causes streak artifact on the injected side. Narrowing when the arm is abducted is positional, not stenosis.
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Left subcostal vein.note: This vein runs below the left 12th rib, anterior to quadratus lumborum, with the subcostal artery and nerve. At T12 it joins the left ascending lumbar vein to form the hemiazygos. Pitfall: a short or absent 12th rib causes level errors. The small bundle beside the vertebral body is easily mistaken for an intercostal node.

Left superior intercostal vein.note: This vein drains the left 2nd–4th intercostal veins. It arches forward along the left lateral aortic arch, between the phrenic and vagus nerves, into the left brachiocephalic vein. Pitfall: the small nodular density on the arch, the 'aortic nipple', can mimic a node, an intimal flap or periaortic haematoma. When dilated, it signals collateral flow.

Left superior lobar bronchus.note: This bronchus arises anterolaterally from the left main bronchus. It splits into an upper division (BI+BII, BIII) and a lingular division (BIV, BV). The Arteria pulmonalis sinistra hooks over and behind it, and the left superior pulmonary vein lies in front. Pitfall: lingular bronchi belong to the upper lobe, so do not report a left middle lobe.
passing: Anterior segmental artery of left lung
Superior lingular artery of left lung
neighbours: Apicoposterior segmental bronchus of left lung (BI+BII)
Anterior segmental bronchus of left lung (BIII)
Superior lingular segmental bronchus of left lung (BIV)
Inferior lingular segmental bronchus of left lung (BV)

Left superior pulmonary vein.note: Vena pulmonalis sinistra superior drains the Lobus superior and lingula. It lies anterior and inferior to the Arteria pulmonalis sinistra and anterior to the left main bronchus before entering the Atrium sinistrum. Pitfall: the left atrial appendage sits directly anterior and the ridge between them ('coumadin ridge') can mimic thrombus or a mass.

Left testicular artery.note: Arises from the anterolateral Aorta abdominalis below the renal arteries and descends behind the peritoneum on Psoas major to the deep inguinal ring, where it joins the Ductus deferens. Pitfall: the much larger Vena testicularis sinistra, draining into the left renal vein, is usually the vessel you see. Do not call it the artery.

Left testicular vein.note: Runs up on psoas major in front of the ureter from the deep inguinal ring and joins the vena renalis sinistra at a right angle. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the inferior mesenteric vein, which lies further medial and drains to the splenic vein. Left renal vein (nutcracker) compression can cause reflux and a varicocele.

Left ventricle.note: The Ventriculus sinister is the thick-walled chamber on the left posterior side. Its apex points anterolaterally, and it is bounded by the septum, Atrium sinistrum and Diaphragma. Pitfall: papillary muscles, trabeculations and false tendons mimic thrombus. Thin myocardium at the true apex is normal and is not an infarct.
passing: Inferior papillary muscle of left ventricle

Lens.note: The Lens is a hyperdense biconvex body behind the Iris. The Camera anterior bulbi oculi lies in front and the Corpus vitreum behind. Pitfall: after trauma, compare both globes for subluxation or dislocation into the vitreous. Look for an absent lens (aphakia) or a pseudophakic implant before calling the lens dislocated.

Lentiform nucleus.note: Wedge shape made of the putamen and the globus pallidus. The external capsule lies lateral. The internal capsule lies medial, its anterior limb separating the lentiform from the caudate and its posterior limb from the thalamus. Losing its outline is an early sign of MCA infarct. Do not mistake enlarged perivascular spaces near the anterior perforated substance for lacunar infarcts.

Lesser omentum.note: It runs from the fissure for the ligamentum venosum and the porta hepatis to the lesser curvature and duodenal bulb. Its free edge (hepatoduodenal ligament) contains the portal triad and borders the foramen omentale. Pitfall: the papillary process of segment I can look like a gastrohepatic lymph node. Confirm continuity with the caudate lobe.
neighbours: Left anterior lateral segment of liver (III)

Levator anguli oris.note: Arises from the fossa canina below the foramen infraorbitale and inserts at the modiolus; it lies deep to Levator labii superioris and zygomaticus minor. Pitfall: the infraorbital neurovascular bundle runs between it and Levator labii superioris, and a canine-root periapical abscess spreading here mimics a primary soft-tissue mass.

Levator labii superioris.note: Arises from the infraorbital margin above the foramen infraorbitale, deep to Pars orbitalis musculi orbicularis oculi, and descends into the upper lip. Pitfall: it covers the infraorbital foramen, so perineural tumour spread along V2 can look like simple muscle thickening; compare the foramen side to side.

Levator nasolabialis.note: Runs from the frontal process of the maxilla along the nasomaxillary groove to the ala and upper lip, medial to Levator labii superioris. Pitfall: the angular vein runs in this groove and connects to the superior ophthalmic vein. Medial canthal inflammation here can spread to the orbit, and the vein should not be mistaken for a nodule.
neighbours: Lateral process of nasal septal cartilage

Levator palpebrae superioris.note: Lies directly beneath the orbital roof (frontal bone) and above the superior rectus. It fans out into an aponeurosis to the superior tarsus, passing between the lobes of the lacrimal gland. Pitfall: CT shows levator and superior rectus as one 'superior muscle complex'. Measuring it as one muscle overestimates superior rectus thickening.

Levator scapulae.note: Runs from the posterior tubercles of the C1–C4 transverse processes to the Angulus superior scapulae and forms part of the floor of the posterior cervical triangle. Pitfall: compensatory hypertrophy after accessory nerve injury (e.g., neck dissection) mimics a neck mass or recurrence, especially when the trapezius is atrophic.
landmarks: lm:Posterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4

Levatores breves costarum.note: Each slip runs from the tip of a transverse process (C7–T11) to the rib directly below, between the tubercle and the angle, deep to the erector spinae. Pitfall: an asymmetric slip at the costotransverse level can mimic a small paravertebral nodule, nerve sheath tumour or node. Check its continuity with the adjacent transverse process.
landmarks: lm:Crest of neck of rib|Sixth rib

Levatores longi costarum.note: Mainly in the lower thoracic spine, each slip runs from a transverse process past one rib to insert on the second rib below, lateral to the levatores breves. Pitfall: on CT it blends with the external intercostals and levatores breves, so do not report the oblique fat planes between them as fat infiltration or a mass.

Ligament of head of femur.note: Runs from the incisura acetabuli and transverse ligament, through the fossa acetabuli, to the fovea capitis femoris. Pitfall: the normal fovea should not be called an osteochondral defect or erosion. A fragment in the fovea after dislocation points to a femoral head (Pipkin) fracture.
landmarks: lm:Fovea for ligament of head of femur|Femur

Ligamenta flava.note: Paired ligaments joining the laminae from C2 to S1. They form the posterolateral wall of the spinal canal and blend laterally with the facet joint capsules at the foramen intervertebrale. Pitfall: a hypertrophied, buckled or ossified (thoracic OLF) ligamentum flavum can mimic a disc fragment or epidural mass and causes dorsal canal stenosis.

Linea alba.note: Linea alba is the midline tendinous seam between the two rectus muscles, running from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis and widest around the umbilicus. Pitfall: do not report diastasis recti (a widened linea alba with no fascial defect) as a hernia; an epigastric or umbilical hernia needs a true defect with protruding fat or bowel.

Lingual gyrus.note: A medial-basal occipital gyrus between the Sulcus calcarinus above and the Sulcus collateralis below, continuing forward into the Gyrus parahippocampalis and lying on the Tentorium cerebelli. Pitfall: on axial CT, partial volume of the cerebellar hemisphere through the tentorium can mimic or hide a PCA infarct here.

Lingual nerve.note: It descends between the lateral and medial pterygoid muscles, runs close to the lingual cortex at the third molar, then crosses the ductus submandibularis on the musculus hyoglossus. Pitfall: on the hyoglossus, the nervus hypoglossus lies lower, together with the vena lingualis. Do not mix the two nerves up when a sublingual lesion lies along their course.
neighbours: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Lingual vein.note: Drains the tongue, runs back along hyoglossus near the greater horn of the hyoid, and empties into the common facial vein or the IJV. Pitfall: the vena comitans of the hypoglossal nerve runs on hyoglossus, superficial to it, while the lingual artery runs deep to it. Do not mistake the venous channels for the artery or for a node.

Lingula of cerebellum.note: The Lingula cerebelli is a thin vermian lamina on the superior medullary velum. It roofs the upper fourth ventricle between the Pedunculi cerebellares superiores. Pitfall: CT cannot resolve it, so the thin roof of the fourth ventricle should not be read as a mass. The trochlear nerve exits dorsally at this level.
