Lingular vein of left lung.note: Vena lingularis pulmonis sinistri forms from the superior and inferior lingular veins and joins the lowest part of the Vena pulmonalis sinistra superior. Pitfall: it can drain separately into the left atrium or into the inferior pulmonary vein. Report this variant before pulmonary vein isolation.
passing: Superior lingular vein of left lung
Inferior lingular vein of left lung

Liver.note: It sits under the right hemidiaphragm, bordered by the right kidney and suprarenal gland behind, the stomach on the left and the IVC in the bare area. The Couinaud segments are divided by the venae hepaticae and the portal plane. Pitfall: focal fatty sparing or infiltration next to the gallbladder fossa or in segment IV can look like a mass. It has no mass effect on vessels.

lm:(Canal for vertebral artery)|Atlas (C.note: The sulcus arteriae vertebralis runs over the posterior arch of the Atlas, behind the lateral mass. The V3 segment of the Arteria vertebralis loops through it toward the foramen magnum. Pitfall: a ponticulus posticus (arcuate foramen) closes the groove into a canal. It can be mistaken for a widened lateral mass, which matters for screw placement.

lm:(External occipital crest)|Occipital.note: The external occipital crest runs in the midline from the external occipital protuberance to the foramen magnum. It anchors the Ligamentum nuchae between the paired suboccipital muscles. Pitfall: the midline ridge, nearby vascular channels or a persistent midline synchondrosis can mimic a nondisplaced occipital fracture.

lm:(Internal occipital crest)|Occipital.note: The internal occipital crest runs from the internal occipital protuberance down to the foramen magnum, between the cerebellar hemispheres. It carries the falx cerebelli and the occipital sinus. Pitfall: a prominent occipital sinus or a dense falx cerebelli on CT brain can mimic a midline posterior fossa subdural haemorrhage.

lm:(Mandibular symphysis)|Mandible.note: The midline symphysis runs from the alveolus between the central incisors down to the gnathion, with the mental spines on its lingual cortex. Pitfall: the lingual foramen and midline vascular canals, or an unfused symphysis in infants, can mimic a fracture. Also look for a paired fracture of the condyles or angles.

lm:(Middle clinoid process)|Sphenoid bon.note: The middle clinoid process is a small inconstant spur at the anterolateral sella turcica, medial to the cavernous internal carotid artery. Pitfall: an ossified carotico-clinoid ligament bridging it to the anterior clinoid forms a bony ring around the ICA. Do not mistake this for calcification or an aneurysm wall; it matters surgically.

lm:(Posterior obturator tubercle)|Hip bo.note: The posterior obturator tubercle lies on the ischial margin of the Foramen obturatum and forms the posterior lip of the obturator canal, where the Membrana obturatoria attaches. Pitfall: this small bony prominence can be mistaken for an avulsion fragment or an ossicle. Compare with the other side.

lm:(Supra-orbital notch)|Frontal bone.note: Notch in the supra-orbital margin at the junction of its medial and middle thirds. The supra-orbital neurovascular bundle (from V1) passes through it. Pitfall: it may be a closed foramen, which can look like a cortical defect or fracture line through the orbital rim. Compare with the other side.

lm:(Third trochanter)|Femur.note: The third trochanter is a normal variant: an enlarged upper end of the Tuberositas glutea, where the Musculus gluteus maximus inserts. It lies below the greater trochanter on the back and side of the femur. Pitfall: do not report it as an osteochondroma, periosteal reaction or avulsion. Its cortex and marrow are continuous with the femur and it often occurs on both sides.

lm:(Trochlear spine)|Frontal bone.note: Small bony spicule in the anteromedial orbital roof that anchors the cartilaginous trochlea of the Musculus obliquus superior. Pitfall: calcification of the trochlea is a common age-related finding. Do not mistake it for an orbital foreign body or a fracture fragment.

lm:(Vermian fossa)|Occipital bone.note: The vermian fossa is a midline hollow on the lower internal occipital crest just above the foramen magnum. It holds the inferior vermis between the tonsils. Pitfall: a deep vermian fossa or a mega cisterna magna can mimic a retrocerebellar arachnoid cyst or Dandy–Walker spectrum; check vermis shape and the fourth ventricle.

lm:Acetabular fossa|Hip bone.note: The Fossa acetabuli is the non-articular floor of the acetabulum, surrounded by the Facies lunata and open inferiorly at the notch. It contains the pulvinar fat and the ligamentum capitis femoris. Pitfall: the fossa's thin quadrilateral wall, and the joint space widened by pulvinar fat, should not be read as protrusio or a central fracture.

lm:Acetabular margin|Hip bone.note: The Margo acetabuli is the bony rim to which the Labrum acetabuli attaches. It is interrupted inferiorly by the Incisura acetabuli. Pitfall: an os acetabuli or rim ossification at the anterosuperior margin can mimic a rim fracture. A smooth cortex suggests a normal variant or femoroacetabular impingement-related change.

lm:Acetabular notch|Hip bone.note: The Incisura acetabuli is the inferior gap in the acetabular rim between the ends of the Facies lunata. The transverse acetabular ligament bridges it, and the acetabular branch of the obturator artery enters through it. Pitfall: on axial CT the notch can mimic a defect or fracture of the inferior wall.

lm:Acetabulum|Hip bone.note: The acetabulum is formed by the ilium, ischium and pubis meeting at the triradiate cartilage. It is described by its anterior and posterior columns and walls. Pitfall: in adolescents, the open triradiate cartilage and secondary ossification centres (os acetabuli) can mimic fractures. Classify fractures (Letournel) on 3D reconstructions and reformats.

lm:Acromial angle|Scapula.note: The Angulus acromii is the posterolateral corner where the Spina scapulae turns into the acromion. The deltoid pars spinalis attaches here. Pitfall: an unfused acromial apophysis (os acromiale) near this corner can look like a fracture. Check for smooth corticated margins and compare with the other side.
neighbours: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

lm:Acromial end|Clavicle.note: Extremitas acromialis is the flattened lateral clavicle. It articulates with the acromion, with the deltoid inserting in front and the trapezius behind. Pitfall: the normal AC joint width and height step vary, and distal clavicular osteolysis or resection can look like separation. Compare with the other side.

lm:Acromial facet|Clavicle.note: Facies articularis acromialis is the small oval lateral clavicular facet facing the clavicular facet of the acromion, with a variable discus between them. Pitfall: an os acromiale, which is an unfused acromial apophysis, can mimic the AC joint or a fracture on axial CT. Find the true AC joint first.

lm:Acromion|Scapula.note: The acromion roofs the subacromial space above the supraspinatus and meets the clavicle at the Articulatio acromioclavicularis. Pitfall: os acromiale, an unfused apophysis with corticated sclerotic margins, can be mistaken for an acute fracture. Acromial shape and undersurface spurs matter for impingement.

lm:Adductor tubercle|Femur.note: The Tuberculum adductorium sits on top of the medial femoral condyle. The tendon of the Adductor magnus inserts here, and the medial patellofemoral ligament attaches nearby. Pitfall: a cortical irregularity at the medial distal femur (cortical desmoid) is a benign stress reaction. Do not mistake it for an aggressive lesion.

lm:Ala of ilium|Hip bone.note: The Ala ossis ilium is the wing of the ilium, with the Musculus iliacus in the iliac fossa on its inner surface and the gluteal muscles on its outer surface. Pitfall: the central part is often very thin and can look like an osteolytic lesion. Nutrient foramina can mimic fracture lines.

lm:Ala of sacrum|Sacrum.note: Ala ossis sacri is the upper lateral sacral mass, lying lateral to the S1 body and in front of the articulatio sacroiliaca, with psoas major and the lumbosacral trunk on its anterior surface. Pitfall: vertical alar insufficiency fractures are faint sclerotic lines that are easily missed axially. Check coronal reformats, which can show the H-pattern.

lm:Angle of mandible (gonion)|Mandible.note: Gonion is where the posterior ramus border meets the lower border of the body, held by masseter laterally and medial pterygoid medially (pterygomasseteric sling), with the parotid tail behind. Pitfall: angle fractures often run through a third-molar socket; do not dismiss this as a follicular space. Look for a second fracture on the opposite side.

lm:Angle of rib|Sixth rib.note: Angulus costae is the posterior bend of the rib, lateral to the tubercle, where the iliocostalis attaches. It is the weakest point and a common fracture site. Pitfall: under the scapula, angle fractures are easily missed on axial slices. Count ribs on coronal/3D views so you do not mislabel the level.

lm:Annular epiphysis|Vertebra L3.note: Epiphysis anularis is the ring apophysis around the endplate rim, anchoring the outer fibres of the annulus (Sharpey fibres) and lying under the anterior longitudinal ligament. Pitfall: a limbus vertebra (corticated triangular fragment from intraosseous disc herniation) and persistent apophyses mimic fractures; in adolescents, a posterior ring apophysis avulsion can mimic a calcified disc herniation.

lm:Anterior arch of atlas|Atlas (C1).note: The Arcus anterior atlantis articulates posteriorly with the Dens axis at the Fovea dentis, which defines the atlantodental interval. Longus colli and longus capitis lie anterior to it. Pitfall: congenital midline clefts with smooth corticated margins mimic a Jefferson fracture. A fracture has sharp, non-corticated edges.

lm:Anterior border of fibula|Fibula.note: The Margo anterior fibulae gives attachment to the Septum intermusculare anterius cruris, which divides the anterior compartment from the lateral compartment. The Membrana interossea attaches to the separate medial (interosseous) border, so keep the two borders apart. Pitfall: the fibular nerves pass close to this border. Proximal fibular fractures or plates risk injuring them, and the superficial fibular nerve pierces the fascia distally.

lm:Anterior border of ulna|Ulna.note: Margo anterior ulnae separates the anterior and medial surfaces of the shaft. It gives origin to Musculus flexor digitorum profundus and, distally, to pronator quadratus. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the sharp interosseous border, which faces the radius and carries the Membrana interossea antebrachii.
neighbours: Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris

lm:Anterior clinoid process|Sphenoid bon.note: Processus clinoideus anterior is the posterior extension of the lesser wing. It lies lateral to the optic canal and above the clinoid segment of the internal carotid artery. Pitfall: pneumatisation from the sphenoid sinus can mimic a lytic lesion. A paraclinoid aneurysm can be hidden by the bony overlap on CTA.

lm:Anterior inferior iliac spine|Hip bon.note: The Spina iliaca anterior inferior lies above the acetabulum and is the origin of the direct head of the Musculus rectus femoris. Pitfall: in adolescents, its apophysis or an old avulsion can mimic a tumour or a loose fragment. A prominent spine can also cause subspine impingement.

lm:Anterior limb of internal capsule|Whi.key: lm:Anterior limb of internal capsule|White matter of telencephalon
lm:Anterior limb of internal capsule|Whi.note: Crus anterius capsulae internae lies between the caput nuclei caudati (medial) and the nucleus lentiformis (lateral). Pitfall: the lenticulostriate perivascular spaces and the boundary with the striatum can mimic small lacunar infarcts. Compare both sides and correlate with the clinical picture.

lm:Anterior limb of stapes|Stapes.note: Thinner, straighter crus running from the stapes head to the front of the footplate in the oval window niche, below the tympanic Nervus facialis. Pitfall: the crura are often blurred by partial volume, so do not call absence or fracture without thin oblique reformats. Fenestral otosclerosis begins just anterior to it (fissula ante fenestram).

lm:Anterior obturator tubercle|Hip bone.note: The Tuberculum obturatorium anterius lies on the superior pubic ramus at the anterior end of the Sulcus obturatorius and borders the obturator canal. Pitfall: the obturator nerve and vessels exit the canal here. A hernia in the obturator canal is easily missed, so compare both sides.

lm:Anterior process of malleus|Malleus.note: The Processus anterior mallei is a thin spur that projects from the Collum mallei toward the petrotympanic fissure, held by the anterior mallear ligament. Pitfall: ossification of the anterior mallear ligament (anterior malleal fixation) can be mistaken for this normal process. Pure partial volume can also make the process look fractured.

lm:Anterior sacral foramina|Sacrum.note: Foramina sacralia anteriora (four pairs) carry the ventral rami of S1–S4 onto the pelvic surface, where piriformis arises between them. Pitfall: fracture lines running through the foramina (Denis zone II) carry a higher risk of nerve injury. Asymmetric foraminal size or a perineural (Tarlov) cyst can mimic a fracture or a lytic lesion.
passing: Anterior root of posterior femoral cutaneous nerve

lm:Anterior surface of petrous part|Temp.key: lm:Anterior surface of petrous part|Temporal bone
lm:Anterior surface of petrous part|Temp.note: Facies anterior partis petrosae forms the posterior floor of the middle cranial fossa. It carries the arcuate eminence, tegmen tympani and the hiatus for the greater petrosal nerve, and meets the sphenoid at the sphenopetrosal fissure. Pitfall: a thin tegmen or arachnoid pits can mimic dehiscence or fracture; confirm on coronal reconstructions.

lm:Anterior tubercle of atlas|Atlas (C1).note: The Tuberculum anterius atlantis is the midline prominence of the anterior arch. The Ligamentum longitudinale anterius and the superior oblique part of longus colli attach to it, and the prevertebral space lies anterior. Pitfall: amorphous calcification anterior to C1–C2 is calcific tendinitis of longus colli, not an avulsion fracture. Look for an associated prevertebral effusion.

lm:Anterior tubercle of transverse proce.key: lm:Anterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4
lm:Anterior tubercle of transverse proce.note: Tuberculum anterius forms the ventral margin of the Foramen transversarium and gives origin to Musculus longus capitis and Musculus scalenus anterior, with longus colli lying medially. Pitfall: an enlarged C6 tubercle (carotid tubercle) or an elongated C4 tubercle can mimic a fracture fragment or prevertebral calcification; check symmetry with the other side.
landmarks: lm:Posterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4

lm:Anterolateral surface of arytenoid ca.key: lm:Anterolateral surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage
lm:Anterolateral surface of arytenoid ca.note: The Facies anterolateralis faces the paraglottic space and carries the Fovea oblonga and Fovea triangularis, which the Crista arcuata separates. The thyroarytenoid and lateral cricoarytenoid muscles attach here. Pitfall: arytenoid ossification is often asymmetric, and sclerosis can be mistaken for cartilage invasion by tumour.

lm:Anterolateral surface of humerus|Hume.note: Facies anterolateralis humeri carries the tuberositas deltoidea in its middle third and gives origin to brachialis distally. Pitfall: the radial nerve in the sulcus nervi radialis and its course through the lateral intermuscular septum are near this surface, so mid- and distal-shaft fractures here (e.g. Holstein–Lewis) risk radial nerve palsy. The deltoid tuberosity itself should not be called periosteal reaction.

lm:Apex of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid.note: The Apex cartilaginis arytenoideae curves posteromedially and carries the Cartilago corniculata within the aryepiglottic fold. The Pars laryngea pharyngis lies posterior to it. Pitfall: an ossified corniculate cartilage can be mistaken for a fractured arytenoid apex or a foreign body.
neighbours: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle

lm:Apex of coccyx|Coccyx.note: Apex ossis coccygis is the caudal tip of the last coccygeal segment. The anococcygeal levator fibres attach here, with the gluteus maximus at the sides. Pitfall: the tip often angles forward or is unfused and fragmented as a normal variant. Do not call this a fracture unless there is a cortical break and soft-tissue swelling.

lm:Apex of dens axis|Axis (C2).note: The apex dentis points toward the basion and anchors the apical and alar ligaments. Use it for the basion–dens interval (normal at most 12 mm). Pitfall: the ossiculum terminale (a persistent apical ossification centre) is a normal variant. Do not call it a type I dens fracture or an os odontoideum.

lm:Apex of head of fibula|Fibula.note: The Apex capitis fibulae projects upward behind and lateral to the tibiofibular facet. The Ligamentum popliteofibulare and arcuate ligament attach to it, and the biceps femoris and fibular collateral ligament insert next to it. Pitfall: a small apex fragment (arcuate sign) means posterolateral corner injury, not a trivial chip. The common fibular nerve passes just below, around the fibular neck.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of fibula|Fibula
neighbours: Articular capsule of superior tibiofibular joint

lm:Apex of petrous part|Temporal bone.note: Apex partis petrosae points anteromedially between the sphenoid body and clivus, roofing foramen lacerum, with Dorello canal (VI) medially. Pitfall: asymmetric pneumatisation or fatty marrow of one apex mimics a lesion; compare both sides, and don't diagnose effusion versus cholesterol granuloma on CT alone.
landmarks: lm:Internal opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone
lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipital bone

lm:Apex of sacrum|Sacrum.note: Apex ossis sacri is the narrow caudal end of S5, joined to the basis ossis coccygis at the symphysis sacrococcygea. Pitfall: the angle at the sacrococcygeal junction varies a lot and a non-fused joint is normal, so neither should be reported as a fracture without a cortical break or soft-tissue swelling. Use sagittal reformats.

lm:Arch of cricoid cartilage|Cricoid car.note: The Arcus cartilaginis cricoideae forms the front of the only complete cartilage ring in the airway. It lies below the Ligamentum cricothyreoideum medianum and above the first tracheal ring. Pitfall: the cartilage ossifies in patches, so partly calcified cartilage can look like a fracture or tumour invasion. Check whether the cortex is continuous.

lm:Arcuate crest|Arytenoid cartilage.note: The Crista arcuata is a ridge on the anterolateral surface. It separates the Fovea triangularis above from the Fovea oblonga below and ends at the Colliculus. Pitfall: CT cannot resolve this ridge. Do not read irregular ossification along it as erosion.
landmarks: lm:Anterolateral surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage
neighbours: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle

lm:Arcuate eminence|Temporal bone.note: Eminentia arcuata bulges from the anterior surface of the pars petrosa over the superior semicircular canal, with tegmen tympani lateral to it. Pitfall: thin bone plus partial volume mimics superior canal dehiscence; confirm on Pöschl/Stenvers reformats, and note the eminence does not always sit exactly over the canal.
landmarks: lm:Petrous part of temporal bone|Temporal bone
lm:Posterior surface of petrous part|Temporal bone

lm:Arcuate line of ilium|Hip bone.note: Linea arcuata ossis ilium is the curved inner ridge that marks the boundary between the true and false pelvis. It runs from the sacroiliac joint to the pecten pubis, with psoas major lying anterior to it. Pitfall: on axial CT, an oblique cortical step at this line can mimic a nondisplaced fracture of the pelvic ring. Check coronal reformats.

lm:Articular facet for malleus|Incus.note: This is the incudomallear joint in the epitympanic recess. On axial CT it is the 'ice-cream cone': caput mallei anteriorly, corpus incudis posteriorly. Pitfall: thick slices or oblique planes blur the joint space and can mimic or hide a subluxation. Use thin bone reconstructions and compare with the other side.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of malleus|Malleus

lm:Articular facet for stapes|Incus.note: This is the incudostapedial joint in the mesotympanum, lateral to the oval window. The tympanic segment of the facial nerve runs just above it. Pitfall: the joint is near CT resolution, so partial volume can fake a separation. A true traumatic incudostapedial disruption needs consistent findings on axial and coronal planes.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of stapes|Stapes

lm:Articular facet of head of fibula|Fib.key: lm:Articular facet of head of fibula|Fibula
lm:Articular facet of head of fibula|Fib.note: Flat, round facet facing anteromedially and superiorly on the fibular head; it meets the posterolateral facet of the lateral tibial condyle at the Articulatio tibiofibularis superior. Pitfall: the obliquely oriented joint space looks widened or incongruent on axial slices. Assess it on reformats before calling it subluxation.
neighbours: Articular capsule of superior tibiofibular joint

lm:Articular facet of head of malleus|Ma.key: lm:Articular facet of head of malleus|Malleus
lm:Articular facet of head of malleus|Ma.note: This saddle-shaped facet on the posterior Caput mallei joins the Corpus incudis in the epitympanum. On axial CT the joint looks like an 'ice-cream cone'. Pitfall: a slightly wider joint gap from obliquity or partial volume can mimic incudomallear dislocation. Confirm on both planes against the other side.

lm:Articular facet of head of radius|Rad.key: lm:Articular facet of head of radius|Radius
lm:Articular facet of head of radius|Rad.note: Fovea articularis capitis radii is the concave proximal surface articulating with the capitulum humeri, inside the joint capsule. Pitfall: subtle impacted or marginal radial head fractures are easy to miss on axial slices alone. Check sagittal and coronal reformats for a step-off, and look for joint effusion or a raised fat pad.

lm:Articular facet of head of stapes|Sta.key: lm:Articular facet of head of stapes|Stapes
lm:Articular facet of head of stapes|Sta.note: Concave facet on the stapes head that forms the incudostapedial joint with the Processus lenticularis incudis, just below the tympanic Nervus facialis. Pitfall: this is the most common site of ossicular discontinuity after trauma or cholesteatoma. However, the thin lenticular process often looks falsely discontinuous from partial volume, so confirm in two planes.

lm:Articular facet of medial malleolus|T.note: The Facies articularis malleoli is the lateral surface of the Malleolus medialis. It articulates with the medial facet of the talus and is continuous with the plafond. The deltoid ligament arises from the colliculi. Pitfall: an os subtibiale with smooth corticated margins is a normal variant. Do not mistake it for a medial malleolar avulsion fracture.

lm:Articular surface for cuboid|Calcaneu.note: This saddle-shaped facies articularis cuboidea at the front of the calcaneus forms the calcaneocuboid joint, part of the Chopart joint line. Pitfall: an avulsion of the anterior process of the calcaneus at the bifurcate ligament is easy to miss on axial images. It can also be confused with an os calcaneus secundarium, which has smooth corticated margins.

lm:Articular surface of arytenoid cartil.key: lm:Articular surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage
lm:Articular surface of arytenoid cartil.note: The Facies articularis on the arytenoid base meets the Facies articularis arytenoidea on the upper border of the cricoid lamina, forming the cricoarytenoid joint. Pitfall: after intubation trauma, check for arytenoid dislocation or subluxation. Compare joint alignment with the other side, because a unilateral cord palsy can look similar.

lm:Articular tubercle|Temporal bone.note: The Tuberculum articulare forms the anterior boundary of the Fossa mandibularis. The Discus articularis rests on its posterior slope, and the Caput mandibulae moves onto it when the mouth opens. Pitfall: a pneumatized articular tubercle is a normal variant that can mimic a lytic lesion or fracture.
passing: Accessory branch of middle meningeal artery
neighbours: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

lm:Arytenoid articular surface|Cricoid c.note: The Facies articularis arytenoidea sits on the upper edge of the Lamina cartilaginis cricoideae and forms the cricoarytenoid joint with the Basis cartilaginis arytenoideae. Pitfall: the two sides often ossify asymmetrically and patients may rotate in the scanner. Either can mimic arytenoid dislocation. Use the joint alignment and the vocal fold position to decide.
landmarks: lm:Articular surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage

lm:Atlas (C1)|Atlas (C1).note: The atlas is a ring with no body. Its anterior arch lies behind the longus colli and longus capitis muscles and the prevertebral soft tissue, and it articulates with the dens. Pitfall: congenital clefts of the anterior or posterior arch have smooth corticated margins. Do not call them a Jefferson fracture, which has sharp non-corticated edges and displaced lateral masses.

lm:Auricular surface of ilium|Hip bone.note: Facies auricularis ossis ilium forms the synovial, anteroinferior part of the sacroiliac joint opposite the auricular surface of the sacrum. Posterosuperior to it lies the ligamentous part, the iliac tuberosity. Pitfall: normal iliac-side subchondral sclerosis and accessory sacroiliac joints mimic sacroiliitis. Judge erosions only within the synovial part.

lm:Auricular surface of sacrum|Sacrum.note: Facies auricularis ossis sacri is the ear-shaped sacral surface of the articulatio sacroiliaca, facing the iliac auricular surface. Only its anteroinferior part is synovial. Pitfall: normal subchondral sclerosis on the iliac side, the posterior ligamentous part and an accessory SI joint can mimic sacroiliitis. Assess erosions on the lower synovial part, on both sides.

lm:Axis (C2)|Axis (C2).note: The axis has the dens above the body, large superior facets for C1, and the first bifid spinous process. Pitfall: the subdental synchondrosis is a normal growth line until about age 6. Do not mistake it, or the Mach band where the arch overlaps, for a type II/III dens fracture.

lm:Base of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid.note: The Basis cartilaginis arytenoideae sits on the cricoid lamina. The Processus vocalis projects anteriorly from it and the Processus muscularis posterolaterally. On axial CT it marks the level of the true vocal cords. Pitfall: dense ossification of the base varies between sides. Do not call it sclerotic tumour invasion without an adjacent soft-tissue mass.
landmarks: lm:Articular surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage

lm:Base of coccyx|Coccyx.note: Basis ossis coccygis is the upper surface of the first coccygeal segment, meeting the sacral apex at the symphysis sacrococcygea, with the cornua coccygea behind. Pitfall: the angle of the sacrococcygeal joint and segment fusion vary a lot, so a sharp angle is not a dislocation. Use sagittal reformats.

lm:Base of mandible|Mandible.note: The Basis mandibulae is the thick lower cortical border of the body. The facial artery and vein cross it just in front of the masseter insertion, at the antegonial notch. Pitfall: this vascular groove is a normal cortical notch, not erosion. Also, the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve runs close by and is at risk in surgical approaches.

lm:Base of metatarsal bone|Third metatar.key: lm:Base of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone
lm:Base of metatarsal bone|Third metatar.note: The base articulates proximally with the Os cuneiforme laterale and on its sides with the bases of MT2 and MT4. It is part of the tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) joint line. Pitfall: small flake avulsions or slight dorsal step-off at the base point to a subtle Lisfranc injury. Check sagittal and coronal reformats rather than calling it normal on axial images alone.

lm:Base of phalanx of foot|Proximal phal.key: lm:Base of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
lm:Base of phalanx of foot|Proximal phal.note: Basis phalangis is concave and articulates with the third metatarsal head at the MTP joint. Collateral ligaments sit on each side and the plantar plate attaches plantarly. Pitfall: miscounting rays on oblique axial foot CT. Always count from the hallux and confirm intra-articular extension on sagittal reformats.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve
landmarks: lm:Head of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone
lm:Body of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot

lm:Base of sacrum|Sacrum.note: Basis ossis sacri is the upper surface of S1: the endplate facing discus L5–S1, flanked by the alae and the superior articular processes. Pitfall: transitional lumbosacral anatomy (sacralised L5, lumbarised S1) changes how levels are counted. Count from C2 or the last rib-bearing vertebra before naming segments.

lm:Base of stapes|Stapes.note: The footplate sits in the oval window, closing off the Vestibulum, with the tympanic Nervus facialis just above it. Pitfall: an overhanging facial nerve or partial volume can mimic a thickened footplate or otosclerotic plaque. After trauma, air in the vestibule (pneumolabyrinth) suggests footplate subluxation and should not be missed.
landmarks: lm:Geniculum of facial nerve (geniculate ganglion)|Temporal bone

lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipi.key: lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipital bone
lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipi.note: Pars basilaris forms the lower clivus and joins the sphenoid body at the spheno-occipital synchondrosis, with the pons and basilar artery behind and the nasopharynx in front. Pitfall: an unfused spheno-occipital synchondrosis in adolescents mimics a clival fracture. Patchy fatty marrow can also mimic a lytic lesion such as chordoma.

lm:Body of clavicle|Clavicle.note: Corpus claviculae is the S-shaped shaft. It is convex forward medially and concave forward laterally, and lies above the first rib and the subclavian vessels. Pitfall: the nutrient canal, or the rhomboid fossa near the medial end, can be mistaken for a fracture or a lytic lesion.
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

lm:Body of femur|Femur.note: The Corpus ossis femoris is the femoral shaft. The vasti muscles surround it, and the Linea aspera runs down its back. Pitfall: the normal canal for the nutrient artery runs obliquely through the posterior cortex. Do not mistake it for a fracture line. Also look at the outer cortex for focal thickening, which can come before an atypical femoral fracture.
passing: Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery

lm:Body of hyoid bone|Hyoid bone.note: Corpus ossis hyoidei sits at about C3 and separates the suprahyoid from the infrahyoid neck. The pre-epiglottic space lies posterior to it and the thyrohyoid membrane below. Pitfall: an unfused synchondrosis between body and greater horn is a normal finding, not a fracture. Look for thyroglossal duct cysts closely related to the body.

lm:Body of ilium|Hip bone.note: Corpus ossis ilium forms the superior part of the acetabulum and the supra-acetabular bone stock. Rectus femoris arises anteriorly at the inferior iliac spine, and gluteus minimus covers it externally. Pitfall: in adolescents, the unfused triradiate cartilage and apophyses at the anterior inferior iliac spine mimic fractures or avulsions.

lm:Body of incus|Incus.note: Corpus incudis lies in the epitympanic recess, posterior to the malleus head and below the tegmen tympani, with the aditus ad antrum behind it. Pitfall: on axial images the incus body is the 'cone' and the malleus head is the anterior 'scoop'. Swapping them leads to mislabelled erosions in attic cholesteatoma.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of malleus|Malleus

lm:Body of ischium|Hip bone.note: Corpus ossis ischii forms the posteroinferior acetabulum and posterior column, and the ischiofemoral ligament attaches to it. Obturator internus lies medial to it, with the gemelli posterior. Pitfall: posterior column and posterior wall fractures are easily confused. Trace the fracture line on axial and 3D images to assign the correct Letournel type.

lm:Body of mandible|Mandible.note: The Corpus mandibulae runs from the symphysis to the angle. The alveolar part sits above, the Basis below, and the canalis mandibulae runs inside carrying the inferior alveolar nerve. Pitfall: the corticated canal and nutrient canals can look like fracture lines. Trace the canal across consecutive slices and both cortices.
landmarks: lm:Root of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

lm:Body of metatarsal bone|Third metatar.key: lm:Body of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone
lm:Body of metatarsal bone|Third metatar.note: The shaft lies between the dorsal and plantar interossei, with the extensor tendons on its dorsal side. Pitfall: stress (march) fractures often affect the MT2 and MT3 shafts. Early cases show only faint periosteal reaction or endosteal sclerosis. Do not mistake the oblique nutrient canal for a fracture line.
passing: Perforating branches of plantar metatarsal arteries
Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

lm:Body of phalanx of foot|Proximal phal.key: lm:Body of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
lm:Body of phalanx of foot|Proximal phal.note: Corpus phalangis is the shaft between the base and the head. Extensor tendons run dorsally and the flexor digitorum longus/brevis tendons run plantarly. Pitfall: in a clawed or hammer toe, the shaft is cut obliquely and partial volume can mimic a fracture. Confirm along the long axis with a curved or sagittal reformat.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve
landmarks: lm:Base of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
lm:Head of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
Proximal phalanx of second finger of foot

lm:Body of pubis|Hip bone.note: Corpus ossis pubis forms the anterior acetabulum and continues medially to the symphysis pubica, with the pecten pubis on its superior edge. Iliopsoas and the femoral vessels pass anterior to it. Pitfall: in young patients, irregular symphyseal margins and the parasymphyseal cleft mimic osteitis pubis or a fracture.

lm:Body of rib|Sixth rib.note: Corpus costae is the long curved shaft between the angle and the costal cartilage. It is bounded by the intercostal muscles above and below and by the pleura internally. Pitfall: nondisplaced fractures parallel to the axial plane are missed. Use curved/MIP reformats, and confirm the rib count from the first rib.

lm:Body of sphenoid bone|Sphenoid bone.note: Corpus ossis sphenoidei is the cuboid central part that contains the sinus. The sella and clivus lie above and behind it, and its inferior surface faces the nasopharynx roof, joining the vaginal processes and pterygoid plates. Pitfall: incomplete clival or arrested sinus pneumatisation (fatty marrow) mimics a lytic lesion. Do not report it as a tumour.
landmarks: lm:Vaginal process of sphenoid bone|Sphenoid bone

lm:Body of talus|Talus.note: Corpus tali carries the trochlea above, malleolar facets on both sides and the posterior calcaneal facet below. Medially it borders the deltoid ligament and tibialis posterior tendon. Pitfall: tell body fractures (into both talocrural and subtalar joints) apart from neck fractures; classification and avascular necrosis risk differ.

lm:Body of ulna|Ulna.note: Corpus ulnae is a triangular shaft that tapers distally. It is bordered by flexor digitorum profundus anteriorly, the flexor carpi ulnaris aponeurosis medially, extensor carpi ulnaris posteriorly and the interosseous membrane laterally. Pitfall: a shaft fracture is not isolated until a radial head dislocation (Monteggia) is excluded. Always image the elbow.
neighbours: Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris

lm:Calcaneal sulcus|Calcaneus.note: Sulcus calcanei is the groove between the posterior and middle talar facets. Together with the sulcus ossis tali it forms the canalis/sinus tarsi, which holds the ligamentum talocalcaneum interosseum. Pitfall: on oblique slices the sulcus can look like a widened subtalar joint or a fracture line.

lm:Calcaneal tubercle|Calcaneus.note: Tuberculum calcanei is the anterior plantar tubercle, where the ligamentum plantare longum and the ligamentum calcaneocuboideum plantare attach, deep to the quadratus plantae. Pitfall: do not mix it up with the processus medialis/lateralis tuberis calcanei at the posterior heel. Enthesophytes here are not plantar fascia spurs.

lm:Calcaneal tuberosity|Calcaneus.note: Tuber calcanei is the posterior heel prominence where the tendo calcaneus inserts, with the bursa subcutanea calcanea lying superficial to it. Pitfall: a posterosuperior prominence (Haglund) or an insertional enthesophyte can be mistaken for an avulsion fracture. Look for a cortical defect and a displaced fragment.

lm:Carotid sulcus|Sphenoid bone.note: Shallow S-shaped groove on the lateral Corpus ossis sphenoidei, lining the medial wall of the Sinus cavernosus and running from the Foramen lacerum to the clinoid region. Pitfall: lateral sphenoid sinus pneumatization leaves only a paper-thin or dehiscent wall here; this is a normal variant, not erosion, but report it before endoscopic surgery.

lm:Carpal articular surface|Radius.note: Facies articularis carpea is biconcave, with scaphoid and lunate fossae separated by a sagittal ridge. Dorsal radiocarpal ligaments run along its rim. Pitfall: the interfossal ridge can mimic an intra-articular fracture line. Report true articular step-off or gap of 2 mm or more on coronal and sagittal reformats.

lm:Cerebellar fossa|Occipital bone.note: Fossa cerebellaris is the paired hollow of the occipital squama below the transverse sinus groove, split by the internal occipital crest and holding the cerebellar hemispheres. Pitfall: beam-hardening streaks from the dense posterior fossa bone can mimic a low-density infarct or high-density extra-axial blood.

lm:Cerebral fossa|Occipital bone.note: Fossa cerebralis is the paired upper hollow of the occipital squama above the transverse sinus groove. It holds the occipital poles on either side of the superior sagittal sinus groove. Pitfall: the lambdoid suture, accessory sutures and wormian bones crossing this area can mimic linear fractures in paediatric trauma.
landmarks: lm:Squamous part of occipital bone|Occipital bone

lm:Cerebral surface of greater wing|Sphe.key: lm:Cerebral surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
lm:Cerebral surface of greater wing|Sphe.note: Concave anterior floor of the middle cranial fossa that cradles the Polus temporalis. It meets the squamous Os temporale posterolaterally. Pitfall: beam-hardening and partial volume against this curved bone mimic temporal pole contusion or a thin extra-axial collection. Check bone and brain windows in coronal reformats.
landmarks: lm:Temporal surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone

lm:Cervical vertebra|Vertebra C4.note: C4 is typical: small body with Processus uncinati, bifid Processus spinosus, and transverse processes pierced by the Foramen transversarium, with the C3–C4 and C4–C5 discs above and below. Pitfall: miscounting levels; count down from C2 on sagittal reconstructions, not by thyroid cartilage or hyoid height.

lm:Chiasmatic sulcus|Sphenoid bone.note: Transverse groove between the Limbus sphenoidalis in front and the Tuberculum sellae behind. Laterally it leads to both Canales optici, and the sphenoid sinus lies directly below. Pitfall: the Chiasma opticum usually lies above and behind the sulcus, not inside it. Don't use the groove to place the chiasm.

lm:Clavicular facet|Scapula.note: The Facies articularis clavicularis on the medial acromion faces the Facies articularis acromialis of the clavicle. Normal AC joint width is about 1–7 mm. Pitfall: normal joint width differs between people and narrows with age. Compare with the other side and assess the coracoclavicular distance before calling an AC separation.

lm:Clavicular notch|Manubrium of sternum.note: Incisura clavicularis is the superolateral manubrial facet that meets the medial clavicle through the Discus articularis, with the first costal cartilage just below. Pitfall: the unfused medial clavicular epiphysis (until about age 25) can mimic a fracture. Compare both sides at the same level so posterior sternoclavicular dislocation is not missed.

lm:Coccygeal horn|Coccyx.note: The Cornua coccygea project upward from the dorsal Basis ossis coccygis. They meet the Cornua sacralia through the Ligamentum intercornuale and border the opening of the Hiatus sacralis. Pitfall: the gap between the sacral and coccygeal horns is a normal feature. Do not read it as a fracture, and do not mistake an unfused horn for a fracture fragment.

lm:Coccyx|Coccyx.note: The Os coccygis lies below the Symphysis sacrococcygea. The pelvic floor muscles (Musculus coccygeus and the iliococcygeus fibres) attach to it laterally, and the Musculus gluteus maximus covers it from behind. Pitfall: the angle of the coccyx varies a lot, and its segments may or may not be fused. Neither finding means a fracture or dislocation unless there is cortical disruption or soft-tissue swelling.

lm:Colliculus of arytenoid cartilage|Ary.note: The Colliculus is a small prominence near the apex where the Crista arcuata ends. It lies at the level of the vestibular fold. Pitfall: this level sits above the glottis. Do not use it as the glottic level in staging, because it is easily confused with the vocal process plane.
neighbours: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle

lm:Condylar canal|Occipital bone.note: Canalis condylaris runs from the condylar fossa behind the occipital condyle to the sigmoid sinus and carries an emissary vein. It lies behind and above the hypoglossal canal. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the Canalis nervi hypoglossi. It is often missing or asymmetric on one side, and that is a normal variant.

lm:Condylar fossa|Occipital bone.note: Fossa condylaris is the hollow behind each occipital condyle. It receives the posterior rim of the atlas facet in extension and opens into the condylar canal. Pitfall: uneven depth, or the opening of the condylar emissary canal, can mimic an occipital condyle fracture; confirm on coronal and sagittal reformats.

lm:Condylar process (head of mandible)|M.note: Caput mandibulae sits in the Fossa mandibularis, with the Tuberculum articulare in front and the tympanic plate and external acoustic meatus behind; the lateral pterygoid inserts anteromedially. Pitfall: in an open-mouth scan the condyle normally sits under the tubercle, which is not dislocation. A bifid condyle variant can look like a sagittal intracapsular fracture.
landmarks: lm:External acoustic meatus (medial end, tympanic membrane)|Temporal bone
neighbours: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

lm:Condyle of humerus|Humerus.note: Condylus humeri includes the trochlea and capitulum together with the fossae; the epicondyles flank it. It articulates with the incisura trochlearis of the ulna and with the radial head. Pitfall: in children, unfused ossification centres (CRITOE order) can mimic fracture fragments, and an entrapped medial epicondyle can be overlooked.
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris

lm:Conoid tubercle|Clavicle.note: Tuberculum conoideum is on the posteroinferior lateral clavicle, where the ligamentum conoideum attaches, medial to the trapezoid line. Pitfall: a prominent tubercle, or a variant coracoclavicular joint, can look like an exostosis or a fracture fragment. Its tilt also changes how coracoclavicular distance is measured.
passing: Anterior division of superior trunk of brachial plexus
Anterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus

lm:Coracoid process|Scapula.note: The Processus coracoideus projects anterolaterally above the subscapularis. The conjoint tendon (short head of biceps, coracobrachialis) and pectoralis minor attach to it. Pitfall: the coracoid base growth plate and the unfused tip apophysis in young patients can look like fractures. Look for coracoid fractures in AC injuries.

lm:Coronoid fossa|Humerus.note: Fossa coronoidea is the anterior depression above the trochlea that holds the processus coronoideus in flexion. It is intracapsular and covered by the anterior fat pad and brachialis. Pitfall: thin bone between it and the olecranon fossa can be perforated (supratrochlear foramen), a variant that should not be called a lytic lesion. A displaced anterior fat pad suggests an effusion.

lm:Coronoid process (tip)|Mandible.note: Processus coronoideus projects up under the zygomatic arch, wrapped by the temporalis insertion, in front of the mandibular notch. Pitfall: on axial CT the coronoid tip under the arch can look like a loose bony fragment. Coronoid hyperplasia, or a depressed arch fracture pressing on it, causes trismus.

lm:Coronoid process of ulna|Ulna.note: Processus coronoideus forms the anterior buttress of the Incisura trochlearis. Musculus brachialis inserts below it, and the radial notch lies laterally. Pitfall: a small tip flake is a marker of the terrible triad or of posteromedial instability. Report the fragment size and anteromedial facet involvement on sagittal and 3D CT.

lm:Costal groove|Sixth rib.note: Sulcus costae runs along the inferior internal margin of the rib. It shelters the intercostal neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve from superior to inferior) between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. Pitfall: the normal scalloped thin inferior cortex can mimic erosion. The groove is shallow anteriorly, so needles should pass just above the lower rib.

lm:Costal notches|Body of sternum.note: The incisurae costales on the lateral edges of the sternal body receive costal cartilages 2–7, with the internal thoracic vessels and parasternal nodes just behind them. Pitfall: calcified costal cartilage, or irregular ossification at the sternocostal junction, can look like a fracture or a lytic lesion. Compare with the opposite side.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

lm:Costal part of transverse process|Ver.key: lm:Costal part of transverse process|Vertebra L3
lm:Costal part of transverse process|Ver.note: Lumbar transverse processes are costal elements: Musculus psoas major lies anterior and quadratus lumborum lateral, with lumbar plexus branches inside psoas. Pitfall: transverse process fractures are easily missed on axial images and are markers of high-energy trauma; also check for psoas haematoma and renal injury. L3 has the longest process, which helps level counting.
landmarks: lm:Lateral part of transverse process|Vertebra L3
neighbours: Dorsal parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles

lm:Costal surface of scapula|Scapula.note: The Facies costalis faces the thoracic wall. Subscapularis fills the Fossa subscapularis, and the serratus anterior lies between the scapula and the ribs. Pitfall: on axial slices the thin scapular body can overlap a rib and suggest a rib lesion or fracture. Follow each rib across consecutive slices.

lm:Crest of head of rib|Sixth rib.key: lm:Crest of head of rib|Sixth rib
lm:Crest of head of rib|Sixth rib.note: Crista capitis costae is the ridge between the two articular facets of the rib head. It points at the T5–T6 disc and is tethered there by the ligamentum intraarticulare. Pitfall: the sixth rib articulates with both T5 and T6, so do not assign it to a single vertebra when counting levels.
neighbours: Intra-articular ligament of head of rib
Radiate ligament of head of rib

lm:Crest of lesser tubercle|Humerus.note: Crista tuberculi minoris forms the medial lip of the sulcus intertubercularis and is where teres major and latissimus dorsi insert. Pectoralis major inserts on the opposite lateral lip. Pitfall: lateral and medial lips can be swapped on rotated arms; an empty sulcus indicates the long biceps tendon has dislocated medially over this crest.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle
Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

lm:Crest of neck of rib|Sixth rib.key: lm:Crest of neck of rib|Sixth rib
lm:Crest of neck of rib|Sixth rib.note: Crista colli costae is the sharp superior ridge of the rib neck, between the head and the tubercle. The superior costotransverse ligament and internal intercostal membrane attach here. Pitfall: in a thin-slice partial volume, the ridge can look like a spur or periosteal reaction. Compare it with the contralateral rib.

lm:Crown of tooth|Lower first molar toot.key: lm:Crown of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Crown of tooth|Lower first molar toot.note: Corona dentis is the enamel-covered part above the gingiva and alveolar crest. It sits between the second premolar (mesial) and the second molar (distal) and occludes with the upper first molar. Pitfall: streak artefact from crown restorations hides caries and adjacent structures. State laterality by FDI number (36 left, 46 right).
landmarks: lm:Occlusal surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Neck of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Vestibular surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Root of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

lm:Cruciform eminence|Occipital bone.note: Eminentia cruciformis is the cross formed by the transverse and superior sagittal sinus grooves and the internal occipital crest. It is centred on the internal occipital protuberance at the confluence of sinuses (torcular). Pitfall: normally dense sinus blood or an asymmetric torcular can mimic a tentorial subdural haematoma or sinus thrombosis.

lm:Cusp of tooth|Lower first molar tooth.key: lm:Cusp of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Cusp of tooth|Lower first molar tooth.note: Cuspides of the lower first molar (usually five) rise from the occlusal surface and interdigitate with the upper first molar. Pitfall: in a closed-mouth scan, partial volume between interlocking upper and lower cusps can mimic fused or bridged crowns. Separate the arches on coronal or sagittal reconstructions.
landmarks: lm:Occlusal surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Lingual surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Mesial surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Crown of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Neck of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

lm:Deltoid tubercle|Scapula.note: The Tuberculum deltoideum is on the inferior lip of the Spina scapulae near its medial root, where the trapezius tendon inserts and rhomboid minor attaches nearby. Pitfall: this normal bony bump at a tendon insertion can be mistaken for a periosteal reaction or an osteochondroma.

lm:Dens axis|Axis (C2).note: The dens sits against the anterior arch of C1 at the fovea dentis and is held from behind by the transverse ligament. Pitfall: an os odontoideum has smooth corticated margins and a hypertrophied anterior arch. Do not mistake it for an acute type II fracture at the base of the dens.

lm:Digastric fossa|Mandible.note: The Fossa digastrica is a shallow paired depression on the inner surface of the base, beside the midline. The anterior belly of the digastric arises here, below the mylohyoid. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the Fovea sublingualis, which lies above the mylohyoid line, or with the submandibular fossa further back. Its normal shallow cortical scalloping is not erosion.

lm:Distal surface of tooth|Lower first m.key: lm:Distal surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Distal surface of tooth|Lower first m.note: Facies distalis faces backward along the arch and contacts the mesial surface of the lower second molar above the interdental alveolar septum. Pitfall: beam hardening between two adjacent enamel surfaces produces dark interproximal bands. These mimic interproximal caries or septal bone loss.
landmarks: lm:Neck of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Occlusal surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Root of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Lingual surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Crown of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

lm:Dorsal radial tubercle|Radius.note: Tuberculum dorsale radii (Lister) separates the 2nd extensor compartment (ECRL/ECRB) from the 3rd (EPL), which turns around its ulnar side. Pitfall: a non-displaced distal radius fracture through the tubercle, or a protruding dorsal screw, can lead to later EPL rupture. Comment on the EPL groove.

lm:Dorsal surface of sacrum|Sacrum.note: Facies dorsalis ossis sacri is convex and rough. It carries the median, intermediate and lateral sacral crests and the posterior sacral foramina, and is covered by the erector spinae origin and the thoracolumbar fascia. Pitfall: an unfused posterior arch (spina bifida occulta of S1) is a common variant and should not be called a fracture.

lm:Dorsum sellae|Sphenoid bone.note: Bony plate forming the posterior wall of the Fossa hypophysialis. It continues down into the clivus, with the basilar artery and pons directly behind it. Pitfall: thinning or demineralization signals chronic raised intracranial pressure or a sellar mass. Don't dismiss it as an oblique-slice artifact; compare midline sagittal reformats.

lm:Ethmoidal notch|Frontal bone.note: Midline gap between the orbital plates that holds the cribriform plate of the ethmoid. The roofs of the ethmoid cells (foveolae) join here. Pitfall: a deep olfactory fossa (Keros III) and an asymmetric skull base height raise the risk of iatrogenic CSF leak. Report the canal of the A. ethmoidea anterior when it hangs below the roof.
landmarks: lm:Foramen caecum of frontal bone|Frontal bone

lm:External acoustic meatus (medial end,.key: lm:External acoustic meatus (medial end, tympanic membrane)|Temporal bone
lm:External acoustic meatus (medial end,.note: The Membrana tympanica closes the medial end of the meatus and is attached to the Manubrium mallei. The tympanic cavity lies beyond it, and the anterior wall borders the TMJ. Pitfall: a persistent foramen tympanicum (Huschke) in the anteroinferior wall is a normal variant, not erosion. Cerumen against the membrane can also mimic a mass.

lm:External occipital protuberance|Occip.note: Protuberantia occipitalis externa (inion) is the midline bump where the superior nuchal lines meet, anchoring the Ligamentum nuchae and trapezius. It sits slightly below the internal protuberance and torcular. Pitfall: a prominent occipital spur (enthesophyte) is a normal variant; do not call it an exostosis or a fracture fragment.

lm:External opening of carotid canal|Tem.key: lm:External opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone
lm:External opening of carotid canal|Tem.note: Apertura externa canalis carotici lies on the inferior petrous surface, anteromedial to the jugular foramen and separated from it by the caroticojugular spine. Pitfall: an aberrant ICA (absent vertical canal, enlarged inferior tympanic canaliculus, vessel crossing the promontory) mimics glomus tympanicum; never biopsy it.
landmarks: lm:Internal opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone

lm:External surface of parietal bone|Par.key: lm:External surface of parietal bone|Parietal bone
lm:External surface of parietal bone|Par.note: This convex outer table lies deep to the galea and scalp, with the temporal lines and parietal eminence on it. Pitfall: parietal foramina, vascular grooves and the thinning of senile parietal atrophy (which is bilateral) mimic fractures or lytic lesions. Compare both sides and use 3D VR.

lm:External surface of squamous part of.key: lm:External surface of squamous part of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:External surface of squamous part of.note: Convex outer table of the frontal squama, covered by the Galea aponeurotica and scalp. Pitfall: diploic vein channels and arachnoid granulation pits on the inner side can mimic fractures or lytic lesions. A true fracture has sharp, non-corticated margins and usually overlying soft-tissue swelling.

lm:Facet for dens|Atlas (C1).note: The fovea dentis is on the posterior surface of the anterior arch and forms the median atlantoaxial joint with the dens. Measure the atlantodental interval here on midsagittal reformats. Pitfall: an oblique or off-midline plane falsely widens the interval. Normal is at most 3 mm in adults and 5 mm in children.

lm:Facet for plantar calcaneonavicular l.note: Inferomedial facet of caput tali resting on the spring ligament between sustentaculum tali and navicular, part of the acetabulum pedis. Pitfall: the ligament itself is barely visible on CT; plantar sag and uncovering of the talar head point to spring ligament failure in acquired flatfoot, not to coalition.

lm:Femur|Femur.note: The Os femoris is surrounded by the Musculus vastus intermedius in front and the Musculus vastus lateralis on the side. The short head of the biceps femoris arises from the lower part of the Linea aspera. Pitfall: the ridge of the Linea aspera can look like periosteal reaction on axial slices. Do not mistake it for a periosteal reaction.

lm:Fibula|Fibula.note: Thin diaphysis lying posterolateral to the tibia. The fibular muscles lie lateral to it and the deep flexors (Flexor hallucis longus, Tibialis posterior) posteromedial. Pitfall: the nutrient canal runs obliquely through the cortex and mimics a nondisplaced fracture. A fibular fracture far from an ankle injury can be a Maisonneuve pattern, so image the whole bone.

lm:Fifth metatarsal bone|Fifth metatarsa.note: Lateral metatarsal that articulates proximally with the cuboid. The Fibularis brevis inserts on its tuberosity. Pitfall: the longitudinal apophysis in adolescents and an os vesalianum mimic fracture. Also separate a tuberosity avulsion from a Jones fracture at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction, which carries a worse prognosis.

lm:First metatarsal bone|First metatarsa.note: Shortest, thickest metatarsal; its base articulates with the Os cuneiforme mediale. The Fibularis longus inserts plantarolaterally on the base. Pitfall: in Lisfranc injury, subtle misalignment at the first and second tarsometatarsal joints is easy to miss. The hallucal sesamoids, including a bipartite sesamoid, are not fractures of the head.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
neighbours: Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis
Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis

lm:Foramen caecum of frontal bone|Fronta.key: lm:Foramen caecum of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Foramen caecum of frontal bone|Fronta.note: Small midline pit between the frontal crest and the crista galli of the ethmoid, where the falx cerebri attaches. Pitfall: in children, a persistent wide foramen caecum, especially with a bifid crista galli, suggests a nasal dermoid sinus tract or encephalocele. A small one in adults is normal.

lm:Foramen lacerum|Temporal bone.note: Foramen lacerum is a cartilage-filled gap between the petrous apex, sphenoid body and basiocciput, with the ICA crossing over its upper surface. Pitfall: don't confuse it with foramen ovale (posterolateral) or the carotid canal. It is a route for nasopharyngeal carcinoma to spread to the cavernous sinus.
landmarks: lm:Internal opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone
lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipital bone

lm:Foramen magnum|Occipital bone.note: The opening is bounded anteriorly by the basion, laterally by the condyles and posteriorly by the opisthion. It carries the medulla oblongata, the Arteriae vertebrales and the spinal roots of XI. Pitfall: cerebellar tonsils normally lie up to 5 mm below the basion–opisthion line. Measure on a true midsagittal reformat before calling Chiari I.

lm:Foramen ovale|Sphenoid bone.note: Oval opening in the posterior Ala major for the Nervus mandibularis (V3) and the accessory meningeal artery. It lies anteromedial to the Foramen spinosum and opens into the infratemporal fossa. Pitfall: don't confuse it with the smaller spinosum (posterolateral) or the inconstant foramen of Vesalius (anteromedial). Mild left-right asymmetry is normal.
passing: Accessory branch of middle meningeal artery
landmarks: lm:Internal opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone
neighbours: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

lm:Foramen rotundum|Sphenoid bone.note: Short horizontal canal in the root of the Ala major, below the superior orbital fissure. It carries the Nervus maxillaris (V2) from the middle cranial fossa to the pterygopalatine fossa, lateral to the sphenoid sinus. Pitfall: on coronal CT it lies superolateral to the Canalis pterygoideus, which is inferomedial. Don't swap the two.

lm:Foramen spinosum|Sphenoid bone.note: Small round foramen posterolateral to the Foramen ovale and anteromedial to the Spina ossis sphenoidei. It carries the Arteria meningea media. Pitfall: an absent or tiny spinosum suggests a persistent stapedial artery or an ophthalmic origin of the middle meningeal artery, not a fracture. A fracture through it raises the risk of epidural haematoma.
passing: Accessory branch of middle meningeal artery
landmarks: lm:Internal opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone

lm:Foramen transversarium|Vertebra C4.note: The foramen lies between the anterior and posterior tubercles, lateral to the body and anterior to the Sulcus nervi spinalis, and carries the Arteria and Vena vertebralis. Pitfall: asymmetric or duplicated foramina are normal variants; a fracture line running into the foramen needs CTA to exclude vertebral artery injury.
landmarks: lm:Anterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4

lm:Fossa for lacrimal gland|Frontal bone.note: Shallow depression in the anterolateral orbital roof, behind the zygomatic process, that holds the Glandula lacrimalis. Pitfall: scalloping or remodelling of the fossa by a slowly growing mass, such as a pleomorphic adenoma or dermoid, is easy to miss. Destructive erosion suggests malignancy. Compare with the other side.
landmarks: lm:Orbital surface of frontal bone|Frontal bone

lm:Fovea for ligament of head of femur|F.key: lm:Fovea for ligament of head of femur|Femur
lm:Fovea for ligament of head of femur|F.note: The Fovea capitis ossis femoris is a pit just below and behind the centre of the femoral head, where the Ligamentum capitis femoris attaches. It faces the acetabular fossa. Pitfall: this normal pit and its irregular edges can look like an osteochondral defect, an impaction fracture or a subchondral cyst. The fovea is the only place without articular cartilage.

lm:Frontal crest|Frontal bone.note: Midline ridge on the inner surface of the frontal squama that anchors the falx cerebri. Higher up, it divides to form the sulcus for the Sinus sagittalis superior. Pitfall: calcification or ossification of the falx next to the crest is normal. Do not call it a subdural or interhemispheric haemorrhage.
landmarks: lm:Septum of frontal sinuses|Sinus of frontal bone

lm:Frontal eminence|Frontal bone.note: Paired rounded bulge of the frontal squama above each superciliary arch, overlying the frontal lobes. Pitfall: normal asymmetry in prominence, plagiocephaly, or a positioning tilt can look like a calvarial deformity. Check cortical integrity and both sides before suggesting a lesion.
passing: Frontal branch of superficial temporal artery

lm:Frontal margin of greater wing|Spheno.key: lm:Frontal margin of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
lm:Frontal margin of greater wing|Spheno.note: Serrated upper edge of the Ala major that joins the Os frontale at the sphenofrontal suture, forming the anterior part of the pterion. Pitfall: the suture can mimic a fracture. A suture is symmetric, corticated and serrated; a fracture is sharp, non-corticated and often has an overlying haematoma. Always compare with the opposite side.
landmarks: lm:Parietal margin of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
neighbours: Orbital part of  inferior frontal gyrus

lm:Frontal part of orbital margin|Fronta.key: lm:Frontal part of orbital margin|Frontal bone
lm:Frontal part of orbital margin|Fronta.note: The Pars frontalis marginis orbitalis forms the superior orbital rim, running from the nasal part to the frontozygomatic suture, with the Glandula lacrimalis behind its lateral third. Pitfall: the supraorbital notch/foramen is a smooth cortical defect in the rim and should not be called a fracture.
landmarks: lm:Zygomatic process of frontal bone|Frontal bone

lm:Fundus of internal acoustic meatus (a.key: lm:Fundus of internal acoustic meatus (approx.)|Temporal bone
lm:Fundus of internal acoustic meatus (a.note: Fundus meatus acustici interni is divided by the crista transversa (falciform crest) and Bill's bar: the facial nerve is anterosuperior, the cochlear nerve anteroinferior, and the vestibular nerves posterior. Pitfall: don't mistake the crista for a fracture. A cochlear aperture narrower than about 1.4 mm suggests a deficient cochlear nerve.
landmarks: lm:Geniculum of facial nerve (geniculate ganglion)|Temporal bone

lm:Geniculum of facial nerve (geniculate.key: lm:Geniculum of facial nerve (geniculate ganglion)|Temporal bone
lm:Geniculum of facial nerve (geniculate.note: Geniculum nervi facialis is the anterior genu where the labyrinthine segment turns into the tympanic segment, anterolateral to the cochlea and beneath the middle fossa floor; the greater petrosal nerve leaves anteriorly. Pitfall: the labyrinthine segment is easily confused with the basal turn of the cochlea. Transverse fractures often cross the geniculate fossa.
landmarks: lm:Fundus of internal acoustic meatus (approx.)|Temporal bone

lm:Genion|Mandible.note: The genion is the midline point on the lingual surface of the symphysis, at the Spinae mentales (the origin of the genioglossus and geniohyoid). Pitfall: do not confuse genion with gonion, the angle of the mandible. They are paired and sound alike, and the label here may sit wrongly near the angle.

lm:Genu of internal capsule|White matter.key: lm:Genu of internal capsule|White matter of telencephalon
lm:Genu of internal capsule|White matter.note: Genu capsulae internae lies at the level of the foramen interventriculare, at the apex of the V between the caudate head, the thalamus and the globus pallidus. Pitfall: calcification of the globus pallidus next to the genu can be mistaken for haemorrhage. A pallidal calcification is symmetric and much denser.

lm:Glabella|Frontal bone.note: Smooth midline prominence between the superciliary arches, above the nasion and in front of the frontal sinuses. Pitfall: fractures here can involve the anterior table only or extend to the posterior table and frontal sinus outflow tract. Assess both tables and the nasofrontal duct region separately.
landmarks: lm:Nasal margin of frontal bone|Frontal bone

lm:Glenoid fossa|Scapula.note: The Fossa glenoidea is the shallow, pear-shaped articular surface that holds the humeral head. The labrum surrounds its rim. Pitfall: a normal bare-area or notch-like contour in the anteroinferior glenoid can look like a bony Bankart lesion. Assess glenoid bone loss en face on sagittal reformats with the humerus subtracted.

lm:Glenoid process of scapula|Scapula.note: The Processus glenoideus is the lateral articular mass of the scapula, joined to the body by the Collum scapulae. The supraglenoid and infraglenoid tubercles sit above and below it. Pitfall: the ring-like secondary ossification centres at the glenoid rim in adolescents can look like rim fractures.

lm:Gluteal surface of ilium|Hip bone.note: Facies glutea ossis ilium is the external surface of the iliac wing, covered by gluteus minimus and gluteus medius. The iliac fossa with iliacus lies on the opposite, inner surface. Pitfall: iliac bone-marrow biopsy tracts and nutrient vascular foramina mimic lytic lesions or fracture lines.

lm:Gluteal tuberosity|Femur.note: The Tuberositas glutea is on the back and side of the upper femoral shaft, where the deep fibres of the Musculus gluteus maximus insert. It continues downward into the lateral lip of the Linea aspera. Pitfall: a prominent tuberosity, sometimes called a third trochanter, or enthesophytes at this site can mimic periosteal reaction or an exostosis.

lm:Gnathion|Mandible.note: The gnathion is the lowest, most anterior midline point of the mandibular symphysis, between pogonion and menton. It is used for cephalometric and facial-height measurements. Pitfall: in obliquely positioned heads, a point off the midline or the Tuberculum mentale can be taken by mistake. Define it on a true midsagittal reformat.

lm:Greater horn of hyoid bone|Hyoid bone.key: lm:Greater horn of hyoid bone|Hyoid bone
lm:Greater horn of hyoid bone|Hyoid bone.note: Cornu majus runs posterolaterally along the lateral pharyngeal wall. Its tip lies medial to the carotid bifurcation and the internal jugular vein. Pitfall: a calcified triticeous cartilage in the lateral thyrohyoid ligament, between the horn tip and the superior thyroid horn, mimics a fracture fragment, foreign body or carotid calcification.

lm:Greater sciatic foramen|Hip bone.note: Foramen ischiadicum majus is bounded by the greater sciatic notch, the sacrospinous ligament and the sacrotuberous ligament, and piriformis divides it. The sciatic nerve and inferior gluteal and internal pudendal vessels exit below piriformis. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the lesser sciatic foramen below the ischial spine, which carries the pudendal nerve back into the perineum.

lm:Greater sciatic notch|Hip bone.note: Incisura ischiadica major is the deep posterior concavity of the os coxae between the posterior inferior iliac spine and the ischial spine, and piriformis passes through it. Pitfall: fractures extending into the notch put the superior gluteal artery at risk, as it hugs the bone above piriformis. Look for active extravasation on CT angiography.

lm:Greater trochanter|Femur.note: The Trochanter major has facets where the Musculus gluteus minimus (front) and the Musculus gluteus medius (side and top) insert. The Tractus iliotibialis lies over it, with bursae in between. Pitfall: an isolated trochanter fracture may continue into the intertrochanteric region without being visible on CT. Also, enthesophytes at the tendon insertions are not avulsion fragments.
neighbours: Trochanteric bursa of gluteus minimus muscle

lm:Greater tubercle|Humerus.note: Tuberculum majus is the posterolateral prominence of the proximal humerus, with facets for supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor, under the bursa subdeltoidea and deltoid. Pitfall: undisplaced fractures of the greater tubercle are often missed after anterior dislocation; normal cortical irregularity or cysts at the footprint should not be overcalled as erosions.

lm:Greater wing|Sphenoid bone.note: The Ala major separates the middle cranial fossa from the orbit and the temporal and infratemporal fossae. It is bounded by the sphenofrontal, sphenoparietal and sphenosquamosal sutures. Pitfall: wing thickening has three look-alikes. Meningioma hyperostosis is reactive, fibrous dysplasia has ground-glass bone, and NF1 wing dysplasia is a defect. Don't call asymmetry normal without characterizing it.
landmarks: lm:Temporal surface of frontal bone|Frontal bone
neighbours: Orbital part of  inferior frontal gyrus

lm:Groove for marginal sinus|Occipital b.note: This shallow groove on the endocranial rim of the foramen magnum holds the Sinus marginalis, which links the occipital sinus to the vertebral venous plexus. Pitfall: a prominent marginal sinus or a smooth notch in the rim can mimic an erosive lesion or a fracture. Check for symmetry and an intact cortex.

lm:Groove for occipital sinus|Occipital.note: The groove runs along the internal occipital crest, from the confluens sinuum down to the foramen magnum, and holds the falx cerebelli. Pitfall: a large occipital sinus, which is common in children, can look like a midline dural venous sinus thrombosis or a subdural collection. A midline vascular channel can also mimic a fracture line.

lm:Groove for popliteus muscle|Femur.note: The Sulcus popliteus lies on the lateral condyle just below and behind the Epicondylus lateralis. The popliteus tendon origin sits in it, inside the capsule, and the Ligamentum collaterale fibulare origin is just anterosuperior. Pitfall: a small posterolateral avulsion fragment here (from the popliteus or collateral ligament) means posterolateral corner injury. Do not dismiss it as a fabella.

lm:Groove for spinal nerve|Vertebra C4.note: Sulcus nervi spinalis runs on the upper surface of the transverse process, behind the Foramen transversarium and between the tubercles, and carries the exiting C4 nerve (C5 runs over C5). Pitfall: on axial images the groove can be mistaken for the foramen transversarium; the foramen is fully enclosed by bone and the groove is open superiorly.
landmarks: lm:Posterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4
lm:Anterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4

lm:Groove for subclavius muscle|Clavicle.note: Sulcus musculi subclavii runs along the underside of the clavicular shaft, where the subclavius sits above the subclavian vein. Pitfall: the shallow groove and the nutrient foramen can look like cortical erosion. The subclavius muscle can protect the vessels in shaft fractures, but there is still a risk of vascular injury.
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis.key: lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of calcaneus|Calcaneus
lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis.note: This groove runs on the underside of the sustentaculum tali, and the flexor hallucis longus tendon passes through it. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the talar groove for the same tendon, which lies between the posterior talar tubercles, or with an os trigonum. Sustentacular fractures can trap this tendon.

lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis.key: lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of talus|Talus
lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis.note: Sulcus between the tuberculum mediale and laterale of the posterior process, carrying the FHL tendon down to the groove under sustentaculum tali. Pitfall: an os trigonum or Stieda process lateral to the groove can mimic a lateral tubercle fracture; smooth corticated margins favour the normal variant.

lm:Groove for transverse sinus|Occipital.note: The groove runs horizontally along the tentorial attachment, from the internal occipital protuberance to the mastoid angle of the parietal bone. Pitfall: the right side is usually dominant and left hypoplasia is common. Do not call an asymmetric groove or a dense sinus thrombosis without venography, and do not mistake arachnoid granulations for clot.

lm:Groove for ulnar nerve|Humerus.note: Sulcus nervi ulnaris lies on the back of the medial epicondyle, forming the floor of the cubital tunnel under Osborne's retinaculum. The ulnar nerve runs in it alongside the superior ulnar collateral artery. Pitfall: an accessory anconeus epitrochlearis or osteophytes can narrow the tunnel; medial epicondyle fractures risk injuring the nerve.
neighbours: Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

lm:Groove for vertebral artery|Atlas (C1.note: The sulcus arteriae vertebralis runs along the upper surface of the posterior arch, behind the lateral mass. It carries the V3 segment of the vertebral artery. Pitfall: a ponticulus posticus (arcuate foramen) turns the groove into a bony canal. Do not mistake it for a fracture fragment, and report it before C1 lateral mass screw placement.

lm:Groove of pterygoid hamulus|Sphenoid.note: Groove at the base of the Hamulus pterygoideus, at the lower tip of the medial pterygoid plate. Here the tendon of the tensor veli palatini turns medially into the soft palate. Pitfall: an elongated or separately ossified hamulus can mimic a fracture fragment or foreign body. Hamular bursitis can mimic a palatal mass.

lm:Handle of malleus|Malleus.note: The Manubrium mallei runs down and back inside the Membrana tympanica, in the mesotympanum. On coronal CT it lies parallel and lateral to the Crus longum incudis. Pitfall: do not swap the manubrium and the long limb of the incus. These two parallel lines are easy to confuse, especially when looking for erosion in cholesteatoma.
landmarks: lm:External acoustic meatus (medial end, tympanic membrane)|Temporal bone

lm:Head of femur|Femur.note: The Caput ossis femoris sits in the acetabulum of the Os coxae. Its only gap in articular cartilage is at the fovea. Pitfall: the physeal scar and herniation pits (synovial cysts at the femoral neck) are normal findings. Do not mistake them for a fracture line or early osteonecrosis. On CT, osteonecrosis shows as subchondral sclerosis or a crescent of collapse.

lm:Head of humerus|Humerus.note: Caput humeri articulates medially with the glenoid cavity of the scapula. The capsule and supraspinatus tendon cover it superiorly, and the deltoid covers it laterally. Pitfall: a Hill-Sachs defect lies posterolaterally at or above coracoid level. Flattening of the posterolateral head below that level is the normal neck contour, not an impaction fracture.

lm:Head of malleus|Malleus.note: The Caput mallei sits in the epitympanic recess, below the tegmen tympani, and joins the Corpus incudis behind it. Pitfall: soft tissue around the head in Prussak space or the attic may be a cholesteatoma, not a normal fold. Check whether the scutum and ossicles are eroded.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of malleus|Malleus

lm:Head of metatarsal bone|Third metatar.key: lm:Head of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone
lm:Head of metatarsal bone|Third metatar.note: The head articulates with the base of the proximal phalanx and is held by the plantar plate, collateral ligaments and the Ligamentum metatarseum transversum profundum. Pitfall: dorsal flattening with subchondral sclerosis is Freiberg infraction, which is less common at MT3 than MT2. Count rays carefully so the wrong metatarsal is not reported.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
landmarks: lm:Base of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot

lm:Head of phalanx of foot|Proximal phal.key: lm:Head of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
lm:Head of phalanx of foot|Proximal phal.note: Caput phalangis forms the proximal interphalangeal joint with the middle phalanx base. Collateral ligaments sit on each side and the plantar plate lies plantarly. Pitfall: PIP flexion deformity (hammer toe) gives oblique sections. These can mimic condylar fracture or erosion, so assess on reformats aligned to the toe.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve
landmarks: lm:Trochlea of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
Middle phalanx of third finger of foot
Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints of foot

lm:Head of radius|Radius.note: Caput radii articulates with the capitulum and the Incisura radialis ulnae, held by the Ligamentum anulare radii.
