Pitfall: an isolated-looking radial head fracture may be part of a terrible triad or Monteggia injury. Check radiocapitellar alignment on all reformats and look for an associated coronoid fracture.

lm:Head of rib|Sixth rib.note: Caput costae forms the costovertebral joint with the T5 and T6 bodies and the T5–T6 disc, just anterolateral to the neural foramen. The sympathetic trunk lies on its anterior surface. Pitfall: costovertebral osteoarthritis or a rib-head lesion can be misattributed to the vertebral body or a paraspinal mass.
landmarks: lm:Crest of head of rib|Sixth rib
neighbours: Radiate ligament of head of rib

lm:Head of talus|Talus.note: Caput tali articulates in front with the os naviculare and below with the spring ligament and the anterior/middle calcaneal facets. Pitfall: an accessory navicular (os tibiale externum) beside the tuberositas ossis navicularis is not a talar head fragment; corticated, rounded margins identify it.

lm:Head of ulna|Ulna.note: Caput ulnae articulates with the radial sigmoid notch at the distal radio-ulnar joint. It is capped distally by the Discus articularis (TFCC), with the extensor carpi ulnaris groove dorsally. Pitfall: DRUJ subluxation is only judged reliably on bilateral axial CT in identical forearm rotation. Report ulnar variance.
neighbours: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint
Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint

lm:Hook of hamate bone|Hamate bone.note: The Hamulus ossis hamati projects palmarly. It forms the radial wall of Guyon's canal and the ulnar border of the carpal tunnel, and it is distal and radial to the Os pisiforme. Pitfall: an os hamuli proprium (unfused ossification centre) can mimic a hook fracture. Look for smooth corticated margins on axial CT.
neighbours: Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand

lm:Hypoglossal canal|Occipital bone.note: The canal passes through the base of the occipital condyle, anteromedial to and below the jugular foramen. It carries XII and a venous plexus. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the jugular foramen or the condylar canal, which lies posterior to the condyle. A canal partly divided by a bony septum is a normal variant, not a fracture.
landmarks: lm:Intrajugular process of occipital bone|Occipital bone
lm:External opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone
lm:Occipital margin of temporal bone|Temporal bone

lm:Hypophysial fossa|Sphenoid bone.note: Bounded by the Tuberculum sellae in front, the Dorsum sellae behind, the sphenoid sinus below and the Sinus cavernosi on each side. Pitfall: a tilted head creates a 'double floor' that mimics erosion. A CSF-filled empty sella is a common variant and should not be called a cystic lesion. Microadenomas are invisible on CT.

lm:Iliac crest|Hip bone.note: Crista iliaca is the superior margin of the iliac wing, with attachments for the three lateral abdominal wall muscles. Iliacus lies on its inner side. Pitfall: in young patients, the unfused iliac crest apophysis mimics an avulsion fracture. Bone-graft harvest defects mimic lytic lesions.

lm:Iliac fossa|Hip bone.note: Fossa iliaca is the smooth concave inner surface of the iliac wing, lined by iliacus and bounded inferiorly by the linea arcuata. On the right, the caecum and colon lie in front of it. Pitfall: the iliac wing is thin centrally, so partial volume makes the cortex look discontinuous or lytic. Confirm on bone-window reformats.

lm:Iliac tubercle|Hip bone.note: Tuberculum iliacum is a thickening on the outer lip of the iliac crest about 5 cm behind the anterior superior iliac spine, where the iliotibial tract attaches. Pitfall: its thick cortex and bony bulge can mimic an osteochondroma or periosteal reaction. It is also a common site for graft harvest, which leaves postoperative defects.

lm:Iliac tuberosity|Hip bone.note: Tuberositas iliaca is the rough area behind the auricular surface where the interosseous sacroiliac ligament attaches. It forms the ligamentous, non-synovial part of the sacroiliac joint. Pitfall: irregular margins and vacuum gas here are normal. Do not report them as erosive sacroiliitis, which affects the synovial part.

lm:Iliopubic eminence|Hip bone.note: Eminentia iliopubica marks where the ilium and pubis fuse above the acetabulum. Iliopsoas glides over it, with the femoral nerve lateral. Pitfall: in children, the adjacent unfused triradiate cartilage mimics a fracture. In adults, iliopsoas bursitis anterior to the eminence can be mistaken for a mass.

lm:Impression for costoclavicular ligame.note: Impressio ligamenti costoclavicularis (rhomboid fossa) is on the inferior medial clavicle, above the first costal cartilage. Pitfall: a deep, irregular fossa is often misread as a lytic lesion or an erosion. It is a normal variant and is often bilateral.

lm:Inferior angle of scapula|Scapula.note: The Angulus inferior lies at about T7–T8. Teres major attaches dorsally and the serratus anterior ventrally, and latissimus dorsi wraps over it. Pitfall: elastofibroma dorsi, a soft-tissue mass deep to the serratus at the inferior angle that is often bilateral, should not be called a sarcoma.

lm:Inferior articular facet of vertebra|.key: lm:Inferior articular facet of vertebra|Vertebra L3
lm:Inferior articular facet of vertebra|.note: Facies articularis inferior of L3 faces anterolaterally and articulates with the superior articular process of L4, forming the posterior L3–L4 zygapophyseal joint, with the ligamentum flavum lying anteromedially. Pitfall: confusing L3 inferior with L4 superior facets, and missing a pars defect; a facet joint vacuum phenomenon is degenerative, not a fracture.

lm:Inferior articular surface of atlas|A.note: This facet forms the lateral atlantoaxial joint with the superior facet of C2, and the vertebral artery lies just lateral to it. Pitfall: in children, and with head rotation, the C1 masses normally overhang C2 (pseudospread). Do not mistake this for Jefferson-type displacement. In adults, a combined overhang over 7 mm suggests transverse ligament rupture.

lm:Inferior articular surface of tibia|T.note: The tibial plafond (Facies articularis inferior) articulates with the trochlea of the talus and continues medially into the malleolar facet. Pitfall: posterior malleolus fractures and plafond impaction are easily missed on axial images, so use sagittal and coronal reformats. The sclerotic distal tibial physeal scar can mimic a fracture line.

lm:Inferior costal facet|Vertebra T8.note: The Fovea costalis inferior is a demifacet at the posterolateral lower margin of the T8 body. Together with the superior demifacet of T9, it receives the head of the ninth rib. Pitfall: costovertebral joint degeneration or a rib head fracture is easily assigned to the wrong rib. Count ribs on coronal reformats.

lm:Inferior gluteal line|Hip bone.note: Linea glutea inferior is a faint ridge on the gluteal surface just above the acetabulum. It marks the lower limit of the gluteus minimus origin, near the reflected head of rectus femoris. Pitfall: it is rarely visible on CT. A subtle cortical ridge here should not be read as periosteal reaction or a healed fracture.

lm:Inferior horn of thyroid cartilage|Th.key: lm:Inferior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage
lm:Inferior horn of thyroid cartilage|Th.note: The Cornu inferius articulates with the Facies articularis thyreoidea of the cricoid at the cricothyroid joint. The recurrent laryngeal nerve passes just behind it. Pitfall: asymmetric or patchy ossification of the horn mimics a fracture or cricothyroid dislocation. Compare with the other side and look for soft-tissue swelling.

lm:Inferior mental spine|Mandible.note: The Spina mentalis inferior is a lingual midline tubercle on the symphysis. The geniohyoid arises here, and the genioglossus arises from the superior spine above it. Pitfall: the lingual foramen and its vascular canal next to the spines can mimic a midline fracture or a lytic focus.

lm:Inferior nuchal line|Occipital bone.note: This ridge lies on the squama between the superior nuchal line and the foramen magnum. The Musculi recti capitis posteriores and obliquus superior attach here, and the cerebellar fossa lies directly deep to it. Pitfall: thin bone between muscle ridges can mimic lytic lesions. Small enthesophytes are normal.

lm:Inferior pubic ramus|Hip bone.note: Ramus inferior ossis pubis forms the inferomedial margin of the foramen obturatum and joins the ischial ramus. Obturator externus lies outside and obturator internus inside it, and the adductors arise from it. Pitfall: pubic ramus fractures are often bilateral or paired with a posterior ring injury. Search for sacral insufficiency fractures.

lm:Inferior thyroid notch|Thyroid cartil.note: This midline notch sits on the lower border of the laminae, directly above the Ligamentum cricothyreoideum medianum, which is the cricothyrotomy site. The infrahyoid strap muscles lie in front. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the deeper Incisura thyreoidea superior. Unossified midline cartilage in young patients can mimic a fracture gap.

lm:Inferior thyroid tubercle|Thyroid car.note: The tubercle marks the lower end of the Linea obliqua on the outer surface of the lamina. Sternothyroid, thyrohyoid and the inferior constrictor attach here, and the thyroid lobe lies just below. Pitfall: a focal ossified tubercle can be mistaken for a calcified thyroid nodule or lymph node.
landmarks: lm:Oblique line of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage
lm:Inferior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

lm:Inferior vertebral notch|Vertebra L3.note: Incisura vertebralis inferior is the deep concavity under the L3 pedicle that forms the roof of the L3–L4 intervertebral foramen, through which the L3 nerve root exits. Pitfall: the deeper inferior notch is the upper half of the foramen below, not the foramen above; label foramina by the two adjacent levels (L3–L4).
landmarks: lm:Costal part of transverse process|Vertebra L3
lm:Lateral part of transverse process|Vertebra L3
neighbours: Dorsal parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles

lm:Infraglenoid tubercle|Scapula.note: The Tuberculum infraglenoideum lies just below the glenoid and is the origin of the long head of triceps. Pitfall: avulsion or enthesophyte here, such as the Bennett lesion seen posteroinferiorly in throwers, can be confused with an anteroinferior bony Bankart fragment. Note the exact position on the clock face.

lm:Infraspinous fossa|Scapula.note: The Fossa infraspinata is the dorsal concavity below the Spina scapulae and holds the infraspinatus. Pitfall: infraspinatus atrophy limited to this fossa points to suprascapular nerve compression at the spinoglenoid notch. It should not be attributed to a rotator cuff tear alone. Also, the very thin central bone can look like a lytic area.

lm:Infratemporal surface of greater wing.key: lm:Infratemporal surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
lm:Infratemporal surface of greater wing.note: Horizontal underside of the Ala major forming the roof of the infratemporal fossa. The infratemporal crest separates it from the temporal surface, and the foramina ovale and spinosum pierce it. Pitfall: an ossified pterygospinous ligament (Civinini bar) can hide the Foramen ovale and mimic a fracture fragment.
neighbours: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

lm:Inner lip of iliac crest|Hip bone.key: lm:Inner lip of iliac crest|Hip bone
lm:Inner lip of iliac crest|Hip bone.note: Labium internum cristae iliacae is the medial edge of the iliac crest, where transversus abdominis attaches above and iliacus attaches below. The ilio-inguinal nerve runs nearby. Pitfall: the inner, intermediate and outer lips cannot be separated on routine CT, so describe findings relative to the crest and the anterior superior iliac spine.
landmarks: lm:Outer lip of iliac crest|Hip bone

lm:Intercondylar eminence|Tibia.note: The eminence lies between the medial and lateral tibial articular surfaces. The anterior intercondylar area in front holds the ACL footprint, and the PCL attaches to the posterior area. Pitfall: an ACL tibial-eminence avulsion can be subtle. Look for a displaced or elevated fragment on sagittal images instead of accepting a prominent tubercle as normal.

lm:Intercondylar fossa|Femur.note: The Fossa intercondylaris lies between the femoral condyles and holds the cruciate ligaments. The ACL attaches on the inner wall of the lateral condyle and the PCL on the inner wall of the medial condyle. The Linea intercondylaris marks the back border. Pitfall: a small ACL avulsion fragment from the femoral side is easy to miss. Bony spurs narrowing the notch also need to be reported.

lm:Intercondylar line|Femur.note: The Linea intercondylaris is the back edge of the intercondylar fossa, separating it from the Facies poplitea. The joint capsule and the Ligamentum popliteum obliquum attach along it, and the Arteria poplitea runs just behind. Pitfall: the line is used as a landmark (Blumensaat line) for patellar height and ACL position. Do not mistake it for a fracture line.

lm:Intermediate sacral crest|Sacrum.note: Crista sacralis medialis is a row of fused articular processes on each side of the median crest, just medial to the posterior sacral foramina. Its lowest part forms the cornua sacralia. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the median crest (the spinous processes) or with the lateral crest (the transverse processes) on axial images.

lm:Intermediate zone|Hip bone.note: Linea intermedia lies between the inner and outer lips of the iliac crest and gives origin to internal oblique. Pitfall: in adolescents, the crest apophysis sits on this zone. Its fragmented ossification mimics an avulsion, so compare with the other side.
landmarks: lm:Inner lip of iliac crest|Hip bone
lm:Outer lip of iliac crest|Hip bone

lm:Internal acoustic opening (porus of i.key: lm:Internal acoustic opening (porus of internal acoustic meatus)|Temporal bone
lm:Internal acoustic opening (porus of i.note: Porus acusticus internus opens on the posterior petrous surface into the cerebellopontine angle, lateral to the pons and flocculus. Pitfall: mild left–right asymmetry is normal. Flaring or erosion of the porus, or a side-to-side difference over about 2 mm, suggests vestibular schwannoma. An AICA loop can enter the canal.
passing: Lateral pontine branches of basilar artery
landmarks: lm:Occipital margin of temporal bone|Temporal bone

lm:Internal occipital protuberance|Occip.note: The protuberance sits at the centre of the cruciform eminence, where the falx and tentorium attach. The confluens sinuum lies against it. Pitfall: a dense confluens or an unevenly divided torcular can mimic thrombosis or a parafalcine subdural haematoma, and an inverted 'delta' does not exclude clot without contrast.

lm:Internal opening of carotid canal|Tem.key: lm:Internal opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone
lm:Internal opening of carotid canal|Tem.note: Apertura interna canalis carotici opens at the petrous apex, where the horizontal petrous ICA passes over foramen lacerum, beside the lingula, into the cavernous sinus. The trigeminal ganglion lies above it. Pitfall: the ICA runs over the lacerum, not through it. A thin or dehiscent canal roof is a normal variant.
landmarks: lm:External opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone

lm:Internal surface of squamous part of.key: lm:Internal surface of squamous part of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Internal surface of squamous part of.note: Concave inner table that faces the frontal lobes, with impressions of gyri and grooves for meningeal vessels. Pitfall: hyperostosis frontalis interna is a common benign, symmetric thickening in older women. Do not mistake it for meningioma-related hyperostosis or a metastasis.

lm:Intertrochanteric crest|Femur.note: The Crista intertrochanterica runs on the back of the femur between the greater and lesser trochanters. The Musculus quadratus femoris inserts on the Tuberculum quadratum along this crest. Pitfall: the junction of the trochanter and neck has normal sclerosis and vascular channels. Do not mistake these for an intertrochanteric fracture line. Follow the cortex in multiplanar reconstructions.

lm:Intertrochanteric line|Femur.note: The Linea intertrochanterica is the anterior ridge between the trochanter major and trochanter minor. The Capsula articularis coxae and Ligamentum iliofemorale attach along it. Pitfall: a fracture line along it is extracapsular (intertrochanteric), whereas a fracture just proximal to it is a basicervical or intracapsular neck fracture. Use the capsular attachment to classify it.

lm:Intervertebral foramen|Vertebra L3.note: The L2–L3 foramen is bounded by the L2 and L3 pedicles above and below, the disc and vertebral bodies anteriorly, and the L3 superior articular process with the ligamentum flavum posteriorly. It contains the L2 ganglion. Pitfall: a foraminal disc herniation affects the exiting L2 root, not L3; assess stenosis on sagittal reconstructions.
landmarks: lm:Superior articular process of vertebra|Vertebra L3
neighbours: Ventral parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles

lm:Intervertebral foramina|Sacrum.note: In the sacrum, the foramina intervertebralia are the internal canals that run laterally from the sacral canal. Each one splits into an anterior and a posterior sacral foramen for the ventral and dorsal rami. Pitfall: do not confuse these internal canals with the surface foramina on axial images. A perineural (Tarlov) cyst widening a canal is not an erosive lesion.

lm:Intervertebral surface|Vertebra L3.note: Facies intervertebralis is the superior endplate of L3, a central cortical plate surrounded by the annular epiphysis and lying against the L2–L3 disc and nucleus pulposus. Pitfall: Schmorl nodes and Modic-type sclerosis can mimic compression fractures or discitis; look for endplate cortical continuity and preserved vertebral height.

lm:Intrajugular process of occipital bon.key: lm:Intrajugular process of occipital bone|Occipital bone
lm:Intrajugular process of occipital bon.note: This spur projects into the jugular foramen and, with its temporal counterpart, separates the anteromedial pars nervosa (IX, inferior petrosal sinus) from the posterolateral pars vascularis (jugular bulb, X, XI). Pitfall: a complete bony bridge is a normal variant and should not be mistaken for a fracture or a calcified mass.
landmarks: lm:Occipital margin of temporal bone|Temporal bone

lm:Ischial spine|Hip bone.note: Spina ischiadica separates the greater sciatic foramen above from the lesser sciatic foramen below. The sacrospinous ligament and coccygeus attach to it, and the internal pudendal vessels and pudendal nerve hook around its tip. Pitfall: ischial spine avulsion fragments may be missed, and a medially projecting spine on CT is a marker of retroversion, not a fracture.

lm:Ischiopubic ramus|Hip bone.note: Ramus ischiopubicus forms the inferior margin of the foramen obturatum and the lateral wall of the pubic arch. Gracilis and adductor magnus arise from it, and the crus of the corpus cavernosum attaches medially. Pitfall: in children, the ischiopubic synchondrosis can be expanded and irregular (van Neck appearance), mimicking a fracture, tumour or osteomyelitis.

lm:Ischium|Hip bone.note: Os ischii forms the posteroinferior hip bone, with the tuber ischiadicum giving origin to the hamstrings. Gluteus maximus covers it, and quadratus femoris lies lateral. Pitfall: in adolescents, the ischial tuberosity apophysis looks irregular. Distinguish a normal unfused apophysis from an avulsion by comparing both sides.
neighbours: Sciatic bursa of gluteus maximus muscle
Superior bursa of biceps femoris muscle

lm:Jugular foramen|Temporal bone.note: Foramen jugulare lies between the temporal and occipital bones and is split by the intrajugular process. The pars nervosa (IX, inferior petrosal sinus) is anteromedial; the pars vascularis (X, XI, jugular bulb) is posterolateral. Pitfall: a right-dominant, high-riding or diverticular bulb mimics a mass; smooth cortex argues against paraganglioma, which erodes it in a permeative pattern.
landmarks: lm:Intrajugular process of occipital bone|Occipital bone
lm:Occipital margin of temporal bone|Temporal bone
lm:External opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone

lm:Jugular notch of occipital bone|Occip.key: lm:Jugular notch of occipital bone|Occipital bone
lm:Jugular notch of occipital bone|Occip.note: This notch forms the posteromedial margin of the jugular foramen, opposite the jugular fossa of the temporal bone. Pitfall: the jugular foramina are normally asymmetric (usually larger on the right), and a high jugular bulb is common. Look for cortical erosion before suggesting a paraganglioma or schwannoma.

lm:Jugular process|Occipital bone.note: This process lies lateral to the condyle and forms the posterior wall of the jugular foramen. It joins the temporal bone at the petro-occipital synchondrosis, and the Musculus rectus capitis lateralis inserts on it. Pitfall: the jugulotemporal synchondrosis can mimic a fracture, and an enlarged paracondylar process is an anatomical variant.
landmarks: lm:Jugular notch of occipital bone|Occipital bone
lm:Occipital margin of temporal bone|Temporal bone

lm:Lamina of cricoid cartilage|Cricoid c.note: The Lamina cartilaginis cricoideae is the tall back plate of the cricoid, at about the level of C6. The postcricoid hypopharynx and the start of the oesophagus lie directly behind it. Pitfall: the postcricoid soft tissue is normally thick, and the cartilage calcifies unevenly. Either can mimic a postcricoid tumour or cartilage invasion.
landmarks: lm:Inferior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

lm:Lamina of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid c.note: The paraglottic space and the Membrana quadrangularis lie medial to the lamina, and the strap muscles lie lateral. The piriform sinus sits posteromedially. Pitfall: normal irregular, asymmetric ossification with unossified gaps mimics tumour invasion or sclerosis. Only call invasion when there is tumour on the extralaryngeal side.
landmarks: lm:Oblique line of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

lm:Lamina of vertebral arch|Vertebra L3.note: Lamina arcus vertebrae joins the articular pillars to the spinous process and forms the posterior wall of the canal, with the ligamentum flavum on its inner surface and the transversospinal muscles behind. Pitfall: a laminar fracture or spina bifida occulta can be overlooked on axial images; a pars interarticularis defect lies more ventrolaterally, between the facets.
landmarks: lm:Superior articular facet of vertebra|Vertebra L3

lm:Laryngeal prominence|Thyroid cartilag.note: The prominence is where the two laminae fuse in the anterior midline, lying under the strap muscles and platysma. The pre-epiglottic fat and anterior commissure lie behind it. Pitfall: unossified midline cartilage between ossified laminae mimics a vertical fracture. Assess for anterior commissure soft-tissue swelling or air.

lm:Lateral angle of scapula|Scapula.note: The Angulus lateralis is the thick corner that carries the glenoid and the Collum scapulae, with the coracoid base just superomedial to it. Pitfall: fractures through this region need to be classed as glenoid, scapular neck or coracoid base. The classification decides whether the injury is intra-articular and whether surgery is needed.

lm:Lateral border of scapula|Scapula.note: The Margo lateralis runs from the infraglenoid tubercle to the inferior angle and is the thickest edge of the scapula. Teres minor attaches dorsally along it. Pitfall: the circumflex scapular artery crosses this border and grooves the bone, which can look like a non-displaced fracture line.

lm:Lateral condyle of femur|Femur.note: The Condylus lateralis femoris sits on the Meniscus lateralis and the lateral tibial plateau. The Sulcus popliteus lies on its lateral surface, and the posterolateral corner structures lie behind it. Pitfall: a shallow lateral femoral notch (sulcus terminalis) is normal. A notch deeper than 1.5–2 mm suggests an ACL-related impaction fracture.

lm:Lateral epicondyle of femur|Femur.note: The Epicondylus lateralis is the most prominent point on the lateral surface of the condyle. The Ligamentum collaterale fibulare originates here, with the Sulcus popliteus just below it. The Tractus iliotibialis passes superficially. Pitfall: avulsion fragments here (the fibular collateral ligament or popliteus origin) are small and easily missed. Do not confuse them with a fabella, which lies posteriorly in the lateral gastrocnemius head.

lm:Lateral intercondylar tubercle|Tibia.note: The Tuberculum intercondylare laterale is the lateral peak of the eminence. The roots of the lateral meniscus attach next to it, and the ACL sits anteromedially. Pitfall: a loose body or meniscal ossicle in the notch can be mistaken for a tubercle fracture fragment, and the reverse. Look for a donor-site defect.

lm:Lateral lip of linea aspera|Femur.note: The Labium laterale lineae asperae is the posterolateral ridge of the femoral shaft. The Musculus vastus lateralis attaches on its lateral side, and the Septum intermusculare laterale and biceps short head attach to it. Pitfall: cortical irregularity at muscle insertions (such as the cortical desmoid pattern) can mimic periosteal reaction or a tumour. Check whether it is bilateral and symmetric.

lm:Lateral malleolar facet|Talus.note: Triangular facet on the lateral talar body facing the malleolus lateralis, with its apex on the processus lateralis tali. Pitfall: judge mortise congruity on true coronal reconstructions, looking at clear spaces and tibiofibular overlap together; subtle lateral talar shift means syndesmotic injury even when this joint looks preserved.

lm:Lateral mass|Atlas (C1).note: The massa lateralis carries the occipital condyle above and C2 below. The transverse foramen and vertebral artery lie lateral to it. Pitfall: the medial transverse ligament tubercle, or a small avulsion fragment, can look like a loose body. A bony fragment here indicates transverse ligament avulsion (an unstable injury).
landmarks: lm:Jugular notch of occipital bone|Occipital bone

lm:Lateral part of occipital bone|Occipi.key: lm:Lateral part of occipital bone|Occipital bone
lm:Lateral part of occipital bone|Occipi.note: The pars lateralis lies on each side of the foramen magnum and bears the condyle, jugular process and hypoglossal canal. It meets the basilar part and the squama at synchondroses. Pitfall: in children, the unfused anterior and posterior intraoccipital synchondroses mimic fractures. Use their symmetry and smooth sclerotic margins to tell them apart.

lm:Lateral part of sacrum|Sacrum.note: Pars lateralis ossis sacri is the bone lateral to the sacral foramina, made of fused costal and transverse elements. It forms the ala and carries the auricular surface. Pitfall: fractures confined to this part (Denis zone I) can extend into the foramina (zone II), so trace every fracture line medially on coronal reformats.

lm:Lateral part of transverse process|Ve.key: lm:Lateral part of transverse process|Vertebra L3
lm:Lateral part of transverse process|Ve.note: The lateral tip of the L3 transverse process gives attachment to quadratus lumborum and the thoracolumbar fascia, with psoas anteromedially and the kidney anterolateral. Pitfall: an unfused apophysis or a lumbar rib can mimic a tip fracture; fractures usually have sharp edges and may come with an adjacent haematoma or lumbar artery bleeding.
landmarks: lm:Costal part of transverse process|Vertebra L3
neighbours: Dorsal parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles

lm:Lateral process of calcaneal tuberosi.note: Processus lateralis tuberis calcanei is the smaller plantar-lateral prominence of the tuber, where the abductor digiti minimi pedis originates. Pitfall: an apophysis that has not fused, or the normal notch between the two processes, can look like a fracture. Check the other side and the cortical margins.

lm:Lateral process of malleus|Malleus.note: The Processus lateralis mallei is a short knob at the top of the manubrium that pushes against the pars flaccida, just medial to the scutum. It forms the lateral-inferior boundary of Prussak space. Pitfall: because it is small and touches the Membrana tympanica, it can be mistaken for a retraction pocket, debris or a scutum fragment.
landmarks: lm:External acoustic meatus (medial end, tympanic membrane)|Temporal bone

lm:Lateral process of talus|Talus.note: Processus lateralis tali carries the apex of the lateral malleolar facet and part of the posterior subtalar facet, below the fibular tip. Pitfall: lateral process ('snowboarder's') fractures are often missed and labelled lateral ankle sprain; check coronal CT for subtalar extension.

lm:Lateral pterygoid plate|Sphenoid bone.note: Thin plate forming the medial wall of the infratemporal fossa. The medial pterygoid arises from its medial surface and the inferior head of the lateral pterygoid from its lateral surface. Pitfall: a pterygoid plate fracture is required for any Le Fort fracture. These thin plates are easily missed on axial images alone, so check coronal bone reformats.
landmarks: lm:Vaginal process of sphenoid bone|Sphenoid bone
neighbours: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

lm:Lateral sacral crest|Sacrum.note: Crista sacralis lateralis is made of the fused transverse processes and lies lateral to the posterior sacral foramina. It anchors the posterior and interosseous sacroiliac ligaments and part of gluteus maximus. Pitfall: ossification of the ligament insertions and enthesophytes here can look like fracture fragments or bridging of the SI joint.
passing: Posterior root of posterior femoral cutaneous nerve

lm:Lateral supracondylar line|Femur.note: The Linea supracondylaris lateralis continues the lateral lip of the linea aspera down to the Epicondylus lateralis. The Musculus plantaris and the lateral head of gastrocnemius attach to it. Pitfall: keep laterality strict. The medial supracondylar line carries the adductor tubercle, and its structures (adductor magnus and the medial gastrocnemius head) do not belong to this line.

lm:Lateral tubercle|Talus.note: Tuberculum laterale forms the lateral lip of the FHL groove, takes the posterior talofibular ligament and sits just above the posterior calcaneus. Pitfall: os trigonum versus Shepherd fracture; smooth corticated margins and a synchondrosis favour os trigonum, while sharp non-corticated edges favour fracture.
landmarks: lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of talus|Talus

lm:Lenticular process of incus|Incus.note: Processus lenticularis is the medial-pointing tip of the long limb and joins the stapes head above the oval window. Pitfall: it is the ossicular part most often eroded in chronic otitis media and cholesteatoma. Because it is so small, partial volume can mimic erosion. Confirm on thin coronal and axial reconstructions.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of stapes|Stapes

lm:Lesser horn of hyoid bone|Hyoid bone.key: lm:Lesser horn of hyoid bone|Hyoid bone
lm:Lesser horn of hyoid bone|Hyoid bone.note: Cornu minus is a small cone at the junction of body and greater horn. The stylohyoid ligament attaches here. Pitfall: segmental calcification of the stylohyoid ligament (Eagle syndrome) or a separate lesser-horn ossicle mimics a fracture or foreign body. Follow the chain up to the processus styloideus.

lm:Lesser sciatic foramen|Hip bone.note: Foramen ischiadicum minus lies between the incisura ischiadica minor, the ligamentum sacrospinale above and the ligamentum sacrotuberale behind. It carries the obturator internus tendon out of the pelvis and the pudendal vessels and nerve into Alcock's canal. Pitfall: the ligaments are hard to see on CT, so it is easily confused with the greater sciatic foramen, which carries the sciatic nerve.

lm:Lesser sciatic notch|Hip bone.note: Incisura ischiadica minor is the smooth concavity of the ischium between the spina ischiadica and the tuber ischiadicum, lined by cartilage where the obturator internus tendon turns. Pitfall: avoid confusing it with the larger incisura ischiadica major above the spine; the spina ischiadica separates them.

lm:Lesser trochanter|Femur.note: The Trochanter minor is posteromedial at the junction of the neck and shaft and receives the iliopsoas tendon. Pitfall: an isolated avulsion of the lesser trochanter in an adult is a pathological fracture until proven otherwise, so look for an underlying lytic metastasis. Its apparent size also varies with femoral rotation.

lm:Limbus of sphenoid|Sphenoid bone.note: Ridge at the back edge of the planum sphenoidale (Jugum sphenoideum) that marks the front border of the Sulcus chiasmaticus. The sphenoid sinus lies directly below. Pitfall: hyperostosis or blistering here suggests a planum or tuberculum meningioma. Don't mistake it for pneumosinus dilatans, a normal expansion of the sinus air space.
passing: Orbitofrontal branches of anterior cerebral artery

lm:Linea aspera|Femur.note: The Linea aspera is the posterior ridge of the femoral shaft, with lateral and medial lips. The adductors, vastus muscles, biceps short head and both intermuscular septa attach to it. Pitfall: on axial CT the normally thick, irregular posterior cortex here can mimic periosteal reaction or cortical thickening. Nutrient canals near it can mimic fracture lines.

lm:Lingual surface of tooth|Lower first.key: lm:Lingual surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Lingual surface of tooth|Lower first.note: Facies lingualis faces the tongue and the floor of the mouth, above the lingual cortex of the mandible. Pitfall: lower molars normally tilt lingually (curve of Wilson), so the lingual cusps sit lower than the buccal ones. Do not report this as malposition or as alveolar bone loss on the lingual side.
landmarks: lm:Cusp of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Occlusal surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Neck of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Root of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Distal surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

lm:Long limb of incus|Incus.note: Crus longum incudis descends into the mesotympanum posterior and parallel to manubrium mallei, ending in the lenticular process. Pitfall: on axial CT the long limb and the manubrium appear as two parallel dots or lines. Do not confuse the posterior one (incus) with the anterior one (malleus) when reporting erosion or dislocation.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of stapes|Stapes

lm:Lunate surface|Hip bone.note: Facies lunata is the horseshoe-shaped articular surface of the acetabulum around the non-articular fossa acetabuli and open inferiorly at the incisura acetabuli. Pitfall: the fossa acetabuli and the supra-acetabular fossa are normal non-articular areas and should not be called cartilage loss or erosions; assess joint space only along the lunate surface.

lm:Malleolar fossa|Fibula.note: Pit on the posteromedial surface of the lateral malleolus, behind the talar facet. The Ligamentum talofibulare posterius attaches here. Pitfall: avulsion fragments of this ligament can be mistaken for an os subfibulare or an accessory ossicle. Look for donor-site irregularity of the cortex.

lm:Malleolar groove of fibula|Fibula.note: Retromalleolar groove on the posterior lateral malleolus. The fibularis brevis tendon runs in it, deep to the longus, held by the Retinaculum fibulare superius. Pitfall: a flat or convex groove and a small cortical flake avulsion (fleck sign) point to retinacular tear and tendon dislocation. Do not dismiss the flake as an ossicle.

lm:Mandibular dental arch|Mandible.note: The Arcus dentalis mandibularis is the row of lower teeth set in the alveolar part. It has a buccal and a lingual cortical plate, with the gingiva on top. Pitfall: tooth numbering by laterality. FDI 36 (left) and 46 (right) are easily swapped on axial images, so check the patient's orientation.
landmarks: lm:Root of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Crown of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Vestibular surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Lingual surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

lm:Mandibular foramen|Mandible.note: Opens in the centre of the medial ramus surface into the Canalis mandibulae, with Musculus pterygoideus medialis medially (pterygomandibular space) and masseter lateral to the ramus. Pitfall: the lingula and the mylohyoid groove below it can mimic a ramus fracture. Do not confuse it with the Foramen mentale on the mandibular body.
passing: Mylohyoid branch of inferior alveolar artery

lm:Mandibular fossa|Temporal bone.note: Fossa mandibularis holds the condyle and disc, with the articular tubercle in front, the tympanic part and external acoustic meatus behind, and a thin roof beneath the middle cranial fossa. Pitfall: an empty fossa with the condyle in front of the tubercle means dislocation; check the roof for intracranial condylar intrusion.
landmarks: lm:External acoustic meatus (medial end, tympanic membrane)|Temporal bone
neighbours: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

lm:Mandibular notch|Mandible.note: Incisura mandibulae is the curve between the Processus coronoideus in front and the condylar neck behind, with the infratemporal fossa medially and the masseteric nerve and vessels crossing it. Pitfall: on axial slices the notch splits the ramus into two separate bony profiles (coronoid and condyle), which is not a fracture.
landmarks: lm:Infratemporal surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
neighbours: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

lm:Manubrium of sternum|Manubrium of ste.note: Manubrium sterni lies in front of the great vessels at T3–T4. It articulates with the clavicles and first costal cartilages, and with the Corpus sterni at the Angulus sterni. Pitfall: the manubriosternal synchondrosis or an unfused joint can mimic a fracture; a true fracture shows a cortical step-off and retrosternal haematoma.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

lm:Mastoid angle of parietal bone|Pariet.key: lm:Mastoid angle of parietal bone|Parietal bone
lm:Mastoid angle of parietal bone|Pariet.note: This posteroinferior angle meets the occipital and temporal bones at the asterion, internally where the transverse sinus turns into the sigmoid sinus. Pitfall: sutural Wormian bones and the parietomastoid suture mimic fractures. A fracture here is an epidural risk for the venous sinus.

lm:Mastoid border of occipital bone|Occi.key: lm:Mastoid border of occipital bone|Occipital bone
lm:Mastoid border of occipital bone|Occi.note: This border forms the occipitomastoid suture with the temporal bone, posteromedial to the sigmoid sinus. Pitfall: the suture and the mastoid emissary vein canal mimic a fracture. An enlarged emissary canal has corticated margins and connects to the sigmoid sinus, which has surgical relevance.

lm:Mastoid notch|Temporal bone.note: Incisura mastoidea is the digastric groove on the medial side of the mastoid tip, where the posterior belly of the digastric arises. Its anterior end points to the stylomastoid foramen. Pitfall: don't confuse it with the occipital artery groove just medial to it.

lm:Mastoid process|Temporal bone.note: Processus mastoideus lies posterior to the external acoustic meatus and gives insertion to the SCM, splenius and longissimus. Pitfall: fluid in the cells or asymmetric/sclerotic pneumatisation does not by itself mean coalescent mastoiditis; look for septal or cortical erosion. Mastoid emissary canals mimic fractures.
landmarks: lm:Tympanic part of temporal bone|Temporal bone

lm:Maxillary dental arch|Maxilla.note: Arcus dentalis maxillaris is the alveolar process carrying the upper teeth, with the maxillary sinus floor above and the Tuber maxillae behind. Pitfall: molar roots projecting into the sinus floor, or periapical lucencies, can mimic erosion of the sinus wall. Trace odontogenic sinusitis to the causative root apex on coronal CT.

lm:Maxillary surface of greater wing|Sph.key: lm:Maxillary surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
lm:Maxillary surface of greater wing|Sph.note: Anterior surface of the Ala major facing the pterygopalatine fossa, below the inferior orbital fissure. It contains the opening of the Foramen rotundum. Pitfall: loss of fat in the pterygopalatine fossa indicates perineural spread along V2. Don't confuse this fossa with the adjacent inferior orbital fissure on axial slices.

lm:Medial border of scapula|Scapula.note: The Margo medialis runs parallel to the spine. Rhomboids attach on its dorsal lip and the serratus anterior on its ventral lip. Pitfall: if the border sits asymmetrically far from the ribs, consider winging of the scapula from a long thoracic or accessory nerve lesion rather than a mass. Compare with the other side.

lm:Medial border of tibia|Tibia.note: Margo medialis tibiae separates the subcutaneous medial surface from the posterior surface. Flexor digitorum longus and soleus attach along it, and the Vena saphena magna and Nervus saphenus run superficially. Pitfall: medial tibial stress syndrome and stress fractures occur here. Do not mistake the oblique nutrient canal of the posterior surface for a fracture line.

lm:Medial condyle of femur|Femur.note: The Condylus medialis femoris rests on the Meniscus medialis. The Ligamentum cruciatum posterius attaches to its intercondylar (lateral) surface, and the medial gastrocnemius head originates above it posteriorly. Pitfall: subchondral insufficiency fracture or osteonecrosis of the weight-bearing surface is subtle on CT. Do not dismiss a flattened subchondral contour as partial-volume artefact.

lm:Medial epicondyle of femur|Femur.note: The Epicondylus medialis is the origin of the Ligamentum collaterale tibiale. The Tuberculum adductorium lies just above it, and the pes anserinus tendons pass posterior to it. Pitfall: ossification at the medial collateral ligament origin (Pellegrini–Stieda) indicates an old injury. Do not report it as an acute avulsion fragment.
neighbours: Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament
Deep part of tibial collateral ligament

lm:Medial epicondyle of humerus|Humerus.note: Epicondylus medialis carries the common flexor origin and the ulnar collateral ligament. Nervus ulnaris runs in its posterior groove. Pitfall: in children, an avulsed medial epicondylar apophysis can be trapped in the joint and mistaken for the trochlear ossification centre. Check the ossification order (CRITOE).
passing: Posterior branch of medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve
neighbours: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

lm:Medial intercondylar tubercle|Tibia.note: The Tuberculum intercondylare mediale is usually the taller peak of the eminence. It borders the medial articular surface, the posterior root of the medial meniscus and the PCL attachment behind. Pitfall: on coronal reformats, make sure medial and lateral tubercles are not swapped when you localise an eminence fracture.

lm:Medial lip of linea aspera|Femur.note: The Labium mediale lineae asperae is the posteromedial ridge of the shaft. The Septum intermusculare mediale, vastus medialis and adductors attach to it. Distally the femoral vessels pass through the adductor hiatus to become the popliteal vessels close to the bone. Pitfall: fracture fragments or exostoses here put the femoral and popliteal vessels at risk, so assess the vessels on contrast phases.

lm:Medial malleolar facet|Talus.note: Comma-shaped facet on the medial talar body facing the facies articularis malleoli tibiae, continuous with the trochlea; deep deltoid fibres insert below it. Pitfall: a medial clear space wider than the superior joint space means deltoid injury, but oblique planes widen it artificially, so measure on true coronal reconstructions.

lm:Medial process of calcaneal tuberosit.note: Processus medialis tuberis calcanei is the larger plantar-medial process, where the aponeurosis plantaris, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor hallucis originate. Pitfall: a plantar heel spur sits in the flexor digitorum brevis origin, not inside the aponeurosis. Do not call it an avulsion fragment.

lm:Medial pterygoid plate|Sphenoid bone.note: Narrow plate forming the lateral border of the posterior nasal opening (choana) and the nasopharynx. It ends below in the Hamulus pterygoideus and gives origin to the superior constrictor. Pitfall: despite its name, the medial pterygoid muscle arises from the lateral plate, not this one. Assign masses and fractures to the correct plate.
landmarks: lm:Vaginal process of sphenoid bone|Sphenoid bone

lm:Medial supracondylar line|Femur.note: The Linea supracondylaris medialis runs from the medial lip of the linea aspera down to the Tuberculum adductorium. The adductor magnus tendon inserts there, and the femoral vessels cross it at the adductor hiatus. Pitfall: keep laterality strict. The plantaris and the lateral gastrocnemius head arise from the lateral supracondylar line, not this one.

lm:Medial surface of arytenoid cartilage.key: lm:Medial surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage
lm:Medial surface of arytenoid cartilage.note: The Facies medialis is covered by mucosa and faces the posterior glottis (interarytenoid region), opposite the other arytenoid. Pitfall: with the glottis closed or a cord in adduction, the apposed mucosa can mimic posterior commissure thickening or a mass. Judge the commissure on images acquired during quiet breathing.
landmarks: lm:Posterior surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage

lm:Medial tubercle|Talus.note: Tuberculum mediale forms the medial lip of the FHL groove and anchors the posterior tibiotalar ligament; the tibial neurovascular bundle lies posteromedially. Pitfall: a Cedell fracture here is subtle and mimics a medial sprain; do not dismiss it as os trigonum, which lies laterally.
landmarks: lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of talus|Talus

lm:Median sacral crest|Sacrum.note: Crista sacralis mediana is the midline ridge of fused spinous tubercles (usually S1–S4) forming the roof of the canalis sacralis. Below it lies the hiatus sacralis. Pitfall: a midline gap, usually at S1, is spina bifida occulta, a common variant that is neither a fracture nor a lytic defect.

lm:Mental foramen|Mandible.note: The Foramen mentale opens on the outer surface, usually below the apex of the second premolar or between the premolars, halfway up the body. The mental nerve exits through it, under the depressor anguli oris. Pitfall: on CT it can mimic a periapical lesion. Accessory mental foramina and an anterior loop of the canal matter before implants or surgery.

lm:Mental tubercle|Mandible.note: The Tuberculum mentale is a paired bony bump at the lower lateral corner of the mental protuberance, on each side of the midline. Pitfall: an asymmetric tubercle or cortical thickening can look like a callus or an osteoma. Do not take it for a midline point when measuring.

lm:Mesial surface of tooth|Lower first m.key: lm:Mesial surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Mesial surface of tooth|Lower first m.note: Facies mesialis faces forward along the arch and contacts the distal surface of the lower second premolar. Pitfall: missing teeth or retained deciduous molars shift the count. Count from the midline and use root number (two for a molar, one for a premolar) to confirm 36/46 before reporting.
landmarks: lm:Crown of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Cusp of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Vestibular surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Lingual surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

lm:Middle facet for calcaneus|Talus.note: Facies articularis calcanea media sits on the sustentaculum tali, anteromedial to the sinus tarsi. Pitfall: talocalcaneal coalition here is often fibrous or cartilaginous; look for joint narrowing, irregular subchondral sclerosis and a downsloping facet, not only an osseous bridge.

lm:Muscular process|Arytenoid cartilage.note: The Processus muscularis projects posterolaterally and is the attachment of the posterior and lateral cricoarytenoid muscles. The piriform sinus lies lateral to it. Pitfall: in vocal cord palsy the arytenoid tips anteromedially and the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle atrophies. Do not mistake the healthy side for the abnormal one.
landmarks: lm:Articular surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage

lm:Mylohyoid line|Mandible.note: The Linea mylohyoidea is an oblique ridge on the inner surface of the body where the mylohyoid attaches. It divides the sublingual space and Fovea sublingualis above from the submandibular fossa below. Pitfall: the roots of the second and third molars reach below the line, so their infection drains into the submandibular space, not the sublingual space.
landmarks: lm:Distal surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

lm:Nasal margin of frontal bone|Frontal.key: lm:Nasal margin of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Nasal margin of frontal bone|Frontal.note: The serrated Margo nasalis articulates with the Ossa nasalia and the frontal processes of the Maxilla below the glabella. Pitfall: the frontonasal suture is often irregular or asymmetric, which can look like a nasofrontal fracture. Check the anterior wall of the Sinus frontalis and the soft tissues before diagnosing a fracture.
landmarks: lm:Nasal spine of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Nasal part of frontal bone|Frontal bone

lm:Nasal part of frontal bone|Frontal bo.key: lm:Nasal part of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Nasal part of frontal bone|Frontal bo.note: The Pars nasalis lies between the orbits and carries the Spina nasalis that supports the nasal bones, with the Apertura sinus frontalis draining into the frontal recess. Pitfall: in naso-orbito-ethmoidal fractures, check whether the frontal sinus outflow tract is involved. Agger nasi cells can mimic it.
landmarks: lm:Nasal spine of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Nasal margin of frontal bone|Frontal bone

lm:Nasal spine of frontal bone|Frontal b.key: lm:Nasal spine of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Nasal spine of frontal bone|Frontal b.note: Midline downward projection from the nasal part of the frontal bone that supports the nasal bones in front and the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid behind. Pitfall: normal sutures between the nasal bones and the frontal spine mimic nasal fractures. Look for displacement and soft-tissue swelling.
landmarks: lm:Nasal part of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Nasal margin of frontal bone|Frontal bone

lm:Navicular articular surface|Talus.note: Convex anterior surface of caput tali articulating with the concave os naviculare, forming the medial Chopart joint. Pitfall: a dorsal talar beak suggests tarsal coalition rather than simple osteoarthritis; also check the central third of the navicular for stress fracture.

lm:Neck of femur|Femur.note: The Collum femoris links the caput femoris to the trochanters. It is intracapsular anteriorly as far as the intertrochanteric line, and the Musculus obturator externus wraps it posteroinferiorly. Pitfall: an undisplaced subcapital fracture can be occult on CT and can be confused with the overlapping physeal scar or a herniation pit. Use MRI if clinical suspicion persists.

lm:Neck of malleus|Malleus.note: The Collum mallei is the narrow part between the Caput and the Manubrium, where the anterior and lateral processes arise. It lies medial to Prussak space. Pitfall: the neck is thin, so slice obliquity or partial volume can look like a fracture or erosion. Assess in two planes.

lm:Neck of radius|Radius.note: Collum radii is the constricted segment below the head, encircled by the annular ligament and wrapped by Musculus supinator. Pitfall: in children, the proximal radial physis looks like a lucent line and can be mistaken for a neck fracture. Also note that the deep branch of the radial nerve runs close by and is at risk in displaced fractures.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of radius|Radius

lm:Neck of rib|Sixth rib.note: Collum costae runs from the head to the tubercle, anterior to the transverse process of T6. The costotransverse ligament and the parietal pleura lie in front of it. Pitfall: posterior neck fractures in non-accidental injury or trauma are subtle. The overlap with the transverse process on axial slices mimics a fracture or hides one.

lm:Neck of scapula|Scapula.note: The Collum scapulae is the narrowing between the glenoid and the body. Pitfall: the anatomical neck lies lateral to the coracoid and the surgical neck lies medial to it. A surgical neck fracture combined with a clavicle fracture makes a 'floating shoulder', so state where the fracture line is relative to the coracoid base.

lm:Neck of talus|Talus.note: Collum tali links body and head; its underside roofs the sinus tarsi and canalis tarsi. Pitfall: neck fractures cut the retrograde blood supply, so report displacement and subtalar or talonavicular subluxation (Hawkins). Minimally displaced lines are easily missed on axial images; use sagittal reconstructions.

lm:Neck of tooth|Lower first molar tooth.key: lm:Neck of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Neck of tooth|Lower first molar tooth.note: Cervix dentis is the cemento-enamel junction at the gingival margin, normally 1–2 mm above the alveolar crest. Pitfall: cervical burnout, a normal relative lucency between enamel and bone, mimics cervical or root caries. Measure periodontal bone loss from the cemento-enamel junction, not from the gingiva.
landmarks: lm:Occlusal surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Lingual surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Distal surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Root of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Crown of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

lm:Oblique line of thyroid cartilage|Thy.key: lm:Oblique line of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage
lm:Oblique line of thyroid cartilage|Thy.note: The Linea obliqua runs between the superior and inferior thyroid tubercles on the outer lamina. Sternothyroid, thyrohyoid and the inferior constrictor attach along it. Pitfall: the ridge is rarely seen as a separate line on CT. Its ossified ends are easily misread as calcified jugular nodes next to the internal jugular vein.
landmarks: lm:Superior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

lm:Oblong fovea|Arytenoid cartilage.note: The Fovea oblonga is the lower depression on the anterolateral surface, below the Crista arcuata. The thyroarytenoid (vocalis) muscle inserts here at the glottic level. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the Fovea triangularis above, which belongs to the vestibular level.
landmarks: lm:Anterolateral surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage

lm:Obturator crest|Hip bone.note: Crista obturatoria runs from the pubic tubercle to the acetabular notch along the anterior margin of the superior pubic ramus, and the ligamentum pubofemorale attaches to it. Pitfall: an irregular cortex here at the enthesis is a normal finding and should not be mistaken for a non-displaced fracture of the superior pubic ramus.

lm:Obturator foramen|Hip bone.note: Foramen obturatum is framed by the pubic and ischial rami and closed by the membrana obturatoria, with obturator internus inside and obturator externus outside. Only the canalis obturatorius, superolateral, carries the obturator vessels and nerve. Pitfall: an obturator hernia lies between pectineus and obturator externus and can be missed; compare both sides.

lm:Obturator groove|Hip bone.note: Sulcus obturatorius is on the underside of the superior pubic ramus and forms the roof of the canalis obturatorius, together with the membrana obturatoria. The obturator nerve and vessels run through it. Pitfall: fractures of the superior pubic ramus through the groove can injure the obturator nerve or vessels, including an aberrant corona mortis.

lm:Occipital border of parietal bone|Par.key: lm:Occipital border of parietal bone|Parietal bone
lm:Occipital border of parietal bone|Par.note: Margo occipitalis forms the lambdoid suture with the occipital squama, deep to Musculus occipitalis. Pitfall: the serrated suture, sutural (Wormian) bones and accessory sutures can mimic a linear fracture. A real fracture has sharp, non-corticated edges and no matching suture on the other side. Use 3D/MIP reformats.

lm:Occipital condyle|Occipital bone.note: The condyles lie anterolateral to the foramen magnum and articulate with the lateral masses of C1. The hypoglossal canal runs above them and the vertebral artery runs posterior to them. Pitfall: condylar fractures (Anderson–Montesano) are easy to miss on axial slices alone, so use coronal reformats. A third condyle or a condylar canal can mimic a fracture fragment.

lm:Occipital margin of temporal bone|Tem.key: lm:Occipital margin of temporal bone|Temporal bone
lm:Occipital margin of temporal bone|Tem.note: Margo occipitalis meets the occipital bone at the petro-occipital fissure, which carries the inferior petrosal sinus and leads down to the jugular foramen. Pitfall: the normal fissure or synchondrosis mimics a fracture. An expansile lesion centred here suggests chondrosarcoma rather than chordoma, which is midline.
landmarks: lm:Intrajugular process of occipital bone|Occipital bone
lm:Internal acoustic opening (porus of internal acoustic meatus)|Temporal bone

lm:Occipital plane|Occipital bone.note: This is the external surface of the squama above the superior nuchal line, deep to the occipital pole. Pitfall: the mendosal suture, Wormian bones and an interparietal (Inca) bone can mimic fractures. In children this matters especially in suspected non-accidental injury, so assess with 3D VR.

lm:Occlusal surface of tooth|Lower first.key: lm:Occlusal surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Occlusal surface of tooth|Lower first.note: Facies occlusalis is the chewing surface. It carries the cusps and fissures and faces the upper first molar across the occlusal plane. Pitfall: in occlusion, axial slices through the plane mix upper and lower crowns. Assign findings to the maxillary or mandibular tooth on sagittal or coronal views.
landmarks: lm:Cusp of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Lingual surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Neck of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Distal surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Crown of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

lm:Olecranon fossa|Humerus.note: Fossa olecrani is a thin-floored depression on the posterior distal humerus. It takes the olecranon in extension and holds the posterior fat pad, deep to triceps. Pitfall: a septal aperture (supratrochlear foramen) is a normal variant, not osteolysis. Also check the fossa for hidden loose bodies.
neighbours: Subtendinous bursa of triceps brachii muscle

lm:Olecranon|Ulna.note: The olecranon forms the posterior proximal ulna and the posterior wall of the Incisura trochlearis. The triceps inserts on it, and in extension it engages the Fossa olecrani. Pitfall: an unfused olecranon apophysis or a patella cubiti (accessory sesamoid) mimics a fracture. Compare with the other side and check for corticated margins.
neighbours: Subtendinous bursa of triceps brachii muscle

lm:Opening of frontal sinus|Frontal bone.note: Drainage opening on the floor of the frontal sinus that leads into the frontal recess and then the middle meatus. Pitfall: agger nasi and frontal ethmoidal cells can narrow the outflow and mimic the sinus on axial images. Trace the drainage pathway on sagittal reformats.
landmarks: lm:Nasal part of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Nasal spine of frontal bone|Frontal bone

lm:Optic canal|Sphenoid bone.note: Canal between the two roots of the lesser wing, superomedial to the superior orbital fissure; the optic strut separates the two. Its medial wall borders the sphenoid sinus. Pitfall: a sphenoethmoidal (Onodi) cell or a dehiscent canal wall puts the optic nerve at surgical risk. Don't mistake the optic strut for a fracture.

lm:Orbital part of frontal bone|Frontal.key: lm:Orbital part of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Orbital part of frontal bone|Frontal.note: The Pars orbitalis forms the orbital roof and separates the orbit from the anterior cranial fossa. Medially it meets the Os ethmoideum at the frontoethmoidal suture, where the anterior ethmoidal foramina lie. Pitfall: the thin roof shows partial-volume pseudodehiscence on axial images. Confirm roof fractures and blowup fractures on coronal reformats.

lm:Orbital plate of frontal bone|Frontal.key: lm:Orbital plate of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Orbital plate of frontal bone|Frontal.note: Thin plate that forms most of the orbital roof and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa beneath the Gyri orbitales. Pitfall: on axial CT its thinness and partial volume can hide or mimic roof fractures. Assess it on coronal and sagittal reformats, and look for orbital emphysema or an extraconal haematoma.

lm:Orbital surface of frontal bone|Front.key: lm:Orbital surface of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Orbital surface of frontal bone|Front.note: Concave inferior surface of the orbital roof. It meets the zygomatic bone at the frontozygomatic suture and the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid behind. Pitfall: the frontozygomatic and frontosphenoidal sutures mimic fracture lines. Check the other side and the alignment of the suture.

lm:Orbital surface of greater wing|Sphen.key: lm:Orbital surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
lm:Orbital surface of greater wing|Sphen.note: Forms the posterior lateral orbital wall between the superior and inferior orbital fissures. It joins the Os zygomaticum in front, and the temporal pole lies just behind it. Pitfall: the sphenozygomatic suture mimics a fracture. Lateral wall fractures in zygomaticomaxillary complex (tripod) injuries are off-axis, so check axial and coronal views.

lm:Outer lip of iliac crest|Hip bone.key: lm:Outer lip of iliac crest|Hip bone
lm:Outer lip of iliac crest|Hip bone.note: Labium externum cristae iliacae gives attachment to obliquus externus abdominis and fascia lata. Obliquus internus arises from the linea intermedia and transversus abdominis from the inner lip. Pitfall: in adolescents, the iliac crest apophysis is a separate ossification centre that should not be called an avulsion fracture.
landmarks: lm:Inner lip of iliac crest|Hip bone

lm:Parietal eminence|Parietal bone.note: Eminentia parietalis is the most convex point of the Facies externa ossis parietalis, above the temporal lines and Musculus temporalis, overlying the Gyrus supramarginalis. Pitfall: symmetric senile biparietal thinning, where the outer table is lost, can mimic an osteolytic lesion or a depressed fracture.
passing: Parietal branches of middle cerebral artery
landmarks: lm:External surface of parietal bone|Parietal bone

lm:Parietal foramen|Parietal bone.note: Foramen parietale is a small paramedian foramen near the posterior sagittal suture. It carries an emissary vein to the Sinus sagittalis superior. Pitfall: the foramina are often asymmetric, unilateral or enlarged as a normal variant. A well-corticated, smooth defect is normal anatomy and should not be called a lytic lesion or fracture.

lm:Parietal margin of frontal bone|Front.key: lm:Parietal margin of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Parietal margin of frontal bone|Front.note: The Margo parietalis forms the coronal suture with the Ossa parietalia, over the frontal convexity. Pitfall: a normal coronal suture, especially an asymmetric or wormian-bearing one, can mimic a linear fracture. Look for suture symmetry and the zigzag margins, and call it a diastasis only if the suture is clearly widened.

lm:Parietal margin of greater wing|Sphen.key: lm:Parietal margin of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
lm:Parietal margin of greater wing|Sphen.note: Upper tip of the Ala major, where it meets the sphenoidal angle of the Os parietale at the pterion. It lies deep to the Musculus temporalis. Pitfall: the H-shaped sutures at the pterion and the groove of the frontal branch of the middle meningeal artery mimic a fracture. Fractures here carry a risk of epidural haematoma.
landmarks: lm:Frontal margin of greater wing|Sphenoid bone

lm:Patellar surface of femur|Femur.note: The Facies patellaris is the anterior trochlear groove that articulates with the patella. The suprapatellar recess and the quadriceps tendon lie above it. Pitfall: shallow trochlear depth (trochlear dysplasia) must be assessed on the most proximal axial slice through the cartilage. Distal slices make the trochlea look falsely normal.

lm:Pecten pubis|Hip bone.note: Pecten ossis pubis is the sharp upper ridge of the superior pubic ramus and forms part of the linea terminalis, the pelvic inlet. Pectineus arises from it and the lacunar ligament attaches to it. Pitfall: in children the triradiate cartilage is close by and should not be mistaken for a fracture; the corona mortis can run over the pecten.

lm:Pectineal line of femur|Femur.note: The Linea pectinea runs from the trochanter minor down to the linea aspera, and the pectineus inserts on it. The Tuberositas glutea lies lateral to it. Pitfall: do not mix up the medial pectineal line with the lateral gluteal tuberosity. A prominent gluteal tuberosity (third trochanter) is a normal variant, not an exostosis.

lm:Pedicle of vertebral arch|Vertebra L3.note: Pediculus arcus vertebrae connects the posterolateral body to the arch and forms the roofs and floors of the L2–L3 and L3–L4 foramina, with the exiting L3 root running beneath it. Pitfall: unilateral pedicle sclerosis may be a stress reaction to a contralateral pars defect, not a blastic metastasis; check for medial breach after screw placement.
neighbours: Dorsal parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles

lm:Pelvic surface of sacrum|Sacrum.note: Facies pelvica ossis sacri is the concave anterior surface, with the transverse lines marking fused discs and the anterior sacral foramina on either side. It lies behind the mesorectum, rectosigmoid and presacral vessels. Pitfall: the transverse lines and residual disc remnants can mimic transverse fractures. A true fracture shows a cortical step on sagittal reformats.

lm:Petrous part of temporal bone|Tempora.key: lm:Petrous part of temporal bone|Temporal bone
lm:Petrous part of temporal bone|Tempora.note: Pars petrosa is the pyramid between the middle and posterior cranial fossae; its superior ridge carries the tentorium attachment and the superior petrosal sinus. It houses the otic capsule. Pitfall: on CT brain, beam-hardening streaks between the petrous ridges mimic pontine hypodensity. Classify fractures as otic-capsule sparing or violating.
landmarks: lm:Posterior surface of petrous part|Temporal bone
lm:Fundus of internal acoustic meatus (approx.)|Temporal bone

lm:Pharyngeal tubercle|Occipital bone.note: This tubercle on the inferior surface of the basiocciput anchors the pharyngeal raphe. The Musculi longus capitis and rectus capitis anterior insert lateral to it, and the nasopharynx lies anterior to it. Pitfall: do not mistake a prominent tubercle, or the adjacent canalis basilaris medianus, for a clival fracture or erosion by a nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
landmarks: lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipital bone

lm:Popliteal surface of femur|Femur.note: The Facies poplitea is the flat triangle between the supracondylar lines and forms the floor of the popliteal fossa. The Arteria poplitea lies directly on it, with the vena poplitea superficial to the artery. Pitfall: a distal femoral fracture or osteochondroma here can injure the popliteal artery. A posterior cortical irregularity (cortical desmoid) is benign and should not be called aggressive.

lm:Posterior arch of atlas|Atlas (C1).note: The arcus posterior atlantis forms the dorsal rim of the C1 canal, under the suboccipital muscles. Pitfall: congenital aplasia or a midline cleft has smooth corticated margins. Do not report it as a fracture. A true fracture usually occurs at the junction with the lateral mass, near the vertebral artery groove.

lm:Posterior articular facet of dens axi.key: lm:Posterior articular facet of dens axis|Axis (C2)
lm:Posterior articular facet of dens axi.note: The facies articularis posterior dentis is where the transverse ligament glides over the back of the dens, in front of the dura and the cervicomedullary junction. Pitfall: pannus or calcium deposition here (crowned dens, rheumatoid arthritis) can look like a retro-odontoid mass. Look for calcification on CT.

lm:Posterior border of ulna|Ulna.note: Margo posterior ulnae is subcutaneous and palpable along its whole length. It serves as a shared aponeurotic attachment for flexor carpi ulnaris, extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum profundus. Pitfall: a direct-blow (nightstick) fracture here can be subtle and non-displaced. Do not mistake the thick cortical ridge for callus.
neighbours: Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris

lm:Posterior calcaneal articular facet|T.note: Largest, concave facet on the talar undersurface, forming the posterior subtalar joint; the sulcus tali and sinus tarsi separate it from the middle facet. Pitfall: in calcaneal fractures, measure posterior facet step-off and depression on coronal reconstructions (Sanders); axial images underestimate them.

lm:Posterior clinoid process|Sphenoid bo.note: Paired tubercles at the top of the Dorsum sellae where the tentorium attaches. The Nervus oculomotorius passes laterally, between the PCA and SCA. Pitfall: a pneumatized posterior clinoid or calcified interclinoid ligament (sella bridging) can mimic a calcified PCoA or basilar tip aneurysm. Confirm on bone-window reformats.

lm:Posterior gluteal line|Hip bone.note: Linea glutea posterior is a faint ridge on the posterior ala ossis ilii in front of the sacroiliac joint. Behind it, the bone gives origin to gluteus maximus; in front of it, gluteus medius arises. Pitfall: the line is subtle and the bone around it is thin, so partial volume can make it look like a fracture line on oblique slices.

lm:Posterior intercondylar area|Tibia.note: Area intercondylaris posterior lies behind the eminentia intercondylaris and slopes onto the posterior tibial surface. It carries the posterior meniscal root attachments and, most posteriorly, the PCL insertion. Pitfall: a posterior cortical fragment on sagittal CT is a PCL avulsion. Do not call it an ACL tibial eminence avulsion or a meniscal root ossicle.

lm:Posterior limb of internal capsule|Wh.key: lm:Posterior limb of internal capsule|White matter of telencephalon
lm:Posterior limb of internal capsule|Wh.note: Crus posterius capsulae internae lies between the thalamus (medial) and the nucleus lentiformis (lateral), and it carries the corticospinal tract. Pitfall: in early ischaemia, faint hypodensity here is easily missed. Hypertensive bleeds usually arise in the neighbouring putamen or thalamus, so name which compartment is involved.

lm:Posterior limb of stapes|Stapes.note: Crus posterius stapedis runs from caput stapedis to basis stapedis in the fenestra vestibuli, just below the tympanic facial canal. Pitfall: the crura are sub-millimetre and often invisible on routine CT; non-visualisation alone does not prove fracture or erosion, so check ultra-thin axial and oblique reconstructions.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of stapes|Stapes

lm:Posterior malleolus|Tibia.note: Malleolus posterior is the posterior lip of the tibial plafond and the attachment of the Ligamentum tibiofibulare posterius. Flexor hallucis longus lies posteromedially and the fibula lies laterally. Pitfall: posterior malleolar fragments are often missed on axial images. Measure fragment size and articular involvement on sagittal reformats, and do not confuse the fragment with an os trigonum.

lm:Posterior process of talus|Talus.note: Processus posterior tali has medial and lateral tubercles on either side of the FHL groove, lying above the posterior calcaneus and in front of Kager fat. Pitfall: an os trigonum or prominent Stieda process is a normal variant; diagnose fracture or impingement only with irregular, non-corticated margins or surrounding change.
landmarks: lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of talus|Talus

lm:Posterior sacral foramina|Sacrum.note: Foramina sacralia posteriora lie between the intermediate and lateral sacral crests, carry the dorsal rami, and are covered by the erector spinae. Pitfall: they are smaller than and not aligned with the anterior foramina, and their symmetry depends on how the sacrum is tilted in the scan. Compare both sides on a reformat angled along the sacrum before calling widening.

lm:Posterior surface of arytenoid cartil.key: lm:Posterior surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage
lm:Posterior surface of arytenoid cartil.note: The Facies posterior is concave and the transverse and oblique arytenoid muscles attach to it. Postcricoid hypopharyngeal mucosa lies behind it. Pitfall: collapsed postcricoid mucosa and venous plexus can mimic a postcricoid mass. Use a modified Valsalva acquisition to separate them.
landmarks: lm:Articular surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage

lm:Posterior surface of petrous part|Tem.key: lm:Posterior surface of petrous part|Temporal bone
lm:Posterior surface of petrous part|Tem.note: Facies posterior forms the anterolateral wall of the posterior fossa and cerebellopontine angle. It carries the porus acusticus internus and the vestibular aqueduct opening, between the superior and inferior petrosal sulci. Pitfall: the subarcuate canal or vestibular aqueduct can be misread as a fracture; an aqueduct wider than 1.5 mm is enlarged.
landmarks: lm:Petrous part of temporal bone|Temporal bone
lm:Occipital margin of temporal bone|Temporal bone
lm:Intrajugular process of occipital bone|Occipital bone

lm:Posterior surface of radius|Radius.note: Facies posterior radii lies between the interosseous and posterior borders. Musculus supinator covers it proximally and abductor pollicis longus arises from its middle third. Pitfall: the rough lateral pronator teres insertion at mid-shaft can mimic periosteal reaction or a healing fracture. Compare with the other side.

lm:Posterior surface of scapula|Scapula.note: The Facies posterior is split by the Spina scapulae into the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae, which hold the supraspinatus and infraspinatus. Pitfall: nutrient foramina and the thin, partly translucent bone of the scapular body can look like fracture lines or lytic lesions.

lm:Posterior surface of ulna|Ulna.note: Facies posterior ulnae lies between the posterior and interosseous borders. It gives origin to the deep extensors (abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis longus, extensor indicis) and, proximally, receives the anconeus. Pitfall: oblique ridges between muscle origins can mimic periosteal reaction. Note also that laterality and pronation change the apparent orientation of this surface.
passing: Posterior branch of medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve
neighbours: Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris

lm:Posterior tubercle of atlas|Atlas (C1.note: The tuberculum posterius is a rudimentary spinous process in the midline of the posterior arch. It anchors the rectus capitis posterior minor and the nuchal ligament. Pitfall: it is much smaller than the C2 spinous process. Do not miscount levels on sagittal reformats; C2 has the first large bifid spinous process.
landmarks: lm:Posterior articular facet of dens axis|Axis (C2)

lm:Posterior tubercle of transverse proc.key: lm:Posterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4
lm:Posterior tubercle of transverse proc.note: Tuberculum posterius closes the transverse process dorsolaterally, behind the Sulcus nervi spinalis, and gives attachment to Musculus scalenus medius, levator scapulae and the splenius and longissimus colli. Pitfall: the tubercle tip seen on a single axial slice can look like a free fragment; confirm continuity on coronal reconstructions.
landmarks: lm:Anterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4

lm:Promontory|Sacrum.note: Promontorium is the anterior upper lip of the S1 body, just below discus L5–S1, and forms the back of the pelvic inlet. The aortic and caval bifurcations and the presacral nerve plexus lie in front of it. Pitfall: with lumbosacral transitional anatomy the true promontory is easily mislabelled, which leads to wrong level reporting.

lm:Pterygoid canal|Sphenoid bone.note: Canal at the base of the pterygoid process, along the sphenoid sinus floor. It runs from the Foramen lacerum to the pterygopalatine fossa and carries the Vidian nerve and artery. Pitfall: it lies inferomedial to the Foramen rotundum, which is superolateral; don't swap them. It may protrude into the sinus on a thin, dehiscent stalk.
landmarks: lm:Internal opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone
lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipital bone

lm:Pterygoid fossa|Sphenoid bone.note: Posteriorly open fossa between the medial and lateral pterygoid plates, filled by the Musculus pterygoideus medialis. Inferiorly it is closed by the pyramidal process of the Os palatinum. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the Fossa pterygopalatina, which lies anterior to the pterygoid process and contains neurovascular fat.

lm:Pterygoid hamulus|Sphenoid bone.note: Hook-shaped inferior tip of the medial pterygoid plate, posterolateral to the Palatum molle. The tendon of tensor veli palatini turns around it, and the pterygomandibular raphe attaches to it. Pitfall: an elongated or separately ossified hamulus can mimic a fracture fragment or foreign body; compare with the other side.

lm:Pterygoid notch|Sphenoid bone.note: Inferior gap between the medial and lateral pterygoid plates, filled by the pyramidal process of the Os palatinum and next to the posterior Maxilla. Pitfall: the palatine–pterygoid suture lines can mimic a pterygoid plate fracture when grading Le Fort injuries; look for a cortical step and soft-tissue changes.

lm:Pterygospinous process|Sphenoid bone.note: Spur on the posterior edge of the lateral pterygoid plate, pointing toward the Spina ossis sphenoidei, below the Foramen ovale. Pitfall: an ossified pterygospinous ligament forms a bony bar (Civinini foramen) that can mimic a fracture. It may also block access to the Foramen ovale or compress the Nervus lingualis.
passing: Accessory branch of middle meningeal artery
neighbours: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

lm:Pubic crest|Hip bone.note: Crista pubica is the upper border of the corpus ossis pubis, running medially from the tuberculum pubicum to the symphysis. Rectus abdominis and pyramidalis insert here. Pitfall: in athletic pubalgia, a rectus–adductor aponeurosis injury causes enthesis irregularity here, which can be misread as degenerative change of the symphysis.

lm:Pubic tubercle|Hip bone.note: Tuberculum pubicum is the lateral end of the crista pubica and the medial attachment of the ligamentum inguinale. The spermatic cord (ductus deferens) passes over it. Pitfall: use it to classify hernias. Inguinal hernias lie superomedial to the tubercle and femoral hernias inferolateral, next to the femoral vein.

lm:Pubis|Hip bone.note: Os pubis consists of the corpus and the superior and inferior rami. It meets the opposite side at the symphysis pubica via the discus interpubicus, with the bladder lying behind in the retropubic space. Pitfall: osteitis pubis or physiological widening around the symphysis (e.g. postpartum) can mimic infection or a traumatic diastasis; correlate with symphyseal width.

lm:Quadrate tubercle|Femur.note: The Tuberculum quadratum is a bump on the Crista intertrochanterica and is the insertion of the Musculus quadratus femoris.
