Pitfall: fracture lines through the posterior intertrochanteric crest here mean posteromedial comminution, which signals an unstable trochanteric fracture. Do not mistake the tubercle's normal prominence for a fragment.
neighbours: Trochanteric bursa of gluteus maximus muscle

lm:Radial groove|Humerus.note: Sulcus nervi radialis spirals obliquely across the posterior mid-shaft, between the origins of the lateral and medial triceps heads. It carries the radial nerve and deep brachial vessels toward the lateral intermuscular septum. Pitfall: distal-third spiral shaft fractures (Holstein-Lewis) put the radial nerve at risk. Do not read the shallow groove as a cortical defect.
neighbours: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

lm:Radial notch|Ulna.note: Incisura radialis is the lateral concave facet of the coronoid process that articulates with the Caput radii at the proximal radio-ulnar joint. The Ligamentum anulare radii is attached to its margins. Pitfall: radial head subluxation (Monteggia) is easily overlooked. Check the radiocapitellar line, and do not confuse the notch with the trochlear notch.

lm:Radial styloid process|Radius.note: Processus styloideus radii is the distolateral tip of the radius, crossed by the 1st extensor compartment (APL/EPB). The radial collateral ligament of the wrist attaches here, with the radial artery just beside it. Pitfall: a styloid (chauffeur) fracture is often associated with scapholunate injury. Assess the scapholunate interval, and do not dismiss an ossicle without checking its edges.
neighbours: Radial collateral ligament of wrist joint

lm:Radial tuberosity|Radius.note: Tuberositas radii lies anteromedially below the neck and receives the biceps tendon, with the bicipitoradial bursa between them. Pitfall: when seen end-on, the tuberosity's cancellous bone looks like a cystic or lytic lesion (pseudolesion). A fluid-filled distended bursa can also mimic a mass next to a biceps tendon rupture.

lm:Radius|Radius.note: The radius is the lateral forearm bone with a lateral bow. The interosseous membrane attaches medially, flexor pollicis longus lies anteriorly and the extensors posterolaterally. Pitfall: an apparently isolated shaft fracture may be a Galeazzi or Monteggia injury, so check both the distal and proximal radioulnar joints. The oblique nutrient canal can mimic a fracture.
neighbours: Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis

lm:Ramus of ischium|Hip bone.note: Ramus ossis ischii runs anteromedially from the tuber ischiadicum to join the inferior pubic ramus, forming the inferior border of the foramen obturatum. Pitfall: in children, the ischiopubic synchondrosis can be bulky and asymmetric (van Neck appearance), which can mimic a fracture or tumour.

lm:Rib|Sixth rib.note: Costa VI is a true rib articulating with T5–T6, with the intercostal spaces above and below and the costal pleura internally. Pitfall: miscounting ribs. Count down from the first rib on coronal or 3D views, because cervical ribs or hypoplastic twelfth ribs shift the numbering.

lm:Root apex|Lower first molar tooth.note: Apex radicis of the mesial and distal roots lies in cancellous mandibular bone just above the canalis mandibulae, which carries the inferior alveolar nerve and vessels. Pitfall: the mandibular canal, or the nearby foramen mentale at premolar level, projected onto the apex can mimic a periapical lucency. Follow the canal across serial slices.
landmarks: lm:Root of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

lm:Root of tooth|Lower first molar tooth.key: lm:Root of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Root of tooth|Lower first molar tooth.note: The Radix dentis usually splits into a mesial and a distal root. Each sits in alveolar bone, lined by a thin periodontal ligament space and lamina dura, above the canalis mandibulae. Pitfall: an extra distolingual root (radix entomolaris) or the canal crossing near the apex can look like a fracture or a periapical lucency.
landmarks: lm:Neck of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Crown of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

lm:Sacral canal|Sacrum.note: Canalis sacralis continues the lumbar canal from S1 to the hiatus sacralis. It contains the cauda equina, the end of the dural sac (usually at S2), the filum terminale and epidural fat. Pitfall: a Tarlov cyst or dural ectasia scalloping the canal can mimic an expansile tumour. The CSF density and a smooth outline favour the benign cause.

lm:Sacral hiatus|Sacrum.note: Hiatus sacralis is the caudal opening of the canalis sacralis, usually at S4–S5 where the laminae fail to fuse. It is bounded by the cornua sacralia and closed by the superficial posterior sacrococcygeal ligament. Pitfall: its level and size vary widely, and a high or absent hiatus is a variant rather than a defect. This matters for caudal epidural access.

lm:Sacral horn|Sacrum.note: Cornu sacrale is the paired downward projection of the intermediate crest that borders the hiatus sacralis and articulates with the cornua coccygea through the ligamentum intercornuale. Pitfall: an unfused or asymmetric cornu, or a small ossicle next to it, can mimic an avulsion fragment. Look for well-corticated margins.

lm:Sacral tuberosity|Sacrum.note: Tuberositas ossis sacri is the rough area behind the auricular surface where the interosseous sacroiliac ligament attaches, facing the tuberositas iliaca. Pitfall: this ligamentous (non-synovial) part of the joint normally looks irregular and widened. Do not read it as erosion or diastasis; judge sacroiliitis on the synovial part instead.

lm:Sacrum|Sacrum.note: The os sacrum consists of five fused vertebrae wedged between the ossa coxae at the sacroiliac joints. It joins L5 above and the coccyx below and contains the sacral canal. Pitfall: sacral insufficiency and other fractures are easily missed on axial CT alone. Review coronal reformats angled along the sacrum and check for transitional segments.

lm:Sagittal border of parietal bone|Pari.key: lm:Sagittal border of parietal bone|Parietal bone
lm:Sagittal border of parietal bone|Pari.note: Margo sagittalis forms the midline sagittal suture with the opposite parietal bone. The Sinus sagittalis superior and Falx cerebri lie directly beneath it. Pitfall: suture vs linear fracture. A fracture crossing the midline needs a check for venous epidural haematoma or sinus injury. A normal suture is serrated and corticated.

lm:Scaphoid fossa|Sphenoid bone.note: Small depression at the upper root of the medial pterygoid plate where tensor veli palatini arises. It lies anteromedial to the Foramen ovale and the exiting mandibular nerve. Pitfall: on thick axial slices this shallow fossa can look like a foramen; do not mistake it for the Foramen ovale or the pterygoid canal.
passing: Accessory branch of middle meningeal artery
neighbours: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

lm:Scapula|Scapula.note: The scapula is a flat triangular bone over ribs 2–7, joined to the trunk by muscle and articulating with the clavicle and humerus. Pitfall: scapular body fractures are easily missed on axial chest CT. Use 3D or sagittal reformats and look for associated rib, lung and thoracic spine injury.

lm:Scapular notch|Scapula.note: The Incisura scapulae is on the superior border, medial to the coracoid base, and is bridged by the Lig. transversum superius scapulae. Pitfall: the suprascapular nerve runs below the ligament and the artery usually runs above it. A calcified ligament can turn the notch into a foramen and is a normal variant linked to nerve entrapment.

lm:Sella turcica|Sphenoid bone.note: Saddle-shaped surface on top of the Corpus ossis sphenoidei, bounded in front by the tuberculum sellae and behind by the dorsum sellae, with the cavernous sinuses on each side. Pitfall: a bridged sella from interclinoid ligament calcification and an empty sella are normal variants. Do not misread them as calcified masses or erosion.

lm:Septum of frontal sinuses|Sinus of fr.key: lm:Septum of frontal sinuses|Sinus of frontal bone
lm:Septum of frontal sinuses|Sinus of fr.note: Septum sinuum frontalium is a thin bony wall dividing the left and right frontal sinuses, between the anterior and posterior tables. It is often off-midline and asymmetric. Pitfall: a deviated septum or accessory septa can be mistaken for fracture lines. Lateralise each sinus by its drainage, not by the midline.

lm:Septum of sphenoidal sinuses|Sinus of.key: lm:Septum of sphenoidal sinuses|Sinus of sphenoid bone
lm:Septum of sphenoidal sinuses|Sinus of.note: Septum sinuum sphenoideorum divides the sphenoid sinus and is often off-midline. Pitfall: the septum or accessory septa can insert onto the carotid canal or optic canal. Report this before transsphenoidal surgery, because fracturing the septum risks injury to the arteria carotis interna.

lm:Soleal line|Tibia.note: Linea musculi solei is an oblique ridge on the proximal posterior tibia. Musculus popliteus inserts above it, and soleus and the deep flexors originate below it. Pitfall: irregular cortex at this tendinous origin is a normal enthesis (tug lesion). Do not call it periostitis, a stress fracture or a tumour.

lm:Sphenoidal crest|Sphenoid bone.note: Midline ridge on the anterior surface of the Corpus ossis sphenoidei that joins the perpendicular plate of the Os ethmoideum and the nasal septum. Pitfall: the intersinus septum of the Sinus sphenoidalis is often off the midline and may insert on the carotid canal, so the crest does not mark the internal septum.
passing: Septal branches of posterior ethmoidal artery

lm:Sphenoidal lingula|Sphenoid bone.note: Small bony spur on the lateral lip of the carotid sulcus, next to the petrous apex above the Foramen lacerum, where the ICA turns into the cavernous sinus. Pitfall: the Foramen lacerum is filled with cartilage and does not carry the ICA, which runs above it. Do not report a normal lingula–apex gap as erosion.
landmarks: lm:Internal opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone
lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipital bone

lm:Sphenoidal margin of frontal bone|Fro.key: lm:Sphenoidal margin of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Sphenoidal margin of frontal bone|Fro.note: The Margo sphenoideus joins the orbital plates to the lesser wing and the greater wing of the Os sphenoideum, forming the sphenofrontal suture at the posterior orbital roof and anterior cranial fossa. Pitfall: the suture and the adjacent superior orbital fissure can be mistaken for a fracture. Use coronal reformats and compare both sides.

lm:Sphenoidal yoke|Sphenoid bone.note: The jugum (planum sphenoidale) is the flat roof of the Sinus sphenoidalis, behind the cribriform plate and in front of the limbus, below the Gyrus recti. Pitfall: the thin plate can look falsely dehiscent from partial volume. Hyperostosis from a planum meningioma can be confused with pneumosinus dilatans.

lm:Spine of scapula|Scapula.note: Spina scapulae is the dorsal bony ridge between the fossa supraspinata and fossa infraspinata. It continues laterally into the acromion and gives attachment to the trapezius and the deltoid spinal part. Pitfall: an unfused os acromiale or an oblique cut through the spine-acromion junction can look like a fracture line.
neighbours: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

lm:Spine of sphenoid bone|Sphenoid bone.note: Downward spur at the posterior corner of the Ala major, medial to the Fossa mandibularis. The sphenomandibular ligament attaches here and the chorda tympani runs on its medial side. Pitfall: the Foramen spinosum lies just anteromedial to it. An absent foramen suggests a persistent stapedial artery and should not be called a lytic defect.
landmarks: lm:External opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone

lm:Spinoglenoid notch|Scapula.note: Incisura spinoglenoidea lies between the lateral spine base and the posterior glenoid neck. It joins the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae and carries the suprascapular nerve and vessels. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the incisura scapulae. A paralabral cyst here compresses only the infraspinatus branch.

lm:Spinous process of axis (tip)|Axis (C.note: The C2 spinous process is large and bifid. It anchors the rectus capitis posterior major and obliquus capitis inferior, and the nuchal ligament attaches at its tip. Pitfall: a normal bifid tip, or a gap from incomplete fusion, can look like a fracture. Look for corticated margins and soft-tissue swelling.

lm:Spinous process|Vertebra L3.note: Processus spinosus projects dorsally from the laminar junction, linked to adjacent spines by the interspinous and supraspinous ligaments and flanked by the erector spinae. Pitfall: Baastrup disease (kissing spines with neoarthrosis) and unfused apophyses mimic fractures; widening of the interspinous distance suggests posterior ligamentous injury.

lm:Squamosal border of parietal bone|Par.key: lm:Squamosal border of parietal bone|Parietal bone
lm:Squamosal border of parietal bone|Par.note: Margo squamosus is overlapped by the bevelled Pars squamosa ossis temporalis, forming the squamosal suture deep to Musculus temporalis. Pitfall: because the overlap is bevelled, axial slices show an oblique lucent line that mimics a temporal fracture. Compare both sides and check coronal reformats.
passing: Temporal branches of middle cerebral artery
landmarks: lm:Squamous part of temporal bone|Temporal bone

lm:Squamosal margin of greater wing|Sphe.key: lm:Squamosal margin of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
lm:Squamosal margin of greater wing|Sphe.note: Posterolateral edge of the Ala major, forming the sphenosquamosal suture with the squamous Os temporale. The Polus temporalis lies inside and the Musculus temporalis outside. Pitfall: the serrated suture mimics a fracture. Small greater-wing defects next to the temporal pole may be meningoencephaloceles, not normal pits.
landmarks: lm:Zygomatic margin of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
lm:Anterior surface of petrous part|Temporal bone

lm:Squamous part of occipital bone|Occip.key: lm:Squamous part of occipital bone|Occipital bone
lm:Squamous part of occipital bone|Occip.note: The squama is bounded by the lambdoid suture above and the foramen magnum below, and the internal occipital protuberance divides its cerebral and cerebellar fossae. Pitfall: accessory sutures (mendosal, Wormian bones) and vascular channels mimic fractures. Small skull-base fractures need contrecoup frontal contusions searched for.

lm:Squamous part of temporal bone|Tempor.key: lm:Squamous part of temporal bone|Temporal bone
lm:Squamous part of temporal bone|Tempor.note: Pars squamosa is a thin plate lying deep to the temporalis, overlapping the parietal bone at the squamosal suture over the temporal lobe. A fracture here can tear the middle meningeal artery and cause an epidural haematoma. Pitfall: the squamosal suture, vascular grooves and axial partial volume of the thin squama mimic fractures.
landmarks: lm:Squamosal border of parietal bone|Parietal bone

lm:Stapes|Stapes.note: Stapes lies medially in the mesotympanum. It articulates with the processus lenticularis incudis, and its basis stapedis closes the fenestra vestibuli under the tympanic facial canal. Pitfall: partial volume easily hides the incudostapedial joint, so confirm dislocation on thin slices; a thickened footplate or fissula lucency suggests otosclerosis.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of stapes|Stapes

lm:Sternal angle|Body of sternum.note: The angulus sterni is the manubriosternal joint, where the second costal cartilages attach, at the level of the T4/T5 disc. Pitfall: this synchondrosis is a normal non-ossified gap that can be mistaken for a sternal fracture. Fractures show displacement or step-off and a retrosternal haematoma.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

lm:Sternal articular surface|Clavicle.note: Facies articularis sternalis is the saddle-shaped medial clavicular surface meeting the clavicular notch of the manubrium, with an intra-articular discus in between. Pitfall: the medial clavicular epiphysis fuses late, up to about 25 years, and can mimic a fracture. Posterior dislocation puts the brachiocephalic vessels at risk.

lm:Sternal end|Clavicle.note: Extremitas sternalis is the enlarged medial end of the clavicle. The sternocleidomastoid clavicular head attaches above and in front, and the sternohyoid behind. Pitfall: asymmetric patient position makes the sternoclavicular joints look subluxed. Judge anterior or posterior displacement relative to the manubrium on symmetric axial slices.

lm:Styloid process of temporal bone|Temp.key: lm:Styloid process of temporal bone|Temporal bone
lm:Styloid process of temporal bone|Temp.note: Processus styloideus divides the prestyloid from the poststyloid parapharyngeal space, with the ECA and parotid lateral and the ICA, IJV and IX–XII medial. Pitfall: an elongated process (over ~30 mm) or a calcified stylohyoid ligament (Eagle syndrome) has segmented ossification that mimics a fracture.

lm:Stylomastoid foramen|Temporal bone.note: Foramen stylomastoideum lies between the styloid and mastoid processes and is where the mastoid segment of the facial nerve exits. Pitfall: don't confuse it with the jugular foramen further medial. Loss of the fat pad at the foramen signals perineural spread, for example from parotid malignancy.
landmarks: lm:External acoustic meatus (medial end, tympanic membrane)|Temporal bone

lm:Sublime tubercle|Ulna.note: Tuberculum sublime is on the medial coronoid margin and is the insertion of the anterior bundle of the Ligamentum collaterale ulnare. Pitfall: a small ossicle here in throwers is a UCL avulsion or enthesophyte. Do not attribute it to the medial epicondyle apophysis, and do not miss an anteromedial coronoid facet fracture.
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris

lm:Sublingual fossa|Mandible.note: The Fovea sublingualis is a shallow anterior depression on the inner surface above the mylohyoid line, holding the sublingual gland beside the mental spines. Pitfall: an anterior lingual salivary bone defect (Stafne variant) or a thin cortex can look like an osteolytic lesion. Do not confuse it with the digastric fossa below.
passing: Mental branch of inferior alveolar artery

lm:Subscapular fossa|Scapula.note: Fossa subscapularis is the concave costal surface of the scapula. It holds the subscapularis, and serratus anterior separates it from the posterior ribs. Pitfall: the thin scapular blade overlapping a rib on axial CT can mimic a rib lesion or fracture, so trace each contour separately.

lm:Sulcus of auditory tube|Sphenoid bone.note: Groove in the petrosphenoidal fissure, between the posterior Ala major and the petrous apex, that holds the cartilaginous Tuba auditiva. Pitfall: the petrosphenoidal fissure can mimic a skull-base fracture. The petrous ICA lies just posteromedial, so any lesion here needs its carotid relationship stated.
landmarks: lm:External opening of carotid canal|Temporal bone

lm:Superciliary arch|Frontal bone.note: The Arcus superciliaris is a ridge above the medial orbital rim, overlying the Sinus frontalis, with the frontal lobes behind it. Pitfall: its prominence depends on how far the sinus is pneumatized and differs between sexes. Fractures of the anterior sinus wall here must be checked separately for involvement of the posterior table.
passing: Frontal branch of superficial temporal artery

lm:Superior angle of scapula|Scapula.note: Angulus superior scapulae is the superomedial corner where the levator scapulae inserts, usually at about the T2 level over the posterior second rib. Pitfall: on axial slices the angle can look like an isolated bony fragment or a rib lesion. A prominent angle or osteochondroma causes snapping scapula.

lm:Superior articular facet of vertebra|.key: lm:Superior articular facet of vertebra|Vertebra L3
lm:Superior articular facet of vertebra|.note: Facies articularis superior of L3 faces posteromedially and articulates with the inferior facet of L2 at the L2–L3 zygapophyseal joint, behind the foramen and lateral to the lamina. Pitfall: laterality and level errors at facet joints; a hypertrophic superior facet causes lateral recess stenosis that affects the traversing L3 root.

lm:Superior articular process of sacrum|.note: The Processus articularis superior ossis sacri forms the S1 side of the L5–S1 zygapophyseal joint, posterolateral to the canal and behind the S1 foramen. Pitfall: lumbosacral transitional anatomy (sacralised L5, lumbarised S1) makes segment numbering unreliable, so count from C2 or T12 before you report facet arthropathy or a fracture.

lm:Superior articular process of vertebr.key: lm:Superior articular process of vertebra|Vertebra L3
lm:Superior articular process of vertebr.note: Processus articularis superior of L3 rises from the pedicle–lamina junction and forms the posterior wall of the L2–L3 foramen and the lateral recess. The mamillary process lies on its posterior margin. Pitfall: osteophytes on the superior articular process narrow the foramen and lateral recess; synovial facet cysts can mimic a sequestered disc fragment.
neighbours: Ventral parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles

lm:Superior articular surface of atlas|A.note: This concave, kidney-shaped facet receives the occipital condyle at the atlanto-occipital joint. Pitfall: in atlanto-occipital dissociation the joint widens. On coronal reformats a condyle–C1 interval over 1.5 mm in children (about 2 mm in adults) is abnormal. A normal facet with a central waist can look like a fracture line.
landmarks: lm:Jugular notch of occipital bone|Occipital bone

lm:Superior costal facet|Vertebra T8.note: The Fovea costalis superior lies at the posterolateral upper margin of the T8 body, at the T7–T8 disc. Together with the inferior facet of T7, it holds the head of the eighth rib. Pitfall: on axial CT, the joint space of the rib head joint can be mistaken for a fracture or for the intervertebral foramen. Check the rib numbering.

lm:Superior facet of talus|Talus.note: Facies superior trochleae tali articulates with the tibial plafond, is wider anteriorly and merges into the malleolar facets. Pitfall: osteochondral lesions on the medial and lateral talar shoulders are easily missed on axial images; check coronal and sagittal reconstructions and do not mistake vascular channels for lesions.

lm:Superior horn of thyroid cartilage|Th.key: lm:Superior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage
lm:Superior horn of thyroid cartilage|Th.note: The Cornu superius points up and back and joins the tip of the greater horn of the hyoid through the lateral thyrohyoid ligament. It lies medial to the carotid bifurcation. Pitfall: a calcified triticeous cartilage inside that ligament mimics carotid plaque, a foreign body or a horn fracture.
landmarks: lm:Oblique line of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

lm:Superior mental spine|Mandible.note: Paired midline tubercles on the lingual surface of the symphysis that give origin to Musculus genioglossus; Spina mentalis inferior below anchors Musculus geniohyoideus. Pitfall: the lingual (genial) foramen just above them carries a small artery and can look like a fracture line or lytic focus on axial CT.

lm:Superior nuchal line|Occipital bone.note: This curved ridge runs laterally from the external occipital protuberance and roughly marks the level of the transverse sinus on the inner surface. The trapezius and semispinalis attach here. Pitfall: tentorial and transverse-sinus level lies near this external line, so a fracture crossing it risks an epidural haematoma involving the venous sinus.

lm:Superior pubic ramus|Hip bone.note: Ramus superior ossis pubis runs from the acetabulum to the symphysis pubica. Musculus pectineus lies in front and below it, and the vesica urinaria lies behind it. Pitfall: in elderly patients, check carefully for subtle insufficiency or ramus fractures, and do not mistake the normal pubic tubercle or the obturator groove for a fracture line.

lm:Superior thyroid notch|Thyroid cartil.note: This V-shaped midline notch sits just above the laryngeal prominence. The Ligamentum thyreohyoideum medianum spans from it to the hyoid, with pre-epiglottic fat behind. Pitfall: a deep notch can look like a midline defect or fracture on axial slices. Confirm on sagittal reformats and check the pre-epiglottic fat.

lm:Superior thyroid tubercle|Thyroid car.note: The tubercle marks the upper end of the Linea obliqua, just in front of the base of the Cornu superius. The thyrohyoid attaches here and the paraglottic space lies medially. Pitfall: the ossified tubercle lies close to level III nodes and the internal jugular vein. Do not report it as a calcified node.
landmarks: lm:Oblique line of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage
lm:Superior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

lm:Superior vertebral notch|Vertebra L3.note: Incisura vertebralis superior is the shallow notch above the L3 pedicle that forms the floor of the L2–L3 foramen, next to the L2–L3 disc. Pitfall: it is much shallower than the inferior notch, so the lower foramen boundary is easily misjudged; disc bulging at this level narrows the inferior part of the foramen, while the L2 ganglion sits higher.
neighbours: Ventral parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles

lm:Supinator crest|Ulna.note: Crista supinatoria runs distally from the posterior margin of the radial notch. It is the ulnar origin of the supinator, and its tubercle receives the lateral ulnar collateral ligament. Pitfall: an avulsion flake here signals posterolateral rotatory instability. Do not dismiss it as a harmless enthesophyte.

lm:Supraglenoid tubercle|Scapula.note: Tuberculum supraglenoideum is the bony prominence at the superior glenoid rim where the long biceps tendon and superior labrum (biceps anchor) attach. It sits intra-articularly under the supraspinatus. Pitfall: a normal sublabral recess or the biceps anchor can mimic an avulsion or SLAP lesion. Do not confuse it with the coracoid base.

lm:Supraspinous fossa|Scapula.note: Fossa supraspinata lies above the spina scapulae and is filled by musculus supraspinatus. It narrows laterally towards the spinoglenoid region and the incisura scapulae. Pitfall: thin fossa bone causes partial-volume lucencies that can mimic osteolysis. Also check whether the supraspinatus muscle has fatty atrophy.

lm:Suprastyloid crest|Radius.note: Crista suprastyloidea is the lateral ridge just above the radial styloid where Musculus brachioradialis inserts. The 1st extensor compartment tendons cross over it. Pitfall: the irregular insertion cortex can mimic periosteal reaction or a non-displaced fracture. The superficial branch of the radial nerve runs close by, which matters for dorsoradial screws.

lm:Supreme nuchal line|Occipital bone.note: This faint ridge lies above the superior nuchal line, and the Galea aponeurotica and Musculus occipitalis attach to it. Pitfall: it is often barely visible on CT. Do not mistake it for the superior nuchal line, and do not read it or normal occipital lymph nodes as a pathology.

lm:Sustentaculum tali|Calcaneus.note: Sustentaculum tali is a medial shelf of the calcaneus. Its upper surface carries the middle facet for the talus, and the flexor hallucis longus runs beneath it. Pitfall: a talocalcaneal coalition at the middle facet, fibrous or cartilaginous, can look like a narrow normal joint. Use coronal reformats.
landmarks: lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of calcaneus|Calcaneus

lm:Talar sulcus|Talus.note: Sulcus tali and sulcus calcanei together form the canalis tarsi and sinus tarsi, which hold the interosseous talocalcaneal ligament between the posterior and middle facets. Pitfall: sinus tarsi fat is normally low density; its loss suggests sinus tarsi pathology. A continuous C-shaped outline around the sinus suggests talocalcaneal coalition.

lm:Tarsal sinus|Calcaneus.note: Sinus tarsi is the lateral funnel-shaped space between the talar neck and the anterior calcaneus. It is filled with fat and the talocalcaneal ligaments. Pitfall: fluid or soft tissue that wipes out the fat is abnormal, but at the narrow medial canalis tarsi partial volume can look like loss of fat.

lm:Tegmen tympani|Temporal bone.note: Tegmen tympani is the thin roof of the tympanic cavity and antrum, separating the epitympanum (malleus head, incus) from the middle fossa and temporal lobe. Pitfall: partial volume of very thin bone mimics dehiscence; assess on coronal reformats before suggesting an encephalocele or CSF leak.
landmarks: lm:Geniculum of facial nerve (geniculate ganglion)|Temporal bone

lm:Temporal line|Frontal bone.note: The Linea temporalis curves up and back from the zygomatic process and marks the upper limit of the temporal fossa and the attachment of the temporal fascia. Pitfall: its cortical ridge and the change in bone thickness can mimic a fracture step or periosteal reaction on CT.
landmarks: lm:Temporal surface of frontal bone|Frontal bone
neighbours: Orbital part of  inferior frontal gyrus

lm:Temporal surface of frontal bone|Fron.key: lm:Temporal surface of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Temporal surface of frontal bone|Fron.note: The Facies temporalis lies below the temporal line, forms the anterior upper temporal fossa under the Musculus temporalis, and meets the greater wing at the pterion. Pitfall: the thin bone near the pterion overlies meningeal vessels. Do not mistake the sphenofrontal suture for a fracture, and check for an epidural hematoma.
neighbours: Orbital part of  inferior frontal gyrus
Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus

lm:Temporal surface of greater wing|Sphe.key: lm:Temporal surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
lm:Temporal surface of greater wing|Sphe.note: Outer convex surface of the Ala major forming the floor of the temporal fossa, where the Musculus temporalis arises. The infratemporal crest marks its lower edge, and the Polus temporalis lies against its inner side. Pitfall: vascular grooves and sutures mimic fractures. Partial volume of bone over the temporal pole can mimic a contusion on CT brain.
landmarks: lm:Cerebral surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone

lm:Thyroid articular surface|Cricoid car.note: The Facies articularis thyreoidea is on the side of the cricoid, where the lamina meets the arch. It forms the cricothyroid joint with the Cornu inferius cartilaginis thyreoideae. Pitfall: the recurrent laryngeal nerve enters the larynx just behind this joint, so cricothyroid dislocation after trauma can injure it. A partly calcified inferior horn can also mimic a fracture.
landmarks: lm:Inferior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

lm:Tibia|Tibia.note: The tibial diaphysis is triangular in cross-section, with a subcutaneous anteromedial surface. The posterior surface is covered by the deep flexors and soleus. Pitfall: the obliquely running nutrient canal mimics a non-displaced fracture. An anterior cortical transverse lucency ("dreaded black line") is a stress fracture.

lm:Tibial tuberosity|Tibia.note: Tuberositas tibiae is the anterior insertion of the patellar ligament. The Bursa infrapatellaris profunda lies deep to the ligament, and the subcutaneous bursae lie superficially. It is also the reference point for TT–TG distance. Pitfall: in adolescents, a fragmented apophyseal ossification centre is normal. Do not call it a tuberosity avulsion or Osgood–Schlatter disease without soft-tissue swelling.
neighbours: Subcutaneous bursa of tuberosity of tibia

lm:Transverse costal facet|Vertebra T8.note: The Fovea costalis processus transversi is on the anterior tip of the T8 transverse process. It forms the costotransverse joint with the tubercle of the eighth rib, with the Longissimus behind. Pitfall: on axial slices, the costotransverse joint looks like a transverse process fracture. Follow the rib in sequence and compare with the other side.

lm:Transverse foramen of atlas|Atlas (C1.note: The foramen transversarium of C1 lies in the transverse process, lateral to the lateral mass. It carries the vertebral artery in its upward-and-backward course into V3. Pitfall: a fracture running into this foramen calls for CT angiography to look for vertebral artery dissection. An incomplete foramen is a normal variant, not a fracture.

lm:Transverse foramen of axis|Axis (C2).note: The C2 foramen transversarium is angled steeply up and out, so the vertebral artery turns laterally here toward C1. Pitfall: a high-riding vertebral artery thins the C2 isthmus and pars, which matters for C2 screws. A fracture involving the foramen calls for vascular imaging.

lm:Transverse ligament tubercle|Atlas (C.note: The tuberculum ligamenti transversi sits on the medial surface of each lateral mass and anchors the transverse ligament behind the dens. Pitfall: a small bone fragment medial to the lateral mass means a bony avulsion of the transverse ligament (Dickman type II). Do not dismiss it as an ossicle, because it changes stability.

lm:Transverse process of atlas (tip)|Atl.note: The C1 transverse process is the widest in the upper cervical spine and is palpable between the mastoid and the mandibular angle. It anchors the obliquus muscles and levator scapulae. Pitfall: a prominent or asymmetric tip can be mistaken for a mass or lymph node. It can also compress the internal carotid artery or the cranial nerves next to it.

lm:Transverse process|Vertebra L3.note: The Processus transversus of L3 is usually the longest lumbar transverse process. It projects laterally between the Psoas major in front and the Musculus quadratus lumborum behind and lateral to it. Pitfall: on axial CT, a transverse process fracture with only slight displacement looks like an unfused apophysis or a vascular groove. Check the cortical margins and look for haematoma in the Psoas major.
neighbours: Dorsal parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles

lm:Transverse ridges|Sacrum.note: The Lineae transversae on the Facies pelvica mark the fused intervertebral discs between the sacral bodies, medial to the anterior sacral foramina. Pitfall: these ridges and remnant disc spaces can look like a transverse sacral fracture on sagittal reformats. A true fracture has a cortical step-off or extends into the foramina.

lm:Trapezoid line|Clavicle.note: Linea trapezoidea is an oblique ridge on the inferior lateral clavicle, running anterolaterally from the conoid tubercle, where the ligamentum trapezoideum attaches. Pitfall: the ridge can be mistaken for a periosteal reaction or a non-displaced fracture line. Coracoclavicular ligament calcification after injury can look similar.

lm:Triangular fovea|Arytenoid cartilage.note: The Fovea triangularis is the upper depression on the anterolateral surface, above the Crista arcuata. It relates to the vestibular ligament and the supraglottic level. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the Fovea oblonga, which lies at the glottic level. Mixing them up assigns a lesion to the wrong laryngeal subsite.
landmarks: lm:Anterolateral surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage
neighbours: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle

lm:Trochanteric fossa|Femur.note: The Fossa trochanterica is the pit on the medial surface of the trochanter major. The Musculus obturator externus tendon inserts there, and the obturator internus–gemelli complex and piriformis attach just above it. Pitfall: it is the starting point for antegrade nailing. Do not confuse it with the trochanter tip, and do not mistake the normal fossa cortex for a lytic lesion.

lm:Trochlea of phalanx of foot|Proximal.key: lm:Trochlea of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
lm:Trochlea of phalanx of foot|Proximal.note: Trochlea phalangis is the bicondylar articular surface facing the middle phalanx base at the PIP joint. Pitfall: on axial or coronal slices, the intercondylar groove can look like a vertical split or unicondylar fracture. A true fracture line is cortex-breaking and continues on adjacent slices.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve
landmarks: lm:Head of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
Middle phalanx of third finger of foot
Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints of foot

lm:Trochlea of phalanx of hand|Proximal.key: lm:Trochlea of phalanx of hand|Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
lm:Trochlea of phalanx of hand|Proximal.note: Trochlea phalangis manus is the bicondylar head forming the PIP joint with the middle phalanx base. The volar plate and FDS/FDP tendons lie palmarly and the extensor apparatus dorsally. Pitfall: a small fragment at the palmar base of the middle phalanx is a volar plate avulsion, not a condylar fracture. Check sagittal reformats.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
Middle phalanx of third finger of hand
Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints
Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

lm:Trochlea of talus|Talus.note: Trochlea tali, made of the superior and both malleolar facets, sits in the malleolar mortise and is wider anteriorly. Pitfall: partial volume of the curved tibial plafond can mimic a subchondral defect; confirm suspected osteochondral lesions (typically posteromedial or anterolateral) in two planes.

lm:Trochlear fovea|Frontal bone.note: The Fovea trochlearis is a small depression in the anteromedial orbital roof that holds the Trochlea musculi obliqui superioris. Pitfall: dense calcification of the trochlea is a common normal finding in older patients. It should not be mistaken for a foreign body, a bone fragment or an orbital mass.

lm:Trochlear notch|Ulna.note: Incisura trochlearis is bounded by the olecranon posteriorly and the coronoid process anteriorly, and articulates with the humeral trochlea. Pitfall: the normal transverse cartilage-free bare area at mid-notch causes a cortical notch on sagittal CT. Do not mistake it for a fracture or erosion.

lm:Tubercle of rib|Sixth rib.note: Tuberculum costae articulates with the transverse process of T6 at the costotransverse joint, lateral to the neck. The lateral costotransverse ligament and the deep back muscles cover it posteriorly. Pitfall: costotransverse joint degeneration or the joint line itself can mimic a transverse process fracture.

lm:Tubercle of trapezium bone|Trapezium.note: Tuberculum ossis trapezii is a palmar ridge that anchors the radial Retinaculum flexorium. The flexor carpi radialis tendon runs in the groove on its ulnar side, and thenar muscles arise from it. Pitfall: fractures of this tubercle are radiographically occult and best seen on axial CT. Do not confuse it with the tubercle of the scaphoid just proximal to it.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of flexor carpi radialis

lm:Tuberculum sellae|Sphenoid bone.note: Front rim of the hypophysial fossa, behind the chiasmatic sulcus and below the Chiasma opticum. Pitfall: a middle clinoid process or a caroticoclinoid bridge can look like a fracture or calcification next to it. Tuberculum sellae meningiomas cause subtle hyperostosis that is easily missed.

lm:Tuberosity for coracoclavicular ligam.note: Tuberositas ligamenti coracoclavicularis is the inferior lateral clavicular area that includes the conoid tubercle and the trapezoid line, above the coracoid. Pitfall: lateral clavicle fractures need to be described as medial or lateral to these attachments, because that decides stability. Do not confuse a coracoclavicular bar or joint with a fracture.

lm:Tuberosity of cuboid bone|Cuboid bone.note: The Tuberositas ossis cuboidei is a plantar ridge on the cuboid. The Ligamentum plantare longum attaches to it, and the groove for the fibularis longus tendon runs just in front of it. Pitfall: the Os peroneum, a small accessory bone in the fibularis longus tendon, sits next to the tuberosity. Do not mistake it for an avulsion fragment.

lm:Tuberosity of distal phalanx of foot|.key: lm:Tuberosity of distal phalanx of foot|Distal phalanx of third finger of foot
lm:Tuberosity of distal phalanx of foot|.note: The Tuberositas phalangis distalis pedis is the widened tip of the distal phalanx. It supports the nail bed above and the pulp of the toe below. Pitfall: in the lesser toes the middle and distal phalanges are often fused. Do not read this as a fracture, an erosion or a missing bone.
neighbours: Distal phalanx of third finger of foot
Middle phalanx of third finger of foot
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints of foot

lm:Tuberosity of distal phalanx of hand|.key: lm:Tuberosity of distal phalanx of hand|Distal phalanx of third finger of hand
lm:Tuberosity of distal phalanx of hand|.note: The Tuberositas phalangis distalis manus is the tuft of the distal phalanx. It supports the nail bed on the dorsal side and the finger pulp on the palmar side. Pitfall: tufts are normally irregular and spiky. Do not mistake this for erosion (acro-osteolysis) or a comminuted tuft fracture. Compare with the neighbouring fingers.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
neighbours: Distal phalanx of third finger of hand

lm:Tuberosity of navicular bone|Navicula.note: Tuberositas ossis navicularis projects plantar-medially and takes the main insertion of Musculus tibialis posterior, with the talar head proximal and the medial cuneiform distal. Pitfall: an accessory navicular (os tibiale externum) with a synchondrosis can mimic an avulsion fracture. It has smooth corticated margins and is often present on both sides.

lm:Tuberosity of ulna|Ulna.note: Tuberositas ulnae is a rough area just distal to the coronoid process on the anterior proximal ulna. It is the insertion of Musculus brachialis, with the Chorda obliqua attached nearby. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the radial tuberosity, which receives the biceps tendon. Normal irregular cortex here is not periostitis.
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

lm:Tympanic part of temporal bone|Tempor.key: lm:Tympanic part of temporal bone|Temporal bone
lm:Tympanic part of temporal bone|Tempor.note: Pars tympanica forms the anterior and inferior walls and part of the posterior wall of the external acoustic meatus. It sits behind the mandibular fossa, separated by the petrotympanic and tympanosquamous fissures. Pitfall: a persistent foramen tympanicum (Huschke) mimics erosion or fracture.

lm:Ulna|Ulna.note: The ulna is the medial forearm bone. It is broad proximally, forming the trochlear notch, and narrow distally, ending in the head and styloid process. It is joined to the radius by the Membrana interossea. Pitfall: the forearm acts as a ring, so with an ulnar fracture always check both radio-ulnar joints (Monteggia, Galeazzi).
neighbours: Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris

lm:Ulnar notch|Radius.note: Incisura ulnaris is the concave medial facet of the distal radius that articulates with the caput ulnae at the articulatio radioulnaris distalis, capped distally by the discus articularis (TFCC). Pitfall: judge DRUJ congruity on true axial slices with both wrists in the same forearm rotation, because pronation/supination mimics subluxation.
neighbours: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint

lm:Ulnar styloid process|Ulna.note: Processus styloideus ulnae projects distally from the dorsomedial Caput ulnae, with the ECU tendon in its dorsal groove and the TFCC (Discus articularis) attaching at its base. Pitfall: an os triangulare or lunula and an ununited ossification centre look like an acute styloid fracture; look for sharp, non-corticated margins before calling a fracture.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
neighbours: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint
Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint
Humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris

lm:Uncinate process of first thoracic ve.key: lm:Uncinate process of first thoracic vertebra|Vertebra T1
lm:Uncinate process of first thoracic ve.note: The Processus uncinatus of T1 is a small posterolateral lip on the upper endplate of T1. It forms the front of the C7–T1 intervertebral foramen, where the C8 root exits. Pitfall: because T1 has uncinate processes, it is easily mistaken for C7. Identify T1 by its rib articulation and its upward-pointing transverse processes.

lm:Uncinate process of vertebra|Vertebra.note: Processus uncinatus rises from the posterolateral upper endplate of C4 to form the uncovertebral (Luschka) joint with C3. It forms the anteromedial wall of the C3–C4 foramen, with the vertebral artery lying laterally. Pitfall: uncovertebral osteophytes narrow the foramen and can displace the vertebral artery, yet are easily missed on axial images; assess on oblique sagittal reconstructions.
landmarks: lm:Anterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4

lm:Vaginal process of sphenoid bone|Sphe.key: lm:Vaginal process of sphenoid bone|Sphenoid bone
lm:Vaginal process of sphenoid bone|Sphe.note: Thin plate running medially from the root of the medial pterygoid plate under the Corpus ossis sphenoidei. It joins the vomer ala and the sphenoidal process of the Os palatinum, and borders the nasopharyngeal roof. Pitfall: the palatovaginal canal it forms is smaller and lies inferomedial; do not confuse it with the pterygoid (Vidian) canal.

lm:Vertebra|Vertebra L3.note: L3 lies between the L2-L3 and L3-L4 discs, with the Psoas major on each side and the vena cava inferior and aorta in front. Pitfall: level counting errors with lumbosacral transitional vertebrae or 11 or 13 rib pairs. Count down from C2 or confirm on the scout before labelling L3.

lm:Vertebral arch|Vertebra L3.note: The Arcus vertebrae (pedicles, laminae, articular, transverse and spinous processes) closes the vertebral foramen behind the body. The Musculus multifidus and Longissimus lie on its dorsal surface. Pitfall: spondylolysis of the pars interarticularis looks like a facet joint gap on axial slices. Confirm it on sagittal reformats, where it shows as the 'incomplete ring' sign.

lm:Vertebral body|Vertebra L3.note: The Corpus vertebrae is bounded by the endplates above and below and by the Ligamentum longitudinale anterius in front. The aorta lies anterolaterally on the left, and the lumbar arteries wrap around its waist. Pitfall: the basivertebral venous channel in the posterior cortex looks like a fracture line or osteolysis. Schmorl nodes can also mimic lesions.

lm:Vertebral foramen|Vertebra L3.note: At L3 the Foramen vertebrale is bounded by the vertebral body in front, the pedicles on each side and the laminae and Ligamenta flava behind. It holds the dural sac with the cauda equina, not spinal cord. Pitfall: the conus medullaris normally ends at L1–L2. A cord-like structure at L3 suggests a low-lying or tethered cord.

lm:Vestibular surface of tooth|Lower fir.key: lm:Vestibular surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Vestibular surface of tooth|Lower fir.note: The Facies vestibularis (buccal surface) faces the oral vestibule, with the gingiva and Bucinator on its outer side. Pitfall: streak artefact from fillings and the thin buccal cortical plate can hide or mimic buccal bone loss or a fenestration. Check bone windows and multiplanar reformats.
landmarks: lm:Crown of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Lingual surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Mesial surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Distal surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Occlusal surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

lm:Vocal process|Arytenoid cartilage.note: The Processus vocalis projects anteriorly from the base. The vocal ligament attaches to it, and it marks the true cord and glottic plane on axial CT. Pitfall: a calcified vocal process can be mistaken for a foreign body or a cartilage fragment. Check that it matches the other side.
landmarks: lm:Medial surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage

lm:Zygomatic margin of greater wing|Sphe.key: lm:Zygomatic margin of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
lm:Zygomatic margin of greater wing|Sphe.note: Anterior serrated edge of the Ala major that forms the sphenozygomatic suture in the lateral orbital wall. The Musculus temporalis lies behind it. Pitfall: a normal suture can be mistaken for diastasis in zygomaticomaxillary complex fractures. Compare both sides and check for orbital wall alignment.
landmarks: lm:Squamosal margin of greater wing|Sphenoid bone

lm:Zygomatic process of frontal bone|Fro.key: lm:Zygomatic process of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Zygomatic process of frontal bone|Fro.note: The Processus zygomaticus forms the lateral orbital rim and meets the Os zygomaticum at the frontozygomatic suture, with the Fossa glandulae lacrimalis on its inner side. Pitfall: the normal frontozygomatic suture can mimic diastasis. In zygomaticomaxillary complex fractures, compare the width with the other side.
landmarks: lm:Frontal part of orbital margin|Frontal bone

lm:Zygomatic process of temporal bone (t.key: lm:Zygomatic process of temporal bone (tip)|Temporal bone
lm:Zygomatic process of temporal bone (t.note: The tip of the Processus zygomaticus meets the temporal process of the Os zygomaticum at the temporozygomatic suture, completing the zygomatic arch. The Musculus temporalis lies medial to it and the masseter arises from below. Pitfall: the oblique sutura temporozygomatica mimics an arch fracture. Check for corticated margins and compare with the other side.

Long head of biceps brachii.note: Arises inside the joint from the supraglenoid tubercle and superior labrum, crosses over the humeral head and runs through the intertubercular groove under the Ligamentum transversum humeri. Pitfall: an empty bicipital groove means a medially dislocated or torn tendon. Fluid in the sheath usually comes from the glenohumeral joint.

Long head of biceps femoris.note: Arises from the ischial tuberosity in a conjoint tendon with the semitendinosus, runs posterolaterally in the thigh and inserts on the fibular head with the ligamentum collaterale fibulare. Pitfall: a small avulsion from the fibular head (arcuate sign) means a posterolateral corner injury, not a trivial fleck.

Long head of triceps brachii.note: Arises from the tuberculum infraglenoideum and runs between teres minor (above) and teres major (below), joining the common tendon to the olecranon. It divides the quadrangular space (lateral) from the triangular space (medial, with the a. circumflexa scapulae). Pitfall: mixing up the two spaces when describing axillary nerve or circumflex vessel pathology.

Long plantar ligament.note: Runs from the plantar calcaneus, in front of the calcaneal tubercles, to the cuboid tuberosity and the bases of metatarsals 2–5. It roofs the tunnel for the fibularis longus tendon. Pitfall: an os peroneum next to the cuboid groove mimics an avulsion fragment. It is smooth and corticated, and fragmentation suggests painful os peroneum syndrome.
landmarks: lm:Base of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone

Long posterior ciliary arteries.note: Two intraconal branches that pierce the sclera next to the nervus opticus and run medially and laterally in the horizontal meridian to the ciliary body and iris. Pitfall: they are not separable from the optic nerve sheath on CT. Thickening around the nerve is a sheath or nerve finding, not vascular.

Long thoracic nerve.note: Formed from C5–C7 roots. It pierces scalenus medius, passes behind the plexus over the first rib and descends on the lateral surface of serratus anterior in the midaxillary line. Pitfall: its injury causes medial winging of the scapula. Do not confuse it with lateral winging from trapezius (accessory nerve) or the dorsal scapular nerve pattern.

Longissimus capitis muscle.note: Arises from the upper thoracic transverse processes and the articular processes of the lower cervical vertebrae and inserts on the posterior Processus mastoideus, deep to splenius capitis. Pitfall: the Arteria occipitalis runs deep to it next to the mastoid notch, and it should not be mistaken for a node or for the posterior digastric belly.
landmarks: lm:Posterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4

Longissimus colli muscle.note: Runs from the transverse processes of T1–T5 to the posterior tubercles of C2–C6, medial to iliocostalis colli and lateral to semispinalis. Pitfall: the name is easily confused with Longus colli, which is prevertebral. Longissimus colli is posterior to the transverse processes; do not mix them up in the report.
landmarks: lm:Posterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4

Longissimus thoracis muscle.note: Intermediate erector spinae column, lateral to multifidus and medial to iliocostalis, running from the sacrum and iliac crest to the transverse processes and ribs. Pitfall: in the lumbar region the multifidus–longissimus border is a fat plane used for the Wiltse approach. Do not mistake asymmetric fatty infiltration for a tumour.
landmarks: lm:Superior articular facet of vertebra|Vertebra L3

Longus capitis muscle.note: Prevertebral muscle running from the anterior tubercles of C3–C6 to the basilar Os occipitale lateral to the Tuberculum pharyngeum. The retropharyngeal space lies directly anterior to it. Pitfall: diffuse prevertebral fluid without rim enhancement is usually oedema or effusion, not a drainable abscess.
landmarks: lm:Anterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4

Longus colli muscle.note: Lies directly on the vertebral bodies from the Tuberculum anterius atlantis to T3, deep to the Ligamentum longitudinale anterius, with the oesophagus and pharynx anterior. Pitfall: amorphous calcification anterior to C1–C2 with prevertebral effusion is acute calcific tendinitis of longus colli, not a retropharyngeal abscess or fracture fragment.
landmarks: lm:Anterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4

Lower canine.note: The lower canine (FDI 33/43) has the longest root in the anterior mandible, lying between the lateral incisor and the first premolar, with the incisive branch of the Nervus alveolaris inferior below its apex. Pitfall: the nearby Foramen mentale can simulate a periapical lucency. Confirm continuity with the mandibular canal before diagnosing periapical disease.
passing: Mental branch of inferior alveolar artery

Lower first molar tooth.note: Two-rooted molar (mesial and distal roots) seated in the alveolar part of the mandibula, with the canalis mandibulae running below the apices. Thin lingual cortex: abscess spreads to the sublingual or submandibular space depending on mylohyoid level. Pitfall: do not mistake the canalis mandibulae or a normal interradicular trabecular gap for a periapical lucency.
landmarks: lm:Root of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Crown of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Occlusal surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Lingual surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

Lower first premolar.note: Single-rooted tooth between the canine and the second premolar in the alveolar part of the mandibula. Its buccal cortex lies deep to the depressor anguli oris. Pitfall: the anterior loop of the canalis mandibulae and the canalis incisivus near the apex look like periapical lucencies. Follow them on curved reformats before calling a lesion.

Lower lateral incisor.note: The lower lateral incisor (FDI 32/42) sits in thin alveolar bone between the medial incisor and the canine, with the Fovea sublingualis on the lingual side. Pitfall: the labial and lingual cortical plates are very thin, so partial volume can mimic fenestration or a root fracture. Confirm laterality with FDI numbering on axial versus 3D views.

Lower medial incisor.note: The lower medial incisor (FDI 31/41) flanks the midline symphysis, with the genial spines and the Musculus genioglossus/geniohyoideus attachments behind it. Pitfall: midline lingual foramina and vascular canals can mimic a symphyseal fracture or periapical lesion. These canals are corticated and lie in the midline.

Lower second molar tooth.note: Two-rooted molar distal to the first molar. Its apices sit close to the canalis mandibulae and the thin lingual cortex, below the linea mylohyoidea, so infection spreads into the submandibular space. Pitfall: when teeth are missing or a third molar is unerupted, the tooth number is easy to get wrong. Count from the midline and use FDI notation (37/47).

Lower second premolar.note: Single-rooted tooth between the first premolar and the first molar. The foramen mentale usually lies just below or between the premolar apices. Pitfall: on axial CT the foramen mentale can mimic a periapical lesion or an osteolytic defect. Trace its continuity with the canalis mandibulae.

Lumbar arteries.note: Paired segmental arteries from the back of the Aorta abdominalis. They wrap around the middle of the L1–L4 vertebral bodies deep to Psoas major and send spinal branches through the intervertebral foramina. Pitfall: they can feed a type II endoleak after EVAR, and the accompanying lumbar veins look the same on venous phase.
landmarks: lm:Lateral part of transverse process|Vertebra L3
lm:Costal part of transverse process|Vertebra L3

Lumbar branch of iliolumbar artery.note: Ascends behind the Psoas major to supply it and the quadratus lumborum, anastomosing with the fourth lumbar artery. Pitfall: the testicular vessels run on the anterior surface of the psoas. Do not confuse them with this branch, which lies posterior to the muscle, or with a segmental lumbar artery.

Lumbar veins.note: Segmental veins wrap around the lumbar vertebral bodies deep to the psoas with the lumbar arteries. They drain into the IVC and connect with the ascending lumbar vein. Pitfall: in IVC obstruction or variants, enlarged lumbar and ascending lumbar collaterals mimic paravertebral lymph nodes. Check the contrast phase.

Lumbrical muscles of foot.note: Four small muscles that arise from the FDL tendons and pass medial to the MTP joints 2–5, plantar to the ligamentum metatarseum transversum profundum. Pitfall: in the intermetatarsal spaces, a Morton neuroma or intermetatarsal bursa sits next to the lumbrical. CT does not resolve these structures, so do not call a soft-tissue nodule a muscle.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
neighbours: Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis
Proximal phalanx of second finger of foot

Lumbrical muscles of hand.note: Four small muscles arising from the FDP tendons in the palm. They pass radial and palmar to the deep transverse metacarpal ligament and insert into the extensor hoods. Pitfall: lumbricals pass palmar to this ligament and interossei dorsal to it; on flexed-hand scans lumbrical bellies can extend into the carpal tunnel and mimic a mass.
passing: Common palmar digital branches of median nerve
Common palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand

Lunate bone.note: Central proximal-row carpal in the radial lunate fossa, between Os scaphoideum and Os triquetrum, capped by Os capitatum distally and facing the TFCC ulnarly. Pitfall: lunate/perilunate dislocation is missed on axial slices—check radius–lunate–capitate collinearity and lunate tilt (DISI/VISI) on sagittal reformats.
neighbours: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint

Lunate sulcus.note: Inconstant curved sulcus on the lateral occipital convexity, just in front of the occipital pole, separating the lateral occipital gyri from the striate cortex at the pole. On CT it is usually not separately identifiable. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the calcarine sulcus. The calcarine sulcus lies on the medial surface and is the true landmark for the visual cortex.

Lunotriquetral interosseous ligament.note: C-shaped proximal ligament joining the os lunatum and os triquetrum, with dorsal, membranous and palmar parts. Pitfall: an LT gap is rarely seen; look for a break in the Gilula arcs or a VISI pattern. Do not confuse a type II lunate (hamate facet) or lunotriquetral coalition with pathology.

Major alar cartilage.note: Cartilago alaris major forms the nasal tip and ala around the nasal vestibule. Its medial crus lies alongside the caudal septum and its lateral crus lies below the upper lateral cartilage. Pitfall: it has soft-tissue density and is invisible in bone window, so nasal tip injury must be assessed in soft-tissue window.
neighbours: Lateral process of nasal septal cartilage

Malleus.note: Caput mallei sits in the epitympanum in front of corpus incudis. Manubrium mallei is embedded in the membrana tympanica, and processus lateralis bounds Prussak space below the scutum. Pitfall: the tensor tympani tendon or chorda tympani can be mistaken for the manubrium, and the normal malleoincudal joint line is not a fracture.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of malleus|Malleus

Mamillary body.note: Paired round bumps at the back of the floor of the Ventriculus tertius. They sit just in front of the Fossa interpeduncularis, between the Bases pedunculi, where the fornix columns end. On axial CT, partial volume with the interpeduncular cistern and basilar tip can make them look like a small suprasellar mass or a basilar tip aneurysm.

Mandible.note: The Corpus mandibulae carries the Canalis mandibulae containing the Nervus alveolaris inferior, which exits at the Foramen mentale below the premolars. The Linea mylohyoidea separates the sublingual space from the submandibular space. Pitfall: the mandibular canal, mental foramen or lingual foramina can mimic fracture lines. Trace them in 3D. Mandible fractures are often paired (e.g. symphysis plus contralateral condyle).

Mandibular node.note: Lies on the outer surface of the mandibular body, deep to the Platysma and M. depressor anguli oris, near the facial vessels. Pitfall: it can look like a submandibular (level IB) node or a soft-tissue reaction around a tooth. Do not confuse the Foramen mentale with a lytic lesion.

Manubrium of sternum.note: Manubrium sterni meets the clavicles at the Incisura clavicularis, the first costal cartilages laterally and the Corpus sterni at the Angulus sterni. The Vena brachiocephalica sinistra crosses right behind it. Pitfall: asymmetric sternoclavicular degeneration with subchondral sclerosis can mimic septic arthritis or tumour, so compare both sides and look for soft-tissue swelling.

Marginal artery.note: A continuous arterial arcade along the mesenteric border of the colon, linking the SMA and IMA territories. Pitfall: it can be interrupted at the splenic flexure (Griffiths point) and the rectosigmoid (Sudeck point). Distinguish it from the meandering mesenteric artery (arc of Riolan), which runs closer to the mesenteric root.
passing: Ascending branch of left colic artery
Descending branch of left colic artery

Masseteric fascia.note: This fascia covers the masseter from the zygomatic arch to the mandibular ramus and angle. Posteriorly it continues into the parotid fascia, and the Ductus parotideus crosses over it. Pitfall: accessory parotid tissue along the parotid duct on the masseter can look like a mass. Unilateral masseter hypertrophy can also look like a mass.

Mastoid nodes.note: Retroauricular nodes in the subcutaneous fat on the Processus mastoideus, at the insertion of the M. sternocleidomastoideus. Pitfall: on bone window they are easy to confuse with an emissary vein, a sebaceous cyst or soft tissue from mastoiditis. Check the mastoid cells and cortex.

Maxilla.note: The body encloses the maxillary sinus, with the infraorbital canal in its roof and the alveolar process below. The palatine process forms the anterior hard palate. Pitfall: vascular grooves for the posterior superior alveolar artery in the posterolateral wall can look like fracture lines, and so can molar roots projecting into the sinus floor.

Maxillary artery.note: Terminal ECA branch. It arises behind the mandibular neck and crosses the masticator space, superficial or deep to the lateral pterygoid, into the pterygopalatine fossa. Pitfall: the surrounding pterygoid venous plexus enhances and is often asymmetric. Don't report it as a masticator-space mass or vascular malformation.
neighbours: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Maxillary nerve.note: It runs in the lower lateral wall of the Sinus cavernosus, through the foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa, then along the infraorbital groove and canal to the infraorbital foramen. Pitfall: the foramen rotundum lies superolateral; the pterygoid (vidian) canal lies inferomedial. Effaced fat in the pterygopalatine fossa suggests perineural spread.

Maxillary veins.note: A short trunk from the pterygoid venous plexus in the infratemporal fossa. It passes medial to the condylar neck with the maxillary artery and joins the superficial temporal vein in the parotid. Pitfall: an asymmetric, strongly enhancing pterygoid plexus can look like a masticator space tumour or perineural spread.

Medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve.note: It comes from the medial cord, runs medial to the arteria brachialis between the axillary artery and vein, and pierces the deep fascia with the vena basilica halfway down the arm. Pitfall: in the axilla it can be mistaken for the ulnar nerve or the medial brachial cutaneous nerve. Check where it branches off before naming it.
passing: Anterior branch of medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve
Posterior branch of medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve

Medial basal segmental artery of left lu.key: Medial basal segmental artery of left lung
Medial basal segmental artery of left lu.note: Supplies the medial basal territory next to the heart and runs with the medial basal bronchus (BVII). Pitfall: on the left, segment VII is usually fused with VIII (anteromedial basal segment). Do not expect a separate artery, and do not misread a missing one as an occlusion.
passing: Posterior basal segmental artery of left lung
Lateral basal segmental artery of left lung
Superior segmental artery of left lung
neighbours: Medial basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BVII)
Superior segmental bronchus of left lung (BVI)

Medial basal segmental artery of right l.key: Medial basal segmental artery of right lung
Medial basal segmental artery of right l.note: A7 is the smallest basal branch. It runs medially into the paracardiac lower lobe, next to the inferior vena cava, the pulmonary ligament and the diaphragm. Pitfall: it often comes off A8 or is absent as a separate branch. Seen in cross-section near the oesophagus, it can mimic a paraoesophageal node.
passing: Posterior basal segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Posterior basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BX)

Medial basal segmental bronchus of left.key: Medial basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BVII)
Medial basal segmental bronchus of left.note: On the left, BVII rarely arises on its own. It usually shares an anteromedial basal stem with BVIII and runs medially toward the heart and the Ligamentum pulmonale. Pitfall: the inferior pulmonary vein beside it, seen in cross-section, mimics a nodule or node. Follow the vessel to the left atrium.
passing: Medial basal segmental artery of left lung
Inferior basal vein of left lung
Posterior basal segmental artery of left lung
neighbours: Lateral basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BIX)
Superior segmental bronchus of left lung (BVI)

Medial basal segmental bronchus of right.key: Medial basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BVII)
Medial basal segmental bronchus of right.note: First basal branch. It runs anteromedially and inferiorly toward the inferior vena cava and the paracardiac diaphragm. Pitfall: a separate BVII exists regularly only on the right; on the left, medial and anterior basal bronchi usually share an anteromedial trunk (BVII+VIII).
passing: Superior basal vein of right lung
neighbours: Anterior basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BVIII)
Superior segmental bronchus of right lung (BVI)

Medial brachial cutaneous nerve.note: The smallest branch of the medial cord crosses behind or medial to the vena axillaris along the medial arm and joins the nervus intercostobrachialis. Pitfall: its territory overlaps that of the intercostobrachialis (T2), so numbness after axillary dissection does not prove injury to the plexus.
passing: Anterior division of inferior trunk of brachial plexus

Medial circumflex femoral artery.note: It arises posteromedially from the Arteria profunda femoris and passes between the iliopsoas and pectineus. It then winds around the Musculus obturator externus to the posterior femoral neck and is the main supply of the femoral head. Pitfall: it may arise from the femoral artery. A displaced femoral neck fracture can tear its retinacular branches and cause avascular necrosis.

Medial circumflex femoral veins.note: Run posteriorly between the musculus pectineus and the iliopsoas, then along the obturator externus to the trochanteric fossa, together with the main arterial supply of the femoral head. Pitfall: do not confuse them with the obturator vessels, which pass through the canalis obturatorius higher up and further medially.

Medial common iliac nodes.note: These nodes sit in the triangle between the two common iliac arteries below the aortic bifurcation, anterior to L4–L5. Pitfall: the left common iliac vein crossing posterior to the right artery, or an anterior disc osteophyte, can mimic a precaval/presacral node.

Medial crural cutaneous branches of saph.key: Medial crural cutaneous branches of saphenous nerve
Medial crural cutaneous branches of saph.note: These branches leave the nervus saphenus below the knee and run in the subcutaneous fat of the medial leg, alongside the vena saphena magna. CT cannot resolve them separately from the vein. Pitfall: do not report the vein or its tributaries as a nerve lesion. Saphenous vein harvest or stripping is the usual cause of medial leg numbness.

Medial cuneiform bone.note: The largest cuneiform. It lies between the navicular and the first metatarsal base, and the tibialis anterior and fibularis longus insert on it. Its lateral surface anchors the Lisfranc ligament to the second metatarsal base. Pitfall: a bipartite medial cuneiform (dorsal/plantar halves separated by a smooth cleft) mimics a fracture.

Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot.key: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot.note: The nerve runs subcutaneously over the inferior extensor retinaculum and the extensor hallucis longus tendon to the medial hallux and the second to third toes. Pitfall: it lies superficial to the retinaculum, whereas the nervus fibularis profundus and arteria dorsalis pedis run deep to it. Do not mix them up when describing dorsal midfoot ganglia or hardware.
passing: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve

Medial external iliac nodes.note: These nodes lie medial and posterior to the external iliac vein on the pelvic sidewall, continuous with the obturator group, and are the main nodes for prostate and cervix. Pitfall: unopacified small-bowel loops and the ductus deferens on the sidewall mimic nodes. Use oral contrast and follow them on contiguous slices.

Medial femoral intermuscular septum.note: Separates vastus medialis from the adductors and attaches to the Labium mediale lineae asperae. It forms the anterolateral wall of the adductor canal. Pitfall: the femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery at the adductor hiatus. Do not confuse the superficial femoral artery with the deep femoral artery (A. profunda femoris), which runs deeper and more lateral.

Medial geniculate body.note: Small swelling under the pulvinar, medial to the Corpus geniculatum laterale. The brachium of the Colliculus inferior connects it to the inferior colliculus and it borders the ambient cistern. It is an auditory relay, not visual. Do not mix it up with the lateral geniculate body, which is the end point of the optic tract.

Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis.key: Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis
Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis.note: Lies along the plantar-medial first metatarsal, deep to the abductor hallucis. It inserts through the medial (tibial) sesamoid, medial to the FHL tendon. Pitfall: a bipartite tibial sesamoid (smooth corticated margins, often bilateral, fragments larger in total than normal) must not be called a fracture (sharp, non-corticated margins).
passing: Superficial branch of medial plantar artery
Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
neighbours: Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis

Medial head of gastrocnemius.note: Arises from the posterior medial femoral condyle and forms the inferomedial border of the fossa poplitea. A popliteal (Baker) cyst arises between its tendon and the semimembranosus tendon. Pitfall: a popliteal artery aneurysm or an abnormal medial-head origin causing entrapment can mimic a cyst, so check on contrast phase.
neighbours: Medial subtendinous bursa of gastrocnemius muscle

Medial head of triceps brachii.note: Deepest head; lies on the posterior humeral shaft distal to the sulcus nervi radialis and runs down to the olecranon, with the medial intermuscular septum and ulnar nerve along its medial edge. Pitfall: in a shaft fracture, the radial nerve and a. profunda brachii run in the groove between the medial and lateral heads, not inside the muscle belly.
neighbours: Subtendinous bursa of triceps brachii muscle

Medial intermuscular septum of arm.note: Septum intermusculare mediale brachii runs from the medial supracondylar ridge to fascia brachii, with brachialis in front and the medial head of triceps behind. Pitfall: the nervus ulnaris pierces it to enter the posterior compartment while the arteria brachialis stays anterior. Do not mistake enlarged nodi supratrochleares beside it for a nerve-sheath tumour.

Medial meniscus.note: C-shaped fibrocartilage with a broader posterior horn, fixed peripherally to the pars profunda of the tibial collateral ligament. On CT it is only seen as soft-tissue density or with chondrocalcinosis. Pitfall: the ligamentum transversum genus insertion mimics an anterior horn tear.
neighbours: Deep part of tibial collateral ligament

Medial occipital artery.note: Terminal PCA branch along the medial occipital surface. It gives the calcarine and parieto-occipital branches that supply the Cuneus, Gyrus lingualis and visual cortex. Pitfall: on axial CT, an occipital infarct along the Falx cerebri is easily hidden by the dense falx and tentorium; check the calcarine cortex on both sides.

Medial occipitotemporal gyrus (Parahippo.note: Mediobasal temporal gyrus bounded laterally by the Collateral sulcus. It lies below the Hippocampus and temporal horn, with the uncus facing the Basis pedunculi at the tentorial incisura, where the PCA runs. Pitfall: effacement of the ambient cistern by uncal herniation is subtle. Calcified Choroid plexus in the temporal horn is not haemorrhage.
landmarks: lm:Petrous part of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Medial patellar retinaculum.note: Runs from the medial patellar margin to the medial femoral epicondyle, superficial to the capsule and blending posteriorly with the Ligamentum collaterale tibiale. Pitfall: after lateral patellar dislocation, a small avulsion fragment at the medial patellar margin can be misread as an intra-articular loose body. Check the lateral femoral condyle for an impaction injury.
neighbours: Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament
Deep part of tibial collateral ligament

Medial pectoral nerve.note: Arises from the medial cord behind the arteria axillaris and runs forward between artery and vein. It pierces musculus pectoralis minor and goes on to pars sternocostalis of pectoralis major; CT shows only the fat plane it runs in. Pitfall: it is named for its cord of origin but lies lateral to the lateral pectoral nerve.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Medial plantar artery.note: The smaller terminal branch of the a. tibialis posterior. It runs along the medial sole deep to the abductor hallucis, beside the n. plantaris medialis and near the FHL tendon. Pitfall: the posterior tibial bifurcation can lie high inside the tarsal tunnel. Do not mistake the smaller medial branch for a hypoplastic or occluded lateral plantar artery.
passing: Superficial branch of medial plantar artery
neighbours: Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis

Medial plantar nerve.note: Arises from the Nervus tibialis in the tarsal tunnel below the sustentaculum tali. It runs forward deep to the Abductor hallucis with the Arteria plantaris medialis. Pitfall: it is not resolved on CT, so locate it by its vessels. Do not confuse it with the Nervus plantaris lateralis, which crosses laterally deep to flexor digitorum brevis.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
landmarks: lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of calcaneus|Calcaneus
neighbours: Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis

Medial plantar veins.note: Run with the medial plantar artery and nerve deep to the abductor hallucis, then between it and the flexor digitorum brevis towards the hallux. Pitfall: at the knot of Henry, where the FDL and FHL tendons cross, the nerve can be entrapped (jogger's foot). Vessel prominence here should not be taken for a mass.
neighbours: Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis

Medial pontine branches of basilar arter.key: Medial pontine branches of basilar artery
Medial pontine branches of basilar arter.note: Paramedian perforators run from the dorsal A. basilaris into the basis pontis, up to the midline. An infarct gives a sharply midline-bounded, unilateral paramedian pontine hypodensity. Pitfall: posterior fossa beam-hardening (Hounsfield bar) artefact mimics paramedian infarcts; confirm with MRI DWI.
passing: Lateral pontine branches of basilar artery

Medial pterygoid muscle.note: Runs from the Fossa pterygoidea and maxillary tuberosity to the medial side of the mandibular angle. Parapharyngeal fat separates it from the superior constrictor. Pitfall: asymmetry from denervation, or pterygoid venous plexus enhancement, can mimic a masticator-space tumour. Check V3 at the foramen ovale.
landmarks: lm:Infratemporal surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
neighbours: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Medial rectus muscle.note: Runs along the lamina papyracea of the ethmoid bone from the anulus to the medial globe, inferomedial to the superior oblique. Pitfall: a congenital dehiscence of the lamina papyracea with fat herniation can look like a medial wall fracture. Look for the muscle being displaced into the ethmoid cells and for hematoma before calling it a fracture.
landmarks: lm:Orbital part of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Medial reticulospinal tract.note: Pontine reticulospinal fibres in the medial anterior funiculus, between the Fissura mediana anterior and the Cornu anterius. CT does not show the tract. Pitfall: confusing it with the Tractus reticulospinalis lateralis, which is medullary in origin and lies in the lateral funiculus.

Medial segmental artery of right lung.key: Medial segmental artery of right lung
Medial segmental artery of right lung.note: A5 runs anteromedially with BV toward the right heart border and the anterior diaphragm. Pitfall: the medial vein and the Vena pulmonalis dextra superior lie right next to the artery. Pulsation artefact from the heart border can also mimic a filling defect.
passing: Middle lobar artery of right lung
neighbours: Medial segmental bronchus of right lung (BV)
