Medial segmental bronchus of right lung.key: Medial segmental bronchus of right lung (BV)
Medial segmental bronchus of right lung.note: Medial branch of the middle lobe bronchus. It runs anteromedially toward the right heart border and the anterior diaphragm. Pitfall: collapse of the medial segment is a thin wedge next to the right atrium that can be mistaken for a pericardial fat pad or cardiac contour.
passing: Medial segmental artery of right lung
Lateral segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Lateral segmental bronchus of right lung (BIV)

Medial subtendinous bursa of gastrocnemi.key: Medial subtendinous bursa of gastrocnemius muscle
Medial subtendinous bursa of gastrocnemi.note: Lies deep to the origin of the Caput mediale musculi gastrocnemii on the posteromedial femoral condyle and communicates with the semimembranosus bursa and the knee joint. Pitfall: when distended it forms the Baker (popliteal) cyst neck between the gastrocnemius and semimembranosus; do not mistake it for a popliteal artery aneurysm or DVT. Use contrast to check.

Medial sural cutaneous nerve.note: Branches from the Nervus tibialis in the popliteal fossa and descends deep to the crural fascia in the groove between the two heads of the gastrocnemius. It joins the sural communicating branch to form the Nervus suralis. Pitfall: the nerve itself is not visible on CT; the enhancing Vena saphena parva beside it is the marker and must not be mistaken for the nerve.

Medial talocalcaneal ligament.note: Runs from the medial tubercle of the processus posterior tali to the posterior margin of the sustentaculum tali, deep to the FHL groove and tibial nerve. Pitfall: a flake at the medial tubercle (Cedell fracture) is easily missed or called an accessory ossicle. Compare cortication and check both tubercles.
landmarks: lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of calcaneus|Calcaneus

Medial vein of right lung.note: Vena medialis pulmonis dextri drains middle lobe segment S5 along the right heart border and joins the middle lobe vein or the Vena pulmonalis dextra superior. Pitfall: it lies against the Atrium dextrum, so partial volume of the right heart border can mimic middle lobe disease. Its own atrial ostium is a common variant.
passing: Medial segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Medial segmental bronchus of right lung (BV)
Lateral segmental bronchus of right lung (BIV)

Medial vestibulospinal tract.note: Continuation of the medial longitudinal fasciculus in the medial anterior funiculus, next to the Fissura mediana anterior. It reaches only the cervical and upper thoracic cord. CT cannot resolve it. Pitfall: shown in a lumbar or lower thoracic section, it is a mislabel because the tract does not reach those levels.

Median antebrachial vein.note: The Vena mediana antebrachii runs up the middle of the volar forearm in the subcutaneous fat, superficial to the antebrachial fascia and the superficial flexors. Pitfall: where it ends varies (median cubital, basilic or cephalic vein), and it must not be mistaken for a deep vein running with the median nerve.
passing: Anterior branch of medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Median cricothyroid ligament.note: Midline membrane between the lower border of the thyroid cartilage and the arcus cartilaginis cricoideae. It forms the anterior wall of the subglottis and is the cricothyrotomy site. Pitfall: on axial slices this normal non-ossified gap can be misread as a cartilage fracture or tumour erosion. A Delphian node or pyramidal lobe may lie directly in front of it.

Median cubital vein.note: The Vena mediana cubiti crosses the cubital fossa obliquely from the cephalic vein to the basilic vein. It lies superficial to the bicipital aponeurosis, which separates it from the brachial artery and median nerve. Pitfall: contrast extravasation from an antecubital cannula spreads in the subcutaneous fat and can be mistaken for cellulitis or haematoma.

Median nerve.note: In the arm it runs with the arteria brachialis and crosses it from lateral to medial. It passes between the two heads of the pronator teres, then between the superficial and deep finger flexors, into the canalis carpi. Pitfall: a processus supracondylaris on the humerus with the ligament of Struthers can trap the nerve. Do not mistake it for an osteochondroma.
passing: Common palmar digital branches of median nerve
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Median sacral artery.note: Small midline branch from the back of the aorta just above the bifurcation. It descends over L4–L5 and the Promontorium onto the Facies pelvica ossis sacri. Pitfall: the tiny enhancing midline dot in front of the sacrum can be mistaken for a presacral node. It is also an overlooked source of presacral bleeding.

Median sacral nodes.note: These nodes lie in the presacral fat along the median sacral artery, anterior to the promontorium and upper sacrum, posterior to the mesorectum. Pitfall: the presacral venous plexus and median sacral vessels in cross-section mimic small midline nodes, so judge them by shape on contiguous slices.

Median thyrohyoid ligament.note: Thickened midline part of the thyrohyoid membrane, from the incisura thyreoidea superior to the back of the corpus ossis hyoidei. It forms the anterior boundary of the fat-filled pre-epiglottic space. Pitfall: do not confuse a midline thyroglossal duct cyst embedded in the strap muscles with a mixed laryngocele, which pierces the membrane laterally.

Medulla oblongata.note: It extends from the pontomedullary sulcus to the foramen magnum, behind the clivus and in front of the fourth ventricle and cisterna magna. Pitfall: an ectatic or dominant vertebral artery indenting the medulla can mimic a mass. Cerebellar tonsils lying more than 5 mm below the foramen magnum indicate Chiari I, not a normal variant.
landmarks: lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipital bone

Meningeal branch of maxillary nerve.note: It leaves the maxillary nerve in the middle cranial fossa before the foramen rotundum and follows the frontal branch of the arteria meningea media to supply the dura. It is not visible on CT. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the ramus meningeus of the mandibular nerve (nervus spinosus), which comes back through the foramen spinosum.
passing: Accessory branch of middle meningeal artery

Meniscopatellar ligament.note: Thin capsular band running from the patellar margin to the anterior horn of each meniscus, deep to the retinacula. It is not separable on CT. Pitfall: do not mistake it for the retinacula or for an anterior horn tear on reformats.

Mental branch of inferior alveolar arter.key: Mental branch of inferior alveolar artery
Mental branch of inferior alveolar arter.note: Exits the canalis mandibulae at the foramen mentale, usually below the second premolar, and supplies the chin and lower lip under the depressor muscles. Pitfall: on CT the mental foramen can mimic a periapical lucency or lytic lesion. Accessory mental foramina are a normal variant.

Mental nerve.note: The terminal branch of the inferior alveolar nerve leaves through the foramen mentale, usually below the premolar apices, and lies deep to the musculus depressor anguli oris. Pitfall: the foramen mentale seen in profile can look like a periapical lucency. Accessory mental foramina and the anterior loop are also important before implant planning.

Mentalis muscle.note: Paired muscle that arises from the incisive fossa of the mandible beside the symphysis and inserts into the chin skin, deep to Depressor labii inferioris. Pitfall: the foramen mentale lies more laterally, below the premolars, not under mentalis; also, the midline symphyseal suture or vascular foramina should not be called a fracture.
passing: Mental branch of inferior alveolar artery

Meso-appendix.note: A triangular peritoneal fold runs from behind the terminal ileal mesentery to the appendix and carries the arteria appendicularis. Pitfall: right lower quadrant fat stranding near the pelvic brim can come from a distal ureteric stone instead of appendicitis. Trace the ureter and confirm the appendix itself is abnormal.

Mesocolic taenia.note: Taenia mesocolica is a longitudinal muscle band along the attachment of the Mesocolon on the Colon transversum, and lies posteromedially on the ascending and descending colon. CT does not show it as a separate structure. Pitfall: in a collapsed colon, contracted taeniae and haustral folds can look like wall thickening.

Mesocolon.note: The root of the transverse mesocolon runs across the anterior pancreatic head and body and the duodenum. It separates the supramesocolic and inframesocolic compartments and carries the colic vessels. Pitfall: pancreatitis tracks directly into the mesocolon. Fluid or stranding here does not by itself mean a primary colonic disease.

Metatarsal interosseous ligaments.note: Short bands between adjacent metatarsal bases, just distal to the tarsometatarsal joints. They are strongest between bases 2–5, and the deep plantar artery passes through the first space. Pitfall: the first and second metatarsal bases normally have no strong intermetatarsal tie. Diastasis or a fleck there is a Lisfranc injury, not an intermetatarsal sprain.

Midbrain.note: Lies between the diencephalon and the Pons. The crura are anterior, the tectum is posterior around the Aquaeductus, and the ambient cisterns are lateral. Pitfall: interpetrous beam-hardening can mimic a hypodensity. Effaced perimesencephalic cisterns or Duret haemorrhage point to transtentorial herniation.

Middle cardiac vein.note: Vena media cordis runs in the sulcus interventricularis posterior on the diaphragmatic surface, between Ventriculus dexter and sinister, and drains into the Sinus coronarius close to its ostium. Pitfall: it runs right next to the posterior descending branch of the Arteria coronaria dextra, so on non-gated or venous-phase CT the vein is easily mistaken for the artery.

Middle cells of ethmoid bone.note: Cellulae mediae lie between the anterior and posterior groups. Laterally a thin lamina orbitalis separates them from the Musculus rectus medialis, and the Os frontale forms the roof. Pitfall: a congenitally dehiscent lamina orbitalis with herniated orbital fat can mimic a blowout fracture. Look for acute signs such as haemorrhage or emphysema.

Middle cerebral artery (M1-segment).note: Runs laterally from the ICA terminus beneath the substantia perforata anterior to the limen insulae, below the frontal lobe and above the temporal pole. Pitfall: the hyperdense MCA sign. A high haematocrit or calcification mimics a clot, so compare with the other side and look at density.
passing: Insular branches of middle cerebral artery (M2)

Middle cerebral artery (M3 segment).note: The opercular segment. It runs from the circular sulcus of the insula over the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula to the surface of the Sylvian fissure, where it becomes the cortical M4 branches. Pitfall: a hyperdense vessel in the fissure can be the superficial middle cerebral vein. Trace it on thin MIP before calling a distal 'dot sign'.
passing: Insular branches of middle cerebral artery (M2-segment)
Temporal branches of middle cerebral artery
Parietal branches of middle cerebral artery
neighbours: Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus
Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci*)

Middle cerebral artery (M3-segment).note: Opercular segment: it runs from the sulcus circularis insulae over the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula to the surface of the lateral (Sylvian) fissure. Pitfall: the Sylvian 'dot sign' can mean M2/M3 thrombus, but calcified walls or a high haematocrit can mimic it; check both sides and measure HU.
passing: Insular branches of middle cerebral artery (M2)
Temporal branches of middle cerebral artery
Parietal branches of middle cerebral artery
neighbours: Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci*)
Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Middle colic artery.note: Arises from the anterior SMA just below the pancreatic neck and enters the transverse mesocolon. Pitfall: the middle colic vein and the gastrocolic trunk (Henle) run close by and vary widely. Tumour spread along the transverse mesocolon root should not be missed.

Middle colic nodes.note: Lie in the root of the Mesocolon transversum along the A./V. colica media, in front of the head of the pancreas and the Duodenum. Pitfall: the gastrocolic trunk and its branches near the pancreatic head look like nodes. Trace the vessels on portal-venous phase before calling a node enlarged.

Middle colic vein.note: Runs in the transverse mesocolon and drains into the Vena mesenterica superior at the inferior border of the pancreatic neck, often via the gastrocolic trunk (Henle). Pitfall: on axial slices the vein seen in cross-section in the mesocolon can mimic a middle colic lymph node. Follow it to the SMV.

Middle collateral artery.note: Posterior terminal branch of the deep brachial artery. It descends within the medial head of triceps to the back of the epicondylus lateralis and anastomoses with the recurrent interosseous artery. Pitfall: it is tiny and usually not separable on CT. Do not report a small enhancing focus at its position near the olecranon fossa as a lesion or a loose body.

Middle frontal gyrus.note: Gyrus frontalis medius is bounded above by the sulcus frontalis superior, below by the sulcus frontalis inferior and behind by the sulcus precentralis. It lies under the frontal bone close to the coronal suture. Pitfall: on high axial slices, its posterior end can be mistaken for the gyrus precentralis. Trace the superior frontal sulcus back to where it meets the precentral sulcus.
landmarks: lm:Parietal margin of frontal bone|Frontal bone
neighbours: Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Middle genicular artery.note: It arises from the anterior wall of the Arteria poplitea and pierces the oblique popliteal ligament and posterior capsule. It enters the intercondylar fossa of the Os femoris and supplies the cruciate ligaments and synovium. Pitfall: it is tiny and normally not resolved. It is a source of haemarthrosis after cruciate injury or reconstruction, so do not dismiss contrast blush there.

Middle glenohumeral ligament.note: Runs obliquely from the anterosuperior labrum and glenoid neck to the lesser tubercle, crossing deep to the subscapularis tendon. Its size varies widely. Pitfall: a thick cord-like ligament with an absent anterosuperior labrum (Buford complex) is a normal variant, not a labral tear.

Middle layer of thoracolumbar fascia.note: Lamina media fasciae thoracolumbaris runs laterally from the tips of the lumbar transverse processes, between erector spinae (posterior) and quadratus lumborum (anterior). Lateral to quadratus lumborum it fuses with the posterior layer and gives origin to transversus abdominis. Pitfall: do not mistake its attachment at a transverse-process tip for a fracture line.

Middle lobar artery of right lung.key: Middle lobar artery of right lung
Middle lobar artery of right lung.note: The middle lobar artery leaves the front of the interlobar artery, roughly opposite A6, and runs anterolaterally with the middle lobar bronchus. Pitfall: A4 and A5 may arise separately, so a duplicated origin is normal. The middle lobe vein runs close by to join the Vena pulmonalis dextra superior and should not be read as the artery.
passing: Inferior lobar artery of right lung

Middle lobar bronchus.note: Arises anteriorly from the Bronchus intermedius, roughly opposite the origin of BVI, and runs anteroinferiorly into the lobe between the horizontal and oblique fissures. Pitfall: its oblique course causes partial volume on axial slices that mimics stenosis, so confirm on MPR before reporting obstruction.
passing: Middle lobar artery of right lung

Middle lobe of right lung.note: The middle lobe is bounded above by the horizontal fissure and behind by the oblique fissure. Its medial segment lies against the right atrium and right heart border. Pitfall: the horizontal fissure lies almost in the axial plane. It shows as an avascular zone, not a line, so lesions are easily assigned to the wrong lobe. Check sagittal reconstructions.
passing: Lateral segmental artery of right lung
Medial segmental artery of right lung

Medial segmental bronchus of right lung (BV)

Middle meningeal artery.note: Arises from the maxillary artery and enters through the foramen spinosum, posterolateral to the foramen ovale. It then grooves the inner table of the temporal squama and the parietal bone. Pitfall: these vascular grooves mimic fractures because they are branching, tapering and corticated. A true fracture crossing the groove raises concern for epidural hematoma.

Middle phalanx of fifth finger of foot.key: Middle phalanx of fifth finger of foot
Middle phalanx of fifth finger of foot.note: The middle phalanx lies between the PIP and DIP joints, and flexor digitorum brevis inserts on its plantar side. On the fifth toe it is tiny and often rudimentary. Pitfall: fusion with the distal phalanx (symphalangism) is a frequent normal variant and should not be read as post-traumatic ankylosis or a missing bone.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve

Middle phalanx of fifth finger of hand.key: Middle phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Middle phalanx of fifth finger of hand.note: Between the PIP and DIP joints; flexor digitorum superficialis inserts on the palmar shaft, the central extensor slip on the dorsal base. Pitfall: a short, trapezoid middle phalanx (brachymesophalangy, clinodactyly) or DIP symphalangism is a common normal variant of the fifth digit—do not report it as fracture or ankylosis.

Middle phalanx of fourth finger of foot.key: Middle phalanx of fourth finger of foot
Middle phalanx of fourth finger of foot.note: The middle phalanx lies between the PIP and DIP joints, with flexor digitorum brevis inserting on the plantar side and the extensor tendon running dorsally. Pitfall: this short bone can fuse with the distal phalanx as a normal variant. In a flexed toe, partial volume can hide a fracture, so check reformats along the toe.

Middle phalanx of fourth finger of hand.key: Middle phalanx of fourth finger of hand
Middle phalanx of fourth finger of hand.note: Between the PIP and DIP joints; the palmar plate attaches to the palmar base, and flexor digitorum superficialis inserts on the shaft. Pitfall: a tiny volar plate avulsion at the palmar base is easily lost in partial volume; check sagittal reformats and report dorsal PIP subluxation.

Middle phalanx of second finger of foot.key: Middle phalanx of second finger of foot
Middle phalanx of second finger of foot.note: Short bone between the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints. The flexor digitorum brevis inserts plantarly on it, with the flexor digitorum longus tendon passing beneath. Pitfall: toes lie flexed, so axial slices cut the phalanges obliquely. A partial-volume overlap at the IP joints can mimic a fracture line or fusion, so check sagittal reformats.

Middle phalanx of second finger of hand.key: Middle phalanx of second finger of hand
Middle phalanx of second finger of hand.note: Between the PIP and DIP joints; the central slip of the extensor apparatus (extensor digitorum, extensor indicis) inserts on the dorsal base. Pitfall: a dorsal-base avulsion (central slip, boutonnière precursor) is often overlooked next to palmar plate fragments; inspect both dorsal and palmar base margins on sagittal reformats.

Middle phalanx of third finger of foot.key: Middle phalanx of third finger of foot
Middle phalanx of third finger of foot.note: Articulates proximally with the trochlea phalangis of the proximal phalanx and distally with the distal phalanx. The flexor digitorum longus/brevis lie plantar and the extensor digitorum longus tendon lies dorsal. Pitfall: counting the toes wrongly on axial images. Count from the hallux on a coronal or 3D view before you assign a digit.

Middle phalanx of third finger of hand.key: Middle phalanx of third finger of hand
Middle phalanx of third finger of hand.note: Base articulates with the trochlea phalangis of the proximal phalanx at the PIP joint, head with the distal phalanx at the DIP. Pitfall: a pilon-type intra-articular base fracture can look minor axially—quantify articular surface involvement and dorsal subluxation on sagittal reformats.

Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Middle pharyngeal constrictor.note: Fan-shaped muscle arising from the greater and lesser horns of the os hyoideum and the ligamentum stylohyoideum. It lies outside the superior constrictor and inside the inferior one, with the retropharyngeal space and longus capitis behind it. Pitfall: a calcified stylohyoid ligament next to it is a normal variant (Eagle), not a foreign body.

Middle temporal gyrus.note: Lateral temporal gyrus between the Superior temporal sulcus and the Inferior temporal gyrus. It lies under the temporal squama and continues posteriorly into the Angular gyrus and occipital gyri. Pitfall: thin epidural or subdural collections beneath the temporal squama are hidden by partial volume with bone. Check for a squamous fracture crossing the middle meningeal groove.
passing: Temporal branches of middle cerebral artery
landmarks: lm:Squamosal border of parietal bone|Parietal bone

Middle trunk of brachial plexus.note: The direct continuation of C7, running in the interscalene gap between scalenus anterior and medius, between the superior and inferior trunks. Pitfall: CT cannot separate the individual trunks, so count levels on bone. The prominent C6 anterior tubercle (Chassaignac) and the rudimentary C7 anterior tubercle help avoid miscounting.
passing: Anterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus
Posterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus

Motor nucleus of facial nerve.note: Sits in the ventrolateral caudal pontine tegmentum. Its fibres loop around the abducens nucleus (facial colliculus) before exiting at the pontomedullary junction. Pitfall: a nuclear lesion gives a complete facial palsy including the forehead, which is unlike the forehead-sparing central palsy.

Motor root of trigeminal nerve.note: Small root that leaves the pons anteromedial to the sensory root. It passes under the trigeminal ganglion in Meckel cave and joins V3 at the foramen ovale to supply the muscles of mastication. Pitfall: denervation shrinks the masticator muscles and fills them with fat; do not call the normal opposite side hypertrophic or a mass.

Mucosa of nasal cavity.note: The Tunica mucosa nasi covers the septum (Vomer, Cartilago septi nasi), the conchae and the meatus, and continues back through the choanae into the Pars nasalis pharyngis. Pitfall: the nasal cycle swells the turbinate mucosa on alternating sides. This asymmetric swelling mimics a polyp or mass, so look for bone erosion before calling a lesion.
passing: Posterior septal branches of sphenopalatine artery
Posterior lateral nasal branches of sphenopalatine artery.
Anterior septal branches of anterior ethmoidal artery
landmarks: lm:Nasal spine of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Mucosa of stomach.note: Tunica mucosa gastris forms the rugae. On arterial or portal-phase CT it is the brightly enhancing inner layer, over a low-density submucosa. Pitfall: in an underdistended stomach, the contracted antrum or the cardia–fundus region can look like wall thickening or a tumour. Distend the stomach (water) before calling it.

Multifidus colli muscle.note: Lies deep in the laminar groove from C2 to T1, on the laminae and articular processes, beneath the semispinalis colli. Pitfall: after laminectomy or posterior fusion, denervation atrophy with fatty replacement is expected. Do not misread it as a fluid collection or as primary myopathy.

Multifidus lumborum muscle.note: The largest and most medial lumbar paraspinal muscle. It fills the groove between the spinous process and the facet joints, medial to the longissimus, and extends down onto the sacrum. Pitfall: unilateral segmental fatty atrophy points to denervation of the dorsal ramus (radiculopathy, surgery). Do not dismiss it as age-related symmetric fat.

Multifidus thoracis muscle.note: A thin layer on the thoracic laminae and transverse processes, deep to the semispinalis thoracis and medial to the longissimus. Pitfall: on CT it cannot be told apart from the rotatores and semispinalis. Report the transversospinal group as a whole rather than naming one muscle.

Muscular branches of axillary nerve.note: The anterior branch winds around the surgical neck deep to the deltoid, about 5–7 cm below the acromion. The posterior branch supplies teres minor and the posterior deltoid. Pitfall: isolated teres minor fatty atrophy is a common incidental finding and should not alone be read as quadrangular space syndrome. Deltoid-splitting approaches put the anterior branch at risk.

Muscular branches of deep fibular nerve.key: Muscular branches of deep fibular nerve
Muscular branches of deep fibular nerve.note: This is the lateral terminal branch of the deep fibular nerve. It runs laterally over the talus and navicular to the extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis on the cuboid. Pitfall: an atrophic extensor digitorum brevis points to deep fibular denervation. Do not mistake the normal muscle belly on the dorsolateral foot for a soft-tissue mass.
passing: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

Muscular branches of median nerve.note: Arise around the elbow to pronator teres, FCR, palmaris longus and FDS as the N. medianus passes between the two heads of pronator teres. Pitfall: the A. ulnaris runs deep to the deep head, while the nerve passes between the heads. Do not confuse the two at this level, and remember that palmaris longus is often absent.
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Muscular branches of radial nerve.note: Arise from the N. radialis in the axilla, the sulcus nervi radialis and above the lateral epicondyle to supply triceps, anconeus, brachioradialis and ECRL. CT does not show them. Pitfall: with a midshaft humeral fracture, the spared triceps branches leave elbow extension intact, so this does not exclude radial nerve injury in the groove.

Muscular branches of ulnar nerve.note: Arise just distal to the cubital tunnel and supply flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus. Pitfall: flexor digitorum superficialis is supplied by the median nerve. Fatty atrophy of FCU plus medial FDP points to a lesion at or above the elbow.
neighbours: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Musculocutaneous nerve.note: It pierces the coracobrachialis, runs between the biceps brachii and brachialis, and emerges lateral to the biceps tendon as the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve. Pitfall: a nerve that does not pierce the coracobrachialis, or communicating branches with the median nerve, is a common variant. Do not report it as an absent or injured nerve.

Musculophrenic artery.note: Lateral terminal branch of the A. thoracica interna at the 6th intercostal space, running inferolaterally behind the costal cartilages 7–9 along the costal attachment of the Diaphragma. Pitfall: on CT it is easily mistaken for an enlarged Nodus parasternalis or a cardiophrenic node; follow it on contiguous slices to show it is tubular.

Musculophrenic veins.note: These veins follow the costal margin behind the 7th–9th costal cartilages, along the costal origin of the diaphragm, and drain into the venae thoracicae internae. Pitfall: in cross-section, small vessels in the cardiophrenic angle can look like enlarged cardiophrenic or parasternal nodes. Check for tubular continuity on adjacent slices.

Mylohyoid branch of inferior alveolar ar.key: Mylohyoid branch of inferior alveolar artery
Mylohyoid branch of inferior alveolar ar.note: Branches off just before the foramen mandibulae and runs with the Nervus mylohyoideus in the sulcus mylohyoideus on the medial ramus, beneath the medial pterygoid muscle. Pitfall: the sulcus mylohyoideus or a bifid canalis mandibulae can be misread as a fracture line on the medial ramus.

Mylohyoid muscle.note: Muscular sling from the mylohyoid line to the hyoid body and a midline raphe. It separates the sublingual space above from the submandibular space below. Pitfall: a mylohyoid boutonnière (normal defect) with herniated sublingual gland or fat can look like a mass. Molar roots sit below the mylohyoid line, so molar infection drains into the submandibular space.

Nasal bone.note: The paired nasal bones articulate with the frontal bone above, the frontal processes of the maxillae laterally and each other in the midline. The upper lateral cartilages attach to their inferior edges. Pitfall: the nasomaxillary suture and the groove for the external nasal nerve can look like fractures. Displacement or soft-tissue swelling supports a true fracture.
landmarks: lm:Nasal spine of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Nasal part of frontal bone|Frontal bone
neighbours: Lateral process of nasal septal cartilage

Nasal septal cartilage.note: Cartilago septi nasi forms the anterior septum. Posteroinferiorly it joins the Vomer and the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, and it rests on the maxillary crest. Pitfall: a cartilaginous septal fracture or haematoma is missed in bone window. Check soft-tissue window for bilateral septal thickening, and do not confuse a normal chondro-vomerine spur with a fracture.
passing: Posterior septal branches of sphenopalatine artery
neighbours: Lateral process of nasal septal cartilage

Nasalis muscle.note: Arises from the maxilla above the incisors and canine and spreads over the dorsum of the upper lateral cartilage, joining Procerus over the Os nasale. Pitfall: the thin soft tissue over the nasal dorsum is easy to miss in nasal bone fracture assessment, and the nasomaxillary suture should not be mistaken for a fracture line.
neighbours: Lateral process of nasal septal cartilage

Nasolabial node.note: Lies in the subcutaneous fat of the nasolabial fold over the Maxilla, along the angular and facial vessels. Pitfall: the V. angularis seen in cross-section looks like a node. Infection here can spread through the angular vein to the cavernous sinus.

Nasolacrimal duct.note: Runs in the bony nasolacrimal canal, formed by the maxilla, lacrimal bone and inferior concha. It opens into the inferior meatus under the inferior turbinate (Hasner valve). Pitfall: on axial images the canal is a round lucency anteromedial to the maxillary sinus. Do not confuse it with the infraorbital canal, which lies in the sinus roof.

Nasopharynx.note: The roof is the sphenoid body and clivus. The posterior wall lies on the Musculus longus capitis, the floor is the Palatum molle and the front opens into the choanae. Pitfall: an asymmetric lateral pharyngeal recess (fossa of Rosenmüller) or adenoid tissue in young adults can mimic carcinoma, so check for deep invasion and skull-base erosion.
passing: Posterior septal branches of sphenopalatine artery
landmarks: lm:Vaginal process of sphenoid bone|Sphenoid bone

Navicular bone.note: Articulates proximally with the caput tali and distally with the three cuneiforms. The tibialis posterior inserts on the tuberositas ossis navicularis, and the spring ligament supports it plantarly. Pitfall: an accessory navicular (os tibiale externum) mimics a tuberosity avulsion. Also, central-third stress fractures are sagittal and subtle on axial slices.

Nerve to mylohyoid muscle.note: It branches from the inferior alveolar nerve just before the foramen mandibulae and runs in the sulcus mylohyoideus on the medial ramus. It reaches the lower surface of the mylohyoid muscle and the venter anterior of the digastric muscle. Pitfall: on thin-slice CT the sulcus mylohyoideus can look like a nondisplaced fracture of the ramus.
passing: Mylohyoid branch of inferior alveolar artery

Nerve to piriformis muscle.note: This is a short branch from S1–S2 that enters the pelvic (anterior) surface of the musculus piriformis close to the os sacrum. CT cannot show it. Pitfall: piriformis atrophy or hypertrophy after denervation can look like asymmetry from a mass. Always compare both sides at the greater sciatic foramen.

Nerve to quadratus femoris muscle.note: This nerve (L4–S1) leaves the pelvis through the infrapiriform foramen, deep (anterior) to the nervus ischiadicus. It then descends on the posterior ischium and hip capsule, deep to the gemelli. It supplies the musculus quadratus femoris and the hip joint. Pitfall: quadratus femoris oedema or atrophy from ischiofemoral impingement is easy to mistake for a primary nerve problem.

Neurohypophysis.note: The posterior lobe sits in the back of the hypophysial fossa against the dorsum sellae and continues upward into the infundibulum and Hypothalamus. Pitfall: CT cannot separate it from the Adenohypophysis or show the T1 bright spot, so a suspected ectopic posterior pituitary or stalk lesion needs MRI.

Ninth rib.note: False rib that articulates with T8 and T9. Its cartilage joins the costal margin, and the diaphragm and pleural recess lie on its inner surface. Pitfall: nutrient canals and the costal groove can mimic a non-displaced fracture on axial slices. Confirm a fracture on curved or MIP reformats before reporting it.

Node of arch of azygos vein.key: Node of arch of azygos vein
Node of arch of azygos vein.note: This node lies in the right tracheobronchial angle, just below the arch of the Vena azyga and above the Bronchus principalis dexter (station 4R/10R). Pitfall: without contrast, the azygos arch cut in cross-section looks like a node. Follow it on adjacent slices back to the paravertebral azygos vein.

Node of ligamentum arteriosum.note: This node lies in the aortopulmonary window (station 5), between the underside of the aortic arch and the left pulmonary artery, next to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and the left upper lobe. Pitfall: partial volume of the aortic arch or pulmonary artery, or fluid in the superior pericardial recess, can look like a node.

Nodule of vermis.note: The Nodulus vermis is the most anteroinferior part of the vermis and projects into the roof of the lower fourth ventricle. The uvula lies behind it and the tonsils sit on either side. Pitfall: normal calcified choroid plexus in the roof of the fourth ventricle should not be mistaken for a lesion. A hyperdense midline mass here in a child suggests medulloblastoma.

Non-coronary leaflet.note: Posterior aortic cusp with no coronary ostium, sitting next to the interatrial septum between Atrium dextrum and Atrium sinistrum. Pitfall: the non-coronary sinus is the one that touches the atria. Do not confuse a non-coronary sinus aneurysm or rupture with an atrial mass.

Nuchal ligament.note: Midline fibroelastic septum running from the protuberantia occipitalis externa and crista occipitalis externa to the C7 spinous process. It separates the paired posterior neck muscles. Pitfall: a calcification or ossicle in the ligamentum nuchae (Barsony) can mimic an avulsed spinous process (clay-shoveler) fracture. Look for a well-corticated margin and an intact spinous process.

Nucleus ambiguus.note: It lies in the lateral medullary tegmentum, dorsal to the olive, in the territory of the vertebral artery and PICA. Pitfall: a lateral medullary (Wallenberg) infarct causing dysphagia is often invisible on CT because of posterior fossa artefact, so a normal CT does not exclude it and MRI DWI is needed.

Nucleus of abducens nerve.note: Lies under the facial colliculus in the floor of the Ventriculus quartus, with the facial genu wrapped around it. Pitfall: a nuclear lesion gives horizontal gaze palsy, often with facial palsy, not an isolated CN VI palsy. An isolated VI palsy from raised pressure is a false localising sign.

Nucleus of accessory nerve.note: Lies in the lateral anterior horn from about C1 to C5/6. Its rootlets exit laterally between the anterior and posterior roots and climb through the foramen magnum. Pitfall: the nerve (XI) leaves through the jugular foramen with IX and X, not through the hypoglossal canal (XII). Do not mix up these neighbouring foramina.

Nucleus of hypoglossal nerve.note: It lies paramedian beneath the hypoglossal trigone in the floor of the lower fourth ventricle. Its nerve exits through the preolivary sulcus into the hypoglossal canal. Pitfall: on bone-window CT, do not confuse the hypoglossal canal with the jugular foramen just lateral to it or with the posterior condylar canal.

Nucleus of oculomotor nerve.note: Paired complex ventral to the periaqueductal grey at the level of the superior colliculus, just rostral to the trochlear nucleus. Pitfall: a nuclear lesion gives ptosis on both sides and a contralateral superior rectus palsy, so the laterality differs from a nerve lesion.

Nucleus of solitary tract.note: Sits in the dorsolateral tegmentum of the Medulla oblongata, under the floor of the Ventriculus quartus and lateral to the Nucleus posterior nervi vagi. CT cannot resolve it. Pitfall: lateral medullary infarcts are often CT-occult, and streaks between the petrous bones can hide or mimic hypodensity, so use MRI.

Nucleus of trochlear nerve.note: Sits in the periaqueductal tegmentum at the level of the inferior colliculus, ventral to the Aquaeductus and caudal to the oculomotor complex. Pitfall: the fibres cross dorsally before they exit, so a nuclear lesion gives a superior oblique palsy on the opposite side.

Nucleus proprius.note: Laminae III–IV in the head of the posterior horn, deep to the substantia gelatinosa. It relays sensory input from the posterior roots. It is not visible on CT. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) or the thoracic nucleus (Clarke) at the base of the horn.

Nucleus pulposus C2-C3.note: Central gel core of the C2-C3 disc, enclosed by the anulus fibrosus between the endplates of the axis and C3. CT cannot separate it from the anulus. Pitfall: congenital block vertebra (Klippel-Feil type) is most common at C2-C3. A rudimentary disc with a waisted body means fusion, not degenerative collapse.

Nucleus pulposus C3-C4.note: Central core of the C3-C4 disc between the C3 and C4 endplates. The uncinate processes lie laterally. On CT it is iso-dense with the anulus. Pitfall: uncovertebral hypertrophy at the disc margin narrows the foramen intervertebrale and is easily mistaken for a disc herniation. Assess it on oblique or coronal reformats.

Nucleus pulposus C4-C5.note: Central core of the C4-C5 disc between the C4 and C5 endplates, not separable from the anulus on CT. Pitfall: gas in a degenerated nucleus (vacuum phenomenon) indicates degeneration and argues against infection. Do not mistake it for air from a penetrating injury or discitis.

Nucleus pulposus C5-C6.note: Central core of the C5-C6 disc. The anulus, Ligamentum longitudinale anterius and musculus longus colli are anterior, with the pharyngo-oesophageal junction in front of them. This is the most frequent degenerative level. Pitfall: laryngeal cartilage at the same axial level can suggest calcified disc material. Confirm the disc on sagittal reformats.

Nucleus pulposus C6-C7.note: Central core of the C6-C7 disc between the C6 and C7 endplates, with the Ligamentum longitudinale posterius behind the anulus. Pitfall: CT has poor soft-tissue contrast for posterior nuclear herniation at this level. A normal-looking disc does not exclude foraminal herniation compressing the C7 root, so recommend MRI if radiculopathy is present.

Nucleus pulposus C7-T1.note: Central core of the C7-T1 disc between the C7 and T1 endplates. Pitfall: streak artefact from the shoulders degrades this level and can simulate low-density disc material or hide a herniation. Use thin sagittal reformats and identify T1 by the first rib articulation.

Nucleus pulposus L1-L2.note: Central core of the L1-L2 disc between the L1 and L2 endplates. The conus medullaris and cauda equina lie behind the disc. Pitfall: a Schmorl node (intravertebral nuclear herniation) has a sclerotic rim. Do not confuse it with a lytic lesion or a compression fracture of the endplate.

Nucleus pulposus L2-L3.note: Central gel core of Discus intervertebralis L2-L3, enclosed by the anulus fibrosus and capped by the endplates of L2 and L3. CT cannot separate it from the anulus. Pitfall: intradiscal gas (vacuum phenomenon) means degeneration, not infection. Discitis shows endplate erosion and paravertebral soft tissue.

Nucleus pulposus L3-L4.note: Lies centrally within Discus intervertebralis L3-L4, between the endplates of L3 and L4. On CT it has the same density as the anulus. Pitfall: a Schmorl node (nucleus pushed into the endplate, with a sclerotic rim) can be mistaken for a lytic lesion or fracture.

Nucleus pulposus L4-L5.note: Core of Discus intervertebralis L4-L5, between the endplates of L4 and L5. Herniation through a posterior anular tear compresses the traversing L5 root. Pitfall: partial volume of the endplate or a posterior osteophyte on thick slices looks like disc protrusion. Check on thin sagittal reformats.

Nucleus pulposus L5-S1.note: Core of Discus intervertebralis L5-S1, between the L5 endplate and the base of the Os sacrum. The disc is often narrow and wedge-shaped. Pitfall: a lumbosacral transitional vertebra (sacralised L5 or lumbarised S1) shifts the level count. Count from T12/the ribs and state the counting method.

Nucleus pulposus T1-T2.note: Core of Discus intervertebralis T1-T2, between the endplates of T1 and T2, with the Ligamentum longitudinale posterius behind it. Pitfall: shoulder streak artefact and partial volume at the cervicothoracic junction hide or mimic disc pathology. Identify T1 by its articulation with the first rib.

Nucleus pulposus T10-T11.note: Core of Discus intervertebralis T10-T11, between the endplates of T10 and T11. Pitfall: thoracic disc calcification is common, and a calcified herniation can be mistaken for an osteophyte or an intraspinal meningioma. Check continuity with the disc space.

Nucleus pulposus T11-T12.note: Core of Discus intervertebralis T11-T12, between the endplates of T11 and T12. The thoracolumbar junction is the most common site of thoracic disc herniation. Pitfall: hypoplastic 12th ribs lead to wrong level labelling. Count ribs on coronal reformats.

Nucleus pulposus T12-L1.note: Core of Discus intervertebralis T12-L1, between the endplates of T12 and L1. The Psoas major origin lies anterolaterally. Pitfall: in trauma, apparent widening or gas in this disc can signal a flexion-distraction injury. Always check posterior element alignment.

Nucleus pulposus T2-T3.note: Core of Discus intervertebralis T2-T3, between the endplates of T2 and T3, in front of the Ligamentum longitudinale posterius. Pitfall: thoracic levels are easily mislabelled when the scan has no cervical coverage. Count from the rib heads, not from the sternum.

Nucleus pulposus T3-T4.note: Core of Discus intervertebralis T3-T4, between the endplates of T3 and T4. The thoracic disc is thin and the canal is narrow. Pitfall: costovertebral joint osteophytes projecting into the neural foramen are mistaken for a lateral disc herniation.

Nucleus pulposus T4-T5.note: Core of Discus intervertebralis T4-T5, between the endplates of T4 and T5, with the Ligamentum longitudinale posterius directly behind it. Pitfall: an ossified posterior longitudinal ligament can mimic a calcified central disc herniation. OPLL extends across several vertebral bodies.

Nucleus pulposus T5-T6.note: Core of Discus intervertebralis T5-T6, between the endplates of T5 and T6. Pitfall: partial-volume averaging of the concave endplate on axial slices mimics a broad-based disc bulge. Confirm on sagittal reformats.

Nucleus pulposus T6-T7.note: Core of Discus intervertebralis T6-T7, between the endplates of T6 and T7. Pitfall: in the mid-thoracic spine, discitis with paravertebral soft tissue can be mistaken for a paraspinal mass or lymph nodes. Look for endplate erosion on both sides of the disc.

Nucleus pulposus T7-T8.note: Core of Discus intervertebralis T7-T8, between the endplates of T7 and T8. Pitfall: central intradiscal calcification, which is often incidental, can be mistaken for a fracture fragment. A herniated calcified fragment must be contiguous with the disc and enter the canal.

Nucleus pulposus T8-T9.note: Core of Discus intervertebralis T8-T9, between the endplates of T8 and T9. Pitfall: Scheuermann-type endplate irregularity with Schmorl nodes can be mistaken for compression fractures. Endplate changes over several levels with anterior wedging point to Scheuermann disease.

Nucleus pulposus T9-T10.note: Core of Discus intervertebralis T9-T10, between the endplates of T9 and T10. Pitfall: the lower thoracic levels are the most common site of symptomatic calcified thoracic disc herniation, which is easy to miss on soft-tissue windows. Review bone windows and sagittal reformats.

Oblique cord.note: A small band from the lateral Tuberositas ulnae to the radius just distal to the radial tuberosity. The gap below it, above the interosseous membrane, transmits the posterior interosseous vessels. Pitfall: ossification here mimics proximal radio-ulnar synostosis or heterotopic bone after a distal biceps repair. Correlate with rotation and the biceps footprint.

Oblique head of adductor hallucis.note: A bulky deep muscle from the bases of metatarsals 2–4 and the fibularis longus sheath to the lateral sesamoid and hallux proximal phalanx. The arcus plantaris runs deep to it. Pitfall: an os peroneum or a calcified fibularis longus tendon crossing deep to it near the cuboid is not a loose body or a fracture.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
landmarks: lm:Base of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone
neighbours: Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis

Oblique head of adductor pollicis.note: Arises from the capitate and the bases of the 2nd–3rd metacarpals. It joins the transverse head on the ulnar sesamoid and the base of the thumb's proximal phalanx; the deep palmar arch and deep ulnar branch pass between the heads. Pitfall: the ulnar sesamoid is normal; do not mistake it for an avulsion of the ulnar collateral ligament (Stener lesion).
neighbours: Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus
Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand

Oblique part of cricothyroid muscle.note: An extralaryngeal muscle running from the anterolateral cricoid arch posterolaterally to the Cornu inferius of the thyroid cartilage, near the cricothyroid joint and the upper thyroid pole. Pitfall: it sits outside the cartilage framework, so do not read it as extralaryngeal tumour spread or a thyroid nodule.
landmarks: lm:Inferior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

Oblique popliteal ligament.note: Expansion of the semimembranosus tendon that crosses the posterior capsule obliquely towards the lateral femoral condyle, forming the floor of the fossa poplitea. Pitfall: the popliteal vessels lie directly on it, so do not mistake a posterior capsular effusion or Baker cyst for a popliteal aneurysm.

Obliquus inferior capitis muscle.note: Runs from the C2 spinous process to the C1 transverse process and forms the inferior border of the suboccipital triangle. Pitfall: the V3 loop of the A. vertebralis lies just above it, in the groove on the posterior arch of the atlas. A ponticulus posticus or this loop can be mistaken for calcification or a mass.

Obliquus superior capitis muscle.note: Runs from the C1 transverse process to the Os occipitale between the superior and inferior nuchal lines, forming the lateral border of the suboccipital triangle. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the rectus capitis lateralis. That muscle lies anterior, attaches to the jugular process and marks the posterior border of the jugular foramen.

Obturator artery.note: Runs along the lateral pelvic wall on the Obturator internus, below the Nervus obturatorius, to the obturator canal under the superior pubic ramus. Pitfall: an aberrant origin from the inferior epigastric or external iliac artery (corona mortis) crosses the superior pubic ramus. It bleeds in pubic fractures and is easily mistaken for an obturator node.

Obturator externus.note: Covers the outer surface of the membrana obturatoria. It passes below the femoral neck to the fossa trochanterica, with the hip capsule above it and the quadratus femoris behind it. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the obturator internus, which lies inside the pelvis. An obturator hernia lies between the pectineus and the obturator externus.

Obturator internus.note: Lines the inner surface of the obturator foramen on the pelvic sidewall. It turns around the lesser sciatic notch to reach the trochanteric fossa, and the levator ani arises from its fascia. Pitfall: obturator nodes along its medial surface mimic an intramuscular mass. The pudendal canal (Alcock) runs in its fascia below the levator.

Obturator membrane.note: Closes the Foramen obturatum between obturator internus on the inside and obturator externus on the outside. It leaves the superolateral obturator canal open for the obturator nerve and vessels. Pitfall: an obturator hernia passes through this canal and lies between pectineus and obturator externus. Do not dismiss it as a lymph node or a muscle-asymmetry finding.

Obturator nerve.note: Emerges from the medial border of the psoas major at the pelvic brim, behind the common iliac vessels. It runs along the lateral pelvic wall on the obturator internus, above the obturator vessels, into the canalis obturatorius. Pitfall: do not mistake obturator lymph nodes or an obturator hernia for the nerve on the lateral pelvic wall.

Obturator nodes.note: These nodes lie on the pelvic sidewall in the obturator fossa, medial to obturator internus and below the external iliac vein, along the obturator vessels and nerve. Pitfall: in women the ovary lies against the sidewall here and mimics an obturator node. In men the ductus deferens can also mimic one.

Occipital artery.note: Arises from the posterior ECA and follows the lower border of the posterior digastric. It grooves the temporal bone (occipital groove) medial to the Incisura mastoidea, then runs deep to the SCM and splenius to the scalp. Pitfall: the occipital groove and the nearby mastoid emissary canal can mimic a fracture line on bone windows.

Occipital bone.note: The bone surrounds the foramen magnum. The basilar part forms the clivus up to the spheno-occipital synchondrosis, and the squama meets the parietal bones at the lambdoid suture. Pitfall: do not confuse the condylar canal (an emissary channel behind the condyle) with the hypoglossal canal, which runs above the condyle and carries CN XII.
landmarks: lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipital bone

Occipital nodes.note: Lie in the subcutaneous fat over the Os occipitale near the M. occipitalis, along the occipital vessels. Pitfall: on brain CT a scalp node can look like a scalp haematoma or sebaceous cyst. Check that it is outside the bone and has no intracranial connection.

Occipital pole.note: The posterior tip of the hemisphere. It lies against the squama of Os occipitale near the confluence of sinuses, between the Falx cerebri and the upper surface of the Tentorium cerebelli. Pitfall: contrecoup contusions and thin subdural collections along the falx and tentorium are easily missed, and occipital pole asymmetry (petalia) is a normal variant, not mass effect.

Occipital sinus.note: The smallest dural sinus. It runs in the attached edge of the falx cerebelli along the internal occipital crest, from the margin of the foramen magnum up to the confluence of sinuses. Pitfall: in children a prominent occipital sinus or its groove in the midline occipital bone can be mistaken for a fracture or an extra-axial haematoma.

Occipital vein.note: This scalp vein runs with the arteria occipitalis in the occipital soft tissues, deep to the galea. It drains to the suboccipital plexus or the vena jugularis externa and connects to the sigmoid sinus through the mastoid emissary vein. Pitfall: the emissary foramen and canal can look like a fracture on CT bone windows.

Occipitalis muscle.note: Arises from the lateral superior nuchal line and inserts into the galea over the occipital bone. Pitfall: occipital nodes and scalp vessels in this layer can mimic small subcutaneous masses. The lambdoid suture and accessory sutures beneath must not be read as fractures.
landmarks: lm:Occipital border of parietal bone|Parietal bone

Occipitotemporal sulcus (Lateral part*).note: Basal sulcus that separates the Inferior temporal gyrus laterally from the Lateral occipitotemporal (fusiform) gyrus medially. Pitfall: it runs parallel to the more medial Collateral sulcus and is often discontinuous, so the two are easily confused on axial CT. The collateral sulcus is deeper and indents the temporal horn as the collateral eminence.

Oculomotor nerve (III).note: It leaves the interpeduncular fossa between the PCA and SCA, runs alongside the PComA, and takes the highest position in the lateral wall of the Sinus cavernosus. It enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure inside the anulus tendineus. Pitfall: a III palsy that involves the pupil needs CTA to exclude a PComA aneurysm or uncal herniation.

Oesophagus.note: It starts behind the cricoid lamina at C6 and runs behind the trachea, slightly to the left. It is indented by the aortic arch, left main bronchus and left atrium, and passes through the hiatus at T10. Pitfall: a collapsed oesophagus, especially near the GEJ, looks thick-walled. Judge wall thickness only where the lumen is distended.

Olfactory nerve (I).note: The olfactory fila cross the Lamina cribrosa of the ethmoid. The bulb and tract lie in the olfactory sulcus below the gyrus rectus. Pitfall: a deep olfactory fossa (high Keros type) with a thin lateral lamella is easily breached at surgery. Check this and the anterior ethmoidal artery canal, and look for skull-base fractures that cause CSF leak.

Olfactory sulcus.note: The sulcus olfactorius runs parallel to the midline on the orbital surface. It separates the gyrus rectus (medial) from the gyri orbitales (lateral) and holds the olfactory bulb and tract above the lamina cribrosa. Pitfall: on bone CT the very thin cribriform plate can look dehiscent through partial volume. Also, a shallow or absent sulcus suggests Kallmann syndrome.

Olive.note: Oval bulge on the anterolateral medulla. It lies between the Pyramis (preolivary sulcus, where the XII rootlets exit) and the retro-olivary sulcus (IX, X, XI), and faces the clivus. Pitfall: an ectatic or calcified Arteria vertebralis or PICA loop against the olive can look like a mass or a hyperdensity.

Omental taenia.note: Taenia omentalis runs along the Omentum maius attachment on the Colon transversum and posterolaterally on the ascending and descending colon. It cannot be resolved on CT. All three taeniae meet at the caecal pole, which helps locate the appendix base. Pitfall: omental fat stranding along the colon is easily misread as colitis or epiploic appendagitis.

Omohyoid muscle.note: Two bellies run from the Corpus ossis hyoidei to the scapula near the suprascapular notch. Its intermediate tendon crosses superficial to the internal jugular vein, which is the surgical level III/IV boundary. Pitfall: on axial CT the tendon cut in cross-section next to the internal jugular vein can mimic a small node.

Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus.key: Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus
Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus.note: The pars opercularis lies between the ascending ramus of the lateral sulcus (in front) and the inferior precentral sulcus (behind), below the inferior frontal sulcus. It covers the anterior insula. It is part of Broca's area in the dominant hemisphere. Pitfall: a hyperdense M2/M3 'dot' in the adjacent sylvian fissure can be mistaken for calcification or partial volume of the operculum.
passing: Insular branches of middle cerebral artery (M2)
neighbours: Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus
Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci*)

Ophthalmic artery.note: Arises from the supraclinoid ICA and enters the orbit through the canalis opticus, inferolateral to the optic nerve. It then crosses above the nerve toward the medial wall. Pitfall: do not confuse the canalis opticus with the fissura orbitalis superior. Origin from the middle meningeal artery is a variant.

Ophthalmic nerve.note: It runs in the lateral wall of the Sinus cavernosus below IV and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure. The frontal branch runs above the levator to the supraorbital notch or foramen. Pitfall: a supraorbital foramen instead of a notch is a normal variant and can look like a fracture or erosion on axial CT.

Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand.key: Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand
Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand.note: The deepest hypothenar muscle. It runs from the hamulus ossis hamati and retinaculum to the ulnar border of the fifth metacarpal shaft, and the deep ulnar branch pierces it. Pitfall: it inserts on the metacarpal, not the phalanx, which separates it from the overlying FDM on CT.
passing: Common palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve

Opponens pollicis muscle.note: Lies deep to abductor pollicis brevis. It runs from the trapezium tubercle and flexor retinaculum to the whole radial border of the first metacarpal shaft. Pitfall: it is the only thenar muscle that inserts on the metacarpal; use this to tell it apart from flexor pollicis brevis, which inserts on the phalanx.
neighbours: Superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis
Deep head of flexor pollicis brevis
Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus

Optic chiasm.note: Lies in the suprasellar cistern above the diaphragma sellae and pituitary, in front of the infundibulum and the optic recess of the third ventricle. The Arteria communicans anterior lies in front of and above it. On axial CT, a normal chiasm or an aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery can look like a suprasellar mass. Check the sella and use CTA.

Optic nerve (II).note: It runs from the globe through the muscle cone, then through the Canalis opticus of the lesser wing with the ophthalmic artery below it, and on to the chiasm. Pitfall: do not confuse the optic canal with the superior orbital fissure, which lies inferolateral and is separated by the optic strut. A sphenoethmoidal (Onodi) cell or a pneumatised clinoid can leave the canal dehiscent.

Optic tract.note: Runs from the chiasm backward and outward around the Basis pedunculi to the Corpus geniculatum laterale. It lies above the uncus and medial temporal lobe, with the Arteria cerebri posterior close below. CT cannot show it separately from the vessels and cistern beside it. Do not confuse it with the posterior cerebral artery in the ambient cistern.

Orbicularis oris muscle.note: Sphincter of the lips, lying between skin and oral mucosa; it blends laterally into the modiolus with Bucinator. Pitfall: lip thickness depends on lip closure and position, so apparent asymmetry is often positional. Do not mistake the labial arteries running in the submucosa for foreign bodies or nodules.
passing: Mental branch of inferior alveolar artery

Orbital gyri.note: The gyri orbitales rest on the lamina orbitalis of the frontal bone. Medially the sulcus olfactorius separates them from the gyrus rectus; laterally they meet the pars orbitalis; posteriorly they face the anterior perforated substance and the temporal pole. Pitfall: the ridged orbital roof causes streak artefact that mimics contusion, a common coup–contrecoup site. Confirm on coronal images.
passing: Orbitofrontal branches of anterior cerebral artery
landmarks: lm:Orbital plate of frontal bone|Frontal bone
neighbours: Orbital part of  inferior frontal gyrus

Orbital gyri (Frontomarginal gyrus and s.note: The frontomarginal gyrus forms the anteroinferior rim of the frontal pole, where the convexity turns onto the orbital surface. It sits directly behind the posterior wall of the frontal sinus and above the orbital roof. Pitfall: beam-hardening and partial volume from the sinus wall can mimic a hyperdense contusion or hide one. Check thin coronal reformats.
passing: Orbitofrontal branches of anterior cerebral artery

Orbital part of inferior frontal gyrus.key: Orbital part of  inferior frontal gyrus
Orbital part of inferior frontal gyrus.note: The pars orbitalis lies below the horizontal ramus of the lateral sulcus and continues onto the orbital surface lateral to the lateral orbital sulcus. It rests on the orbital plate near the sphenoid ridge. Pitfall: across the sylvian fissure the temporal pole sits right next to it. Beam-hardening from the sphenoid ridge can lead you to place a contusion in the wrong lobe.
neighbours: Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Orbital part of orbicularis oculi.note: Ring of muscle around the orbital margin, superficial to the septum orbitale and anchored medially at the medial palpebral ligament. Pitfall: swelling superficial to the septum orbitale is preseptal cellulitis and should not be reported as orbital (postseptal) disease. Find the septum before describing the extent.

Orbital sulci (H-shaped orbital sulci*).note: The H-shaped sulci orbitales divide the orbital surface into anterior, posterior, medial and lateral orbital gyri, just above the lamina orbitalis. Pitfall: CSF in these sulci, partial-volumed against the bumpy orbital roof, can be misread as focal atrophy or a thin extra-axial collection. Assess them on coronal reformats.
landmarks: lm:Orbital plate of frontal bone|Frontal bone
neighbours: Orbital part of  inferior frontal gyrus

Orbital sulci (Lateral Orbital sulcus*).note: The lateral orbital sulcus marks the border between the lateral orbital gyrus and the pars orbitalis of the inferior frontal gyrus, at the anterolateral edge of the orbital surface. Pitfall: on axial slices it is easily confused with the ramus anterior horizontalis of the sulcus lateralis, which lies just behind and above it. Confirm using sagittal images.
landmarks: lm:Temporal surface of frontal bone|Frontal bone
neighbours: Orbital part of  inferior frontal gyrus
Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Orbitofrontal branches of anterior cereb.key: Orbitofrontal branches of anterior cerebral artery
Orbitofrontal branches of anterior cereb.note: Run forward from proximal A2 along the gyrus rectus and the medial orbital gyri, above the lamina cribrosa and orbital roof. Pitfall: frontobasal contusions in this region are easily hidden by beam-hardening artefact from the orbital roof. Look at coronal reformats.

Oropharynx.note: Extends from the Palatum molle down to the hyoid level and tip of the epiglottis. It includes the base of tongue, palatine tonsils, vallecula and posterior pharyngeal wall. Pitfall: asymmetric palatine or lingual tonsils are common and can mimic tumour. A medialised retropharyngeal internal carotid artery must not be mistaken for a mass.

Palatine bone.note: The horizontal plate forms the posterior hard palate behind the maxilla. The perpendicular plate forms the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa and the sphenopalatine foramen. Pitfall: the greater palatine canal and foramen are a perineural spread route. Do not mistake them for the lesser palatine foramina or for erosion.
passing: Posterior lateral nasal branches of sphenopalatine artery.

Palatine tonsil.note: The palatine tonsil sits in the tonsillar fossa of the oropharynx, between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches. Laterally it is bounded by the M. constrictor superior pharyngis and the parapharyngeal space, with the M. pterygoideus medialis beyond. Pitfall: tonsilloliths (dense calcified foci) and mild normal asymmetry are common. Do not mistake them for a tumour or a sialolith.

Palatopharyngeus muscle.note: Runs from the palatine aponeurosis through the posterior tonsillar pillar, along the inner side of the constrictors, to the posterior border of the thyroid lamina. Pitfall: a prominent posterior pillar or uneven pharyngeal walls can mimic an oropharyngeal mass. Compare with the other side before calling a lesion.
landmarks: lm:Superior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

Palmar aponeurosis.note: Aponeurosis palmaris is a triangular fibrous sheet just beneath the palmar skin. It continues from the palmaris longus tendon and retinaculum flexorium and fans into digital slips at the metacarpophalangeal level. Pitfall: nodular thickening (Dupuytren) lies superficial to the flexor tendon sheaths and the superficial palmar arch, so do not call it a tendon lesion.
passing: Common palmar digital branches of median nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Synovial sheaths of digits of hand
Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Palmar branch of median nerve.note: Arises about 5 cm above the wrist crease, runs along the ulnar side of the FCR tendon and crosses superficial to the Retinaculum flexorum to the thenar skin. Pitfall: it does not pass through the carpal tunnel, so thenar sensation is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome. It is at risk in FCR approaches and open carpal tunnel release.
passing: Palmar carpal branch of radial artery
neighbours: Tendon sheath of flexor carpi radialis
Superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis

Palmar branch of ulnar nerve.note: Arises in the mid-forearm and runs on the arteria ulnaris. It pierces fascia antebrachii and passes superficial to the retinaculum flexorium to reach the skin of the proximal hypothenar palm. Pitfall: it bypasses Guyon canal, so palm sensation is spared in canal lesions; do not confuse it with the palmar branch of the median nerve.
neighbours: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Palmar capitohamate ligament.note: Short transverse band spanning the palmar capitate–hamate interval in the distal carpal row, deep to the flexor tendons and proximal to the CMC joints. CT does not resolve it as a separate structure. Pitfall: after high-energy trauma, a widened capitohamate interval suggests axial carpal instability and should not be read as a normal joint space.

Palmar carpal branch of radial artery.key: Palmar carpal branch of radial artery
Palmar carpal branch of radial artery.note: Small branch arising at the distal border of Pronator quadratus. It runs ulnarward on the palmar distal radius and carpus, deep to the flexor tendons, to join the ulnar palmar carpal branch. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery, which runs over the thenar muscles.
neighbours: Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Palmar carpometacarpal ligaments.note: Join the palmar surfaces of the distal carpal row to metacarpal bases 2–5, deep to the flexor tendons and the deep palmar arch. Pitfall: the thumb CMC is a separate saddle joint; a fracture at the base of the first metacarpal (Bennett/Rolando) is not a lesion of these ligaments.

Palmar digital veins.note: The Venae digitales palmares are small veins on the volar-lateral sides of the phalanges, running with the proper palmar digital arteries and nerves on either side of the flexor tendon sheath. Most of the finger drains through the dorsal digital veins. Pitfall: the neurovascular bundles can be mistaken for fluid in the flexor tendon sheath, especially through partial-volume effect.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
landmarks: lm:Trochlea of phalanx of hand|Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
Middle phalanx of third finger of hand

Palmar interossei muscles.note: Unipennate muscles on the palmar side of metacarpals 2, 4 and 5 that insert into the extensor hoods; they adduct the fingers toward the middle finger. Pitfall: they share each intermetacarpal space with a dorsal interosseous; the palmar one is volar and single-headed, so do not mislabel them on axial images.
passing: Common palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand

Palmar interphalangeal ligaments.note: The volar plates. They form the palmar floor of the PIP and DIP joints, attach firmly to the base of the distal phalanx and lie deep to the flexor tendons and their sheath. Pitfall: a small palmar base fragment of the middle phalanx means a volar plate avulsion, often with dorsal subluxation. Do not call it a sesamoid.
landmarks: lm:Trochlea of phalanx of hand|Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
neighbours: Middle phalanx of third finger of hand
Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints
Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Palmar lunotriquetral ligament.note: Palmar thickening of the lunotriquetral interval, deep to the ulnocarpal ligaments (Lig. ulnotriquetrum). Pitfall: lunotriquetral tears rarely widen the gap. Look instead for a step-off in the proximal carpal arc and a VISI pattern, and do not mistake a type II lunate's hamate facet for a malalignment.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery

Palmar metacarpal arteries.note: Arise from the deep palmar arch and run distally on the palmar interossei between the metacarpals, deep to the flexor tendons and lumbricals. They join the common palmar digital arteries near the MCP joints. Pitfall: they are deeper than the common palmar digital arteries, which lie superficial to the flexor tendons.

Palmar metacarpal ligaments.note: Short transverse bands joining the palmar bases of metacarpals II–V, just distal to the carpometacarpal joint line and deep to the Arcus palmaris profundus. Not seen as separate structures on CT. Pitfall: do not confuse them with the Ligamenta carpometacarpea palmaria. These ligaments lie at the intermetacarpal level, not across the CMC joint.

Palmar radio-ulnar ligament.note: Palmar limb of the TFCC. It runs from the palmar rim of the incisura ulnaris to the ulnar fovea, deep to pronator quadratus, and gives origin to the ulnolunate and ulnotriquetral ligaments. Pitfall: a fracture at the ulnar styloid base (foveal insertion) suggests DRUJ instability; a styloid tip flake does not.
neighbours: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint

Palmar scaphotriquetral ligament.note: Forms the distal limb of the palmar 'V', crossing palmar to the capitate neck from the scaphoid to the triquetrum. Between it and the radiocarpal ligaments lies the space of Poirier, a weak zone over the capitolunate joint. Pitfall: perilunate dislocation passes through this zone, so check capitolunate alignment on sagittal reconstructions.

Palmar trapezoideocapitate ligament.note: Palmar band joining the trapezoid and capitate in the distal row, deep to the thenar muscles and the flexor pollicis longus sheath. Pitfall: trapezoid fractures are rare and subtle because the bone is wedge-shaped and overlaps neighbouring bones. Assess the trapezoid in all three planes rather than calling it intact from the axial images alone.

Palmaris longus muscle.note: Has a short belly from the medial epicondyle. Its long tendon runs superficial to the flexor retinaculum and continues into the aponeurosis palmaris, with the median nerve directly deep to it. Pitfall: the muscle is absent in about 15% of people, on one or both sides, and can be reversed or duplicated; do not call absence a rupture or a reversed belly a mass.
passing: Anterior branch of medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Palpebral part of orbicularis oculi.note: Thin muscle inside the eyelids, anterior to the tarsi and septum orbitale, running from the medial to the lateral palpebral ligament. Pitfall: on CT the eyelid layers merge into one soft-tissue band, and partial volume with the cornea or a closed lid can mimic eyelid thickening.

Pancreas.note: The head lies in the duodenal C-loop to the right of the SMV, and the uncinate process lies behind the SMV. The body crosses in front of the SMA and aorta, and the tail reaches the splenic hilum with the splenic vein behind it. Pitfall: unopacified duodenum or jejunum can look like a pancreatic head mass.

Pancreatic duct.note: Runs centrally through the tail, body and head of the Pancreas and joins the Ductus biliaris at the major duodenal papilla. Normal calibre is about 3 mm or less in the head. Pitfall: the fat plane or the splenic vein along the posterior gland surface can mimic a dilated duct, so follow it to confirm it stays inside the parenchyma.

Paracentral gyrus and sulcus*.note: The lobulus paracentralis lies on the medial hemisphere next to the falx. Anterior boundary: sulcus paracentralis. Posterior boundary: pars marginalis of the sulcus cinguli. Inferior boundary: sulcus cinguli. The central sulcus notches its upper edge. It belongs to the ACA territory and represents the leg. Pitfall: a hyperdense or calcified falx, or the superior sagittal sinus, can mimic parafalcine SAH or subdural haematoma.
neighbours: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle posterior part)

Paracentral sulcus.note: In this segmentation the label sits in the anterior frontal region, between the superior and middle frontal gyri near the frontal pole, under the frontal bone. Pitfall: the TA sulcus paracentralis lies on the medial surface, rising from the sulcus cinguli in front of the paracentral lobule. Do not use this label as a landmark for the paracentral lobule.

Paracolic superior mesenteric nodes.note: Lie along the mesenteric border of the colon, next to the A. marginalis coli. Pitfall: the paracolic gutter (outside the colon) is a different space from the mesenteric side. Do not confuse these nodes with diverticula, epiploic appendages or the marginal vessels seen in cross-section.

Pararectal nodes.note: These nodes lie in the mesorectal fat inside the mesorectal fascia, along the superior rectal vessels, above levator ani. Pitfall: branches of the superior rectal vessels cut in cross-section mimic small mesorectal nodes. Trace them on contiguous slices, and judge nodes by shape and margins, not size alone.

Parasternal nodes.note: These nodes follow the internal thoracic vessels just lateral to the sternum. They lie behind the costal cartilages and in front of the M. transversus thoracis and the Pleura, mostly in intercostal spaces 1–3. They matter for breast cancer staging. Pitfall: an internal thoracic vein seen in cross-section can mimic a node.

Paratracheal cervical nodes.note: Level VI nodes lie in the tracheoesophageal groove, between the Trachea and Oesophagus on the inner side and the common carotid artery on the outer side, along the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Pitfall: a parathyroid adenoma or an oesophageal diverticulum (Killian–Jamieson) in the groove can mimic a paratracheal node; look for an air or contrast connection, or avid arterial enhancement.

Paratracheal thoracic nodes.note: These nodes run along the Trachea. On the right (2R/4R) they sit between the trachea and the SVC; on the left (2L/4L) they sit medial to the Arcus aortae. The left/right boundary is the left lateral tracheal wall, not the midline. Pitfall: the fluid-density, crescent-shaped superior pericardial recess can mimic a node.

Parietal bone.note: It is bounded by the sagittal, coronal, lambdoid and squamosal sutures, and its mastoid angle touches the sigmoid sinus groove. Pitfall: parietal foramina, accessory parietal sutures (in children) and arachnoid granulations can look like fractures or lytic lesions. Check the 3D reconstructions and compare with the other side.
landmarks: lm:Sagittal border of parietal bone|Parietal bone
lm:Squamosal border of parietal bone|Parietal bone
lm:Mastoid angle of parietal bone|Parietal bone
lm:Occipital border of parietal bone|Parietal bone

Parietal branches of middle cerebral art.key: Parietal branches of middle cerebral artery
Parietal branches of middle cerebral art.note: Leave the posterior Sylvian fissure to supply the gyrus supramarginalis, gyrus angularis and lower lobulus parietalis superior. Pitfall: the arteria temporalis superficialis runs outside the os parietale in the scalp. Do not confuse its contrast or calcification with an intracranial branch, and keep laterality in mind.

Parieto-occipital artery.note: It runs in the Sulcus parietooccipitalis between the Cuneus and the Precuneus, supplying the medial parieto-occipital cortex and anastomosing with the A. pericallosa (ACA). Pitfall: the parieto-occipital sulcus can be confused with the calcarine sulcus on axial slices; the parieto-occipital sulcus is higher and runs more vertically.

Parieto-occipital sulcus.note: A deep medial sulcus separating the Precuneus (parietal lobe) from the Cuneus (occipital lobe). It joins the Sulcus calcarinus anteroinferiorly in a Y shape. Pitfall: on axial CT it is easily mistaken for the Sulcus calcarinus. The parieto-occipital sulcus lies higher and runs obliquely upward and backward.

Parotid duct.note: Ductus parotideus runs forward across the superficial masseter about 1 cm below the zygomatic arch. It then pierces the Bucinator and opens opposite the upper second molar. Pitfall: a sialolith in the duct can be confused with a phlebolith or vascular calcification. Accessory parotid tissue along the duct mimics a buccal-space mass.

Parotid gland.note: The parotid fills the space behind the mandible. The facial nerve plane splits it into superficial and deep lobes, and the Vena retromandibularis marks this plane on CT. The deep lobe extends through the stylomandibular tunnel into the prestyloid parapharyngeal space. Pitfall: tell a deep-lobe mass (no fat plane to the gland) from a true parapharyngeal mass.
landmarks: lm:Styloid process of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Patella.note: The patella is a sesamoid in the quadriceps tendon and articulates with the facies patellaris femoris. The retinacula attach to its medial and lateral margins, and the infrapatellar fat pad lies below the apex. Pitfall: bipartite patella (superolateral fragment, smooth corticated margins, often bilateral) mimics a fracture.

Patellar anastomosis.note: This is a periarticular network around the Patella, in the prepatellar fat and the retinacula. It is fed by the four genicular arteries, the descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery and the anterior tibial recurrent artery. Pitfall: with popliteal occlusion it forms prominent collaterals. After arthroplasty, a focal blush there means pseudoaneurysm, not normal network.
passing: Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery

Pectineus muscle.note: A flat muscle from the pecten ossis pubis to the pectineal line of the femur. It forms the medial floor of the femoral triangle under the femoral vessels, with the iliopsoas lateral and the adductor longus medial. Pitfall: a femoral or obturator hernia can be missed as nodes or vessels. Trace the hernia sac to its origin.

Pectoral branches of thoraco-acromial ar.note: Pierce the Fascia clavipectoralis above Pectoralis minor and descend in the interpectoral plane between pectoralis major and minor.
