Pitfall: in cross-section, these enhancing vessels can look like interpectoral (Rotter) lymph nodes, so follow them across adjacent slices.
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Pectoral fascia.note: Invests pectoralis major, attaches to the clavicle and sternum, and joins the deltoid fascia at the deltopectoral groove where the cephalic vein runs. Pitfall: an intact retromammary fat plane argues against chest-wall invasion. A unilateral sternalis muscle (normal variant) can look like a parasternal mass.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle
Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Pectoralis minor muscle.note: It runs from ribs 3–5 to the coracoid process of the scapula, deep to pectoralis major. It divides the axillary vessels into three parts and the axillary nodes into levels I–III. Pitfall: interpectoral (Rotter) nodes lie between pectoralis major and minor and count as level II, not level I.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle
Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Peduncle of flocculus.note: The Pedunculus flocculi joins the flocculus to the nodulus along the inferior medullary velum. It runs at the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle. Pitfall: the lateral recess, the foramen of Luschka and its choroid plexus lie in the same spot. Do not mistake them for a CPA lesion or a dilated recess.
landmarks: lm:Posterior surface of petrous part|Temporal bone

Perforating branches of plantar metatars.key: Perforating branches of plantar metatarsal arteries
Perforating branches of plantar metatars.note: Proximal perforators pass between the heads of the dorsal interossei near the metatarsal bases, and distal perforators near the heads. Both link the plantar and dorsal metatarsal arteries. Pitfall: if the a. arcuata is hypoplastic, the dorsal metatarsal arteries normally fill retrogradely through these perforators. This is not a pathological collateral.
landmarks: lm:Body of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone

Perforating femoral arteries.note: There are usually three to four branches of the Arteria profunda femoris; the terminal profunda counts as the fourth. They pierce the Adductor magnus close to the linea aspera of the Os femoris to supply the posterior compartment. Pitfall: they hug the posterior femoral shaft and are a source of haematoma or pseudoaneurysm after shaft fractures, nailing or cerclage. The femoral nutrient artery arises from one of them.
passing: Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery

Perforating veins.note: These are the venae perforantes that travel with the perforating arteries. They pierce the adductor magnus close to the linea aspera and drain the posterior thigh into the vena profunda femoris. Pitfall: do not confuse them with the superficial-to-deep perforator veins of venous insufficiency, such as the Dodd and Hunterian perforators.
passing: Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery

Pericallosal artery.note: Runs in the sulcus corporis callosi over the genu and truncus of the corpus callosum. Posteriorly it anastomoses with the splenial branches of the PCA. Pitfall: an azygos or triplicated ACA is a variant. Calcified falx or a lipoma of the corpus callosum can mimic vessel calcification.
neighbours: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle anterior part)
Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle posterior part)

Pineal gland.note: Sits in the quadrigeminal cistern behind the Ventriculus tertius, above the Colliculus superior and below the splenium. Pitfall: physiological calcification is common in adults, but calcification before about age 10 or an expanded gland over about 1 cm needs workup. Do not confuse it with habenular or choroid plexus calcification.

Piriformis fascia.note: Invests piriformis from the anterior sacrum through the incisura ischiadica major to the greater trochanter. It divides the suprapiriform foramen (superior gluteal vessels and nerve) from the infrapiriform foramen (sciatic nerve, inferior gluteal vessels). Pitfall: in normal variants the sciatic nerve divides early or pierces piriformis.

Piriformis muscle.note: Arises from the anterior sacrum around the S2–S4 foramina, exits through the greater sciatic foramen and inserts on the greater trochanter. It divides the foramen into suprapiriform and infrapiriform spaces. Pitfall: mild side-to-side asymmetry in size is normal. The sciatic nerve may pierce the muscle as a variant, so do not mistake a split nerve for a mass.

Pisiform bone.note: Sesamoid within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon; it articulates only dorsally with Os triquetrum and forms the ulnar wall of Guyon's canal. Pitfall: fragmented or multiple ossification centres in adolescents mimic fracture; also assess the pisotriquetral joint, a frequently overlooked source of ulnar wrist pain and arthrosis.
neighbours: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Pisohamate ligament.note: Continues the flexor carpi ulnaris from the pisiform to the hook of the hamate and forms the floor of the distal canalis ulnaris (Guyon). The deep branch of the ulnar nerve passes the pisohamate hiatus. Pitfall: an os hamuli proprium has smooth, corticated margins. Do not confuse it with a hamulus fracture, which has sharp, uncorticated edges.
neighbours: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand

Pisometacarpal ligament.note: Distal extension of the flexor carpi ulnaris from the pisiform to the base of the fifth metacarpal, ulnar to the hamate. Pitfall: in adolescents the pisiform can ossify from several fragmented centres. Do not report this as a fracture unless the margins are uncorticated and there is soft-tissue swelling.
neighbours: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Pisotriquetral ligament.note: Capsular reinforcement of the pisotriquetral joint, palmar to the triquetrum and within the flexor carpi ulnaris insertion. This joint often communicates with the radiocarpal joint. Pitfall: an oblique slice can make the pisotriquetral joint look incongruent. Judge its parallelism and width on true sagittal or carpal tunnel reconstructions.
neighbours: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint

Plantar aponeurosis.note: Starts at the Processus medialis tuberis calcanei; its thickest part is the central cord, which splits into slips to the toes. Pitfall: the plantar calcaneal spur lies in the origin of flexor digitorum brevis, deep to the aponeurosis, not inside it. Proximal thickening over about 4 mm suggests plantar fasciitis.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
neighbours: Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis

Plantar arch.note: Continues the a. plantaris lateralis from the base of MT5 and runs medially across the bases of MT2–4. It lies deep to the oblique head of the adductor hallucis, superficial to the interossei, and joins the a. plantaris profunda in the first space. Pitfall: an incomplete arch is a common variant and should not be reported as occlusion.
landmarks: lm:Base of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone
neighbours: Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis

Plantar calcaneocuboid ligament.note: Short plantar ligament: runs from the anterior calcaneal tubercle to the plantar cuboid, deep (dorsal) to the ligamentum plantare longum. Pitfall: an os peroneum near the cuboid tuberosity can mimic a plantar avulsion fragment. Look for smooth cortication and a position within the fibularis longus tendon.

Plantar calcaneonavicular ligament.note: Spring ligament: runs from the sustentaculum tali to the plantar-medial navicular and cradles the caput tali, with the tibialis posterior tendon directly superficial. Pitfall: CT cannot show the ligament reliably, so the tendon should not be read as the ligament. Infer failure from plantar talar head sag or peritalar subluxation.

Plantar cuboideonavicular ligament.note: Short band joining the plantar lateral navicular to the plantar medial cuboid, just proximal to the os cuneiforme laterale. Pitfall: the cuboideonavicular articulation is variable (fibrous or synovial). A narrow, irregular interface can mimic a coalition or a fracture line, so check for bony bridging on all three planes.

Plantar cuneocuboid ligament.note: Spans the plantar surfaces of the os cuneiforme laterale and os cuboideum, just proximal to the 3rd/4th tarsometatarsal joints and next to the fibularis longus tendon. Pitfall: small cuneocuboid avulsion flakes are often dismissed, but they can be the only CT sign of a lateral-column midfoot (Lisfranc-spectrum) injury.

Plantar cuneonavicular ligaments.note: Run from the plantar navicular to the three cuneiforms and blend with the tibialis posterior tendon slips. Pitfall: an os naviculare accessorium (type II synchondrosis) or a tibialis posterior insertion spur mimics a navicular tuberosity avulsion. Look for smooth corticated margins and a symmetric contralateral finding.

Plantar digital veins.note: Small veins in the plantar subcutaneous fat of the toes, superficial to the flexor tendon sheaths, draining into the Venae metatarseae plantares. They are not resolved on non-contrast CT. Pitfall: a punctate plantar density here is more likely a foreign body or calcified digital artery (diabetic medial calcinosis) than a vein.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
landmarks: lm:Head of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
lm:Trochlea of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot
Proximal phalanx of second finger of foot
Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot

Plantar intercuneiform ligaments.note: Join the plantar surfaces of the three cuneiforms, proximal to the tarsometatarsal joints, with the fibularis longus and tibialis posterior tendons close by. Pitfall: medial–intermediate cuneiform diastasis is a proximal Lisfranc variant that is easily missed on non-weight-bearing CT. Compare intercuneiform spacing with the other side.

Plantar interossei muscles.note: Three unipennate muscles on the plantar-medial surfaces of metatarsals 3–5, inserting on the medial bases of the corresponding proximal phalanges. Pitfall: they blend with the dorsal interossei on CT. Fluid or a mass in a web space should be reported by intermetatarsal space number, not assigned to a single muscle.
passing: Perforating branches of plantar metatarsal arteries
Common plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
landmarks: lm:Body of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone
lm:Base of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
lm:Head of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fourth finger of foot

Plantar interphalangeal ligaments.note: These are the plantar plates of the interphalangeal joints, lying directly dorsal to the long flexor tendons. Pitfall: on CT the plate and the flexor tendon cannot be told apart, so partial volume can mimic a thickened tendon. A plantar base fleck of the distal phalanx is a plate avulsion, not a tendon rupture.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
landmarks: lm:Head of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
lm:Trochlea of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
neighbours: Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints of foot
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints of foot
Articular capsule of interphalangeal joint of great toe
Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot

Plantar metatarsal arteries.note: Four arteries arise from the arcus plantaris and run distally on the plantar interossei in the intermetatarsal spaces. They give off perforating branches and continue as the common plantar digital arteries. Pitfall: the first plantar metatarsal artery usually comes from the a. plantaris profunda, not the arch.
passing: Perforating branches of plantar metatarsal arteries
landmarks: lm:Base of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone

Plantar metatarsal ligaments.note: Transverse bands on the plantar surfaces of the metatarsal bases. They lie deep to the fibularis longus tendon and the arcus plantaris. Pitfall: small plantar flecks at the metatarsal bases are easily missed on axial images alone. Check sagittal reformats, because plantar avulsions point to Lisfranc instability.
passing: Perforating branches of plantar metatarsal arteries
landmarks: lm:Base of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone

Plantar metatarsal veins.note: Run in the intermetatarsal spaces plantar to the interossei, from the metatarsal heads back to the plantar venous arch. Pitfall: next to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament, soft tissue from these vessels or the intermetatarsal bursa can mimic a Morton neuroma.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
landmarks: lm:Head of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone

Plantar metatarsophalangeal ligaments.note: Plantar plates: fibrocartilaginous thickenings of the plantar capsule that are firmly attached to the phalangeal base and lie deep to the flexor tendons. At the hallux they contain the sesamoids. Pitfall: CT cannot show a plantar plate tear (classically 2nd MTP). Infer it from dorsal subluxation of the proximal phalanx or sesamoid retraction.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of second finger of foot

Plantar tarsometatarsal ligaments.note: Strong plantar bands joining the cuneiforms and cuboid to the metatarsal bases, near the insertions of fibularis longus (1st MT base/medial cuneiform) and tibialis posterior. Pitfall: an os intermetatarseum or os peroneum can be mistaken for a Lisfranc avulsion fragment, or the reverse. Corticated ossicles are usually well-defined and often bilateral.
landmarks: lm:Base of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone

Plantar tendon sheath of fibularis longu.key: Plantar tendon sheath of fibularis longus muscle
Plantar tendon sheath of fibularis longu.note: Surrounds the fibularis longus tendon in the cuboid groove, under the ligamentum plantare longum, as it crosses the sole to the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base. Pitfall: an os peroneum near the cuboid is a normal sesamoid, not a fracture, although fragmenting or proximal migration means a tendon tear.

Plantar venous arch.note: A deep arch running with the arterial arcus plantaris across the metatarsal bases, between the oblique head of the adductor hallucis and the interossei. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the subcutaneous plantar venous network or with the dorsal venous arch of the foot, which drains into the saphenous veins.

Plantaris muscle.note: Small belly above the lateral femoral condyle, deep to the lateral gastrocnemius head. Its long thin tendon runs between the gastrocnemius and soleus to the medial side of the tendo calcaneus. Pitfall: it is absent in about 10% of people, and a retained tendon can mimic intact Achilles fibres.

Platysma.note: Thin subcutaneous muscle sheet spanning from the Mandibula to below the Clavicula. The external jugular vein and superficial nodes lie deep to it. Pitfall: thickening and stranding after radiotherapy or neck dissection is a treatment effect and should not be read as tumour or cellulitis; the muscle is normally deficient in the midline.

Pleura.note: Parietal pleura lines the ribs, the Musculi intercostales intimi, the mediastinum and the diaphragm. Normally it is seen only as part of the 1–2 mm intercostal stripe. Pitfall: the posterior costophrenic recess reaches down to about T12, below the liver dome, so lung or effusion on upper abdominal slices is not intra-abdominal.

Pons.note: The prepontine cistern, basilar artery and clivus lie in front, the fourth ventricle behind, and the middle cerebellar peduncles to the sides. Pitfall: beam-hardening artefact between the petrous bones (Hounsfield bar) mimics a pontine hypodensity or infarct, and a dense or ectatic basilar artery can mimic haemorrhage.
landmarks: lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipital bone
lm:Internal acoustic opening (porus of internal acoustic meatus)|Temporal bone

Popliteal artery.note: It runs from the adductor hiatus to the lower border of the Musculus popliteus. It is the deepest member of the bundle, lying on the Os femoris, posterior capsule and popliteus, with the vein and then the Nervus tibialis more superficial. Pitfall: a partly thrombosed popliteal aneurysm can look like a Baker cyst. Also check for entrapment by the medial head of gastrocnemius.

Popliteal fascia.note: Roof of the fossa poplitea. It is continuous with the Fascia lata above and the Fascia cruris below, and the small saphenous vein pierces it to join the popliteal vein. Pitfall: a Baker cyst comes from between the medial gastrocnemius head and semimembranosus deep to this fascia, so do not call it a subcutaneous lesion.

Popliteal vein.note: Runs from the adductor hiatus to the lower border of the musculus popliteus. It lies between the popliteal artery (deeper) and the tibial nerve (more superficial). Pitfall: duplication is common, and inflow mixing artefact can mimic thrombus. Do not mistake a Baker cyst between the medial gastrocnemius and semimembranosus for the vein.

Popliteofibular ligament.note: Short band running from the musculotendinous junction of the popliteus to the posteromedial fibular head, and a key posterolateral corner stabiliser. Pitfall: a small fibular styloid avulsion fragment (arcuate sign) is easy to miss. Always check the adjacent nervus fibularis communis.
neighbours: Articular capsule of superior tibiofibular joint

Popliteus muscle.note: A triangular muscle on the posterior tibia above the linea musculi solei. Its tendon runs inside the capsule, through the popliteal hiatus between the lateral meniscus and the capsule, to the lateral femoral condyle, deep to the fibular collateral ligament. Pitfall: on CT arthrography, contrast in the popliteus tendon sheath or hiatus can mimic a tear of the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus.

Postcentral arterial branch.note: Anterior parietal branch. It ascends in the sulcus postcentralis behind the gyrus postcentralis, in front of the gyrus supramarginalis. Pitfall: the postcentral and central sulci are easily swapped on axial CT. The postcentral sulcus usually joins the intraparietal sulcus; the central sulcus does not.
passing: Temporal branches of middle cerebral artery
neighbours: Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci*)

Postcentral gyrus.note: Primary somatosensory cortex between the Central sulcus in front and the Postcentral sulcus behind, reaching down to the Sulcus lateralis. Pitfall: the precentral and postcentral gyri are easily swapped on axial CT. Identify the central sulcus first (pars marginalis sign, or the precentral knob, which is thicker than the postcentral gyrus).
neighbours: Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci*)

Postcentral sulcus.note: Lies behind the Postcentral gyrus and separates it from the Superior parietal lobule and Supramarginal gyrus. It is often continuous with the Intraparietal sulcus. Pitfall: it runs parallel to the Central sulcus and can be mistaken for it. The central sulcus does not join the intraparietal sulcus, and the postcentral sulcus is often discontinuous.

Posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve.note: Branches from the N. radialis in the spiral groove, pierces the lateral head of triceps and runs subcutaneously over the lateral epicondyle to the dorsal forearm. It is purely sensory. Pitfall: a lateral elbow approach can injure it, and the resulting sensory loss should not be mistaken for a lesion of the posterior interosseous nerve.

Posterior auricular vein.note: This vein runs subcutaneously behind the auricle over the processus mastoideus. It joins the posterior division of the retromandibular vein to form the v. jugularis externa. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the mastoid emissary vein, which runs through a bony foramen into the sinus sigmoideus. Small mastoid nodes lie right beside this vein.
landmarks: lm:Tympanic part of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Posterior axillary nodes.note: The nodi subscapulares follow the subscapular vessels on the posterior axillary wall. They lie anterior to subscapularis, latissimus dorsi and teres major, near the humeral neck. Pitfall: tortuous subscapular or circumflex humeral vessels cut in cross-section mimic nodes, so trace them on contiguous slices before calling a node.

Posterior basal segmental artery of left.key: Posterior basal segmental artery of left lung
Posterior basal segmental artery of left.note: Supplies segment X, the largest basal artery, running back toward the posterior costophrenic recess next to the Diaphragma. Pitfall: dependent atelectasis and respiratory motion at the lung base can mimic filling defects. The inferior pulmonary vein runs close by, so confirm that the vessel is an artery.
passing: Lateral basal segmental artery of left lung
Medial basal segmental artery of left lung
Superior segmental artery of left lung

Posterior basal segmental artery of righ.key: Posterior basal segmental artery of right lung
Posterior basal segmental artery of righ.note: A10 is the end of the basal trunk. It runs posteroinferiorly with BX into the posterior costophrenic recess. Pitfall: partial volume from the diaphragm, dependent atelectasis and poor contrast mixing in dependent arteries can mimic filling defects.
passing: Inferior lobar artery of right lung
Medial basal segmental artery of right lung
Anterior basal segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Posterior basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BX)
Lateral basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BIX)

Posterior basal segmental bronchus of le.key: Posterior basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BX)
Posterior basal segmental bronchus of le.note: BX is the most posterior basal bronchus. It runs toward the posterior costophrenic recess beside the spine and descending aorta. Pitfall: in supine patients this segment is where dependent atelectasis and aspiration collect. Subpleural density here may be positional, so confirm with prone imaging before calling fibrosis.
passing: Anterior basal segmental artery of left lung
Superior basal vein of left lung
neighbours: Lateral basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BIX)

Posterior basal segmental bronchus of ri.key: Posterior basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BX)
Posterior basal segmental bronchus of ri.note: Most posterior and caudal basal branch. It runs into the posterior costophrenic recess beside the spine. Pitfall: dependent subpleural atelectasis in supine patients mimics posterior basal consolidation or fibrosis; prone images help tell them apart.
passing: Posterior basal segmental artery of right lung
Inferior basal vein of right lung
Medial basal segmental artery of right lung

Posterior belly of digastric muscle.note: Runs from the incisura mastoidea to the intermediate tendon. It crosses superficial to the internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, accessory nerve and hypoglossal nerve, and forms the deep boundary of the parotid. Pitfall: the jugulodigastric node just below it is normally the largest neck node (up to about 15 mm short axis). Do not call it pathological on size alone.
landmarks: lm:Styloid process of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Posterior branch of medial antebrachial.key: Posterior branch of medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve
Posterior branch of medial antebrachial.note: Runs in the subcutis with the vena basilica, anterior to and then over the epicondylus medialis, onto the posteromedial forearm. Pitfall: an enlarged nodus supratrochlearis next to the basilic vein can mimic a neuroma. The branch is also at risk during cubital tunnel surgery and should not be confused with the deeper ulnar nerve.
passing: Anterior branch of medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve
neighbours: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Posterior branch of obturator nerve.note: Pierces the obturator externus and descends between the adductor brevis (in front) and the adductor magnus (behind), sending an articular twig to the knee. Pitfall: medial knee pain can be referred along this branch, and it lies posterior, not anterior, to the adductor brevis.

Posterior branch of renal artery.note: The posterior division of the right renal artery runs behind the renal pelvis and supplies the posterior segment. Pitfall: it is at risk during posterior percutaneous access. Its retropelvic course can compress the pelviureteric junction, which can mimic stenosis.

Posterior cells of ethmoid bone.note: Cellulae posteriores lie behind the basal lamella and in front of the Os sphenoideum, and drain to the superior meatus. The Arteria ethmoidea posterior runs along their roof. Pitfall: an Onodi (sphenoethmoidal) cell extends above the sphenoid sinus around the optic canal and can be mistaken for the sphenoid sinus. This poses a surgical risk to the optic nerve.
passing: Septal branches of posterior ethmoidal artery

Posterior cerebral artery.note: It arises at the basilar tip above the Dorsum sellae and curves around the Mesencephalon in the ambient cistern above the Tentorium, supplying the occipital lobe, medial temporal lobe and thalamus. CN III runs between the PCA and the SCA. Pitfall: a fetal-type PCA (dominant A. communicans posterior with a hypoplastic P1) is a normal variant, not an occlusion.

Posterior circumflex humeral artery.note: Arises from the third part of the axillary artery. It passes with the axillary nerve through the quadrilateral space (teres minor, teres major, long head of triceps, humerus) to wind round the collum chirurgicum. Pitfall: it is the dominant supply to the humeral head. Do not confuse the quadrilateral space with the triangular space, which carries the circumflex scapular artery.

Posterior circumflex humeral vein.note: This vein runs with the posterior circumflex humeral artery and the axillary nerve through the quadrangular space, around the back of the surgical neck of the humerus, below the glenohumeral capsule. It drains into the Vena axillaris. Pitfall: in surgical neck fractures, bleeding from this bundle and injury to the axillary nerve are easy to overlook.

Posterior cochlear nucleus.note: Lies on the dorsolateral inferior cerebellar peduncle at the pontomedullary junction, beside the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle where CN VIII enters. Pitfall: at the cerebellopontine angle, streak artefact from the petrous bones mimics hypodensity. Also, CN VII enters anterior to VIII, so do not swap them.

Posterior commissure.note: White-matter band in the back wall of the Ventriculus tertius. It sits just under the pineal recess and above the opening of the Aquaeductus mesencephali. It is the back reference point of the AC–PC line. Do not confuse it with the habenular commissure, which lies just above the pineal recess and often calcifies.

Posterior communicating artery.note: It runs posteromedially from the supraclinoid Carotis interna to the P1/P2 junction. It lies above and medial to the Nervus oculomotorius and next to the Basis pedunculi. Pitfall: a junctional infundibulum (conical, under 3 mm, vessel arising from its apex) is easily mistaken for an aneurysm. A fetal-type PComm is a normal variant, not ectasia.

Posterior cord of brachial plexus.note: Formed by all three posterior divisions. It lies posterior to the second part of the A. axillaris, deep to pectoralis minor and anterior to subscapularis, and ends as the axillary and radial nerves. Pitfall: cords are named by their position relative to the axillary artery. CT cannot separate them, so use the artery as the reference.
passing: Posterior division of superior trunk of brachial plexus
Posterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus

Posterior crico-arytenoid muscle.note: Lies on the posterior surface of the Lamina cartilaginis cricoideae, runs to the Processus muscularis, and forms the anterior wall of the postcricoid hypopharynx. Pitfall: the enhancing postcricoid venous plexus and collapsed mucosa here can mimic postcricoid carcinoma, so compare with a scan done during phonation or a modified Valsalva.

Posterior cruciate ligament.note: Intracapsular, extrasynovial ligament running from the medial femoral condyle to the posterior intercondylar area below the joint line. Pitfall: its tibial avulsion fragment sits posteriorly in the area intercondylaris posterior. Do not mistake it for an ACL tibial-spine avulsion, which lies anteriorly at the eminence.

Posterior deep temporal artery.note: Branch of the maxillary artery that ascends deep to the Musculus temporalis against the squamous temporal bone. It lies extracranially, superficial to the temporal pole. Pitfall: don't confuse its outer-table course with the intracranial middle meningeal artery. Deep temporal bleeding produces an intramuscular hematoma, not an epidural one.
neighbours: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Posterior division of inferior trunk of.key: Posterior division of inferior trunk of brachial plexus
Posterior division of inferior trunk of.note: The divisions lie in the costoclavicular space, behind the clavicula and above the first rib, lateral to the scalene gap. CT cannot separate individual divisions. Pitfall: this is the smallest division and joins the posterior cord, not the medial cord, so do not attribute lower-trunk posterior fibres to medial cord lesions.
passing: Anterior division of inferior trunk of brachial plexus
Anterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus

Posterior division of internal iliac art.key: Posterior division of internal iliac artery
Posterior division of internal iliac art.note: Short trunk that runs posteriorly toward the lumbosacral trunk and the upper greater sciatic foramen. It gives the iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal arteries. Pitfall: it is easily confused with the anterior division in axial slices. Check on MIP or coronal views, because non-selective embolization here risks gluteal ischaemia.
passing: Anterior division of internal iliac artery

Posterior division of mandibular nerve.note: It runs down between the pterygoid muscles, medial to the ramus mandibulae and lateral to the ligamentum sphenomandibulare, and splits into the nervus lingualis and the nervus alveolaris inferior. Pitfall: fat in the pterygoid space normally looks asymmetric. Do not call perineural tumour unless the foramen ovale is widened or eroded, or the denervated masticator muscles show atrophy.
neighbours: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Posterior division of middle trunk of br.key: Posterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus
Posterior division of middle trunk of br.note: Runs deep (posterior) to the anterior divisions, behind the clavicula, and merges with the other posterior divisions to form the posterior cord. Pitfall: posterior divisions lie deepest in the cervicoaxillary canal, so do not label the more superficial anterior divisions as the posterior cord origin.
passing: Posterior division of superior trunk of brachial plexus
Anterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus

Posterior division of retromandibular ve.note: This vein leaves the lower pole of the parotid behind the mandibular ramus and joins the posterior auricular vein to form the v. jugularis externa. Pitfall: the retromandibular vein marks the plane of the facial nerve, which runs just lateral to it. Do not localise a parotid mass to the deep or superficial lobe without checking it, and do not confuse the vein with the ECA, which lies medial to it.
landmarks: lm:Styloid process of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Posterior division of superior trunk of.key: Posterior division of superior trunk of brachial plexus
Posterior division of superior trunk of.note: Lies deep to the anterior division of the superior trunk, behind the clavicula, and contributes the largest share of the posterior cord (axillary and radial fibres). Pitfall: individual divisions cannot be resolved on CT, so report the level (supraclavicular, retroclavicular or infraclavicular) rather than a specific division.
passing: Anterior division of superior trunk of brachial plexus
Posterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus

Posterior ethmoidal artery.note: Crosses the posterior ethmoidal canal at the frontoethmoidal suture, above the cellulae ethmoidales posteriores. Pitfall: the canal lies only about 5–10 mm in front of the canalis opticus. Do not confuse it with the anterior ethmoidal canal or the optic canal, especially when an Onodi cell is present.
passing: Septal branches of posterior ethmoidal artery

Posterior fasciculus proprius.note: Thin band of white matter around the posterior grey column, deep to the Fasciculus gracilis. CT cannot separate it from the rest of the cord. Pitfall: beam-hardening streaks in the cervical canal (from shoulders and dens) can look like an intramedullary hypodensity, so do not assign CT density changes to individual tracts.

Posterior femoral cutaneous nerve.note: The nerve (S1–S3) leaves through the infrapiriform foramen together with the vasa glutea inferiora, medial to the sciatic nerve. It runs deep to the gluteus maximus and then beneath the fascia lata of the posterior thigh. Pitfall: on CT it blends with the inferior gluteal vessels and the sciatic nerve. Enlarged inferior gluteal nodes can mimic a nerve sheath tumour.
passing: Posterior root of posterior femoral cutaneous nerve
Anterior root of posterior femoral cutaneous nerve

Posterior horn of spinal cord.note: The dorsal grey column reaching the posterolateral sulcus, where the posterior roots enter through the posterolateral tract (Lissauer). The posterior funiculus lies medially and the lateral funiculus laterally. Pitfall: the cuneate fasciculus exists only above about T6, so at lower levels the posterior funiculus is the gracile fasciculus alone. Grey and white matter cannot be separated on CT.

Posterior inferior cerebellar artery.note: Branch of the intradural A. vertebralis. It loops around the Medulla oblongata between the rootlets of CN IX–XI, then runs along the Tonsilla cerebelli to the inferior vermis and hemisphere. Pitfall: a low-lying caudal tonsillar loop can be mistaken for tonsillar herniation. An extradural PICA origin is a normal variant.

Posterior intercavernous sinus.note: Runs behind the neurohypophysis, just in front of the dorsum sellae. Together with the anterior intercavernous sinus it forms the circular sinus and drains into the basilar venous plexus. Pitfall: its enhancement at the back of the sella can be mistaken for a lesion of the posterior pituitary or an enhancing dural tail.

Posterior intercostal arteries.note: Arise from the posterior Aorta thoracica and run in the Sulcus costae between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, with the order vein–artery–nerve from above down. Pitfall: near the spine the artery runs tortuously in the middle of the space and is not protected by the groove. Interventions placed medially or close to the lower rib border risk haemothorax.
neighbours: Radiate ligament of head of rib

Posterior intermuscular septum of leg.note: Runs from the Fascia cruris to the posterior border of the fibula and separates the fibular compartment from the superficial posterior compartment. Pitfall: the fibular artery and veins lie in the deep posterior compartment next to FHL, not in the lateral compartment. The common fibular nerve is in contact with the septum only near the fibular neck.

Posterior interosseous artery.note: Arises from the common interosseous artery and passes dorsally over the proximal edge of the interosseous membrane. It then runs between the superficial and deep extensor layers with the posterior interosseous nerve. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the anterior interosseous artery, which stays on the volar surface of the membrane.
neighbours: Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Posterior interosseous nerve of forearm.note: Continuation of the deep branch beyond the supinator, on the dorsal surface of the Membrana interossea, deep to the APL, EPB and EPL. Pitfall: it wraps around the radial neck, so radial head/neck fractures, Monteggia lesions and supinator lipomas put it at risk. Do not confuse it with the anterior interosseous nerve on the volar side of the membrane.

Posterior lateral nasal branches of sphe.key: Posterior lateral nasal branches of sphenopalatine artery.
Posterior lateral nasal branches of sphe.note: Leaves the pterygopalatine fossa through the foramen sphenopalatinum and supplies the lateral nasal wall over the middle and inferior conchae. Pitfall: this is the main source of posterior epistaxis. Do not mistake the foramen sphenopalatinum for the canalis pterygoideus or the foramen rotundum on axial CT.
passing: Anterior septal branches of anterior ethmoidal artery

Posterior lateral segment of liver (VII).note: Segment VII lies posterior to the right hepatic vein and above the portal plane, including the bare area against the diaphragm. Pitfall: fluid behind segment VII can be a pleural effusion or ascites. Use the diaphragm and bare-area signs: ascites does not extend behind the bare area.

Posterior layer of thoracolumbar fascia.note: Lamina posterior fasciae thoracolumbaris covers erector spinae from behind. It attaches to the lumbar and sacral spinous processes and the supraspinous ligament, and is the aponeurotic origin of latissimus dorsi and serratus posterior inferior. Pitfall: it forms a thick band over the crista sacralis mediana; do not read this as postoperative scar or a soft-tissue mass.

Posterior leaflet of left atrioventricul.key: Posterior leaflet of left atrioventricular valve
Posterior leaflet of left atrioventricul.note: Posterior mitral cusp, attached to the posterior annulus between Atrium sinistrum and Ventriculus sinister, with chordae to the inferior (posteromedial) papillary muscle. Pitfall: posterior mitral annular calcification is common and can look like a calcified mass. Note also that this is the left (mitral) valve, not the tricuspid.
passing: Inferior papillary muscle of left ventricle

Posterior ligament of fibular head.note: Reinforces the posterior aspect of the superior tibiofibular joint and is covered by the popliteus tendon. Pitfall: posteromedial fibular head dislocation is subtle on axial CT. Check alignment against the contralateral side and assess the adjacent common fibular nerve.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of fibula|Fibula
neighbours: Articular capsule of superior tibiofibular joint

Posterior longitudinal ligament.note: Runs inside the canal along the dorsal surfaces of the vertebral bodies and discs, ventral to the dura spinalis. It continues cranially as the membrana tectoria and is firmly fixed to the discs. Pitfall: cervical OPLL is a dense band behind several bodies and is easily called an osteophyte or disc calcification. Check the sagittal reformats.

Posterior medial segment of liver (VIII).note: Segment VIII lies between the right and middle hepatic veins, above the portal plane, under the diaphragmatic dome next to the IVC. Pitfall: inflow mixing artefact at the junction of the hepatic veins and IVC mimics thrombus. Partial volume with the lung base hides small lesions at the dome.

Posterior meniscotibial ligament (Latera.note: Posterior root attachment of the lateral meniscus, inserting just behind the tuberculum intercondylare laterale and anterior to the PCL. Pitfall: the meniscofemoral ligaments (Humphry, Wrisberg) arise near this root. Do not mistake them, or a small root avulsion fragment, for a PCL avulsion.

Posterior meniscotibial ligament (Medial.note: Posterior root of the medial meniscus, inserting in the area intercondylaris posterior in front of the PCL tibial footprint. Pitfall: a root avulsion fragment here can be mistaken for a PCL avulsion. Root tears cause meniscal extrusion and early subchondral insufficiency fracture.

Posterior nucleus of vagus nerve.note: Forms the vagal trigone in the floor of the Ventriculus quartus. The Nucleus nervi hypoglossi is medial and the Nucleus tractus solitarii is lateral. Pitfall: partial volume of CSF at the obex and caudal fourth ventricle can mimic a dorsal medullary hypodensity.

Posterior parietal artery.note: Leaves the posterior end of the Sylvian fissure and runs over the planum temporale to the gyrus supramarginalis and gyrus angularis. Pitfall: this territory borders the ACA and PCA watershed zones. Posterior parietal hypodensity may be a border-zone infarct rather than a branch occlusion.

Posterior quadrangular lobule.note: The Lobulus quadrangularis posterior is the hemispheric part of the simple lobule. It lies between the Fissura prima and the posterior superior fissure on the upper surface, directly under the tentorium. Pitfall: the occipitotemporal cortex lies just above the tentorium, so supratentorial and infratentorial lesions are easily confused on axial CT. Use coronal reformats.

Posterior root of posterior femoral cuta.key: Posterior root of posterior femoral cutaneous nerve
Posterior root of posterior femoral cuta.note: This root comes from the posterior divisions of S1–S2. It joins the anterior root on the piriformis and exits below the muscle. CT cannot show it. Pitfall: it lies right next to the nervus pudendalis and the inferior gluteal veins. Do not mistake engorged gluteal veins or a sacral fracture fragment for a nerve lesion.
passing: Anterior root of posterior femoral cutaneous nerve

Posterior root of spinal nerve.note: It enters the posterolateral sulcus of the cord, carries the ganglion spinale in the foramen and lies behind the anterior root. Pitfall: in the foramen, the bulging ganglion on this root can be mistaken for a herniated disc fragment or a nerve sheath tumour.

Posterior sacro-iliac ligament.note: Runs from the posterior superior iliac spine to the lateral sacral crest and continues into the sacrotuberous ligament, superficial to the interosseous ligament. Pitfall: the Foramina sacralia posteriora lie directly beneath it. Fractures through them (Denis zone II) are easy to miss, so trace each foraminal ring on both sides.

Posterior segment of eyeball.note: The posterior segment is the vitreous-filled globe behind the Lens. It is enclosed by Retina, choroid and Sclera, and the Nervus opticus exits posteriorly. Pitfall: optic disc drusen form punctate calcification at the optic nerve head. They mimic an intraocular foreign body or retinoblastoma calcification.
landmarks: lm:Orbital surface of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Posterior segment of liver (I).note: The caudate lobe sits between the IVC behind, the fissure for the ligamentum venosum in front and the portal bifurcation below. It drains directly into the IVC, so it is often spared and enlarged in cirrhosis. Pitfall: a separated papillary process mimics a portocaval lymph node or a pancreatic head mass.
neighbours: Left posterior lateral segment of liver (II)

Posterior segmental artery of left lung.key: Posterior segmental artery of left lung
Posterior segmental artery of left lung.note: The posterior artery arises from the posterosuperior arch of the left pulmonary artery. It runs with BI+BII into the posterior upper lobe, next to the oblique fissure. Pitfall: arterial branching in the left upper lobe is very variable. Assign the segment by the bronchus the artery travels with, not by counting branches.
passing: Apical segmental artery of left lung
Anterior segmental artery of left lung
neighbours: Apicoposterior segmental bronchus of left lung (BI+BII)

Posterior segmental artery of right lung.key: Posterior segmental artery of right lung
Posterior segmental artery of right lung.note: A2 runs posteriorly with BII into the posterior segment, next to the oblique fissure. It is supplied by a recurrent branch of the truncus anterior, by a posterior ascending branch of the interlobar artery, or by both. Pitfall: the ascending branch near the fissure is easily mistaken for A6 of the lower lobe.

Posterior segmental bronchus of right lu.key: Posterior segmental bronchus of right lung (BII)
Posterior segmental bronchus of right lu.note: Runs posterolaterally from the right upper lobe bronchus. Its segment abuts the oblique fissure and the superior segment of the lower lobe. Pitfall: posterior opacities across the oblique fissure may be in BVI rather than BII, which matters when localising a typical tuberculosis reactivation site.
passing: Apical segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Apical segmental bronchus of right lung (BI)
Anterior segmental bronchus of right lung (BIII)

Posterior septal branches of sphenopalat.key: Posterior septal branches of sphenopalatine artery
Posterior septal branches of sphenopalat.note: Leave the sphenopalatine foramen, cross the anterior face of the sphenoid below its ostium, and run along the septum toward the incisive canal. They supply the nasoseptal flap pedicle. Pitfall: these vessels are the source of posterior epistaxis. Locate the sphenopalatine foramen, not the pterygopalatine fossa, when planning ligation.

Posterior spinocerebellar tract.note: Superficial uncrossed tract on the dorsolateral margin of the lateral funiculus, arising from the nucleus thoracicus (C8–L2). CT does not show it. Pitfall: the fibres stay on the same side and enter the cerebellum through the pedunculus cerebellaris inferior, unlike the anterior tract, which crosses.

Posterior sternoclavicular ligament.note: Ligamentum sternoclaviculare posterius is the strongest stabiliser of the sternoclavicular joint. Only sternohyoid and sternothyroid separate it from the brachiocephalic veins and pleura. Pitfall: posterior dislocation is easily missed on radiographs. On CT, look for the clavicular head lying behind the sternum and compressing the veins, trachea or great vessels; this is an emergency.

Posterior superior alveolar artery.note: Arises from the pterygopalatine part of the Arteria maxillaris and enters the alveolar foramina on the tuber maxillae, then runs in canals in the posterolateral maxillary sinus wall. Pitfall: these thin canals in the sinus wall look like fracture lines on bone-window CT.

Posterior talocalcaneal ligament.note: Runs from the lateral tubercle of the processus posterior tali to the upper calcaneus, behind the posterior subtalar facet, lateral to the FHL groove. Pitfall: an os trigonum (smooth, corticated, rounded) can be mistaken for a Shepherd fracture of the lateral tubercle (sharp, non-corticated edges), or the reverse.

Posterior talofibular ligament.note: Runs almost horizontally from the fossa malleoli lateralis to the lateral tubercle of the posterior talar process. Pitfall: an os trigonum or Stieda process looks like a lateral tubercle (Shepherd) fracture. Smooth, corticated margins favour the normal variant.

Posterior temporal branch.note: Runs posteroinferiorly over the posterior gyrus temporalis superior and planum temporale toward the temporo-occipital junction (Wernicke's area in the dominant hemisphere). Pitfall: at the posterior temporal/occipital boundary MCA and PCA territories overlap. Do not assign an infarct to the MCA without checking the PCA.

Posterior tibial artery.note: It descends in the deep posterior compartment on the Musculus tibialis posterior, beneath the transverse septum and soleus. In the tarsal tunnel it lies between the FDL and FHL tendons, then divides into the plantar arteries. Pitfall: behind the medial malleolus the Nervus tibialis lies posterior to the artery and its paired veins. The adjacent fibular artery is easily mislabelled on CTA.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of flexor hallucis longus

Posterior tibial veins.note: A pair of veins running with the posterior tibial artery and the tibial nerve in the deep posterior compartment, deep to the transverse intermuscular septum. Behind the medial malleolus they pass through the tarsal tunnel, between the FDL and FHL tendons. Pitfall: mixing artefact in paired calf veins mimics DVT, so confirm on delayed phase.

Posterior tibiofibular ligament.note: The strongest syndesmotic ligament. It runs from the posterior tibial tubercle (malleolus posterior) to the posterior fibula. Pitfall: it usually pulls off a posterior malleolar (Volkmann) fragment rather than tearing. That fragment is easily missed on axial images, so check the sagittal reformats.

Posterior tibiotalar ligament.note: The strongest deep deltoid band. It runs from the posterior colliculus to the medial talar body, directly deep to the tibialis posterior tendon. Pitfall: its normal striated, fat-streaked look mimics a tear. Infer deep deltoid failure from a medial clear space wider than about 4 mm.

Posterior vein of right lung.note: Drains the posterior segment of the Lobus superior pulmonis dextri. It runs between the segments and empties into the Vena pulmonalis dextra superior. Pitfall: do not mistake it for the posterior segmental artery. Arteries run next to their bronchus, while veins run between segments. Trace the vessel back to the left atrium to confirm it is a vein.

Posterolateral tract.note: Thin bundle (Lissauer tract) capping the apex of the Cornu posterius at the dorsal root entry zone. It lies between the posterior funiculus and the lateral funiculus. CT does not show it. Pitfall: on CT myelography, the dorsal rootlets enter posterolaterally and the ventral rootlets exit anterolaterally, so do not swap them when assigning laterality or level.

Postvesical nodes.note: These nodes lie between the bladder base and the rectum or sigmoid colon, close to the seminal glands and ejaculatory ducts. Pitfall: asymmetric or collapsed seminal glands, or a bowel loop in the rectovesical pouch, mimic a postvesical node mass.

Pre-aortic nodes.note: Nodi preaortici sit anterior to the aorta abdominalis, grouped around the origins of the coeliac trunk, SMA and IMA, posterior to the pancreas and the third part of the duodenum. Pitfall: the left renal vein crossing between SMA and aorta, or a retroaortic/circumaortic variant, can mimic a pre-aortic node.

Pre-auricular nodes.note: Lie in front of the tragus, over the root of the zygomatic arch and the TMJ, next to the superficial temporal vessels. Pitfall: the superficial temporal vein or artery in cross-section looks like a small node. Follow the vessel across slices.

Precaecal nodes.note: Lie on the front of the caecum and lowest part of the Colon ascendens, in the right iliac fossa in front of the M. iliacus. Pitfall: reactive nodes here are common in mesenteric lymphadenitis. Do not mistake them for an inflamed appendix or ileal loops; identify the appendix on its own.

Precaval nodes.note: Nodi precavales lie on the anterior surface of the inferior vena cava, posterior to the duodenum and pancreatic head. Pitfall: an unopacified third or second duodenal part, or the right gonadal vein entering the IVC, mimics a precaval node; use oral contrast and multiplanar views.

Precentral gyrus.note: The gyrus precentralis lies between the sulcus precentralis in front and the sulcus centralis behind. It runs from the paracentral lobule down to the operculum above the lateral sulcus. Pitfall: confusing it with the postcentral gyrus. Find it as the gyrus just behind the junction of the superior frontal and precentral sulci; its cortex is thicker and it carries the 'hand knob'.
neighbours: Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Precentral sulcus (inferior part)*.note: The inferior precentral sulcus forms the front border of the lower precentral gyrus, behind the pars opercularis and the posterior middle frontal gyrus. It usually meets the inferior frontal sulcus. Pitfall: it is often separate from the superior part and can run continuously toward the central sulcus on axial CT. Confirm the central sulcus from the vertex downward.
neighbours: Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus
Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci*)

Precentral sulcus (Superior part)*.note: The superior precentral sulcus forms the front border of the upper precentral gyrus. It makes a T-junction with the sulcus frontalis superior, which is the key axial landmark for the central region. Pitfall: mistaking it for the sulcus centralis shifts every label one gyrus forward. The central sulcus is the next sulcus behind it and does not meet the superior frontal sulcus.

Precuneus.note: Medial parietal cortex bounded anteriorly by the marginal part of the Sulcus cinguli, posteriorly by the Parieto-occipital sulcus and inferiorly by the Subparietal sulcus, next to the Falx cerebri. Pitfall: dense falx or a parafalcine subdural haematoma can mimic or hide cortical haemorrhage. Early precuneus atrophy (Alzheimer disease) is easy to overlook on axial slices.
neighbours: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Posterior dorsal part)

Prefrontal artery.note: Superior-trunk MCA branch. It fans over the pars triangularis and pars opercularis to the sulcus frontalis inferior and the gyrus frontalis medius. Pitfall: in the dominant hemisphere this supplies Broca's area. Infarcts near the superior frontal gyrus may be ACA–MCA watershed rather than MCA territory.
passing: Insular branches of middle cerebral artery (M2)
neighbours: Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus
Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Prepericardial nodes.note: These are anterior mediastinal (prevascular) nodes. They lie behind the sternum and in front of the pericardium and the great veins. Pitfall: in young adults, residual thymic tissue or thymic rebound can mimic nodes. Unopacified internal thoracic or brachiocephalic veins can also look like nodes, so check the contrast phase.

Pretracheal nodes.note: Level VI nodes lie in front of the trachea, below the thyroid isthmus and deep to the Musculus sternothyreoideus and Musculus sternohyoideus. Pitfall: a pyramidal lobe, ectopic thyroid tissue or the inferior thyroid veins can mimic nodes. Thyroid tissue is iodine-hyperdense even without contrast.

Prevertebral nodes.note: These nodes lie directly in front of the thoracic vertebral bodies and the Lig. longitudinale anterius, behind the Oesophagus and next to the Aorta thoracica. Pitfall: the azygos/hemiazygos veins, the thoracic duct, anterior osteophytes or paravertebral haematoma can look like nodes in this narrow space.

Prevesical nodes.note: These nodes lie in the retropubic (Retzius) space between the pubic symphysis and the anterior bladder wall. Pitfall: an underdistended bladder dome, a urachal remnant or retropubic veins can mimic a node. Postoperative fluid collections in this space also mimic nodes.

Procerus muscle.note: Arises from the Os nasale and lower nasal cartilage and inserts into the glabellar skin, merging with Frontalis. Pitfall: glabellar soft-tissue swelling can hide an anterior-wall fracture of the Sinus frontalis or nasofrontal duct involvement; check the outer table on bone windows.
landmarks: lm:Nasal margin of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Pronator quadratus.note: A quadrilateral muscle on the distal anterior radius and ulna, lying on the interosseous membrane deep to the FDP and FPL, just above the radiocarpal joint. Pitfall: a bowed or blurred fat plane in front of this muscle (pronator quadratus sign) can be the only clue to an occult distal radius fracture.

Proper hepatic artery.note: Arteria hepatica propria runs from the gastroduodenal artery origin up the hepatoduodenal ligament, anteromedial to the portal vein and medial to the bile duct, then divides at the porta hepatis. Pitfall: replaced or accessory hepatic arteries from the SMA or left gastric artery. Report variants before liver surgery or TACE.

Proper palmar digital arteries.note: Run along the palmolateral sides of each finger beside the flexor tendon sheath, dorsal to the proper digital nerves, and join in the pulp. Pitfall: the thumb and radial index finger are often supplied via the radial artery (princeps pollicis), and unequal radial/ulnar digital artery size is normal.

Proper palmar digital branches of median.key: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of median.note: Run in the neurovascular bundles along the palmar sides of the fingers, beside the flexor tendon sheaths, from the thumb to the radial side of the ring finger, and supply the dorsal skin of the distal phalanges. Pitfall: in the finger the nerve lies palmar to the proper digital artery, the reverse of the palm.

Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar.key: Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar.note: Run in the palmar-lateral neurovascular bundle next to the flexor sheath of the fifth finger and the ulnar side of the fourth, out to the fingertip. Pitfall: in the finger the nerve lies palmar to the artery (the reverse of the palm). Penetrating injuries and a displaced phalangeal fracture often involve the nerve and artery together.

Proper plantar digital arteries.note: Paired arteries along the plantar medial and lateral margins of the phalanges, beside the flexor tendon sheath and digital nerves. They are the main blood supply of the toes. Pitfall: the medial artery of the hallux and the lateral artery of the fifth toe come directly from the medial and lateral plantar arteries, not from common digital arteries.

Proper plantar digital branches of later.key: Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
Proper plantar digital branches of later.note: Run plantar along both sides of the fifth toe and the lateral side of the fourth toe, beside the flexor tendon sheaths and the Arteriae digitales plantares propriae. Pitfall: the dorsolateral skin of the fifth toe is supplied by the Nervus suralis, not the lateral plantar nerve. Keep this in mind when relating a lesion's position to the nerve involved.

Proper plantar digital branches of media.key: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Proper plantar digital branches of media.note: Supply the medial side of the hallux and the facing sides of toes 1–4, running plantar beside the flexor tendon sheaths with the digital arteries. Pitfall: the medial hallucal nerve passes next to the medial sesamoid. Perineural fibrosis there (Joplin neuroma) can be mistaken for sesamoid or capsule pathology.

Prostate.note: The Prostata lies below the bladder base, behind the pubic symphysis and in front of the rectum, resting on the levator ani (Musculus pubococcygeus). The Urethra runs through it. Pitfall: an enlarged median lobe bulging into the bladder base mimics a bladder tumour. Small calcifications are normal, and CT cannot separate the zones.

Proximal lateral striate branches.note: Medial lenticulostriate branches leave proximal M1 and pass through the substantia perforata anterior to the globus pallidus, the medial putamen and the head of the caudate. Pitfall: physiological basal ganglia calcification is not haemorrhage. Check Hounsfield values and symmetry.

Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of foot.key: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of foot
Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of foot.note: Runs from the fifth MTP joint to the PIP joint. Abductor digiti minimi and flexor digiti minimi insert at its base. Pitfall: middle–distal symphalangism is common in the fifth toe and makes it look two-phalanged. Do not report a fused or 'missing' phalanx as a fracture or amputation.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve

Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand.key: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand.note: Between the fifth MCP and PIP joints; abductor and flexor digiti minimi insert on the ulnar base. Pitfall: in children the basal physis lies at the base—do not mistake it for a fracture, yet look for Salter–Harris II ('extra-octave') fractures with ulnar angulation.

Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot.key: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot
Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot.note: Lies between the first MTP joint (sesamoids plantar to the metatarsal head) and the hallux IP joint. The flexor hallucis longus tendon runs plantar and the extensor hallucis longus dorsal. Pitfall: an interphalangeal sesamoid plantar to the IP joint, or a bipartite basal apophysis in adolescents, can mimic an avulsion fragment.

Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand.key: Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand
Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand.note: The thumb has only two phalanges: the base forms the MCP joint with the first metacarpal, the head the interphalangeal joint; adductor pollicis inserts ulnar, extensor pollicis brevis dorsal at the base. Pitfall: an ulnar-base avulsion (ulnar collateral ligament, skier's thumb) must not be dismissed as a palmar MCP sesamoid.

Proximal phalanx of fourth finger of foo.key: Proximal phalanx of fourth finger of foot
Proximal phalanx of fourth finger of foo.note: Runs from the fourth MTP joint to the PIP joint, with interossei near the base and flexor/extensor tendons plantar and dorsal. Pitfall: the toes of the third to fifth rays overlap and lie flexed on axial slices. Confirm the digit by tracing it back to its metatarsal before reporting a fracture.

Proximal phalanx of fourth finger of han.key: Proximal phalanx of fourth finger of hand
Proximal phalanx of fourth finger of han.note: Between the fourth MCP and PIP joints; the flexor tendons run palmar in the fibrous sheath, the extensor hood dorsal. Pitfall: spiral or oblique shaft fractures can hide rotational malalignment (scissoring) that looks minor axially—compare the rotation of the condyles with the adjacent digits.

Proximal phalanx of second finger of foo.key: Proximal phalanx of second finger of foot
Proximal phalanx of second finger of foo.note: Runs from the second MTP joint (plantar plate below) to the PIP joint. The lumbrical and interossei sit near the base. Pitfall: in hammer or claw toe, the base subluxes dorsally on the second metatarsal head. On oblique axial slices this mimics a joint or fracture abnormality, so assess MTP alignment on sagittal views.

Proximal phalanx of second finger of han.key: Proximal phalanx of second finger of hand
Proximal phalanx of second finger of han.note: Between the second MCP and PIP joints; the first dorsal interosseous inserts on the radial base. Pitfall: a collateral-ligament avulsion at the basal corner can be confused with the normal radial palmar sesamoid of the index MCP joint—sesamoids are round, corticated and lie palmar to the metacarpal head.

Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot.key: Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot.note: Its basis articulates with the third metatarsal head and its caput/trochlea with the middle phalanx. Pitfall: a nutrient canal in the corpus phalangis can be mistaken for a nondisplaced fracture. A true fracture usually crosses the cortex transversely or obliquely and shows soft-tissue swelling.

Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand.key: Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand.note: The base forms the third MCP joint and the distal trochlea phalangis forms the PIP joint. Pitfall: unicondylar fractures of the trochlea run sagittally and are nearly invisible on axial images—check coronal reformats for condylar step-off and angular deformity.

Psoas major.note: Arises from the T12–L4 vertebral bodies and transverse processes, with the lumbar plexus inside it and the ureter on its anterior surface. It inserts on the Trochanter minor. Pitfall: side-to-side asymmetry is common, so look for gas or a rim-enhancing collection before diagnosing an abscess. An isolated lesser trochanter avulsion in an adult suggests a pathological fracture from metastasis.
landmarks: lm:Costal part of transverse process|Vertebra L3

Pterygospinous ligament.note: Runs from the posterior edge of the lateral pterygoid plate to the sphenoid spine, near branches of the Nervus mandibularis. Ossification creates the pterygospinous (Civinini) foramen. Pitfall: the ossified bar can be mistaken for a fracture fragment. The extra foramen must not be confused with the Foramen ovale or Foramen spinosum, and it can block percutaneous access to the foramen ovale.
passing: Accessory branch of middle meningeal artery
neighbours: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Pubic symphysis.note: Secondary cartilaginous joint between the pubic bodies, joined by the discus interpubicus and the superior and inferior pubic ligaments, with the bladder in the retropubic space behind it. A normal width is about 10 mm or less. Pitfall: in children and postpartum women physiological widening and irregular margins mimic diastasis or osteitis pubis.

Pubo-analis muscle.note: Medial part of the levator ani: it runs from the posterior pubic body alongside the prostate and loops around the anorectal junction, blending with the sphincter externus ani. Pitfall: CT cannot separate it from the puborectalis or the sphincter. Asymmetry after prostatectomy or obstetric injury is not a mass.

Pubococcygeus muscle.note: Runs from the posterior pubic body and the anterior arcus tendineus to the anococcygeal body and coccyx, forming the margin of the levator hiatus. Pitfall: CT does not resolve the levator subdivisions, and nearby lateral vesical lymph nodes along it can be mistaken for muscle bulk or the reverse.

Pubofemoral ligament.note: Runs from the iliopubic eminence and superior pubic ramus to the inferomedial capsule and zona orbicularis. Pitfall: the weak spot between it and the iliofemoral ligament lies under iliopsoas. Here the iliopsoas bursa connects with the joint, so a fluid collection at this spot may come from the joint rather than be a separate mass.

Pudendal nerve.note: The nerve (S2–S4) leaves through the infrapiriform foramen and crosses the ligamentum sacrospinale at the ischial spine. It re-enters through the foramen ischiadicum minus into the canalis pudendalis (Alcock) on the obturator internus fascia. Pitfall: do not confuse the greater and lesser sciatic foramina. Entrapment occurs between the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments.

Pulmonary trunk.note: Runs from the RV outflow tract up, back and to the left of the Aorta ascendens to its bifurcation below the aortic arch. Pitfall: diameter is measured at the bifurcation level, and more than about 29 mm suggests pulmonary hypertension. Mixing artefact from unopacified SVC inflow can mimic an embolus.
passing: Right semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valve
Left semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valve

Putamen.note: Lateral part of the Nucleus lentiformis. The external capsule, claustrum and extreme capsule lie lateral, toward the insula, and the globus pallidus lies medial. It is the most common site of hypertensive bleeding. Do not mistake a bleed that only involves the external capsule or claustrum for a putamen bleed. Check its lateral edge.

Pyramid of medulla oblongata.note: Paired anterior columns on either side of the anterior median fissure, bounded laterally by the preolivary sulcus and facing the clivus. The pyramids decussate near the foramen magnum. Pitfall: a calcified or dense Arteria vertebralis lying on the pyramid can mimic haemorrhage. Deficits are contralateral above the decussation.

Pyramidalis muscle.note: Musculus pyramidalis is a small triangular muscle in front of the lower rectus abdominis. It runs from the pubic crest and symphysis to the linea alba. Pitfall: it is often absent or asymmetric, so do not mistake a one-sided pyramidalis for a suprapubic mass, a haematoma or a rectus tear.

Pyramis of vermis.note: The Pyramis vermis is part of the inferior vermis, between the tuber above and the uvula below. It faces the cisterna magna. Pitfall: do not mistake a mega cisterna magna for Dandy-Walker spectrum or vermian hypoplasia. Check that the inferior vermis is intact and that the fourth ventricle is normal on sagittal reformats.

Quadrangular membrane.note: Submucosal sheet running from the lateral epiglottis to the arytenoid. It forms the aryepiglottic fold and ends inferiorly as the vestibular ligament (false cord). It separates the paraglottic space from the piriform sinus. Pitfall: the membrane itself is invisible on CT. Use fat (false cord) versus muscle (true cord) in the paraglottic space to place the level.
landmarks: lm:Superior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

Quadrate ligament.note: Thin band from the inferior border of the incisura radialis ulnae to the medial collum radii, closing the proximal radio-ulnar joint inferiorly below the ligamentum anulare. It is not resolved on CT. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the chorda obliqua or the proximal membrana interossea, which lie more distally.

Quadratus femoris muscle.note: A flat muscle running from the lateral ischial tuberosity to the Tuberculum quadratum on the intertrochanteric crest, with the obturator externus deep to it and the sciatic nerve posterior. Pitfall: ischiofemoral impingement narrows the space between the ischium and the lesser trochanter. On CT, this narrowing is the only clue.

Quadratus lumborum muscle.note: Musculus quadratus lumborum runs from the iliac crest and iliolumbar ligament to the 12th rib and the L1–L4 transverse processes. It lies posterolateral to psoas major and in front of erector spinae. Pitfall: left–right asymmetry is common, so do not call it atrophy, mass or abscess without a change in density or a fascial abnormality.

Quadratus plantae muscle.note: Arises by two heads from the plantar calcaneus and inserts into the lateral border of the FDL tendon. The lateral plantar nerve and vessels cross between it and the FDB. Pitfall: an accessory flexor digitorum accessorius longus in the tarsal tunnel can mimic a mass or cause tarsal tunnel syndrome.

Radial artery.note: Arises from the brachial artery at the radial neck and runs deep to brachioradialis. It lies lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon on pronator quadratus, then curves round the radial styloid through the anatomical snuffbox, deep to the extensor pollicis longus tendon, to the deep palmar arch. Pitfall: a high origin from the axillary or brachial artery is common. Do not report the absent cubital origin as occlusion.

Radial collateral artery.note: Anterior terminal branch of the deep brachial artery. It pierces the septum intermusculare laterale with the radial nerve and descends between brachialis and brachioradialis to anastomose with the radial recurrent artery. Pitfall: it marks the radial nerve. Do not mistake this vessel for the nerve, or the nerve for the vessel, at the lateral elbow.

Radial collateral ligament.note: Fans out from the lateral epicondyle into the ligamentum anulare radii, deep to the common extensor origin and blending with it. Pitfall: on CT it cannot be separated from the extensor tendon origin. Posterolateral instability (lateral ulnar collateral band) shows only indirectly, as radiocapitellar or ulnohumeral malalignment or a small avulsion flake.

Radial collateral ligament of wrist join.key: Radial collateral ligament of wrist joint
Radial collateral ligament of wrist join.note: Capsular thickening running from the processus styloideus radii to the scaphoid tubercle and trapezium, deep to the first extensor compartment. The radial artery crosses it in the anatomical snuffbox. Pitfall: a radial styloid (chauffeur) fracture may sit next to a scaphoid waist fracture. Search for both and do not dismiss a styloid tip ossicle.
neighbours: Tendon sheath - abd. pollicis longus - ext. pollicis brevis

Radial head of flexor digitorum superfic.key: Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Radial head of flexor digitorum superfic.note: A thin sheet arising from the anterior oblique line of the radius. It forms the radial limb of the FDS arch, and the median nerve runs along its deep surface. Pitfall: on CT this thin head blends with flexor pollicis longus; do not mistake the median nerve on its deep surface for the anterior interosseous nerve, which lies between FDP and FPL.
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Radial nerve.note: Runs in the spiral groove between the medial and lateral triceps heads and pierces the septum intermusculare laterale about 10 cm above the elbow. It then runs between brachialis and brachioradialis and divides at the radiocapitellar level. Pitfall: distal-third humeral shaft fractures (Holstein-Lewis) can trap the nerve where it is held against bone by the septum.

Radial veins.note: The Venae radiales are paired veins that run alongside the radial artery, deep to brachioradialis, on flexor pollicis longus and pronator quadratus. They join the ulnar veins below the radial tuberosity to form the brachial veins. Pitfall: next to the bicipitoradial bursa, these paired veins can be mistaken for bursal fluid or a distended bursa.

Radiate carpal ligament.note: Fibres fanning out from the palmar head and neck of the capitate to the surrounding carpal bones, deep to the carpal tunnel contents. Pitfall: in scaphocapitate syndrome the proximal capitate fragment can be rotated 90–180°. On CT this can mimic an intact head, so trace the capitate cortex on sagittal reconstructions.

Radiate ligament of head of rib.key: Radiate ligament of head of rib
Radiate ligament of head of rib.note: Fans out from the front of the rib head to the two adjacent vertebral bodies and the disc. It lies directly behind the pleura, with the truncus sympathicus just anterior to it. Pitfall: costovertebral osteophytes, sympathetic ganglia or intercostal nodes here can mimic a paravertebral mass. Check bone windows and adjacent slices.

Radiocapitate ligament.note: Palmar extrinsic band from the palmar radial rim to the capitate. It lies deep to the FPL tendon and meets the Ligamentum ulnocapitatum to form the distal V (arcuate ligament). Not separately visible on CT. Pitfall: the space of Poirier between the V arms is normal thinning. Do not report it as a ligament tear.

Radioscaphocapitate ligament.note: Arises from the palmar Processus styloideus radii, slings across the palmar scaphoid waist and inserts on the capitate. It is the fulcrum for scaphoid rotation. Pitfall: a radial styloid fracture that includes its origin risks ulnar translocation of the carpus. The space of Poirier is a normal thin area, not a capsular defect.

Radius.note: Caput radii articulates with the capitulum and the ulnar radial notch; distally the carpal surface bears scaphoid and lunate, and the incisura ulnaris forms the DRUJ. Pitfall: in a shaft or head fracture, assess both radioulnar joints (Galeazzi, Essex-Lopresti); the deep radial nerve winds around the neck.
neighbours: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint

Rectus abdominis muscle.note: Musculus rectus abdominis lies beside the midline, from the pubic crest and symphysis to the xiphoid and costal cartilages 5–7, inside the rectus sheath. Pitfall: tendinous intersections cause normal segmental contour changes. A rectus sheath haematoma from the inferior epigastric artery can cross the midline below the arcuate line into the prevesical space.

Rectus anterior capitis muscle.note: Short muscle running from the anterior lateral mass of the atlas to the basilar Os occipitale just anterior to the condyle. It lies deep and posterolateral to longus capitis. Pitfall: it is inseparable from longus capitis on CT, so craniocervical prevertebral swelling should be attributed to the prevertebral space rather than to a single muscle.

Rectus femoris muscle.note: The direct head arises from the Spina iliaca anterior inferior and the reflected head from the supra-acetabular ilium. The muscle runs superficial to the Vastus intermedius into the quadriceps tendon. Pitfall: in adolescents, an AIIS apophyseal avulsion can mimic an os acetabuli or a normal unfused apophysis, so compare with the other side.
passing: Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery

Rectus lateralis capitis muscle.note: Runs from the Processus transversus atlantis to the jugular process of the Os occipitale, immediately posterior to the jugular foramen. Pitfall: the vertebral artery passes medial to it over the atlas, and the internal jugular vein lies anterior; do not mistake the muscle for a jugular foramen or skull-base mass.

Rectus posterior major capitis muscle.note: Runs from the C2 spinous process to the lateral inferior nuchal line and forms the medial border of the suboccipital triangle. Pitfall: it lies lateral to the smaller rectus posterior minor, which attaches to the atlas, not the axis. Use the bony attachment to tell them apart on axial images.

Rectus posterior minor capitis muscle.note: Runs from the Tuberculum posterius atlantis to the medial inferior nuchal line, beside the external occipital crest, and is linked to the dura through a myodural bridge. Pitfall: congenital clefts or aplasia of the posterior arch of the atlas at its origin show smooth corticated margins. Do not report them as fractures.

Recurrent interosseous artery.note: Runs upward from the posterior interosseous artery between Supinator and Anconeus toward the lateral epicondyle, where it joins the Arteria collateralis media behind the elbow. Pitfall: this enhancing periarticular vessel at the posterolateral capsule should not be mistaken for synovitis or a loose body.

Red nucleus.note: Paired tegmental nucleus at the level of the superior colliculus, dorsomedial to the substantia nigra and the Basis pedunculi. CT does not resolve it. Pitfall: CN III fascicles run through it, so a small tegmental lesion (Benedikt syndrome) can be CT-occult despite a clear clinical deficit.

Renal pelvis.note: The Pelvis renalis sits in the renal sinus and leaves at the hilum, posterior to the renal vessels. Inferomedially it narrows at the pelviureteric junction, anterior to Psoas major. Pitfall: an extrarenal pelvis or parapelvic cysts can mimic hydronephrosis. Excretory-phase imaging shows whether contrast fills the structure.

Retina.note: On CT the Retina cannot be separated from the choroid and Sclera along the posterior globe wall. Pitfall: retinal detachment forms a V shape converging on the optic disc. Choroidal detachment forms lentiform collections that spare the optic disc region, so do not confuse the two.

Retro-aortic nodes.note: Nodi retroaortici lie between the posterior wall of the aorta abdominalis and the anterior longitudinal ligament of the L1–L3 vertebral bodies, medial to the diaphragmatic crura. Pitfall: the cisterna chyli, a retroaortic left renal vein or hemiazygos/lumbar veins look like retroaortic nodes; check continuity and contrast phase.

Retrocaecal nodes.note: Lie behind the caecum, between the caecum and the iliopsoas, close to a retrocaecal Appendix vermiformis. Pitfall: a retrocaecal appendix, whether normal or inflamed, can look like a node chain. Follow the tubular, blind-ending structure back to the caecal base.

Retrocaval nodes.note: Nodi retrocavales lie between the posterior wall of the inferior vena cava and the right diaphragmatic crus/upper lumbar vertebral bodies. Pitfall: the right renal artery passing behind the IVC, the right crus and lumbar veins are the usual retrocaval node mimics; confirm on arterial-phase and coronal images.

Retromandibular vein.note: Formed by the superficial temporal and maxillary veins. It runs within the parotid behind the mandibular ramus, lateral to the external carotid artery. Pitfall: CT does not show the facial nerve itself, which lies just lateral to this vein.
