The vein is the reference line for superficial versus deep lobe, so label tumours relative to the vein, not to the nerve.
landmarks: lm:Styloid process of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Retropharyngeal nodes.note: These nodes sit in the retropharyngeal space, behind the Constrictor superior pharyngis and in front of the prevertebral muscles. The lateral group (node of Rouvière) lies medial to the internal carotid artery at the Pars nasalis pharyngis level. Pitfall: a tortuous or medialized internal carotid artery can look like an enlarged lateral retropharyngeal node; follow the enhancing vessel on contiguous slices.

Rhomboid major muscle.note: Runs from the T2–T5 spinous processes to the Margo medialis scapulae below the scapular spine. It lies deep to the trapezius and superficial to the serratus posterior superior and erector spinae. Pitfall: on CT it is not separable from the rhomboid minor. Report 'rhomboids' rather than guessing a boundary.

Rhomboid minor muscle.note: Thin band from the Ligamentum nuchae and C7–T1 spinous processes to the medial scapular border at the root of the Spina scapulae. It lies deep to the Musculus trapezius and above the Musculus rhomboideus major. Pitfall: on CT it usually cannot be separated from rhomboid major, so do not report a fat cleft between them as a tear.

Right ascending lumbar vein.note: This vein runs vertically in the groove between the lumbar vertebral bodies and the psoas, anterior to the transverse processes. It links the lumbar veins and continues through the crus as the v. azygos. Pitfall: when it acts as a collateral in IVC obstruction, the dilated vein mimics retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy or a psoas lesion.

Right atrium.note: The Atrium dextrum forms the right heart border. It receives the SVC, IVC and coronary sinus and lies beside the ascending aorta. Pitfall: dense SVC contrast mixing with unopacified IVC blood mimics thrombus. The crista terminalis or Eustachian valve can mimic a mass.

Right brachiocephalic vein.note: This short, vertical vein starts behind the right sternoclavicular joint. It runs anterolateral to the brachiocephalic trunk and against the right upper lobe pleura down to the SVC. Pitfall: inflow mixing of opacified and unopacified blood creates pseudo-filling defects that mimic thrombus. Streak artifact from a right-arm injection can also hide adjacent nodes.

Right colic artery.note: Runs to the right across the duodenum, in front of the right ureter and gonadal vessels, toward the ascending colon. Pitfall: it is inconstant and often arises from the middle colic or ileocolic artery. Do not report it as absent or occluded without checking these variants.

Right colic nodes.note: Lie along the A./V. colica dextra in the right mesocolon, toward the root of the superior mesenteric vessels, next to the Duodenum and the head of the pancreas. Pitfall: the right colic artery is often missing. Do not mistake the gastrocolic trunk or loops of the duodenum for nodes.

Right colic vein.note: Crosses the right mesocolon anterior to the duodenum and drains into the Vena mesenterica superior, often via the gastrocolic trunk. Pitfall: the vein is frequently absent or joins the gastrocolic trunk. Do not assume a standard direct SMV tributary when describing anatomy before surgery.

Right common carotid artery.note: Arises from the Truncus brachiocephalicus behind the sternoclavicular joint. It ascends in the carotid sheath with the Vena jugularis interna lateral and Nervus vagus posterior, and bifurcates near C3–C4. Pitfall: on non-contrast CT, an asymmetric, collapsed jugular vein or an adjacent lymph node can be mistaken for the artery.

Right coronary artery.note: The RCA arises from the right aortic sinus and runs in the right atrioventricular groove between the Atrium dextrum and Ventriculus dexter to the crux cordis. Pitfall: its mid segment moves the most. On non-gated or poorly gated CT, motion artefact mimics stenosis or dissection.
passing: Right inferolateral branch of right coronary artery

Right coronary leaflet.note: Anterior aortic cusp below the right sinus, which gives off the right coronary artery, facing the RV outflow tract and the pulmonary valve. Pitfall: fusion of the right and left coronary cusps is the most common bicuspid pattern, so check the commissures. Do not confuse it with the adjacent right pulmonary cusp.

Right gastric nodes.note: Nodi gastrici dextri lie in the omentum minus along the right gastric artery, on the lesser curvature of the pylorus, below liver segment IV. Pitfall: partial volume of the pyloric wall or the hepatic artery can be mistaken for a node; review with gastric distension.

Right gastro-omental nodes.note: Nodi gastroomentales dextri lie in the omentum majus along the right gastro-omental vessels on the greater curvature of the gastric antrum, anterior to the pancreatic head. Pitfall: omental vessels seen in cross-section and collapsed transverse colon look like small nodes; check for tubular continuity.

Right gastro-omental vein.note: Runs along the greater curvature toward the pylorus, then descends anterior to the pancreatic head and joins the gastrocolic trunk into the Vena mesenterica superior. Pitfall: this vessel on the anterior pancreatic head can mimic a dilated duct or a small nodule. Follow it into the gastrocolic trunk.

Right inferior lobar bronchus.note: Continues the Bronchus intermedius below the middle lobe origin. It gives BVI posteriorly, then a basal trunk that divides into BVII–BX. Pitfall: the inferior pulmonary vein runs posteromedial to the basal trunk, and when unopacified it can mimic a hilar node or mass.
passing: Inferior lobar artery of right lung
Superior basal vein of right lung
Inferior basal vein of right lung
Middle lobar artery of right lung
neighbours: Superior segmental bronchus of right lung (BVI)
Medial basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BVII)
Anterior basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BVIII)
Lateral basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BIX)
Posterior basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BX)

Right inferior pulmonary vein.note: Vena pulmonalis dextra inferior drains the Lobus inferior dexter and runs horizontally behind the right atrium to the posterior Atrium sinistrum, next to the Oesophagus. Pitfall: its horizontal course and confluence can mimic a subcarinal or hilar mass on non-contrast CT. A separate ostium for the superior segmental vein is a normal variant.
passing: Superior basal vein of right lung
Inferior basal vein of right lung

Right inferolateral branch of right coro.key: Right inferolateral branch of right coronary artery
Right inferolateral branch of right coro.note: In right-dominant hearts this posterolateral branch continues from the RCA beyond the crux cordis. It runs on the inferior Ventriculus sinister wall above the Diaphragma. Pitfall: check coronary dominance first. Do not mistake the parallel inferior vein of the left ventricle for this artery.

Right lobe of thymus.note: Prevascular anterior mediastinal tissue behind the manubrium and in front of the ascending aorta and right atrial appendage. It is usually smaller than the left lobe. Pitfall: the superior pericardial recess next to the ascending aorta mimics a thymic nodule or lymph node. Fluid attenuation and a crescent shape identify the recess.

Right main bronchus.note: The right main bronchus is short, wide and steep, with the azygos arch above it. It gives off the upper lobe bronchus and continues as the Bronchus intermedius. Pitfall: a tracheal bronchus ("pig bronchus") arising from the trachea can be mistaken for the normal upper lobe bronchus. The steep course makes it the usual route for aspiration.
passing: Superior lobar artery of right lung
neighbours: Node of arch of azygos vein

Right pulmonary artery.note: Runs right, behind the Aorta ascendens and the Vena cava superior and in front of the carina. It gives off the truncus anterior, then continues as the interlobar artery in front of the Bronchus intermedius. Pitfall: an early truncus anterior or a nearby pulmonary vein can be confused with hilar nodes or with a pulmonary vein.
passing: Superior lobar artery of right lung
Middle lobar artery of right lung

Right renal artery.note: Arises from the right side of the Aorta abdominalis at L1–L2 and runs behind the Vena cava inferior to the renal hilum. It is longer than the left. Pitfall: retrocaval nodes or the right crus can mimic it, and accessory renal arteries are frequent.

Right renal vein.note: A short vein running anteromedially from the renal hilum, anterior to the right renal artery, into the lateral IVC at about L1–L2. Pitfall: multiple right renal veins are a common variant. Because the vein is short, tumour thrombus from renal cell carcinoma reaches the IVC early, so always assess the cava.

Right semilunar leaflet of pulmonary val.key: Right semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valve
Right semilunar leaflet of pulmonary val.note: Right cusp of the pulmonary valve, next to the right aortic sinus and the origin of the right coronary artery. Pitfall: because it lies so close to the aortic root, do not mix it up with the right coronary cusp. Valve level differs: the pulmonary valve is higher and further anterior-left.
passing: Left semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valve
Anterior semilunar leaflet of pulmonary valve

Right subclavian artery.note: Arises from the Truncus brachiocephalicus and arches over the pleural cupula behind Musculus scalenus anterior and over Costa prima. The Vena subclavia runs in front of the scalenus. Pitfall: an aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria) arises as the last arch branch and runs behind the oesophagus, so always confirm its origin.

Right subclavian vein.note: Runs from the outer edge of the first rib, in front of the M. scalenus anterior and behind the clavicle, to the right venous angle. There it joins the V. jugularis interna. Pitfall: the A. subclavia dextra lies behind the scalenus anterior. Do not mix up the two vessels or mistake streak artifact from dense contrast for a filling defect.
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Right subcostal vein.note: This vein runs along the lower border of the 12th rib, anterior to quadratus lumborum, with the subcostal artery and nerve. It joins the right ascending lumbar vein to form the azygos. Pitfall: miscounting a hypoplastic 12th rib or a lumbar rib shifts the level. Do not report the neurovascular bundle as a node.

Right superior intercostal vein.note: This vein collects the right 2nd–4th posterior intercostal veins along the costovertebral junctions and drains into the arcus venae azygos. The intercostal vessels run in the sulcus costae, with the vein uppermost (V-A-N). Pitfall: a small paravertebral vessel near the rib neck can mimic a node or nerve-sheath tumour. Follow its continuity to the azygos.

Right superior lobar bronchus.note: Arises laterally from the right main bronchus about 2 cm below the carina, at the level of the azygos arch, and splits into BI, BII and BIII. Pitfall: a tracheal bronchus (bronchus suis) arising directly from the trachea is a normal variant and should not be mislabelled as this lobar bronchus.
passing: Superior lobar artery of right lung
Apical segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Apical segmental bronchus of right lung (BI)
Posterior segmental bronchus of right lung (BII)
Anterior segmental bronchus of right lung (BIII)
Node of arch of azygos vein

Right superior phrenic vein.note: This small vein lies on the thoracic surface of the posterior right hemidiaphragm. It drains into the azygos system. Pitfall: it is normally not resolvable on CT. Diaphragmatic partial volume over liver segment VII can mimic a pleural nodule or plaque, so do not mistake it for the inferior phrenic vessels below the diaphragm.

Right superior pulmonary vein.note: Vena pulmonalis dextra superior drains the Lobus superior and medius. It lies anterior and inferior to the Arteria pulmonalis dextra and passes behind the superior vena cava to the Atrium sinistrum. Pitfall: the middle lobe vein can drain separately (a variant), and partial anomalous venous return into the superior vena cava must not be missed.

Right testicular artery.note: Arises from the front of the Aorta abdominalis below the renal arteries, crosses in front of the Vena cava inferior and descends on Psoas major to the deep inguinal ring. Pitfall: unlike the left, the Vena testicularis dextra drains directly into the IVC. Do not mistake the vein or ureter for this tiny artery.

Right testicular vein.note: Leaves the deep inguinal ring and ascends on the psoas, anterior to the ureter, to drain obliquely into the anterolateral IVC below the right renal vein. Pitfall: mind laterality. The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein. On non-contrast CT, do not mistake the vein for the ureter; trace it to the IVC.

Right ventricle.note: The Ventriculus dexter is the most anterior chamber, directly behind the sternum and resting on the Diaphragma. The septum and the LAD mark its left border. Pitfall: the moderator band and coarse trabeculation mimic thrombus or tumour. In pulmonary embolism, measure the RV/LV ratio on axial or four-chamber views.
passing: Anterior papillary muscle of right ventricle
Septal leaflet of right atrioventricular valve

Risorius muscle.note: Thin, variable muscle running from the fascia over the masseter to the modiolus, superficial to Bucinator, often merging with Platysma. Pitfall: it is often absent or not separable on CT. The facial vessels crossing here and the Ductus parotideus, which pierces Bucinator, should not be mistaken for an abnormality.

Roots of brachial plexus.note: The C5–T1 ventral rami leave the intervertebral foramina and run in the Sulcus nervi spinalis, posterior to the A. vertebralis in the Foramen transversarium and between the tubercles, then into the interscalene gap. Pitfall: cervical nerves exit above the vertebra of the same number, so C8 exits at C7–T1. Uncovertebral osteophytes narrow these foramina.
landmarks: lm:Anterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4
lm:Uncinate process of first thoracic vertebra|Vertebra T1

Rotatores.note: The deepest transversospinal layer. Short slips run from a transverse process to the lamina or spinous process base one or two levels above, and are best developed in the thoracic spine. Pitfall: they cannot be resolved as separate muscles on CT. The thin fat plane against the lamina is normal and should not be read as an epidural or facet collection.

Rubrospinal tract.note: Crossed tract from the nucleus ruber that lies just ventral to and partly mixed with the Tractus corticospinalis lateralis in the lateral funiculus. CT cannot resolve it. Pitfall: it overlaps the corticospinal tract, so do not draw a sharp boundary between them.

Sacrococcygeal symphysis.note: Fibrocartilaginous joint between the Apex ossis sacri and the Basis ossis coccygis. The Musculus coccygeus and the sacrospinous ligament attach laterally, and the Musculus gluteus maximus lies posterolaterally. Pitfall: normal variation in coccygeal angulation, segmentation or partial fusion is often mistaken for fracture or dislocation.

Sacrospinous ligament.note: Runs from the lateral sacrum/coccyx to the Spina ischiadica, fused with the coccygeus muscle, and separates the greater from the lesser sciatic foramen. The pudendal bundle crosses behind it at the ischial spine. Pitfall: a small ischial spine fragment is an avulsion of this ligament, which indicates rotational instability. It is not an incidental ossicle.

Sacrotuberous ligament.note: Runs from the posterior iliac spines and lateral sacrum/coccyx to the medial ischial tuberosity, deep to gluteus maximus, and continues into the hamstring origin. It forms the posterior border of the lesser sciatic foramen. Pitfall: linear ossification of this ligament can mimic a fracture fragment or heterotopic bone. Ischial tuberosity avulsions need to be separated from it.

Sacrum.note: The Os sacrum meets L5 at the Basis ossis sacri, the hip bones at the Facies auricularis and the coccyx at its apex. Pitfall: insufficiency fractures of the Ala ossis sacri are subtle on axial images and are best seen on coronal reformats. Report which Foramina sacralia anteriora are involved (Denis zone II).

Saphenous nerve.note: Runs in the canalis adductorius deep to the sartorius, crossing the femoral artery from lateral to anterior. It exits between the sartorius and gracilis at the knee, then follows the great saphenous vein along the medial tibia. Pitfall: it does not pass through the adductor hiatus with the vessels, and in the leg it cannot be told apart from venous tributaries.
passing: Medial crural cutaneous branches of saphenous nerve
neighbours: Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament

Sartorius muscle.note: Arises from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) and crosses the thigh obliquely, roofing the adductor canal over the femoral vessels. It inserts on the medial tibia as part of the pes anserinus. Pitfall: fluid in the Bursa anserina can mimic a meniscal cyst or ganglion. ASIS apophyseal avulsions in adolescents displace inferiorly.

Scalenus anterior muscle.note: Runs from the anterior tubercles of C3–C6 to the scalene tubercle of the Costa prima. Together with scalenus medius it bounds the interscalene triangle. Pitfall: the subclavian vein passes anterior to the muscle, while the subclavian artery and brachial plexus pass posterior to it; do not swap them when assessing thoracic outlet compression or a cervical rib.

Scalenus medius muscle.note: Largest scalene, running from the posterior tubercles of C2–C7 to the Costa prima behind the subclavian groove. It forms the posterior wall of the interscalene triangle. Pitfall: the dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves pierce the muscle, so linear densities within it are normal nerves, not tears or nodes.
landmarks: lm:Posterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4

Scalenus posterior muscle.note: Smallest scalene, running from the posterior tubercles of C5–C7 to the outer surface of the Costa secunda, posterolateral to scalenus medius. Pitfall: on CT it often merges with scalenus medius without a fat plane, so do not report its absence or asymmetry as pathology.

Scaphocapitate ligament.note: Runs from the palmar distal pole of the scaphoid to the capitate waist, radial to the space of Poirier. It stabilises the distal scaphoid. Pitfall: scaphoid distal pole and tubercle fractures are easily missed on axial images. Reconstruct along the long axis of the scaphoid.

Scaphoid bone.note: Bridges both carpal rows: proximal pole in the radial scaphoid fossa, distal pole facing Os trapezium/trapezoideum, ulnarly the lunate and capitate. Pitfall: waist fractures are occult on standard axial planes—reformat along the scaphoid long axis; retrograde blood supply makes proximal-pole fractures prone to avascular necrosis and nonunion.

Scapholunate interosseous ligament.note: C-shaped ligament spanning the proximal scapholunate interval, with its strongest part dorsal. It separates the radiocarpal and midcarpal compartments. Pitfall: measure the scapholunate gap at the mid-portion of the flat facing surfaces on coronal reconstructions, not at the palmar or proximal curvature. Compare with the other side before calling diastasis above 3 mm.

Scaphotrapeziotrapezoidal ligament.note: Palmar-radial ligament complex of the STT joint, lying next to the flexor carpi radialis tendon as it grooves the trapezium. Pitfall: STT osteoarthritis with scaphoid flexion can produce a DISI-like lunate. Do not misattribute this to scapholunate dissociation; check the scapholunate interval directly.

Scapula.note: The Fossa glenoidea articulates with the humeral head, and the acromion and Processus coracoideus project above it. The suprascapular nerve runs through the suprascapular and spinoglenoid notches. Pitfall: an os acromiale (an unfused acromial apophysis persisting into adulthood) can look like an acromial fracture. Look for its smooth, corticated margins.

Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle.key: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle
Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle.note: The posterior part arises from the inferior lip of the spina scapulae and the acromial angle, overlies infraspinatus and teres minor, and inserts on the deltoid tuberosity. The axillary nerve enters its deep surface from the quadrangular space. Pitfall: isolated atrophy of the posterior deltoid together with teres minor suggests axillary nerve compression rather than rotator cuff disease.

Sciatic bursa of gluteus maximus muscle.key: Sciatic bursa of gluteus maximus muscle
Sciatic bursa of gluteus maximus muscle.note: Lies between the Tuber ischiadicum and the Musculus gluteus maximus, superficial to the hamstring origin. Pitfall: ischiogluteal bursitis can look like a hamstring tendon tear or a cystic or soft-tissue tumour. The Nervus ischiadicus lies just lateral, so mass effect explains sciatica.

Sciatic bursa of obturator internus.note: Lies between the Musculus obturator internus tendon and the lesser sciatic notch, where the tendon turns around the bone between the gemelli. Pitfall: this lesser sciatic foramen site must not be confused with the greater sciatic foramen (piriformis) or with the pudendal canal along the medial obturator internus.

Sciatic nerve.note: The nerve (L4–S3) leaves the pelvis through the infrapiriform part of the foramen ischiadicum majus. It then descends on the gemelli and quadratus femoris, between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter, and runs deep to the long head of biceps femoris. Pitfall: in the piriformis variant the nerve is split or passes through the muscle. The nerve is iso-dense to muscle, so trace it in its fat plane.

Sclera.note: The Sclera is the dense outer coat of the globe. It continues into the Cornea anteriorly and the optic nerve sheath posteriorly, and the recti insert on it. Pitfall: senile scleral calcified plaques at the rectus insertions, mainly medial and lateral, mimic intraocular foreign bodies. So does a hyperdense scleral buckle.

Second metacarpal bone.note: The notched base locks against the trapezoid, trapezium, capitate and third metacarpal; extensor carpi radialis longus inserts dorsally and flexor carpi radialis palmar on the base. Pitfall: a carpal boss (os styloideum) at the dorsal 2nd/3rd CMC junction mimics a fracture fragment or osteophyte; it is corticated and well-defined.
passing: Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of second finger of hand

Second metatarsal bone.note: The basis is recessed between the three cuneiforms (the keystone) and is tied to the medial cuneiform by the Lisfranc ligament. The caput articulates with proximal phalanx II. Pitfall: a fleck avulsion, or a medial MT II base out of line with the intermediate cuneiform, means a Lisfranc injury. A flattened caput suggests Freiberg infraction.
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of second finger of foot

Second posterior intercostal artery.note: Runs in the costal groove of the second rib between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, with the vein above and the nerve below. Pitfall: it comes from the supreme intercostal artery, and aortic posterior intercostal arteries usually start at the third space.

Second rib.note: True rib that articulates with T1 and T2. Its cartilage meets the sternum at the angulus sterni, and the tuberositas musculi serrati anterioris lies on its outer surface. Pitfall: calcified costal cartilage near the sternum can mimic a fracture or a lung nodule. A first or second rib fracture means high-energy trauma, so check the subclavian and axillary vessels.

Semimembranosus bursa.note: Lies between the Musculus semimembranosus tendon insertion on the posteromedial tibia and the Ligamentum collaterale tibiale. Pitfall: when distended it forms a U-shaped collection around the tendon that can be mistaken for a Baker cyst or a medial parameniscal cyst. It lies below the joint line with no neck toward the gastrocnemius.
neighbours: Deep part of tibial collateral ligament
Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament

Semimembranosus muscle.note: Arises from the ischial tuberosity anterolateral to the conjoint tendon and lies deep to the semitendinosus. It inserts on the posteromedial tibial condyle. Pitfall: fluid between its tendon and the medial gastrocnemius head is a popliteal cyst, not a meniscal cyst or soft-tissue tumour.
neighbours: Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament

Seminal gland.note: The paired Glandulae seminales lie behind the bladder base and in front of the rectum, above the Prostata, joining the Ductus deferens to form the Ductus ejaculatorius. Pitfall: the fat angle between seminal gland and bladder can disappear with bladder filling or patient positioning. Do not report this as tumour invasion. Mild asymmetry is normal.

Semispinalis colli muscle.note: Runs from the T1–T6 transverse processes to the C2–C5 spinous processes and is bulkiest at the C2 spine. It lies deep to the semispinalis capitis and superficial to the multifidus. Pitfall: it is easily confused with the semispinalis capitis. The fat plane carrying the deep cervical vessels separates the two.

Semispinalis thoracis muscle.note: A thin muscle running from the T6–T10 transverse processes to the C6–T4 spinous processes. It lies superficial to the multifidus and deep to the spinalis/longissimus. Pitfall: it blends with the multifidus thoracis on CT. Do not report its apparent thinness as atrophy.

Semitendinosus muscle.note: Arises from the ischial tuberosity in a conjoint tendon with the biceps, runs superficial to the semimembranosus and inserts on the anteromedial tibia as part of the pes anserinus. Pitfall: after ACL reconstruction the tendon may be missing or regenerated; do not report this as a tear.

Sensory root of trigeminal nerve.note: The trigeminal sensory column runs from the midbrain through the pons and the lateral medulla (spinal tract and nucleus) down to the posterior horn of the upper cervical cord. Pitfall: a lateral medullary (Wallenberg) infarct causes ipsilateral facial sensory loss but is often invisible on early CT, and posterior-fossa beam hardening can mimic hypodensity.

Septal branches of anterior interventric.key: Septal branches of anterior interventricular artery
Septal branches of anterior interventric.note: The septal branches leave the LAD at right angles and penetrate the interventricular septum between the left and right ventricles. The first septal branch marks the end of the proximal LAD segment. Pitfall: small septal branches are easily lost to partial volume. Septal branches that are absent or enlarged may reflect occlusion or collaterals, not variant anatomy.

Septal branches of posterior ethmoidal a.key: Septal branches of posterior ethmoidal artery
Septal branches of posterior ethmoidal a.note: Small branches to the posterosuperior septum near the sphenoethmoidal junction, entering through the posterior ethmoidal foramen. They are not visible on CT. Pitfall: the posterior ethmoidal foramen lies only millimetres anterior to the canalis opticus. Do not mistake one for the other on coronal CT, and do not count the posterior ethmoidal canal as the anterior one.

Septal leaflet of right atrioventricular.key: Septal leaflet of right atrioventricular valve
Septal leaflet of right atrioventricular.note: Cuspis septalis attaches to the interventricular septum, between atrium dextrum and ventriculus dexter, close to the ostium of sinus coronarius. Pitfall: its septal hinge sits slightly apical (lower) to the mitral annulus. Do not mistake this normal offset for Ebstein displacement, and do not mistake the leaflet for a thrombus on non-gated CT.
passing: Septal papillary muscle of right ventricle
Inferior leaflet of right atrioventricular valve

Septal nuclei.note: Grey matter in the paraterminal and subcallosal region, below the rostrum of the corpus callosum. They lie in front of the anterior commissure and lamina terminalis and above the chiasm. Do not confuse them with the thin Septum pellucidum or a cavum septi pellucidi, which lie above the anterior commissure, between the frontal horns.

Septal papillary muscle of right ventric.key: Septal papillary muscle of right ventricle
Septal papillary muscle of right ventric.note: A small, often multiple, muscle arising from the right side of the interventricular septum, holding chordae of the Cuspis septalis. Pitfall: do not mistake it, or the trabecula septomarginalis, for septal thickening or an intracavitary mass in the Ventriculus dexter.
passing: Septal leaflet of right atrioventricular valve

Septum pellucidum.note: Thin midline leaflets between the frontal horns, running from the corpus callosum above to the fornix below. Midline shift is measured here. Pitfall: cavum septi pellucidi or cavum vergae is a normal CSF-filled variant, not a cyst or hydrocephalus. If the septum is absent, think of septo-optic dysplasia.

Serratus anterior muscle.note: It runs from ribs 1–9 to the medial border of the facies costalis scapulae, between subscapularis and the chest wall. Pitfall: a lens-shaped soft-tissue mass deep to it at the inferior scapular angle is typically elastofibroma dorsi, not sarcoma. Its interdigitations with the external oblique can also mimic rib or pleural lesions.

Serratus posterior inferior muscle.note: Thin sheet running from the T11–L2 spinous processes, through the Fascia thoracolumbalis, to ribs 9–12. It lies deep to the Musculus latissimus dorsi and superficial to the Musculus erector spinae. Pitfall: a hypoplastic 12th rib or a lumbar rib causes miscounting of its rib attachments, so count from T1 or the lumbar vertebrae.

Serratus posterior superior muscle.note: Thin sheet running from the C7–T3 spinous processes and Ligamentum nuchae down to ribs 2–5, lateral to the angles. It lies deep to the Musculi rhomboidei and superficial to the Musculi splenii and erector spinae. Pitfall: because it is so thin it partial-volumes with the rhomboids, so do not mistake it for a separate soft-tissue lesion over the posterior ribs.

Sesamoid bones of foot.note: The tibial (medial) and fibular (lateral) sesamoids lie in the flexor hallucis brevis tendons under caput ossis metatarsi I. The flexor hallucis longus tendon runs between them. Pitfall: a bipartite sesamoid (usually tibial, smooth corticated halves, often bilateral) mimics fracture. Fracture edges are sharp and non-corticated.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
neighbours: Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis
Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis

Seventh rib.note: Last true rib. It articulates with T6 and T7, and its cartilage reaches the sternum at the xiphisternal level. The diaphragmatic dome and lower lobe lie on its inner surface. Pitfall: merged cartilages of ribs 7 and 8 at the costal margin can mimic a fracture or a mass. Follow each cartilage separately.

Short head of biceps brachii.note: Arises from the tip of the Processus coracoideus as part of the conjoint tendon, medial to the long head and in front of the subscapularis, then joins the long head in the mid-arm. Pitfall: in a coracoid fracture, the pull of the conjoint tendon can displace the tip fragment downward. Look for it in the soft tissues.

Short head of biceps femoris.note: Arises from the labium laterale lineae asperae and the lateral intermuscular septum, deep to the long head, and joins it to insert on the fibular head. Pitfall: the common fibular nerve runs along its posteromedial border toward the fibular neck, so do not mistake the nerve for a small vessel or tendon slip.

Short posterior ciliary arteries.note: Many small intraconal branches that pierce the sclera around the optic disc to supply the choroid and optic nerve head. Pitfall: CT shows no sign of ischaemic optic neuropathy (as in giant cell arteritis). Calcification at the disc is drusen or scleral plaque, not vessel.

Sigmoid arteries.note: Two to four branches of the inferior mesenteric artery fan out in the sigmoid mesocolon over the left psoas and the left common iliac vessels. Pitfall: enlarged sigmoid nodes along these vessels are easily mistaken for unopacified bowel loops or vessels. Trace them on contiguous slices.
passing: Descending branch of left colic artery

Sigmoid colon.note: It is intraperitoneal on the sigmoid mesocolon and runs from the pelvic brim to the rectosigmoid junction at about S3. The left ureter passes beneath the root of the mesocolon. Pitfall: redundant, collapsed sigmoid loops in the pelvis can look like a bladder-wall or adnexal mass. Trace the bowel continuously.

Sigmoid nodes.note: Nodi sigmoidei lie in the mesocolon sigmoideum along the sigmoid vessels, anterior to the left psoas major and common iliac vessels. Pitfall: they are easily confused with common iliac nodes or the left ureter/gonadal vessels; check that they sit in the mesentery, not on the vessel wall.

Sigmoid sinus.note: Sits in an S-shaped groove in the mastoid part of the temporal bone, behind and inside the mastoid air cells. It runs from the transverse sinus to the jugular bulb. Pitfall: a normally small (hypoplastic) sinus or an arachnoid granulation can mimic thrombosis. A thin or dehiscent sigmoid plate and emissary canals can be mistaken for a fracture.

Sigmoid veins.note: Run in the sigmoid mesocolon with the Arteriae sigmoideae and drain into the Vena mesenterica inferior. The left ureter crosses beneath the root of the mesocolon. Pitfall: on non-contrast CT, the unopacified left ureter and gonadal vein look like these vessels. Trace each tubular structure to its origin.

Sinus of frontal bone.note: Sinus ossis frontalis lies between the anterior table under the glabella and a posterior table facing the anterior cranial fossa and Gyrus rectus. The Septum sinuum frontalium is often off the midline. Pitfall: unilateral aplasia or hypoplasia is a normal variant and must not be reported as opacification or postoperative change.
landmarks: lm:Septum of frontal sinuses|Sinus of frontal bone

Sinus of sphenoid bone.note: Sinus ossis sphenoidei lies under the sella and Adenohypophysis, with the Arteria carotis interna along each lateral wall and the nasopharynx below. Pitfall: the Septum sinuum sphenoideorum often inserts on the bony carotid canal, which may be dehiscent. Report this before transsphenoidal surgery.
landmarks: lm:Septum of sphenoidal sinuses|Sinus of sphenoid bone

Sixth rib.note: True rib. Its caput costae articulates with T5 and T6, its tuberculum costae with the T6 transverse process, and the angulus costae lies lateral to the erector spinae. The neurovascular bundle runs in the sulcus costae. Pitfall: subtle buckle fractures at the angulus costae are missed on axial slices. Use curved reformats.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Small saphenous vein.note: Passes behind the lateral malleolus with the sural nerve, runs up the midline of the calf between the heads of the gastrocnemius, then pierces the popliteal fascia to join the vena poplitea. Pitfall: where it ends varies. A cranial extension (Giacomini vein) to the great saphenous vein or femoral vein can be mistaken for an abnormal vessel.

Soft palate.note: The Palatum molle hangs from the posterior edge of the hard palate (Os palatinum) and separates the nasopharynx from the oropharynx. Its tensor tendon hooks around the pterygoid hamulus. Pitfall: its position and thickness change with breathing and swallowing. Contact with the tongue dorsum can look like a mass or airway narrowing.

Soleus muscle.note: Arises from the linea musculi solei and the fibular head, lying deep to the gastrocnemius and superficial to the deep flexors. Its tendinous arch covers the popliteal vessels and tibial nerve. Pitfall: cortical irregularity at the soleal line is a normal traction finding, not periosteal reaction or a stress fracture.

Sphenoid bone.note: The body contains the sphenoid sinus and the sella. The greater wings form the floor of the middle cranial fossa and the lateral orbital wall, and the pterygoid processes project downward. Pitfall: on coronal images, the foramen rotundum (V2) lies superolateral to the pterygoid canal. Do not swap them, and do not mix up foramen ovale with the smaller posterolateral foramen spinosum.

Sphenomandibular ligament.note: Runs from the sphenoid spine to the mandibular lingula, medial to the ramus and lateral to the medial pterygoid muscle. The inferior alveolar nerve and vessels pass between it and the ramus into the Foramen mandibulae. Pitfall: a prominent lingula or a calcified ligament can mimic a fracture fragment or a foreign body.
neighbours: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Spinal branch of iliolumbar artery.note: Small branch that enters the L5–S1 intervertebral foramen to supply the cauda equina and the vertebral canal. Pitfall: on contrast CT, an enhancing vessel in the foramen can mimic a nerve root, a disc fragment or foraminal pathology. Correlate with the course of the Vena iliolumbalis.

Spinal dura.note: Dura spinalis forms the thecal sac from the foramen magnum to about S2. It is separated from the posterior longitudinal ligament and the ligamenta flava by epidural fat, and its root sleeves reach the spinal ganglia in the foramina. Pitfall: on CT the dura cannot be told apart from CSF or a thickened ligamentum flavum. Perineural (Tarlov) cysts and dural ectasia are not osteolytic lesions.

Spinal ganglion.note: It sits in the upper foramen intervertebrale under the pedicle, outside the dural sac. In the neck it lies behind the arteria vertebralis and next to the processus uncinatus. Pitfall: the ganglion normally enhances and looks bulky, especially at L5 and S1, so it can mimic a schwannoma or disc fragment. Sacral ganglia may lie inside the canal.

Spinal reticular process.note: Net-like zone where the lateral angle of the Cornu posterius meets the lateral funiculus. It is most prominent in the cervical cord. CT cannot resolve it, and the cord appears homogeneous within the thecal sac. Pitfall: beam hardening at C6–T1 from the shoulders can mimic a focal intramedullary hypodensity at this site.

Spinalis capitis muscle.note: Small, inconstant muscle that usually blends with semispinalis capitis and inserts on the occipital bone beside the external occipital crest. Pitfall: it usually cannot be separated from semispinalis capitis on CT, so describe the region as the semispinalis complex. The suboccipital venous plexus should not be mistaken for an abnormality.

Spinalis colli muscle.note: Inconstant medial muscle running from the upper thoracic and C7 spinous processes to the C2–C4 spinous processes, next to the Ligamentum nuchae. Pitfall: it is often absent or merged with semispinalis colli. Do not mistake ossification of the nuchal ligament (a fabella-like nuchal ossicle) for a spinous process fracture.

Spinalis thoracis muscle.note: Most medial column of the erector spinae, running along the spinous processes from about T2 to L2. Longissimus thoracis lies lateral, semispinalis/multifidus lie deep. Pitfall: on CT it cannot be separated from longissimus. Report the erector spinae as a whole, and do not read slight side-to-side bulk differences caused by patient rotation as atrophy.

Spinotectal tract.note: Ascending crossed fibres that run with the spinothalamic tracts in the anterolateral funiculus to the colliculus superior. CT cannot resolve them. Pitfall: the similar name invites confusion with the descending Tractus tectospinalis, which lies medially beside the Fissura mediana anterior.

Spleen.note: Sits in the left upper quadrant under the diaphragm. It borders the stomach anteromedially, the left kidney posteromedially and the splenic flexure inferiorly, and the pancreatic tail reaches the hilum. Pitfall: heterogeneous (zebra) enhancement in the arterial phase mimics infarction or laceration. Confirm in the portal venous phase.

Splenic artery.note: Tortuous course along the upper border of the Pancreas, behind the Gaster, to the splenic hilum; the Vena splenica runs below and behind it. Pitfall: tortuous loops seen in cross-section mimic aneurysms or pancreatic lesions, and wall calcification can be mistaken for pancreatic calcification.

Splenic nodes.note: Nodi splenici lie at the splenic hilum along the splenic vessels, between the pancreatic tail and the posterior gastric fundus. Pitfall: accessory spleens (splenunculi) at the hilum mimic nodes; they match splenic attenuation in every contrast phase.

Splenic vein.note: Runs along the posterior surface of the pancreatic body and tail, caudal to the tortuous Arteria splenica, and joins the Vena mesenterica superior behind the pancreatic neck. Pitfall: in arterial-phase CT, unopacified or mixing blood at the portal confluence can mimic thrombus. Confirm on the portal venous phase.

Splenius capitis muscle.note: Runs from the Ligamentum nuchae and the C7–T3 spinous processes up to the Processus mastoideus and the lateral superior nuchal line. It lies deep to the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid and superficial to the semispinalis capitis. Pitfall: near its insertion, the A. occipitalis seen in cross-section can mimic an occipital lymph node.

Splenius colli muscle.note: Arises from the T3–T6 spinous processes and inserts on the posterior tubercles of the C1–C3 transverse processes, lateral and deep to the splenius capitis. Pitfall: at its upper attachments it merges with the levator scapulae and longissimus colli. Do not try to separate them on axial CT.
landmarks: lm:Posterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4

Stapes.note: Basis stapedis fills the fenestra vestibuli on the vestibulum. The crura run laterally to the processus lenticularis incudis, and the tympanic facial canal lies just above. Pitfall: the crura are sub-millimetre and often not visible, so do not call them absent. Fenestral otosclerosis shows as a hypodense focus just anterior to the oval window.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of stapes|Stapes

Sternocleidomastoid muscle.note: Runs from the Manubrium sterni and medial Clavicula to the Processus mastoideus, covering the carotid sheath and the jugular nodes. Pitfall: after accessory nerve injury the ipsilateral muscle atrophies with fatty change, which can make the normal contralateral sternocleidomastoid look like a mass.

Sternocostal head of pectoralis major mu.key: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle
Sternocostal head of pectoralis major mu.note: It arises from the manubrium, corpus sterni, costal cartilages 1–6 and the external oblique aponeurosis, and converges on the humerus anterior to pectoralis minor. Pitfall: unilateral absence (Poland syndrome) can be mistaken for post-mastectomy change. A parasternal sternalis muscle is a normal variant that can mimic a mass.
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Sternohyoid muscle.note: The most superficial paramedian strap muscle, running from the posterior Manubrium sterni and medial clavicle to the Corpus ossis hyoidei, anterior to sternothyroid and the thyroid gland. Pitfall: a strap muscle thinned or effaced by a goitre does not by itself indicate extrathyroidal invasion.

Sternothyroid muscle.note: Deep strap muscle running from the posterior Manubrium sterni to the Linea obliqua cartilaginis thyreoideae, lying directly on the thyroid lobes, deep and lateral to sternohyoid. Pitfall: unenhanced thyroid is hyperdense, while the muscle is isodense to other muscle; do not mistake a flattened sternothyroid for a rim of thyroid tissue.
landmarks: lm:Oblique line of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

Stomach.note: The fundus sits under the left hemidiaphragm next to the spleen. The lesser curvature faces the lesser omentum and liver, the greater curvature faces the greater omentum and transverse colon, and the posterior wall faces the lesser sac and pancreas. Pitfall: a collapsed antrum or the GEJ can look like a mass or wall thickening. Distend with water before judging.

Straight gyrus (Gyrus rectus).note: The gyrus rectus is the most medial gyrus of the orbital surface. It lies between the interhemispheric fissure and the sulcus olfactorius, above the cribriform plate and the planum sphenoidale. Pitfall: haematoma here is classic for a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm. Do not dismiss it as a contusion or as streak artefact from the anterior cranial fossa.
passing: Orbitofrontal branches of anterior cerebral artery

Straight part of cricothyroid muscle.note: The anterior, more vertical part of cricothyroid, running from the cricoid arch to the inferior border of the thyroid lamina, lateral to the Ligamentum cricothyreoideum medianum. Pitfall: tissue at the cricothyroid membrane level is normal muscle; true subglottic or anterior transglottic spread lies inside the cartilages.

Straight sinus.note: Lies in the falcotentorial junction. It starts where the great cerebral vein and inferior sagittal sinus join and runs back and down to the confluence of sinuses. Pitfall: on non-contrast CT it is normally dense, especially with a high haematocrit. Compare it with the arterial density before calling it a thrombosed 'cord sign'.

Stria medullaris thalami.note: Thin fibre band along the upper medial edge of the thalamus, where the tela choroidea of the third ventricle attaches. It runs backward to the habenula. Habenular calcification is C-shaped and lies a few millimetres in front of the pineal. Do not mistake it for pineal calcification or for a small bleed.

Stria terminalis.note: Not resolvable on CT. It runs in the caudothalamic groove along the floor of the lateral ventricle body and arches through the roof of the temporal horn to the amygdala. Pitfall: the caudothalamic groove is where germinal matrix haemorrhage occurs in preterm infants. Do not confuse it with the thalamostriate vein or subependymal calcification.

Stylohyoid ligament.note: Runs from the tip of the Processus styloideus to the lesser horn of the hyoid, along the lateral oropharyngeal wall next to the carotid arteries. Pitfall: segmental calcification (Eagle syndrome) has pseudo-joints that mimic fractures. Measure the total styloid length (abnormal >30 mm) and report how close it lies to the carotid arteries.
landmarks: lm:Styloid process of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Stylohyoid muscle.note: Runs from the posterior processus styloideus to the junction of the hyoid body and greater horn, parallel to the posterior digastric belly. It splits around the intermediate digastric tendon. Pitfall: an elongated styloid or calcified ligamentum stylohyoideum (Eagle) lies deeper and more medially than the muscle. Do not mistake either for a foreign body.
landmarks: lm:Styloid process of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Stylomandibular ligament.note: A thickening of the deep cervical fascia from the styloid process to the angle and posterior border of the mandible, separating the parotid from the submandibular region. Pitfall: deep-lobe parotid tumours pass through the stylomandibular tunnel into the parapharyngeal space in a dumbbell shape. Do not misread such a mass as primary parapharyngeal.
landmarks: lm:Styloid process of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Stylopharyngeus muscle.note: Runs from the medial base of the processus styloideus, between the internal carotid artery (medial) and the external carotid artery (lateral). It enters the pharynx through the gap between the superior and middle constrictors. Pitfall: the styloid musculature separates the prestyloid parapharyngeal space from the carotid space. Judge the direction of fat displacement to tell where a mass started.
landmarks: lm:Styloid process of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Subacromial bursa.note: Lies deep to the acromion and Ligamentum coracoacromiale, superficial to the supraspinatus tendon, and is usually continuous with the subdeltoid bursa. Pitfall: on CT arthrography, contrast in this bursa is not a normal connection. It means a full-thickness rotator cuff tear.

Subaortic nodes.note: These nodes lie just below the aortic bifurcation, between the common iliac arteries and anterior to L4–L5 and the left common iliac vein. Pitfall: a left common iliac vein compressed or dilated where the right artery crosses it (May–Thurner configuration) mimics a subaortic node.

Subclavian nerve.note: A small branch of the superior trunk (C5–C6). It descends anterior to the plexus and the third part of the A. subclavia, behind the clavicle, to the M. subclavius. Pitfall: it often gives an accessory phrenic nerve, so supraclavicular surgery or a clavicle fracture can cause unexpected hemidiaphragm paresis.

Subclavius muscle.note: It runs from the first costochondral junction to the sulcus musculi subclavii on the underside of the clavicle. It is enclosed by the clavipectoral fascia and lies directly in front of the subclavian vein in the costoclavicular space. Pitfall: the subclavian groove on the clavicle can mimic erosion or fracture, and a hypertrophied muscle can cause venous thoracic outlet compression.
neighbours: Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

Subcostal artery.note: The last parietal branch of the thoracic aorta. It runs below the twelfth rib, behind the kidney and in front of the Musculus quadratus lumborum, passing under the lateral arcuate ligament. Pitfall: it is easily mislabelled as the first lumbar artery or an eleventh intercostal artery. Count from T12 and the twelfth rib, especially when ribs are hypoplastic or there is a transitional vertebra.

Subcutaneous acromial bursa.note: Lies under the skin over the dorsal acromion, superficial to the deltotrapezial aponeurosis, near the acromioclavicular joint. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the deep subacromial bursa. Also rule out a cyst arising from the acromioclavicular joint (geyser sign from a cuff tear).
neighbours: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

Subcutaneous bursa of lateral malleolus.note: Adventitial bursa in the subcutis directly over the lateral malleolus, superficial to the Fascia cruris. Pitfall: distension is often mistaken for fibular tendon-sheath effusion or a soft-tissue hematoma over a fracture; it lies superficial to the Retinaculum fibulare superius.

Subcutaneous bursa of medial malleolus.note: Adventitial bursa in the subcutis over the medial malleolus, superficial to the Fascia cruris and Retinaculum musculorum flexorum. Pitfall: do not confuse it with tibialis posterior tendon-sheath effusion, which lies deep to the retinaculum behind the malleolus.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of tibialis posterior muscle

Subcutaneous bursa of tuberosity of tibi.key: Subcutaneous bursa of tuberosity of tibia
Subcutaneous bursa of tuberosity of tibi.note: Lies in the subcutis over the Tuberositas tibiae, distal to the Bursa subcutanea infrapatellaris and superficial to the Ligamentum patellae insertion. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the deep infrapatellar bursa behind the tendon, and do not report Osgood–Schlatter ossicles as an avulsion fracture.

Subcutaneous calcaneal bursa.note: Lies in the subcutaneous fat behind the distal Tendo calcaneus, at the level of the Tuber calcanei. It is normally not visible. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the Bursa subtendinea calcanea, which lies deep to the tendon in front of the posterosuperior calcaneus; 'pump bump' swelling sits superficial to the tendon.

Subcutaneous infrapatellar bursa.note: Lies in the subcutis in front of the distal patellar ligament, above the Tuberositas tibiae. Pitfall: do not mix it up with the Bursa infrapatellaris profunda, which lies deep to the ligament against the tibia. Fluid in front of the ligament belongs to a superficial bursa, not to Hoffa's fat pad or the joint.
neighbours: Subcutaneous bursa of tuberosity of tibia

Subcutaneous prepatellar bursa.note: This is the most superficial prepatellar layer, between the skin and the anterior surface of the Patella. Pitfall: CT cannot separate the subcutaneous, subfacial and subtendinous layers, so report 'prepatellar bursitis'. It does not communicate with the joint, so do not call it a knee effusion, which collects in the Bursa suprapatellaris.

Subcutaneous trochanteric bursa.note: Lies between the subcutis and the Tractus iliotibialis, over the lateral Trochanter major. Pitfall: superficial fluid here, including a Morel-Lavallée lesion after trauma, is a different thing from deep trochanteric bursitis beneath the gluteal tendons, which involves the gluteus medius/minimus bursae. Report which layer is involved.
neighbours: Trochanteric bursa of gluteus medius muscle
Trochanteric bursa of gluteus minimus muscle

Subdeltoid bursa.note: Lies between the deltoid and the rotator cuff tendons over the Tuberculum majus, usually joined with the subacromial bursa. Pitfall: fluid lateral to the greater tubercle is bursal fluid. Do not mistake it for glenohumeral effusion in the biceps tendon sheath or for deltoid muscle oedema.

Subfacial prepatellar bursa.note: This is the middle prepatellar layer, deep to the superficial fascia and in front of the Patella and quadriceps expansion. Pitfall: on CT it cannot be told apart from the subcutaneous and subtendinous layers, so describe 'prepatellar fluid'. It does not communicate with the knee joint.

Sublingual gland.note: Lies in the sublingual space above the Musculus mylohyoideus, between the Fovea sublingualis of the Mandibula laterally and the Musculus genioglossus medially, with the Ductus submandibularis along its medial side. Pitfall: a plunging ranula passes behind or through the mylohyoid and can be mistaken for a primary submandibular-space lesion.

Submandibular duct.note: Leaves the deep part of the gland, curves around the posterior free border of the Musculus mylohyoideus and runs forward between the Musculus hyoglossus and the sublingual gland to the sublingual caruncle. Pitfall: dental restoration streak artefact or phleboliths can mimic or hide a distal calculus, so check thin bone-window reformats.

Submandibular gland.note: The superficial part fills the submandibular space below the Musculus mylohyoideus, medial to the Mandibula and deep to the Platysma. The deep part wraps around the posterior mylohyoid border. Pitfall: an enlarged level IB node or the Vena facialis next to the gland can look like a gland mass, and atrophy or excision on one side looks like contralateral enlargement.

Submandibular nodes.note: Level IB nodes lie around the submandibular gland, below the Mandibula, lateral to the Musculus mylohyoideus and deep to the Platysma. They are separated from level IA by the anterior belly of the digastric. Pitfall: the submandibular gland itself, or the facial vessels with nodes beside them, can be mistaken for a node mass; identify the gland's density and the vessels first.

Submental artery.note: Arises from the facial artery at the submandibular gland and runs anteriorly on the superficial surface of the Musculus mylohyoideus, beneath the mandible, toward the chin. Pitfall: in axial cross-section, the submental vessels can mimic level IA nodes. Remember the mylohyoid separates the submandibular from the sublingual space.

Submental nodes.note: Level IA nodes lie in the midline triangle between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles, below the Musculus mylohyoideus, deep to the Platysma and behind the mandibular symphysis. Pitfall: these nodes drain both sides and are not assigned a side; a midline cystic lesion here (dermoid, thyroglossal duct cyst) can mimic a necrotic node.

Submental vein.note: The Vena submentalis runs along the outer surface of Musculus mylohyoideus, beside the anterior belly of the digastric and below the mandibular body, and drains into the Vena facialis. Pitfall: in cross-section this small enhancing vessel can look like a level IA submental node. Follow it across consecutive slices.

Subparietal sulcus.note: Continues the Sulcus cinguli posteriorly on the medial surface and separates the Precuneus from the posterior Gyrus cinguli. Pitfall: next to the Falx cerebri, a dense falx or the Pericallosal artery can mimic hyperdense subarachnoid blood in this sulcus.
neighbours: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Posterior dorsal part)

Subscapular artery.note: Largest branch of the third part of the axillary artery, arising at the lower border of subscapularis. It divides into the circumflex scapular artery (through the triangular space) and the thoracodorsal artery (to latissimus dorsi). Pitfall: a common trunk with the posterior circumflex humeral artery is a frequent variant. Do not label that trunk as the main axillary artery.

Subscapular vein.note: The Vena subscapularis runs along the lateral border of the scapula, between subscapularis and serratus anterior, and drains into the axillary vein. It receives the circumflex scapular and thoracodorsal veins. Pitfall: its tributaries in the axillary fat can look like small enhancing axillary nodes in cross-section.

Subscapularis muscle.note: Arises from the fossa subscapularis between the scapula and serratus anterior, then crosses anterior to the capsula articularis to insert on the tuberculum minus. Pitfall: the subtendinous subscapular recess communicates with the glenohumeral joint, so fluid or loose bodies there can look like a cyst or mass.

Subtendinous bursa of iliacus muscle.note: Lies between the iliopsoas tendon and the anterior hip capsule/iliopectineal eminence, lateral to the femoral vessels. Pitfall: when distended, often communicating with the hip joint, it can mimic a cystic groin mass, a lymphocele or a femoral hernia. Trace its neck to the hip joint.

Subtendinous bursa of infraspinatus musc.note: Lies deep to the infraspinatus tendon, between the tendon and the posterior glenohumeral capsule, next to the humeral head. Pitfall: it may connect with the joint. On CT arthrography, filling here can be mistaken for a paralabral cyst or a capsular tear.

Subtendinous bursa of obturator internus.note: Lies deep to the Musculus obturator internus tendon, where the tendon turns around the lesser sciatic notch and crosses the posterior hip capsule between the gemelli. Pitfall: do not confuse obturator internus (posterior, above the gemellus inferior) with obturator externus, whose tendon passes below the femoral neck. The bursa may communicate with the hip joint.

Subtendinous bursa of sartorius muscle.note: Lies at the pes anserinus on the anteromedial proximal tibia, deep to the sartorius and superficial to the Ligamentum collaterale tibiale, below the joint line. Pitfall: anserine fluid can mimic a meniscal cyst, a semimembranosus–tibial collateral ligament bursa or a ruptured Baker cyst. Use its position below the joint line and superficial to the tibial collateral ligament to tell them apart.
neighbours: Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament

Subtendinous bursa of teres major muscle.key: Subtendinous bursa of teres major muscle
Subtendinous bursa of teres major muscle.note: Lies between the teres major and latissimus dorsi tendons near their insertion on the medial lip of the intertubercular groove. Pitfall: a fluid-filled bursa here can be mistaken for an enlarged posterior axillary (subscapular) lymph node.

Subtendinous bursa of tibialis anterior.note: Lies between the distal tibialis anterior tendon and the medial cuneiform at the base of the first metatarsal, on the medial side of the midfoot. Pitfall: a distended bursa can be mistaken for a dorsal ganglion or tendon-sheath effusion. Confirm that it sits beneath the tendon insertion.
neighbours: Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis

Subtendinous bursa of trapezius muscle.note: Lies between the trapezius fibres and the smooth medial end of the Spina scapulae. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the scapulothoracic bursae deep to the serratus anterior, which cause snapping scapula, or with a soft-tissue mass at the medial scapular border.
neighbours: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

Subtendinous bursa of triceps brachii mu.key: Subtendinous bursa of triceps brachii muscle
Subtendinous bursa of triceps brachii mu.note: Lies deep to the triceps tendon, just above its insertion on the olecranon and superficial to the posterior elbow capsule. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the subcutaneous olecranon bursa (much more superficial). Also distinguish it from a raised posterior fat pad caused by joint effusion.

Subtendinous calcaneal bursa.note: This is the retrocalcaneal bursa, between the Tendo calcaneus and the posterosuperior calcaneus, with Kager's fat pad above it. Pitfall: loss of the sharp fat interface or fluid here suggests retrocalcaneal bursitis, often with a Haglund prominence. Do not confuse it with the superficial Bursa subcutanea calcanea, which lies behind the tendon.

Subtendinous prepatellar bursa.note: This is the deepest prepatellar layer, between the quadriceps tendon expansion and the anterior patellar cortex. Pitfall: CT cannot separate it from the subfacial and subcutaneous layers, so do not overcall the layer. Fluid here is extra-articular and is different from a suprapatellar knee effusion.

Sulcus interm_prim-Jensen.note: Jensen's primary intermediate sulcus branches off the Sulcus intraparietalis into the Lobulus parietalis inferior and separates the Gyrus supramarginalis from the Gyrus angularis. Pitfall: it is inconstant and easily confused with the ascending end of the Sulcus temporalis superior.

Superficial anterior cervical nodes.note: These nodes lie superficial to the superficial layer of the investing cervical fascia, deep to the Platysma along the anterior jugular vein, and in front of the infrahyoid muscles. Pitfall: on non-contrast CT the anterior jugular vein seen in cross-section looks like a small node; confirm it is not tubular across slices.

Superficial branch of medial plantar art.key: Superficial branch of medial plantar artery
Superficial branch of medial plantar art.note: Runs distally along the medial border of the first metatarsal, between or within the abductor hallucis and the medial head of the FHB, to the medial side of the hallux. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the deep branch, which runs laterally to join the first plantar metatarsal artery or the arch.
neighbours: Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis

Superficial branch of radial nerve.note: Runs deep to brachioradialis beside the A. radialis. About 8–9 cm above the styloid it emerges between the brachioradialis and ECRL tendons, then crosses superficial to the first extensor compartment. Pitfall: K-wires or plates at the processus styloideus radii and de Quervain release endanger it (Wartenberg syndrome), and it sits next to the cephalic vein.
passing: Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
neighbours: Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Superficial branch of ulnar nerve.note: Arises in Guyon canal, radial to the os pisiforme and superficial to the pisohamate ligament. It supplies palmaris brevis and gives the digital nerves to the fifth and ulnar fourth fingers. Pitfall: the ulnar artery lies right next to it on the radial side; a thrombosed artery (hypothenar hammer) or ganglion can mimic a nerve lesion.
passing: Common palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Superficial dorsal veins of penis.note: Lie in the subcutaneous tissue superficial to Buck's fascia and drain through the external pudendal veins into the great saphenous vein. Pitfall: do not confuse them with the deep dorsal vein, which lies beneath Buck's fascia between the dorsal arteries and drains into the prostatic plexus.

Superficial epigastric artery.note: It arises from the Arteria femoralis just below the Ligamentum inguinale, pierces the cribriform fascia, and runs up through subcutaneous fat over the external oblique towards the umbilicus. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the inferior epigastric artery. That artery comes from the external iliac, runs deep to the rectus abdominis, and is the landmark for rectus sheath haematoma and inguinal hernia type.

Superficial epigastric vein.note: Runs up in the subcutaneous fat of the lower anterior abdominal wall, crosses the inguinal ligament and drains into the vena saphena magna. Pitfall: a dilated, tortuous vein connecting to the lateral thoracic vein (thoracoepigastric collateral) indicates IVC or iliac obstruction. Do not dismiss it as a normal superficial vessel.

Superficial external pudendal artery.note: It arises medially from the Arteria femoralis, pierces the cribriform fascia, and runs medially over the spermatic cord (Ductus deferens) to the pubic and scrotal skin. Pitfall: it crosses close to the saphenofemoral junction. It is easily confused with tributaries of the Vena saphena magna or with the deep external pudendal artery, which runs deep to the fascia lata.

Superficial fibular nerve.note: The nerve runs in the lateral compartment between the fibularis muscles and the extensor digitorum longus, along the anterior intermuscular septum. It pierces the fascia cruris in the distal third of the leg and divides into the medial and intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerves. Pitfall: where it exits the fascia it is at risk from distal fibular plating and anterolateral ankle portals.
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

Superficial head of flexor pollicis brev.key: Superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis
Superficial head of flexor pollicis brev.note: Arises from the flexor retinaculum and trapezium tubercle, medial to abductor pollicis brevis, and inserts via the radial sesamoid. Pitfall: the FPL tendon runs between the superficial and deep heads, so the fluid-filled FPL sheath can look like a cleft or tear in the muscle.
neighbours: Deep head of flexor pollicis brevis
Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus
Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand

Superficial head of pronator teres.note: Arises from the medial epicondyle, forms the medial border of the fossa cubitalis and inserts on the lateral midshaft of the radius. The median nerve passes between its superficial and deep heads. Pitfall: the ulnar artery passes deep to the deep head, not between the heads; do not swap the two when describing pronator syndrome.
neighbours: Radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Superficial investing cervical fascia.note: This layer surrounds the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles and forms the roof of the posterior triangle. It attaches to the mandible, mastoid process, external occipital protuberance, hyoid, clavicle and acromion. It cannot be seen as a separate layer on CT. Pitfall: the V. iugularis externa lies superficial to it and is not part of the carotid space.

Superficial lateral cervical nodes.note: These nodes lie along the external jugular vein, superficial to the Musculus sternocleidomastoideus and deep to the Platysma, and extend toward the posterior triangle in front of the Trapezius. Pitfall: in the posterior triangle, the brachial plexus trunks between the scalene muscles and the transverse cervical vessels can look like small nodes; follow their tubular course.

Superficial layer of temporal fascia.note: This layer runs from the superior temporal line to the lateral lip of the zygomatic arch and covers the temporalis muscle. The superficial temporal fat pad lies between the superficial and deep layers. Pitfall: fluid or blood in this fat pad is not subgaleal. Do not mistake normal fat-pad asymmetry for temporalis atrophy or a tumour.
passing: Frontal branch of superficial temporal artery
landmarks: lm:Squamous part of temporal bone|Temporal bone
lm:Zygomatic process of temporal bone (tip)|Temporal bone
lm:Temporal surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone

Superficial palmar arch.note: Lies deep to the palmar aponeurosis and superficial to the flexor tendons and digital nerves, at the mid-metacarpal level distal to the deep arch. It is fed mainly by the Arteria ulnaris beyond the hook of the hamate. Pitfall: an incomplete arch is a common normal variant and does not mean occlusion.
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Superficial parotid nodes.note: Lie on the surface of the Glandula parotidea, under the superficial investing fascia, over the masseter and mandibular ramus. Pitfall: a node here can look like a small parotid tumour (Warthin tumour, pleomorphic adenoma). Report where it lies relative to the gland surface.

Superficial part of masseter.note: Runs from the zygomatic process of the maxilla and the anterior zygomatic arch to the angle and lateral ramus. The parotid overlaps its posterior border and the Ductus parotideus crosses its surface. Pitfall: accessory parotid tissue along the duct can mimic a buccal-space mass. Match its attenuation to the parotid.

Superficial part of tibial collateral li.key: Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament
Superficial part of tibial collateral li.note: Long band running from the medial epicondyle to the tibia about 5–6 cm below the joint line, deep to the pes anserinus. Pitfall: calcification at its femoral origin (Pellegrini–Stieda) indicates an old injury. Do not mistake it for an acute avulsion or a loose body.
neighbours: Deep part of tibial collateral ligament

Superficial popliteal nodes.note: Lie at the junction of the V. saphena parva with the popliteal vein, in the superficial popliteal fat. Pitfall: the saphenopopliteal junction or a varix of the small saphenous vein looks like a node. Follow the vein toward the calf.

Superficial temporal artery.note: Terminal ECA branch. It leaves the parotid, ascends anterior to the tragus and posterior to the mandibular condyle, and runs superficial to the temporal fascia before dividing into frontal and parietal branches. Pitfall: it is subcutaneous, not deep temporal. A post-traumatic STA pseudoaneurysm can look like a scalp hematoma or nodule.
passing: Frontal branch of superficial temporal artery

Superficial temporal veins.note: Run down in the scalp over the temporal fascia, cross the zygomatic arch root in front of the tragus and the TMJ capsule, and enter the parotid to form the retromandibular vein. Pitfall: in the pre-auricular area, the vein seen end-on can look like an enlarged pre-auricular node. Follow it across slices next to the superficial temporal artery.

Superficial transverse metacarpal ligame.note: Ligamentum metacarpeum transversum superficiale (the natatory ligament) is a transverse band in the web spaces of the distal palm, superficial to the digital neurovascular bundles. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the ligamentum metacarpeum transversum profundum, which joins the MCP palmar plates deep to the lumbricals and the neurovascular bundles.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
neighbours: Synovial sheaths of digits of hand
Proximal phalanx of second finger of hand

Superficial transverse metatarsal ligame.note: Transverse fibres of the plantar aponeurosis lying in the subcutaneous tissue at the level of the metatarsal heads. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the Ligamentum metatarseum transversum profundum, which joins the plantar plates. An interdigital (Morton) neuroma lies plantar to the deep ligament.

Superficial venous palmar arch.note: The Arcus venosus palmaris superficialis lies distal to the flexor retinaculum, deep to the palmar aponeurosis and superficial to the flexor tendons and the digital branches of the median nerve. Pitfall: it can be confused with the deep arch, which lies more proximal at the metacarpal bases and deep to the flexor tendons.
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Superior anorectal artery.note: Terminal continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery. It crosses the left common iliac vessels and descends in the sigmoid mesocolon and then the mesorectum, behind the rectum. Pitfall: mesorectal nodes along it are N-stage relevant in rectal cancer. Do not dismiss them as vessels seen in cross-section.

Superior basal vein of left lung.key: Superior basal vein of left lung
Superior basal vein of left lung.note: Vena basalis superior pulmonis sinistri drains the anterior basal segments of the left lower lobe and joins the Vena pulmonalis sinistra inferior. Pitfall: tracing it is how you tell vein from artery. It runs into the left atrium, while the basal arteries run with the bronchi back to the Arteria pulmonalis sinistra; mixing them up causes false PE calls.
passing: Inferior basal vein of left lung
neighbours: Lateral basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BIX)
Posterior basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BX)

Superior basal vein of right lung.key: Superior basal vein of right lung
Superior basal vein of right lung.note: Vena basalis superior pulmonis dextri drains the anterior and lateral basal segments and joins the Vena pulmonalis dextra inferior. Pitfall: the basal segmental arteries next to it run with the bronchi. Trace each vessel to the left atrium or to the Arteria lobaris inferior before calling a filling defect.
passing: Inferior basal vein of right lung
Anterior basal segmental artery of right lung
Lateral basal segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Lateral basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BIX)
Medial basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BVII)

Superior bursa of biceps femoris muscle.key: Superior bursa of biceps femoris muscle
Superior bursa of biceps femoris muscle.note: Lies at the ischial tuberosity, deep to the common origin of the long head of the biceps femoris and the semitendinosus. Pitfall: it lies right next to the ischiogluteal bursa (Bursa ischiadica musculi glutei maximi), and fluid here can mimic a hamstring origin tear or a cystic mass. The sciatic nerve runs just lateral to it.
neighbours: Sciatic bursa of gluteus maximus muscle

Superior cerebellar artery.note: It arises just below the basilar tip, runs below the Tentorium cerebelli and around the Pons and Mesencephalon, and supplies the superior cerebellum and vermis. CN III separates it from the PCA. Pitfall: its loop touching the trigeminal root entry zone is a common neurovascular-conflict finding in trigeminal neuralgia but is often seen in asymptomatic people.
passing: Medial pontine branches of basilar artery

Superior cerebellar peduncle.note: The Pedunculi cerebellares superiores form the lateral walls of the upper fourth ventricle. They ascend beneath the Colliculi inferiores and decussate in the midbrain tegmentum. Pitfall: CT cannot separate them from the pontine tegmentum. The trochlear nerve, which exits dorsally just below the colliculi, cannot be seen on CT.

Superior colliculus.note: Upper part of the tectum, just below the Glandula pinealis and Commissura posterior, facing the quadrigeminal cistern. Pitfall: normal pineal calcification is common in adults. Calcification in a young child, or a pineal mass over 1 cm pressing on the colliculus (Parinaud syndrome), is abnormal.

Superior diaphragmatic nodes.note: These nodes lie on the thoracic surface of the Diaphragma. There are anterior (cardiophrenic), lateral (at the phrenic nerve entry) and posterior (retrocrural) groups. Pitfall: the epicardial fat pad, or partial volume of the IVC or hepatic veins, can mimic nodes. Cardiophrenic nodes larger than 5 mm short axis suggest spread from the abdomen or ovaries.

Superior epigastric artery.note: Medial terminal branch of the A. thoracica interna. It passes through the sternocostal triangle (Larrey) and runs behind the M. rectus abdominis inside its sheath, where it anastomoses with the A. epigastrica inferior. Pitfall: after trauma or anticoagulation, a rectus sheath haematoma from this vessel can be mistaken for an abdominal wall mass.

Superior epigastric veins.note: These veins continue the venae thoracicae internae through the sternocostal triangle into the rectus sheath. They run behind the musculus rectus abdominis and anastomose with the vena epigastrica inferior. Pitfall: when they are prominent, consider a cavo-caval collateral from SVC or IVC obstruction rather than a normal variant.

Superior extensor retinaculum of ankle.note: Band between the anterior borders of the distal tibia and fibula, just above the malleoli. It holds the extensor tendons and the anterior tibial vessels and deep fibular nerve beneath it. Pitfall: the superficial fibular nerve runs superficial to the retinaculum, not under it. Only tibialis anterior usually has a tendon sheath at this level.

Superior fibular retinaculum.note: Runs from the posterolateral lateral malleolus to the lateral calcaneus and holds the fibularis tendons in the Sulcus malleolaris fibulae. Pitfall: a thin cortical flake off the lateral malleolar rim (fleck sign) is an avulsion of this retinaculum and implies fibular tendon dislocation. It is not an ATFL or CFL avulsion.
neighbours: Common tendon sheath of fibularis muscles

Superior frontal gyrus.note: The gyrus frontalis superior runs from the frontal pole back to the superior precentral sulcus. Its lateral border is the sulcus frontalis superior; on the medial side it extends down to the sulcus cinguli beside the falx. Pitfall: a dense superior sagittal sinus or falx can mimic parafalcine SAH or subdural haematoma. Its parasagittal strip is the ACA–MCA watershed zone.
neighbours: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle anterior part)

Superior frontal sulcus.note: The sulcus frontalis superior runs front to back, separating the superior frontal gyrus from the middle frontal gyrus. Its back end meets the superior precentral sulcus. Pitfall: it is often interrupted. A break in it can lead you to follow the wrong sulcus to the T-junction and then mislabel the central sulcus.

Superior gemellus muscle.note: Arises from the Spina ischiadica just below the piriformis and joins the upper border of the obturator internus tendon to the trochanteric fossa. Pitfall: on CT it is inseparable from the obturator internus tendon. The internal pudendal vessels hook around the nearby ischial spine and should not be mistaken for nodes.

Superior glenohumeral ligament.note: Runs from the superior glenoid next to the biceps anchor to the fovea above the lesser tubercle. With the ligamentum coracohumerale it forms the biceps pulley in the rotator interval. Pitfall: pulley lesions are invisible on plain CT; suspect them when the biceps long head is medially subluxed out of the sulcus.

Superior gluteal artery.note: Exits through the suprapiriform greater sciatic foramen at the greater sciatic notch, then runs between the Musculus gluteus medius and minimus with the superior gluteal nerve. Pitfall: it is fixed against bone at the notch, so it is the most frequently injured pelvic artery in posterior ring fractures. Do not label an infrapiriform vessel as this artery.
passing: Posterior division of internal iliac artery

Superior gluteal nerve.note: The nerve (L4–S1) is the only nerve that leaves through the suprapiriform foramen, together with the superior gluteal artery. It then runs between the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus. Pitfall: do not swap the suprapiriform and infrapiriform compartments. Superior gluteal artery pseudoaneurysm after pelvic fracture can mimic a nerve sheath tumour. Denervation shows as fatty atrophy of gluteus medius and minimus.

Superior gluteal nodes.note: These nodes run along the superior gluteal vessels at the suprapiriform part of the greater sciatic notch, anterior to the sacroiliac joint.
