Pitfall: the superior gluteal vein in cross-section, a gluteal artery aneurysm or the lumbosacral trunk can mimic a node. Contrast phase and continuity settle it.

Superior gluteal veins.note: Leave the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis (suprapiriform), running against the greater sciatic notch to the plane deep to gluteus medius. Pitfall: fractures through the notch can injure these vessels. Do not confuse them with the inferior gluteal vessels, which emerge below piriformis next to the sciatic nerve.
passing: Posterior division of internal iliac artery

Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscl.key: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscl.note: Runs from the infratemporal surface of the greater sphenoid wing to the TMJ disc and capsule, sitting just above the inferior head. Pitfall: on CT the two heads cannot be separated, and the fibres attached to the disc blend with the capsule. Do not read them as an effusion or mass in front of the condyle.
passing: Accessory branch of middle meningeal artery
neighbours: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle

Superior labial artery.note: Arises from the facial artery at the oral commissure and runs tortuously in the upper lip deep to the Musculus orbicularis oris. It gives septal branches to the anterior nasal septum. Pitfall: normal lip enhancement and dental streak artifact can mimic a labial mass. It also supplies Kiesselbach's area, a source of anterior epistaxis.

Superior labial vein.note: The Vena labialis superior runs in the upper lip, deep to Musculus orbicularis oris and in front of the maxillary alveolar process and upper incisors and canine. It drains into the Vena facialis near the modiolus. Pitfall: its enhancement can be mistaken for lip or gingival inflammation, especially when dental streak artefact is present.

Superior lateral brachial cutaneous nerv.note: The end of the posterior branch of the axillary nerve. It winds around the posterior border of the deltoid to the skin over the lower deltoid (the 'regimental badge' area). Pitfall: the correct TA term is Nervus cutaneus brachii lateralis superior; the Latin name 'posterioris femoris' given for it is wrong and belongs to the thigh nerve.
neighbours: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

Superior lateral genicular artery.note: It winds laterally around the Os femoris just above the lateral condyle, deep to the biceps femoris and under the lateral intermuscular septum, into the vastus lateralis and the Rete patellare. Pitfall: it is at risk in supracondylar fractures, plating and lateral retinacular release. A blush there after surgery suggests injury to it.

Superior lingular artery of left lung.key: Superior lingular artery of left lung
Superior lingular artery of left lung.note: A4 runs centrally with BIV in the bronchovascular bundle of the upper lingula, just below the left superior lobar bronchus. Pitfall: the Vena anterior pulmonis sinistri runs between segments and can be mistaken for the artery. Also, a nearby intrapulmonary node can look like a vessel seen end-on, so scroll through adjacent slices.
passing: Inferior lingular artery of left lung
Anterior segmental artery of left lung
neighbours: Superior lingular segmental bronchus of left lung (BIV)
Inferior lingular segmental bronchus of left lung (BV)

Superior lingular segmental bronchus of.key: Superior lingular segmental bronchus of left lung (BIV)
Superior lingular segmental bronchus of.note: Upper branch of the lingular bronchus. It runs anterolaterally within the left upper lobe, above BV and in front of the oblique fissure. Pitfall: the lingular segments split superior/inferior, unlike the lateral/medial split of the right middle lobe, so do not mix up the BIV labels between sides.
passing: Superior lingular artery of left lung
Superior lingular vein of left lung
Inferior lingular artery of left lung
neighbours: Inferior lingular segmental bronchus of left lung (BV)

Superior lingular vein of left lung.key: Superior lingular vein of left lung
Superior lingular vein of left lung.note: Vena lingularis superior pulmonis sinistri drains segment S4 and joins the Vena lingularis next to the left heart border. Pitfall: it sits right next to the epicardial Vena magna cordis and the Ventriculus sinister. Do not mistake the pulmonary vein for a cardiac vein, or pericardial fat for a lingular lesion.
passing: Inferior lingular vein of left lung
neighbours: Superior lingular segmental bronchus of left lung (BIV)

Superior lobar artery of right lung.key: Superior lobar artery of right lung
Superior lobar artery of right lung.note: The truncus anterior is the first branch of the right pulmonary artery. It lies in front of the right main and superior lobar bronchi and behind the Vena cava superior. Pitfall: A2 often comes from a separate ascending branch of the interlobar artery. Do not count that branch as an accessory vessel or a node.
passing: Apical segmental artery of right lung
Anterior segmental artery of right lung

Superior lobe of left lung.note: The left upper lobe includes the lingula and is bounded posteroinferiorly by the oblique fissure. The left lung has no horizontal fissure. Medially it touches the aortic arch, aortopulmonary window and left heart border. Pitfall: the lingula belongs to the upper lobe, so never call lingular disease "left middle lobe". The Vena intercostalis superior sinistra can mimic a node.
passing: Inferior lingular artery of left lung
Inferior lingular vein of left lung
neighbours: Superior lingular segmental bronchus of left lung (BIV)
Inferior lingular segmental bronchus of left lung (BV)

Superior lobe of right lung.note: The right upper lobe lies above the horizontal fissure and in front of the upper oblique fissure. Its apex rises above the first rib into the thoracic inlet. Pitfall: an azygos fissure variant forms an accessory azygos lobe and can mimic a fissural mass or bulla wall. Apical pleural thickening is usually benign.

Superior medial genicular artery.note: Arises from the a. poplitea and winds around the medial femoral metaphysis just above the medial condyle, deep to the adductor magnus tendon and m. vastus medialis, and ends in the rete patellare. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the descending genicular artery, which comes from the a. femoralis in the adductor canal.

Superior mesenteric artery.note: Arises from the front of the Aorta abdominalis at L1 and passes behind the pancreatic neck. It crosses in front of the Vena renalis sinistra and the third part of the Duodenum, with the Vena mesenterica superior on its right. Pitfall: an SMV lying left of the SMA suggests malrotation.

Superior mesenteric vein.note: Lies right of the Arteria mesenterica superior, anterior to the uncinate process and third part of the duodenum, and joins the splenic vein behind the pancreatic neck. Pitfall: an SMV lying left of or anterior to the SMA (reversed relationship) suggests intestinal malrotation. Do not dismiss it as normal variation.

Superior oblique muscle.note: Arises above the optic canal and runs along the superomedial orbital wall to the trochlea at the fovea trochlearis. From there its tendon turns posterolaterally under the superior rectus. Pitfall: calcification of the trochlea is a common normal finding in older patients. Do not mistake it for a foreign body or orbital fracture fragment.
landmarks: lm:Orbital surface of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Superior occipital gyri.note: Dorsal occipital convexity gyri that continue the Superior parietal lobule behind the Parieto-occipital sulcus, next to the falx and the lambdoid region. Pitfall: the parieto-occipital sulcus is mainly a medial-surface sulcus, so the parietal–occipital border on the convexity is uncertain on axial CT. This lobar boundary falls in the PCA–MCA watershed.

Superior ophthalmic vein.note: Forms near the trochlea from the vena angularis, runs posterolaterally beneath the musculus rectus superior and above the optic nerve, and exits through the superior orbital fissure into the sinus cavernosus. Pitfall: mild asymmetry is normal, but a markedly enlarged vein with proptosis suggests a carotid-cavernous fistula or cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Superior pancreatic nodes.note: Nodi pancreatici superiores lie along the splenic artery on the upper border of the pancreatic body and tail, posterior to the stomach. Pitfall: the tortuous splenic artery, seen in cross-section, mimics a chain of nodes; trace it on arterial-phase or MIP images.

Superior pancreaticoduodenal nodes.note: Nodi pancreaticoduodenales superiores lie in the groove between the pancreatic head and the first/second duodenal parts, near the distal bile duct. Pitfall: groove pancreatitis, duodenal diverticula or the gastroduodenal artery can mimic nodes in the pancreaticoduodenal groove.

Superior parathyroid gland.note: Lies on the posterior surface of the upper or mid thyroid lobe near the cricothyroid junction, in the tracheo-oesophageal groove. An enlarged gland can sink into the retro- or paraoesophageal space. Pitfall: an exophytic posterior thyroid nodule or the Zuckerkandl tubercle looks identical, so look for a fat plane and early washout.

Superior parietal lobule.note: Dorsomedial parietal convexity between the Postcentral sulcus anteriorly, the Intraparietal sulcus laterally and the Parieto-occipital sulcus posteriorly, continuous medially with the Precuneus. Pitfall: thin convexity subarachnoid haemorrhage or a subdural collection near the vertex is lost in partial volume with the Parietal bone. Use a subdural window and coronal reformats.
passing: Parietal branches of middle cerebral artery

Superior petrosal sinus.note: Runs along the upper ridge of the petrous temporal bone in the attached tentorial edge, from the back of the cavernous sinus to where the transverse sinus meets the sigmoid sinus. It passes over the trigeminal nerve at the entrance to Meckel cave. Pitfall: streak artifact from the petrous ridge can mimic subdural blood along the tentorium.
landmarks: lm:Petrous part of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Superior pharyngeal constrictor.note: Hangs from the tuberculum pharyngeum by the pharyngobasilar fascia and attaches anteriorly to the pterygomandibular raphe. The palatine tonsil lies medial to it and the parapharyngeal fat lateral. Pitfall: an asymmetric, collapsed lateral pharyngeal recess can look like a nasopharyngeal mass. Do not confuse the lateral retropharyngeal (Rouvière) node with longus capitis.

Superior phrenic arteries.note: These are small paired branches of the distal thoracic aorta. They run to the posterior upper (thoracic) surface of the Diaphragma, below the basal lung lobes, and are usually too small to see on CT. Pitfall: do not confuse them with the Arteriae phrenicae inferiores. Those arise from the abdominal aorta or coeliac trunk and are the usual non-bronchial and hepatic collateral feeders.

Superior pubic ligament.note: Spans the pubic crests and tubercles across the upper symphysis and blends with the rectus abdominis/adductor aponeurosis. Pitfall: this upper margin is where to measure vertical symphyseal step-off. Asymmetry from patient rotation can mimic subluxation, so check the obturator foramina for symmetry.

Superior rectus muscle.note: Runs from the upper anulus tendineus communis, beneath the levator and above the optic nerve, to the superior globe. The superior ophthalmic vein crosses beneath it from medial to lateral. Pitfall: on axial images partial volume with the orbital roof mimics a thickened muscle, so use coronal. An enlarged superior ophthalmic vein here suggests a carotid-cavernous fistula.

Superior sagittal sinus.note: Triangular in cross-section, it lies in the attached upper edge of the falx cerebri. It runs from the frontal crest along the sagittal suture to the confluence at the internal occipital protuberance. Pitfall: arachnoid granulations or a split confluence can mimic the 'empty delta' sign. Normal dense blood in neonates or polycythaemia can mimic a thrombosed sinus.
landmarks: lm:Sagittal border of parietal bone|Parietal bone

Superior salivatory nucleus.note: Lies in the caudal pontine tegmentum, dorsal to the facial motor nucleus. Its fibres leave with the nervus intermedius of CN VII. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the Nucleus salivatorius inferior. The superior nucleus supplies the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands; the inferior supplies the parotid through CN IX.

Superior segmental artery of left lung.key: Superior segmental artery of left lung
Superior segmental artery of left lung.note: The first posterior branch of the left interlobar artery, supplying segment VI and running with bronchus BVI just below the major fissure. Pitfall: it often arises at the same level as the lingular arteries. Do not assign it to the upper lobe, and do not count duplicated origins as extra masses.
passing: Posterior basal segmental artery of left lung
Lateral basal segmental artery of left lung
Medial basal segmental artery of left lung
neighbours: Superior segmental bronchus of left lung (BVI)

Superior segmental artery of right lung.key: Superior segmental artery of right lung
Superior segmental artery of right lung.note: A6 leaves the back of the interlobar artery, about opposite the middle lobar artery, and runs posteriorly with BVI into the apex of the lower lobe. Pitfall: A6 may be duplicated, and the posterior ascending branch to the upper lobe (A2) can look like it. Identify each vessel by the bronchus it follows.
passing: Inferior lobar artery of right lung
Middle lobar artery of right lung
Lateral segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Superior segmental bronchus of right lung (BVI)

Superior segmental bronchus of left lung.key: Superior segmental bronchus of left lung (BVI)
Superior segmental bronchus of left lung.note: First branch of the Bronchus lobaris inferior sinister. It runs posteriorly into the superior segment of the lower lobe, just behind the oblique fissure. Pitfall: an accessory subsuperior bronchus arising lower down the basal trunk can be mistaken for BVI, so trace the origin on MPR.
passing: Superior segmental artery of left lung
neighbours: Medial basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BVII)

Superior segmental bronchus of right lun.key: Superior segmental bronchus of right lung (BVI)
Superior segmental bronchus of right lun.note: Arises posteriorly from the right lower lobe bronchus at or just below the middle lobe origin. It runs posteriorly into the superior segment, which reaches high behind the oblique fissure. Pitfall: posterior upper opacities may lie in this segment rather than the upper lobe, so localise the fissure on sagittal MPR.
passing: Superior segmental artery of right lung
neighbours: Medial basal segmental bronchus of right lung (BVII)

Superior semilunar lobule.note: The Lobulus semilunaris superior lies above the horizontal fissure along the posterolateral margin of the cerebellum. It sits under the tentorium and against the Sinus transversus. Pitfall: the occipital lobe lies just above the tentorium, so lesions can be placed on the wrong side of it. A hyperdense transverse sinus can mimic a tentorial subdural haematoma.

Superior subscapular nerve.note: Arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus (C5–C6) and enters the upper subscapularis on the costal surface of the scapula. Pitfall: it is a brachial plexus branch, not a lumbar plexus branch despite its catalog placement, and CT cannot resolve it; report subscapularis denervation atrophy instead.

Superior tarsus.note: Dense fibrous plate of the upper eyelid. It lies deep to Pars palpebralis musculi orbicularis oculi, receives the Levator palpebrae superioris aponeurosis and faces the cornea across the conjunctival sac. Pitfall: on CT the tarsus, orbicularis and levator aponeurosis merge into one lid band, so partial volume of a closed lid can look like lid thickening.

Superior temporal gyrus (Lateral part).note: Uppermost temporal gyrus forming the lower lip of the Sulcus lateralis, with the Superior temporal sulcus below. Its dorsal surface carries the Transverse temporal gyri and Planum temporale. Pitfall: hyperdense M2/M3 branches in the Sylvian fissure (dot sign) may be mistaken for gyral haemorrhage. Partial volume with the sphenoid greater wing also mimics anterior temporal hyperdensity.
passing: Temporal branches of middle cerebral artery
Parietal branches of middle cerebral artery
landmarks: lm:Temporal surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
neighbours: Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci*)

Superior temporal sulcus.note: Long sulcus between the superior and middle temporal gyri, running parallel to the Sulcus lateralis. Its upturned posterior end is capped by the Angular gyrus. Pitfall: on axial CT it is easily mistaken for the Sylvian fissure. The fissure is deeper, holds MCA branches and leads medially to the insula.

Superior thyroid vein.note: Leaves the upper pole of the thyroid lobe, runs laterally across the common carotid artery, and drains into the vena jugularis interna or the common facial vein. Pitfall: a prominent vein at the upper pole can be mistaken for an exophytic nodule or a small node. The external laryngeal nerve runs next to the upper-pole vessels.

Superior tracheobronchial nodes.note: These nodes lie in the angle between the Trachea and each main bronchus (lower paratracheal 4R/4L). On the left they are just below the Arcus aortae. Pitfall: do not confuse them with the Nodi tracheobronchiales inferiores (subcarinal, station 7), which lie below the carina. Also check laterality against the left tracheal wall.

Superior transverse scapular ligament.note: Bridges the Incisura scapulae medial to the coracoid base. The suprascapular nerve passes below it and the artery and vein pass above. Pitfall: an ossified ligament turns the notch into a scapular foramen. This is a normal variant that can predispose to nerve entrapment. Do not mistake it for a fracture fragment.

Superior trunk of brachial plexus.note: Formed by C5 and C6 at Erb's point, lateral to the scalene gap in the posterior cervical triangle above the inferior belly of omohyoid. It gives off the suprascapular and subclavian nerves. Pitfall: posterior triangle lymph nodes lie next to the trunk. Nodes are ovoid and focal, while plexus elements are tubular and continuous across slices.
passing: Anterior division of superior trunk of brachial plexus
Posterior division of superior trunk of brachial plexus

Superior ulnar collateral artery.note: Arises from the mid-brachial artery and follows the ulnar nerve through the septum intermusculare mediale. It runs on the medial head of triceps to pass behind the epicondylus medialis and joins the posterior ulnar recurrent artery. Pitfall: it lies beside the ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel. Do not report the vessel as a thickened nerve or a soft-tissue nodule.

Superior vein of left lung.note: Vena superior pulmonis sinistri is the superior segmental vein (S6) of the lower lobe and drains into the Vena pulmonalis sinistra inferior. Pitfall: despite its name it does not belong to the Vena pulmonalis sinistra superior. Do not confuse it with the nearby Arteria segmentalis superior, which runs next to bronchus BVI.
passing: Superior segmental artery of left lung
Superior basal vein of left lung
neighbours: Superior segmental bronchus of left lung (BVI)
Anterior basal segmental bronchus of left lung (BVIII)

Superior vein of right lung.note: Vena superior pulmonis dextri is the superior segmental vein (S6) of the right lower lobe and drains into the Vena pulmonalis dextra inferior. Pitfall: despite its name it is not part of the right superior pulmonary vein. It can enter the left atrium through a separate ostium, a variant that matters before ablation.
passing: Superior segmental artery of right lung
Inferior lobar artery of right lung
Superior basal vein of right lung
neighbours: Superior segmental bronchus of right lung (BVI)

Superior vena cava.note: Formed where the two brachiocephalic veins meet behind the first right costal cartilage. It runs down to the right of the Aorta ascendens, in front of the right pulmonary artery, to the right atrium, and the azygos arch joins its back wall. Pitfall: unopacified inflow can mimic a thrombus. A persistent left SVC is a normal variant.

Superolateral superficial inguinal nodes.note: Horizontal chain just below and parallel to the Ligamentum inguinale, lateral to the femoral vessels, in the subcutaneous fat. Pitfall: these nodes drain the buttock and lower abdominal wall, not only the leg. Do not mistake the superficial circumflex iliac or superficial epigastric vessels for nodes.

Superomedial superficial inguinal nodes.note: Lie below the medial part of the Ligamentum inguinale, close to the spermatic cord and the pubic tubercle. They drain the perineum, external genitalia and anal canal. Pitfall: the spermatic cord or an inguinal hernia can look like a node mass. Trace the Ductus deferens through the canal.

Supinator.note: Wraps around the proximal third of the radius, from the crista supinatoria ulnae and the annular/radial collateral ligaments to the radial neck and shaft. The posterior interosseous nerve passes between its two layers under the arcade of Frohse. Pitfall: radial neck fractures and Monteggia lesions put the nerve at risk. Displacement of the supinator fat plane is an indirect fracture sign.

Supra-orbital artery.note: Runs under the orbital roof above the musculus levator palpebrae superioris and leaves through the supraorbital notch or foramen to the forehead. Pitfall: the notch or foramen is a normal variant (sometimes bilateral and asymmetric). Do not report it as a fracture of the supraorbital rim or anterior wall of the sinus frontalis.
passing: Frontal branch of superficial temporal artery

Supraclavicular nodes.note: These nodes lie in the supraclavicular fossa above the clavicle, next to the jugulosubclavian venous confluence and just above the pleural dome. Pitfall: partial volume of the lung apex or pleura, or unopacified venous confluences, can mimic a node. Also note that Virchow's node is typically left-sided, not right.

Supramarginal gyrus.note: Anterior part of the inferior parietal lobule that arches around the upturned posterior end of the Sulcus lateralis. It lies behind the Postcentral sulcus, below the Intraparietal sulcus and in front of the Angular gyrus. Pitfall: it is easily confused with the Angular gyrus, which caps the Superior temporal sulcus instead. Hyperdense M3 branches in the posterior Sylvian fissure can mimic gyral haemorrhage.
passing: Parietal branches of middle cerebral artery

Suprapatellar bursa.note: Lies between the quadriceps tendon/vastus intermedius and the prefemoral fat on the distal femur, and normally communicates with the knee joint. Pitfall: a fat–fluid level here (lipohaemarthrosis) means an intra-articular fracture until proven otherwise. A suprapatellar plica can partition the bursa and mimic a cystic mass.

Suprarenal gland.note: The right gland lies above the upper pole of the kidney, posterior to the IVC, between the bare area of the liver and the right diaphragmatic crus. Normal limbs are about 5 mm thick. Pitfall: the upper renal pole, vessels, a lobulated liver contour or, on the left, a gastric diverticulum can mimic an adrenal nodule.

Suprascapular artery.note: It crosses the M. scalenus anterior and runs behind the Clavicula to the scapular notch. Unlike the nerve, it passes ABOVE the Lig. transversum superius scapulae, then supplies the Mm. supraspinatus and infraspinatus. Pitfall: dilated suprascapular veins or a varix at the notch can mimic a ganglion cyst compressing the N. suprascapularis.

Suprascapular nerve.note: Passes through the suprascapular notch below the Lig. transversum superius scapulae (the artery runs above it), then through the spinoglenoid notch under the inferior ligament. Pitfall: a paralabral cyst at the spinoglenoid notch denervates only infraspinatus. An ossified superior ligament turns the notch into a foramen and is not a fracture.

Suprascapular vein.note: This vein runs behind the clavicle with the a. suprascapularis, passes over the lig. transversum scapulae superius into the fossa supraspinata, and drains into the external jugular vein. Pitfall: the artery and vein pass above the ligament, while the n. suprascapularis passes below it through the incisura scapulae. An ossified ligament turns the notch into a foramen and can compress the nerve.

Supraspinatus muscle.note: Fills the fossa supraspinata deep to the trapezius, then passes beneath the acromion and acromioclavicular joint to the superior facet of the tuberculum majus. Pitfall: calcific tendinopathy above the tuberculum majus looks like an avulsed fracture fragment. Check whether the cortex is intact and whether the density has a trabecular pattern.

Supraspinous ligament.note: Subcutaneous cord joining the tips of the processus spinosi from C7 to about L3–L4. It continues cranially as the ligamentum nuchae and lies dorsal to the ligamenta interspinalia. Pitfall: it is normally thin or absent at L4–S1, so a missing ligament there is not a tear. In flexion injuries, look for a widened interspinous gap instead.

Supratrochlear artery.note: A terminal branch of the ophthalmic artery. It leaves the superomedial orbit next to the trochlea and climbs the medial forehead under the musculus corrugator supercilii. Pitfall: trochlear calcification is a common normal variant with age. Do not call it a foreign body or orbital-roof fracture fragment.

Supratrochlear nodes.note: The epitrochlear nodes lie in the subcutaneous fat above the medial epicondyle, next to the basilic vein. They sit superficial to the medial intermuscular septum and the origin of the flexor–pronator muscles. Pitfall: do not mistake the ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel (posterior to the epicondyle) or the basilic vein for a node.
passing: Posterior branch of medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve

Supreme intercostal artery.note: Descends behind the apical pleura, in front of the necks of the first and second ribs, and gives rise to the first two posterior intercostal arteries. Pitfall: in cross-section this small paravertebral apical vessel can mimic a pleural nodule or apical pleural thickening.

Sural communicating branch of common fib.key: Sural communicating branch of common fibular nerve
Sural communicating branch of common fib.note: This branch leaves the common fibular nerve and runs over the lateral head of gastrocnemius. It joins the medial sural cutaneous nerve to form the nervus suralis next to the vena saphena parva. Pitfall: the level where it joins varies, and it may not join at all. CT cannot separate it from the small saphenous vein.

Sural nerve.note: Descends lateral to the Tendo calcaneus with the Vena saphena parva. It passes behind the lateral malleolus, superficial to the fibular tendons and retinacula, then along the lateral side of the fifth metatarsal. Pitfall: the nerve is invisible on CT, so use the small saphenous vein as its marker. It is at risk from approaches to the calcaneus and the fifth metatarsal base.
passing: Sural communicating branch of common fibular nerve

Suspensory ligament of eyeball.note: Lockwood's hammock under the globe, formed from Tenon's capsule and the sheaths of the inferior rectus and inferior oblique. It attaches to the lacrimal bone medially and the zygomatic bone laterally. Pitfall: it is not seen as a separate structure on CT. The globe can keep its height despite a large orbital floor defect, so do not exclude a floor fracture because the globe position is normal.

Sympathetic nerves.note: Rami and splanchnic branches run from the Truncus sympathicus over the costovertebral joints to the intercostal nerves and the prevertebral plexuses. They are not resolved on CT. Pitfall: small paravertebral soft tissue at the rib heads is usually a ganglion or intercostal vessel; do not call it a lymph node or neurogenic tumour without comparing sides.
neighbours: Radiate ligament of head of rib

Sympathetic trunk.note: In the neck it lies on the Musculus longus colli, behind the carotid sheath. In the thorax it runs over the costal heads, lateral to the vertebral bodies. Pitfall: its fusiform ganglia look like retropharyngeal or paravertebral lymph nodes, and the intercostal veins look like the trunk; follow the structure craniocaudally.
landmarks: lm:Crest of head of rib|Sixth rib
neighbours: Radiate ligament of head of rib

Synovial sheaths of digits of hand.key: Synovial sheaths of digits of hand
Synovial sheaths of digits of hand.note: These sheaths line the palmar surface of the phalanges from the distal phalanx proximally. Those of digits 2–4 end at about the metacarpophalangeal level. Pitfall: only the little finger sheath is normally continuous with the ulnar bursa (and the thumb sheath with the radial bursa). Infection spreads differently depending on the digit.
landmarks: lm:Trochlea of phalanx of hand|Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Cruciform part of fibrous sheath of digit of hand
Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
Middle phalanx of third finger of hand
Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints

Talocalcaneal interosseous ligament.note: Fills the canalis tarsi between the sulcus tali and sulcus calcanei and separates the posterior subtalar joint from the talocalcaneonavicular joint. Pitfall: the cervical ligament lies more laterally in the sinus tarsi. Middle-facet talocalcaneal coalition lies just medial; sclerosis there should not be read as ligament ossification.

Talonavicular ligament.note: Dorsal band running from the collum tali to the dorsal navicular, deep to the tibialis anterior/EHL tendons and the dorsalis pedis bundle. Pitfall: a dorsal capsular avulsion flake or traction spur can be mistaken for a talar beak (a secondary sign of tarsal coalition). An os supratalare can mimic a fracture.

Talus.note: The trochlea fits in the ankle mortise between the tibia and both malleoli. The talus meets the calcaneus below at the subtalar facets and the navicular in front. The flexor hallucis longus runs between the lateral and medial tubercles. Pitfall: an os trigonum behind the lateral tubercle mimics a Shepherd fracture, and lateral process fractures are easily missed.
landmarks: lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of talus|Talus

Tectospinal tract.note: Crossed fibres from the colliculus superior that run in the medial anterior funiculus beside the Fissura mediana anterior. The tract ends in the cervical cord. CT does not show it. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the Tractus spinotectalis, an ascending tract in the anterolateral funiculus.

Temporal bone.note: It has squamous, tympanic, mastoid and petrous parts. The petrous apex points toward the clivus, and the mandibular fossa holds the TMJ. Pitfall: normal fissures and sutures (petrotympanic, tympanomastoid, petrosquamous) and the vestibular and cochlear aqueducts can look like fractures. Trace them on both sides.
landmarks: lm:Anterior surface of petrous part|Temporal bone

Temporal branches of middle cerebral art.key: Temporal branches of middle cerebral artery
Temporal branches of middle cerebral art.note: Supply the lateral temporal gyri, from the Sylvian fissure down to the gyrus temporalis inferior, above the pars petrosa and tentorium. Pitfall: beam hardening from the os temporale makes false hypodensity in the inferior temporal lobe. A dense sinus transversus or tentorium can mimic subarachnoid blood.
neighbours: Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci*)

Temporal plane.note: Triangular upper surface of the superior temporal gyrus behind the Transverse temporal gyri, forming the floor of the posterior Sylvian fissure. Pitfall: normal leftward asymmetry (larger left planum) should not be read as atrophy of the other side. It is visible only obliquely on axial CT, so use coronal or sagittal reformats.
passing: Parietal branches of middle cerebral artery
neighbours: Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci*)

Temporal pole.note: Polus temporalis fills the anterior middle cranial fossa, bounded anteriorly by the greater wing of the sphenoid and medially near the amygdala. Pitfall: beam-hardening and partial volume from the adjacent bone can hide or mimic contusions and thin extra-axial haematomas. Check coronal reformats, and do not mistake a middle fossa arachnoid cyst for atrophy.
landmarks: lm:Cerebral surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
lm:Anterior surface of petrous part|Temporal bone
lm:Temporal surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone

Temporalis muscle.note: Fills the temporal fossa from the Linea temporalis to the coronoid process, passing deep to the zygomatic arch, with the temporal fascia on its lateral side. Pitfall: one-sided atrophy (V3 lesion or after craniotomy) can make the normal side look like a mass. Do not confuse the normal muscle with a sphenoid-wing meningioma spreading outside the skull.
passing: Frontal branch of superficial temporal artery
landmarks: lm:Squamous part of temporal bone|Temporal bone
lm:Temporal surface of greater wing|Sphenoid bone
lm:Temporal surface of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Temporo-occipital branch.note: The most posterior MCA cortical branch. It runs over the posterior gyrus temporalis medius toward the lateral occipital gyri. Pitfall: lateral occipital cortex is often PCA territory. A hypodensity here may be a PCA infarct or MCA–PCA watershed, not an MCA branch occlusion.

Temporoparietalis muscle.note: Thin, variable scalp sheet above the auricle, between frontalis and the auricular muscles, lying on the temporal fascia. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the temporalis. It lies outside the temporal fascia with the superficial temporal vessels, so a collection here is a scalp haematoma, not an intramuscular temporalis haematoma.
landmarks: lm:Squamous part of temporal bone|Temporal bone
lm:Mastoid angle of parietal bone|Parietal bone

Tendinous arch of levator ani.note: A thickening of the obturator fascia running from the pubic body to the spina ischiadica, giving origin to the levator ani. Pitfall: it is not seen as a separate structure on CT, but it is the boundary between compartments. Obturator internus above the arch faces the pelvis; below it, the muscle forms the ischioanal fossa wall, which matters for where collections spread.

Tendon of extensor digitorum longus.note: The tendon passes under the Retinaculum extensorium inferius, then splits into four slips running dorsal to metatarsals II–V to the dorsal aponeuroses of the toes. Pitfall: the thin slips blend with Extensor digitorum brevis tendons and dorsal veins through partial-volume averaging. Do not call this blurring a tear.
passing: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum longus
Proximal phalanx of second finger of foot

Tendon sheath - abd. pollicis longus - e.key: Tendon sheath - abd. pollicis longus - ext. pollicis brevis
Tendon sheath - abd. pollicis longus - e.note: First dorsal compartment, lying over the lateral surface of the processus styloideus radii under the retinaculum extensorium. Pitfall: a septum inside the compartment that separates the extensor pollicis brevis tendon is a common normal variant. It matters in de Quervain disease and should not be mistaken for a tendon split.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensors carpi radialis

Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris.key: Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris
Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris.note: Sixth dorsal compartment, sitting in the groove next to the processus styloideus ulnae within its own fibro-osseous subsheath. Pitfall: the tendon normally shifts ulnarly in supination, so judge subluxation in the neutral position. Do not confuse an ulnar styloid ossicle with a fracture.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensor digiti minimi manus
Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint
Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint

Tendon sheath of extensor digiti minimi.key: Tendon sheath of extensor digiti minimi manus
Tendon sheath of extensor digiti minimi.note: Fifth dorsal compartment, lying directly dorsal to the distal radio-ulnar joint, radial to the extensor carpi ulnaris compartment. Pitfall: it is easily mislabelled as the sixth compartment. A doubled extensor digiti minimi tendon is a normal variant, not a split tear.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris
Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum and extensor indicis

Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum and.key: Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum and extensor indicis
Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum and.note: Fourth dorsal compartment, ulnar to the tuberculum dorsale radii and dorsal to the lunate and capitate. The terminal posterior interosseous nerve runs along its floor. Pitfall: a dorsal ganglion from the scapholunate region lies directly beneath it and can look like tenosynovitis.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensor pollicis longus
Tendon sheath of extensor digiti minimi manus

Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum long.key: Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum longus
Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum long.note: The most lateral anterior ankle sheath, shared by the EDL and fibularis tertius tendons, deep to the extensor retinacula. Pitfall: the anterior tibial vessels and nervus fibularis profundus lie just medial to it, between the EDL and EHL; do not call these vessels tenosynovial fluid.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensor hallucis longus

Tendon sheath of extensor hallucis longu.key: Tendon sheath of extensor hallucis longus
Tendon sheath of extensor hallucis longu.note: The middle anterior sheath, between the tibialis anterior and EDL sheaths, running from the extensor retinacula to the dorsum of the first ray. Pitfall: the EHL crosses over the anterior tibial bundle at the ankle, and the arteria dorsalis pedis lies lateral to the tendon; on non-contrast CT do not call the vessel a tendon.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum longus

Tendon sheath of extensor pollicis longu.key: Tendon sheath of extensor pollicis longus
Tendon sheath of extensor pollicis longu.note: Third dorsal compartment, running ulnar to the tuberculum dorsale radii. The tendon then turns obliquely across the extensor carpi radialis tendons towards the thumb. Pitfall: the tendon can rupture after a minimally displaced distal radius fracture, so check the tubercle for fracture lines or spurs.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensors carpi radialis
Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum and extensor indicis

Tendon sheath of extensors carpi radiali.key: Tendon sheath of extensors carpi radialis
Tendon sheath of extensors carpi radiali.note: Second dorsal compartment, lying radial to the tuberculum dorsale radii on the dorsal distal radius. Pitfall: the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis cross over it 4–8 cm proximal to the wrist (proximal intersection). Inflammation there is intersection syndrome, not de Quervain disease.
neighbours: Tendon sheath - abd. pollicis longus - ext. pollicis brevis
Tendon sheath of extensor pollicis longus

Tendon sheath of flexor carpi radialis.key: Tendon sheath of flexor carpi radialis
Tendon sheath of flexor carpi radialis.note: Lies in its own fibro-osseous tunnel in the trapezium groove, separated from the carpal tunnel by a deep layer of the retinaculum flexorium. Pitfall: tenosynovitis here is usually caused by osteophytes from scaphotrapeziotrapezoidal osteoarthritis. Do not report it as a carpal tunnel process.
passing: Palmar carpal branch of radial artery
neighbours: Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus

Tendon sheath of flexor digitorum longus.key: Tendon sheath of flexor digitorum longus
Tendon sheath of flexor digitorum longus.note: Lies behind the medial malleolus under the Retinaculum flexorium tali, posterior to the tibialis posterior sheath and anterior to the neurovascular bundle and flexor hallucis longus. Pitfall: medial-to-lateral order (TP, FDL, vessels/nerve, FHL) is easily mixed up. In the midfoot, FDL crosses superficial to FHL at the knot of Henry, so it can be mislabelled.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of tibialis posterior muscle
Tendon sheath of flexor hallucis longus

Tendon sheath of flexor hallucis longus.key: Tendon sheath of flexor hallucis longus
Tendon sheath of flexor hallucis longus.note: Runs in the sulcus between the medial and lateral tubercles of the Processus posterior ossis tali, then under the sustentaculum tali, posterolateral to the neurovascular bundle. Pitfall: the sheath connects with the ankle joint in many people, so fluid here may just reflect joint effusion. An os trigonum or Stieda process can mimic a fracture or cause impingement.
landmarks: lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of talus|Talus
lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of calcaneus|Calcaneus
neighbours: Tendon sheath of flexor digitorum longus

Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus.key: Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus
Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus.note: The radial bursa is the most radial structure in the carpal tunnel and continues along the thumb to the distal phalanx. Pitfall: a volar distal radius plate that sits beyond the watershed line can wear through the tendon, so check plate position relative to the volar rim.
passing: Palmar carpal branch of radial artery
Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
neighbours: Tendon sheath of flexor carpi radialis
Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand

Tendon sheath of tibialis anterior.note: The most medial and longest anterior ankle sheath, extending from above the superior extensor retinaculum toward the insertion on the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base. Pitfall: the nearby anteromedial vena saphena magna, especially if thrombosed, can be mistaken for tenosynovitis.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensor hallucis longus

Tendon sheath of tibialis posterior musc.key: Tendon sheath of tibialis posterior muscle
Tendon sheath of tibialis posterior musc.note: The most anterior medial flexor sheath. It sits in the retromalleolar groove directly on the medial malleolus and superficial to the deltoid ligament, running to the navicular tuberosity. Pitfall: an accessory navicular (os naviculare externum) or the normal widening of the tendon near its insertion should not be read as a fracture or a tear.
neighbours: Tendon sheath of flexor digitorum longus

Tensor fasciae latae.note: Arises from the anterior iliac crest and anterior superior iliac spine, lateral to the sartorius and anterolateral to the gluteus medius, and inserts into the tractus iliotibialis. Pitfall: one-sided hypertrophy (pseudohypertrophy) can mimic a soft-tissue mass; it keeps normal muscle density.

Tenth rib.note: Lowest false rib. Its head usually has a single facet for T10 only, and its cartilage forms the lower costal margin. The diaphragm and costodiaphragmatic recess lie deep to it. Pitfall: a free-ending tenth costal cartilage (costa fluctuans decima) is a normal variant. Do not report it as a dislocation, and check the liver and spleen when this rib is fractured.

Tentorium cerebelli.note: Attached to the petrous ridge (superior petrosal sinus) and the groove for the transverse sinus on the occipital bone. Its free edge forms the tentorial incisura around the midbrain, with the superior cerebellar artery below and the posterior cerebral artery above. Pitfall: a normally dense tentorium on CT mimics tentorial subdural haemorrhage. Check symmetry and coronal reformats.
landmarks: lm:Petrous part of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Teres major muscle.note: Arises from the dorsal inferior angle of the scapula and inserts on the medial lip of the intertubercular groove, alongside and behind the latissimus dorsi tendon. Its lower border marks where the axillary artery becomes the brachial artery and forms the floor of the triangular and quadrangular spaces. Pitfall: at insertion it often cannot be separated from latissimus, so avoid calling a pseudo-tear.

Teres minor muscle.note: Arises from the margo lateralis scapulae and inserts on the inferior facet of the tuberculum majus. It forms the upper border of the triangular and quadrangular spaces. Pitfall: on axial CT it merges with the infraspinatus. If only the teres minor shows fatty atrophy, think of axillary nerve compression in the quadrangular space.
neighbours: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

Testis.note: The Testis is an ovoid, homogeneous organ inside the scrotum, wrapped by the tunica albuginea, with the Epididymis on its posterolateral side. Pitfall: an empty hemiscrotum means an undescended testis. In the inguinal canal it can be mistaken for an inguinal lymph node, so check both sides.

Thalamus.note: Paired grey-matter mass. The Ventriculus tertius lies medial, the posterior limb of the internal capsule lateral (separating it from the Nucleus lentiformis), the caudate and lateral ventricle above and in front, and the midbrain below. It is a common site of hypertensive bleeding. Do not call calcified choroid plexus or habenula next to it a thalamic bleed.

Third metacarpal bone.note: The base articulates with Os capitatum and has small facets for metacarpals II and IV. The dorsoradial styloid process takes the Extensor carpi radialis brevis insertion, and the head forms the third MCP joint. Pitfall: a carpal boss or os styloideum at the dorsal base can look like a fracture fragment or an osteophyte.
passing: Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand

Third metatarsal bone.note: The basis articulates with the lateral cuneiform and with MT II and MT IV. The caput articulates with proximal phalanx III. Pitfall: an early march (stress) fracture of the corpus is often occult. Count the rays from MT I to avoid labelling the wrong metatarsal.
passing: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve
landmarks: lm:Base of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone
lm:Body of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone
lm:Head of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone
lm:Base of phalanx of foot|Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot

Third rib.note: True rib that articulates with T2 and T3. Pectoralis minor attaches anteriorly, and the upper lobe and pleura lie on its inner surface. Pitfall: counting ribs anteriorly or on axial slices alone often shifts the number by one. Count from the first rib on coronal or 3D reformats and cross-check with the thoracic vertebrae.

Third ventricle.note: Narrow midline cavity between the thalami, with the hypothalamus forming its floor. The anterior commissure and lamina terminalis lie in front. The posterior commissure, pineal and aqueduct lie behind, and the tela choroidea and fornices lie above. Look carefully at the foramina of Monro: a hyperdense colloid cyst there is easy to miss. Do not mistake a cavum veli interpositi for a dilated third ventricle.

Thoracic aorta.note: Descends left of the vertebral bodies from T4 to T12, behind the Atrium sinistrum and left of the Oesophagus. It passes through the hiatus aorticus to become the Aorta abdominalis. Pitfall: the hemi-azygos vein and adjacent atelectasis can mimic an intramural haematoma or a flap, so check the non-contrast density.

Thoraco-acromial artery.note: Short trunk from the second part of the axillary artery at the upper border of pectoralis minor. It pierces the fascia clavipectoralis and divides into pectoral, acromial, clavicular and deltoid branches. Pitfall: the deltoid branch runs with the cephalic vein in the deltopectoral groove. Do not mistake the opacified vein for the artery, or the artery for an infraclavicular node.

Thoracodorsal artery.note: Continuation of the Arteria subscapularis that descends along the lateral scapular border on Serratus anterior to the deep surface of latissimus dorsi, with the thoracodorsal nerve. Pitfall: it can be mistaken for the more anterior lateral thoracic artery, and it may be absent after a latissimus dorsi flap.

Thoracodorsal nerve.note: Arises from the posterior cord and runs down the posterior axillary wall on subscapularis, then teres major, with the thoracodorsal vessels, entering the deep surface of latissimus dorsi. Pitfall: the long thoracic nerve lies more anteriorly, on the outer surface of serratus anterior. Postoperative latissimus flap changes can be mistaken for an axillary mass.

Thoracodorsal vein.note: This vein descends along the posterior axillary wall on the serratus anterior with the thoracodorsal nerve, toward latissimus dorsi. It drains into the subscapular and axillary veins. Pitfall: it is easily confused with the v. thoracica lateralis, which lies more anteriorly on the serratus. In a post-dissection axilla, a small vessel can also be misread as a residual node.

Thyro-epiglottic part of thyro-arytenoid.note: Thin muscle slips running upward from the inner thyroid lamina to the lateral epiglottis, within the supraglottic paraglottic space lateral to the Membrana quadrangularis. Pitfall: keep the paraglottic space separate from the pre-epiglottic fat in front of the epiglottis; these are different staging compartments.
neighbours: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle

Thyrocervical trunk.note: Short trunk from the first part of the subclavian artery at the medial border of scalenus anterior, above the cupula pleurae. It gives the inferior thyroid, suprascapular and transverse cervical arteries. Pitfall: the vertebral artery arises just medial to it and the internal thoracic artery just opposite. Trace each vessel upward before naming it.

Thyrohyoid muscle.note: Short muscle running from the Linea obliqua of the thyroid lamina to the hyoid, covering the thyrohyoid membrane. Pitfall: a mixed laryngocele herniates through the thyrohyoid membrane deep to this muscle and can be mistaken for a necrotic node or a branchial cleft cyst.
landmarks: lm:Oblique line of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

Thyroid cartilage.note: The two Laminae cartilaginis thyreoideae meet anteriorly at the Prominentia laryngea and enclose the paraglottic space. The Cornua inferiora articulate with the cricoid. Pitfall: unossified segments of irregularly ossified cartilage mimic erosion or tumour invasion. A calcified triticeous cartilage beside the Cornu superius is not a fracture fragment.
landmarks: lm:Superior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage
lm:Inferior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage
lm:Oblique line of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

Thyroid gland.note: The lobes lie beside the larynx and Trachea, deep to the infrahyoid strap muscles and medial to the carotid sheath. The isthmus crosses tracheal rings 2–4. Pitfall: a posterior exophytic nodule or the Zuckerkandl tubercle can mimic a parathyroid or paraoesophageal mass, so trace its continuity with the lobe.
landmarks: lm:Inferior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage
lm:Oblique line of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

Thyroid nodes.note: These nodes lie next to the Glandula thyreoidea capsule, deep to the strap muscles and beside the thyroid and cricoid cartilages. Pitfall: an exophytic thyroid nodule can be mistaken for a node. A claw sign or continuity with the gland parenchyma points to a thyroid nodule.

Tibia.note: The tibial plateau bears the femoral condyles. The fibula meets the tibia at both tibiofibular joints, and the talus articulates with the facies articularis inferior and malleolus medialis. Pitfall: the oblique nutrient canal in the posterior proximal shaft mimics a fracture. Posterior malleolus fractures are easily missed without sagittal reformats.

Tibial nerve.note: In the popliteal fossa the nerve is the most superficial structure, lying over the popliteal vein and artery. It then runs deep to the soleus with the posterior tibial vessels. In the tarsal tunnel it lies between the flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus tendons. Pitfall: in the tarsal tunnel it is easily mistaken for the accompanying venae tibiales posteriores.

Tibialis anterior muscle.note: This is the most medial muscle of the anterior compartment, arising from the lateral tibial surface and the interosseous membrane. Its tendon is the most medial anterior ankle tendon and inserts on the medial cuneiform and the base of the first metatarsal. Pitfall: a distal tendon rupture retracts and can mimic a soft-tissue mass at the ankle. The anterior tibial vessels lie deep to it, on the interosseous membrane.

Tibialis posterior muscle.note: Deepest muscle of the posterior compartment, lying on the membrana interossea cruris. Its tendon is the most anterior in the tarsal tunnel behind the malleolus medialis and inserts on the tuberositas ossis navicularis. Pitfall: an accessory navicular (os tibiale externum) with a smooth corticated synchondrosis is not an avulsion fracture.
landmarks: lm:Base of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone

Tibiocalcaneal ligament.note: A superficial deltoid band. It runs from the anterior colliculus of the medial malleolus to the sustentaculum tali. Pitfall: a sustentaculum fracture is easily missed on axial CT, so check coronal reformats. The flexor hallucis longus groove beneath it should not be read as a fracture line.
landmarks: lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of calcaneus|Calcaneus

Tibionavicular ligament.note: The most anterior superficial deltoid band. It runs from the anterior colliculus past the talar neck to the navicular tuberosity and blends with the spring ligament. Pitfall: an accessory navicular (os tibiale externum) can look like a tuberosity avulsion. Look for a smooth, corticated synchondrosis.

Tongue.note: The oral tongue lies in front of the circumvallate papillae, and the tongue base belongs to the oropharynx. The Musculus mylohyoideus forms the floor and the Hyoid bone the lower anchor. Pitfall: in a hypoglossal palsy, the denervated half atrophies and turns fatty. The normal opposite half can then be misread as a mass. Lingual tonsil asymmetry is a mimic too.
landmarks: lm:Lesser horn of hyoid bone|Hyoid bone

Tonsil of cerebellum.note: The Tonsillae cerebelli sit at the inferomedial margin of each hemisphere. They flank the medulla and the vallecula, and their tips lie near the foramen magnum. Pitfall: tonsils up to 5 mm below the basion–opisthion line are normal. On axial slices, partial volume at the foramen magnum can mimic herniation, so measure on sagittal reformats.

Trachea.note: The Trachea runs from the lower border of the Cartilago cricoidea (C6) to the carina (T4–T5). The Oesophagus lies behind it, the Arcus aortae to the left and the azygos arch to the right. Pitfall: on expiration the posterior membranous wall bows inward. This mimics an intraluminal mass or tracheomalacia. Calcified rings in older patients are normal.

Transversalis fascia.note: This fascia lies deep to the M. transversus abdominis and the rectus sheath, with extraperitoneal fat inside it. The deep inguinal ring lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. Pitfall: an indirect hernia arises lateral to the Vasa epigastrica inferiora and a direct hernia medial to them. Use these vessels, not the hernia sac, to classify the hernia.

Transverse acetabular ligament.note: Bridges the incisura acetabuli and completes the labral ring. The foramen beneath it carries vessels to the fossa acetabuli and the ligamentum capitis femoris. Pitfall: the normal inferior notch defect is easily mistaken for a labral tear or acetabular fracture. The ligament also serves as a reference for cup anteversion.

Transverse arytenoid muscle.note: Unpaired muscle bridging the posterior surfaces of both cartilagines arytenoideae, above the lamina cartilaginis cricoideae. It forms the anterior wall of the postcricoid laryngopharynx. Pitfall: collapsed postcricoid mucosa plus this muscle can look like a postcricoid mass. Asymmetric arytenoid sclerosis is a normal variant and does not mean cartilage invasion.
landmarks: lm:Posterior surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage
neighbours: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle

Transverse cervical artery.note: It runs laterally across the M. scalenus anterior and the brachial plexus through the posterior cervical triangle, above the inferior belly of the M. omohyoideus, towards the trapezius and levator scapulae. Pitfall: it often arises directly from the A. subclavia rather than the Truncus thyrocervicalis; on cross-section it can be mistaken for a supraclavicular lymph node.

Transverse colon.note: It is intraperitoneal and hangs on the transverse mesocolon between the hepatic and splenic flexures. It lies below the greater curvature, in front of the duodenum and pancreas, with the greater omentum draped in front. Pitfall: colon interposed between the liver and diaphragm (Chilaiditi) can look like pneumoperitoneum. Look for haustra.

Transverse facial artery.note: Arises from the Arteria temporalis superficialis inside the parotid gland and runs forward over the masseter, below the zygomatic arch and above the parotid duct. Pitfall: on contrast CT, do not confuse it with the ductus parotideus or with accessory parotid tissue along the masseter.

Transverse frontopolar gyrus and sulcus*.note: The transverse frontopolar gyri form the tip of the frontal pole, behind the frontal squama and the posterior wall of the frontal sinus, on either side of the falx and frontal crest. Pitfall: frontal sinus size varies a lot, from absent to very large. A fracture of the posterior sinus wall with pneumocephalus can hide here, so check bone windows.

Transverse head of adductor hallucis.note: A thin muscle band running across the plantar plates of MTP joints 3–5 to the lateral sesamoid. It lies plantar to the ligamentum metatarseum transversum profundum. Pitfall: in hallux valgus its pull adds to lateral sesamoid subluxation. Do not misread its thin belly as plantar plate thickening.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
landmarks: lm:Head of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone

Transverse head of adductor pollicis.note: A triangular muscle from the palmar ridge of the third metacarpal shaft to the ulnar sesamoid and base of the thumb's proximal phalanx. It forms the deep (dorsal) boundary of the thenar space. Pitfall: the first dorsal interosseous lies directly dorsal to it; the radial artery entering between them can be mistaken for a fluid collection.
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand

Transverse humeral ligament.note: Bridges the sulcus intertubercularis between the greater and lesser tubercles and holds the biceps long head in the groove, under the deltoid. It is largely made of subscapularis tendon fibres. Pitfall: an empty groove means a dislocated (usually medially, with a subscapularis tear) or ruptured biceps tendon, not normal anatomy.

Transverse intermuscular septum of leg.note: Separates the superficial posterior compartment (gastrocnemius, soleus) from the deep one (tibialis posterior, FDL, FHL). The posterior tibial and fibular neurovascular bundles lie just deep to it. Pitfall: the cortical irregularity at the Linea musculi solei is a normal enthesis and should not be called a fracture or periostitis.

Transverse ligament of knee.note: Connects the anterior horns of the two menisci and runs within or behind the Hoffa fat pad. Pitfall: its junction with the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus, and especially the medial meniscus, produces a pseudotear on reformats.

Transverse occipital sulcus.note: Lateral occipital sulcus that continues the posterior end of the intraparietal sulcus. It lies between the Superior occipital gyri and the Lateral occipital gyrus, behind the Angular gyrus. Pitfall: on axial CT it is easily mistaken for the posterior intraparietal sulcus or the parieto-occipital sulcus, so trace it across several slices before naming it.

Transverse part of iliofemoral ligament.note: The strong lateral limb of the Y ligament. It runs from the anterior inferior iliac spine and acetabular rim to the upper intertrochanteric line, deep to rectus femoris. Pitfall: its thick soft-tissue band on CT can be misread as joint effusion or early heterotopic ossification. Compare with the other side.

Transverse part of trapezius muscle.note: Horizontal fibres from the C7–T3 spinous processes to the acromion and the Spina scapulae. They lie superficial to the Musculi rhomboidei and Musculus supraspinatus, and the insertion borders the Articulatio acromioclavicularis. Pitfall: at the AC joint, the trapezio-deltoid insertion and subcutaneous bursa can mimic soft-tissue swelling, so check for joint widening before calling it a hematoma.
neighbours: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

Transverse sinus.note: Runs in the attached outer edge of the tentorium cerebelli, from the confluence at the internal occipital protuberance to the sigmoid sinus at the mastoid angle of the parietal bone. Pitfall: one side, usually the left, is often hypoplastic. Arachnoid granulations cause filling defects. Neither should be reported as venous sinus thrombosis.
landmarks: lm:Mastoid angle of parietal bone|Parietal bone

Transverse temporal gyri.note: Gyri temporales transversi (Heschl) run obliquely on the superior surface of the superior temporal gyrus, deep in the posterior Sylvian fissure. The insula lies medially and the planum temporale posteriorly. Pitfall: a duplicated Heschl gyrus and a larger left planum temporale are normal variants, not mass or atrophy.
passing: Temporal branches of middle cerebral artery
neighbours: Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci*)
Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus

Transverse tibiofibular ligament.note: The deep, lower part of the posterior tibiofibular complex. It runs from the malleolar fossa to the posterior tibial margin and deepens the plafond behind the talar dome, like a labrum. Pitfall: when it is ossified or thickened it can mimic a loose body or a posterior impingement fragment.

Transversus abdominis muscle.note: Musculus transversus abdominis is the innermost flank muscle and lies directly on fascia transversalis. It arises from the inner lip of the iliac crest, the thoracolumbar fascia, the lateral inguinal ligament and the lower costal cartilages. Pitfall: fluid from a TAP block sits in the plane between this muscle and internal oblique; do not call it an abdominal-wall abscess.
landmarks: lm:Inner lip of iliac crest|Hip bone

Transversus thoracis muscle.note: It runs from the inner surface of the lower corpus sterni and xiphoid process to costal cartilages 2–6. It lies deep to the internal thoracic vessels and separates them from the pleura. Pitfall: confusing parasternal (internal mammary) nodes with the paired internal thoracic veins; trace the vessels on consecutive contrast-enhanced slices.

Trapeziotrapezoidal interosseous ligamen.note: Intra-articular ligament binding the trapezium and trapezoid within the distal carpal row, distal to the STT joint. Pitfall: fractures of the trapezial ridge run parallel to the axial plane and are easily missed. Review a carpal tunnel–plane reconstruction.

Trapezium bone.note: It has a saddle facet for metacarpal I distally, Os scaphoideum proximally, and Os trapezoideum and the base of metacarpal II on the ulnar side. The palmar Tuberculum ossis trapezii borders the FCR groove. Pitfall: fractures of the trapezial ridge are often missed on radiographs, so check the axial CT. Do not confuse the trapezium (thumb ray) with the trapezoid.

Trapezoid bone.note: This wedge-shaped bone is wider dorsally. It articulates with the base of metacarpal II distally, Os scaphoideum proximally, Os trapezium radially and Os capitatum ulnarly. Pitfall: overlap on radiographs hides its rare fractures, and dorsal ridges at the CMC II–III joints (carpal boss) can look like avulsion fragments.

Trapezoid ligament.note: Ligamentum trapezoideum spans from the upper surface of the coracoid process to the Linea trapezoidea, anterolateral to the Ligamentum conoideum. Pectoralis minor inserts on the coracoid just below it. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the Ligamentum coracoacromiale, which runs to the acromion and forms the roof of the subacromial space.

Trapezoideocapitate interosseous ligamen.note: Interosseous ligament inside the trapezoid–capitate interval, deep to the extensor carpi radialis brevis insertion. Pitfall: a dorsal bony prominence at the bases of the second and third metacarpals may be a carpal boss or an os styloideum. Do not report it as an avulsion fracture or osteophyte.

Triangular part of inferior frontal gyru.key: Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus
Triangular part of inferior frontal gyru.note: The pars triangularis is a wedge between the horizontal and ascending rami of the lateral sulcus, below the inferior frontal sulcus. It covers the anterior insula. Pitfall: on axial CT the two rami form a V/Y shape that is easily mistaken for the inferior frontal sulcus, which puts the Broca region in the wrong place.
neighbours: Opercular part of inferior frontal gyrus
Orbital part of  inferior frontal gyrus

Trigeminal nerve (V).note: It leaves the midlateral pons, crosses the prepontine cistern into Meckel cave (Cavum trigeminale) at the petrous apex, and divides into V1 (superior orbital fissure), V2 (foramen rotundum) and V3 (foramen ovale). Pitfall: the foramen spinosum is small, posterolateral and carries the middle meningeal artery; do not mistake it for the foramen ovale.

Triquetrocapitate ligament.note: Ulnar limb of the palmar arcuate ligament, running from the triquetrum across the hamate to the capitate neck. It stabilises the ulnar midcarpal joint. Pitfall: a type II lunate's normal articulation with the hamate is a normal variant. Do not mistake it for ulnar midcarpal malalignment or instability.

Triquetrohamate ligament.note: Palmar band across the helicoid triquetrohamate joint, deep to the pisiform. Pitfall: because the joint surface is spiral, an oblique axial slice makes the joint look widened or stepped. Confirm on coronal and sagittal reconstructions before reporting a hamate body fracture or instability.
neighbours: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Triquetrum bone.note: Os lunatum lies radially, Os hamatum distally and Os pisiforme on the palmar side, with the TFCC proximal to it. The dorsal cortex is the usual site of avulsion fractures, best seen on sagittal images. Pitfall: an os triangulare or an ununited fragment of the ulnar styloid can look like an acute dorsal triquetral chip.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
neighbours: Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint

Triradiate cartilage.note: Y-shaped growth cartilage where ilium, ischium and pubis meet at the acetabular floor. It fuses at about 14–16 years. Pitfall: in paediatric CT its open, irregular limbs mimic acetabular fractures, and a fracture that crosses it risks premature closure and acetabular dysplasia.

Trochanteric bursa of gluteus maximus mu.key: Trochanteric bursa of gluteus maximus muscle
Trochanteric bursa of gluteus maximus mu.note: This is the main 'subgluteus maximus' bursa, between the gluteus maximus/Tractus iliotibialis and the posterolateral Trochanter major. Pitfall: trochanteric fluid is often attributed to bursitis when the real cause is a gluteus medius/minimus tendon tear. Check tendon continuity and the deeper medius/minimus bursae.
neighbours: Trochanteric bursa of gluteus medius muscle

Trochanteric bursa of gluteus medius mus.key: Trochanteric bursa of gluteus medius muscle
Trochanteric bursa of gluteus medius mus.note: Lies deep to the gluteus medius tendon, against the lateral and posterior facets of the Trochanter major. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the larger, more superficial gluteus maximus bursa. Fluid confined here, together with tendon thinning or calcification, suggests gluteus medius tendinopathy or a tear rather than simple bursitis.
neighbours: Trochanteric bursa of gluteus minimus muscle
Trochanteric bursa of gluteus maximus muscle

Trochanteric bursa of gluteus minimus mu.key: Trochanteric bursa of gluteus minimus muscle
Trochanteric bursa of gluteus minimus mu.note: Lies deep to the gluteus minimus tendon, at the anterior facet of the Trochanter major. Pitfall: because it is small and anterior, it is easily lost in partial volume with the hip capsule. Do not mistake an anterior trochanteric fluid collection for a joint recess or for the iliopsoas bursa, which lies more medially.
neighbours: Trochanteric bursa of gluteus medius muscle

Trochlea of superior oblique muscle.note: Fibrocartilaginous pulley at the superomedial orbital rim, attached to the Fovea trochlearis of the frontal bone, that redirects the superior oblique tendon. Pitfall: trochlear calcification with age is a common normal finding. Do not mistake it for an orbital foreign body or an osteoma of the frontal sinus floor.

Trochlear nerve (IV).note: The only nerve that leaves the dorsal brainstem, below the inferior colliculus. It wraps around the midbrain in the ambient cistern, runs in the cavernous lateral wall below III, and passes through the superior orbital fissure outside the anulus. Pitfall: it cannot be seen on CT; a IV palsy after minor trauma needs the dorsal midbrain and tentorial edge checked.

Tuber of vermis.note: The Tuber vermis is part of the posterior vermis, below the folium and above the pyramis. It sits in the posterior cerebellar notch with the semilunar lobules on either side. Pitfall: the CSF-filled notch and the dura beside it can mimic a midline cleft or atrophy. Assess vermian size on sagittal reformats.

Twelfth rib.note: Short floating rib on T12 with no tubercle articulation. Quadratus lumborum and the diaphragm attach to it, and medially the posterior pleural recess extends below it. Pitfall: a hypoplastic twelfth rib versus a lumbar rib on L1 leads to vertebral miscounting. Count from C2 or T1 and state the numbering method.

Tympanic membrane.note: Separates the external acoustic meatus from the tympanic cavity, attached to the tympanic annulus with the scutum above. The Manubrium mallei is embedded in it, and the pars flaccida lies above the lateral process (Prussak space). Pitfall: the membrane is often invisible on CT. Cerumen or debris in the meatus can mimic a thickened or retracted membrane, so check for scutum erosion.

Ulna.note: Proximally, the Incisura trochlearis holds the humeral trochlea and the Incisura radialis holds the radial head. Distally, the Caput ulnae sits in the sigmoid notch under the TFCC. Pitfall: the normal transverse bare area across the trochlear notch can look like a fracture line.
neighbours: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint
Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris

Ulnar artery.note: Passes deep to the deep head of pronator teres, which separates it from the median nerve. It runs under flexor digitorum superficialis on flexor digitorum profundus, then enters Guyon's canal superficial to the flexor retinaculum, between the pisiform and the hook of the hamate. Pitfall: hook of hamate fractures and hypothenar hammer injury damage it here. Coronal CT is needed because axial slices miss these fractures.
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Ulnar collateral ligament.note: Its anterior bundle runs from the base of the medial epicondyle to the tuberculum sublime, deep to the common flexor-pronator origin. The ulnar nerve lies posteriorly in the cubital tunnel. Pitfall: a small ossicle at the medial epicondyle or tuberculum sublime in throwers may be chronic ligament calcification rather than an acute avulsion.
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis
Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint.key: Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint
Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint.note: Capsular thickening from the processus styloideus ulnae to the triquetrum and pisiform, next to the extensor carpi ulnaris sheath. Pitfall: a corticated ossicle next to the ulnar styloid may be an os triangulare or lunula. Do not confuse it with an ununited styloid fracture, and remember that base fractures point to TFCC/DRUJ injury.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
neighbours: Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris
Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris.key: Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris.note: Arises from the posterior border of the ulna through an aponeurosis shared with FCU and FDP, and joins the humeral head to run in the sixth compartment next to the caput ulnae. Pitfall: the dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve crosses near the processus styloideus ulnae. Styloid fractures and ECU sheath fluid can look alike, so check the groove carefully.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
neighbours: Humeral head of extensor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris.key: Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris.note: Arises from the medial olecranon and, through an aponeurosis, from the margo posterior ulnae. It forms the ulnar side of the cubital tunnel, behind the sulcus nervi ulnaris. Pitfall: the aponeurosis is shared with ECU and FDP, so the fat planes between them often do not show on CT; do not read this as infiltration.
passing: Posterior branch of medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve
neighbours: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris

Ulnar nerve.note: Runs medial to the axillary and brachial artery and pierces the septum intermusculare mediale at mid-arm. It then passes through the cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle, between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, and into Guyon canal. Pitfall: an accessory anconeus epitrochlearis muscle or ulnar nerve subluxation in flexion are normal variants and should not be read as a mass or dislocation.
neighbours: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Ulnar veins.note: The Venae ulnares are paired veins that run alongside the ulnar artery, between flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, and pass superficial to the flexor retinaculum through Guyon's canal. Pitfall: veins enhancing next to the ulnar nerve can be mistaken for a thickened nerve or a ganglion at the wrist.
neighbours: Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Ulnocapitate ligament.note: The most superficial ulnocarpal ligament. It runs from the ulnar fovea and Ligamentum radioulnare palmare, palmar to the lunate and triquetrum, to the capitate. Pitfall: do not confuse it with the deeper Ligamentum ulnolunatum. Fractures through the ulnar styloid base can disrupt its foveal attachment and destabilize the DRUJ.

Ulnolunate ligament.note: Runs from the palmar radioulnar ligament (part of the TFCC) to the palmar lunate, deep to the ulnocapitate ligament. Pitfall: subchondral sclerosis or cysts in the ulnar lunate with positive ulnar variance indicate ulnocarpal impaction. Do not report them as an incidental intraosseous ganglion or as Kienböck disease.
neighbours: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint

Ulnopisiform ligament.note: Ulnar palmar capsular band from the ulnar head and TFCC to the pisiform, lying alongside the FCU insertion. Pitfall: a pisiform with irregular or multiple ossification centres, or pisotriquetral arthrosis, can mimic a fracture. Assess the pisotriquetral joint on sagittal and oblique reformats.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
neighbours: Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint
Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Ulnotriquetral ligament.note: Runs from the palmar radioulnar ligament (TFCC) to the triquetrum, forming the ulnar wall of the radiocarpal joint near the ECU sheath. Pitfall: a corticated ossicle at the tip of the Processus styloideus ulnae (os triangulare or lunula) mimics a nonunited styloid fracture. Fracture margins are sharp and not corticated.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
neighbours: Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint
Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint
Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris

Upper canine.note: The upper canine (FDI 13/23) has a long root that rises in the canine eminence next to the nasal floor and the canine fossa of the Maxilla. Pitfall: impaction, usually on the palatal side, is common. Localise the canine in 3D and check for root resorption of the adjacent lateral incisor.

Upper first molar tooth.note: Three-rooted molar (two buccal roots, one palatal) in the processus alveolaris maxillae. Its roots indent the floor of the sinus maxillaris. Pitfall: thin or dehiscent bone over the root apices is a normal finding. Focal mucosal thickening at the sinus floor above a periapical lucency points to odontogenic sinusitis, not rhinogenic disease.

Upper first premolar.note: Premolar in the processus alveolaris maxillae, distal to the canine eminence. It is usually two-rooted (buccal and palatal). Pitfall: the second, palatal root is easy to miss on axial slices. Check coronal reformats when you assess periapical lesions or a residual root.

Upper lateral incisor.note: The upper lateral incisor (FDI 12/22) lies between the medial incisor and the canine in the premaxillary alveolus, below the nasal floor. Pitfall: it is often absent or peg-shaped, which is a normal variant. The alveolar cleft in cleft patients lies between this tooth and the canine; do not miscount the teeth.

Upper medial incisor.note: The upper medial incisor (FDI 11/21) flanks the midline, with the incisive canal between the two roots on the palatal side. Pitfall: a wide incisive canal or nasopalatine duct cyst can mimic a periapical lesion, and a midline supernumerary tooth (mesiodens) can be mistaken for an impacted incisor.
passing: Posterior septal branches of sphenopalatine artery

Upper second molar tooth.note: Molar with often fused roots, sitting near the tuber maxillae and the processus pyramidalis of the os palatinum. It is often the tooth closest to the floor of the sinus maxillaris. Pitfall: fused or convergent roots can be misread as a single root or as root resorption. Assess them on oblique or coronal reformats.

Upper second premolar.note: Usually single-rooted tooth between the first premolar and the first molar in the processus alveolaris maxillae. Its apex often lies just under the sinus floor. Pitfall: the anterior recess of the sinus maxillaris projecting over the apex mimics a periapical lucency. Look for an intact lamina dura on sagittal reformats.

Ureter.note: The Ureter descends on Psoas major and crosses the Arteria iliaca communis bifurcation at the pelvic brim. It then runs along the pelvic sidewall and enters the Vesica urinaria obliquely. Pitfall: phleboliths in pelvic veins look like ureteric calculi. Phleboliths have a central lucency; a true stone shows the soft-tissue rim sign.

Urethra.note: The Urethra starts at the bladder neck and passes through the Prostata, where the Ductus ejaculatorius opens into it. Distally it runs inside the Corpus spongiosum penis as far as the Glans penis. Pitfall: prostatic calcifications along the urethra can be mistaken for urethral calculi. Only a stone lies within the lumen itself.
