Urinary bladder.note: The Vesica urinaria lies behind the Symphysis pubica in the prevesical space. Obturator internus and levator ani lie lateral to it, the Glandula seminalis and rectum posterior, and the Prostata inferior. Pitfall: an underdistended bladder gives pseudo-thickening of the wall. Ureteric jets in early contrast phases can mimic filling defects.

Uvula of palate.note: The Uvula palatina is the free midline tip of the soft palate, hanging into the oropharyngeal airway in front of the posterior pharyngeal wall. Pitfall: on axial slices, its cross-section surrounded by air can look like a polyp, foreign body or tonsillar mass. Check continuity on sagittal reformats.

Uvula of vermis.note: The Uvula vermis is part of the inferior vermis, between the pyramis and the nodulus. It sits in the vallecula with the tonsils on either side. Pitfall: when assessing herniation on axial CT, do not mistake the midline uvula for a tonsil. The tonsils lie paramedian, beside the medulla.

Vagus nerve (X).note: It leaves the pars vascularis of the Foramen jugulare and descends in the carotid sheath, behind and between the ICA/CCA and the IJV. The left recurrent nerve loops under the aortic arch. Pitfall: the paralysed vocal cord is the medialised one with a wide piriform sinus. Image from the skull base down to the aortopulmonary window.
landmarks: lm:Superior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage
neighbours: Node of arch of azygos vein

Vastus intermedius muscle.note: Lies directly on the anterior and lateral femoral shaft, deep to the Rectus femoris and between the lateral and medial vasti. Distally it borders the Bursa suprapatellaris. Pitfall: post-traumatic myositis ossificans next to the cortex mimics parosteal osteosarcoma. A peripheral (zonal) ossification pattern and a lucent gap from the cortex favour myositis ossificans.
passing: Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery

Vastus lateralis muscle.note: Arises from the intertrochanteric line, the greater trochanter and the Labium laterale lineae asperae, deep to the Tractus iliotibialis. Posteriorly it is bounded by the lateral intermuscular septum. Pitfall: a Morel-Lavallée collection lies between the subcutaneous fat and the fascia lata. Do not report it as an intramuscular haematoma.
passing: Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery

Vastus medialis muscle.note: Arises from the Labium mediale lineae asperae; its oblique distal fibres insert on the superomedial patella. It forms the anterolateral wall of the adductor canal. Pitfall: the femoral vessels and saphenous nerve in the adductor canal lie between the vastus medialis and the adductors, under the sartorius. They are not intramuscular structures.

Ventral parts of lateral intertransversa.key: Ventral parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles
Ventral parts of lateral intertransversa.note: Small slips between adjacent lumbar transverse processes. They lie at the exit of the Foramen intervertebrale, posteromedial to the Musculus psoas major and medial to the Musculus quadratus lumborum. Pitfall: the spinal ganglion and ventral rami lie directly against them, so do not mistake an extraforaminal disc herniation or nerve-sheath tumour for muscle.
neighbours: Dorsal parts of lateral intertransversarii lumborum muscles

Vermiform appendix.note: It arises from the posteromedial caecum below the ileocaecal valve, where the taeniae coli meet. Its tip can be retrocaecal, pelvic, or lie over the psoas and external iliac vessels. Pitfall: the terminal ileum or the gonadal vein can be mistaken for the appendix. Trace it from the caecal base to a blind end.

Vertebra C3.note: C3 is a typical cervical vertebra between the C2-C3 and C3-C4 discs, with uncinate processes, a bifid spinous process and foramina transversaria for the Arteria vertebralis. Pitfall: in children, normal pseudosubluxation of C2 on C3 can mimic injury; check the posterior cervical (spinolaminar) line.

Vertebra C4.note: C4 sits between the C3-C4 and C4-C5 discs. The Arteria vertebralis passes through the Foramen transversarium, and the spinal nerve runs in the Sulcus nervi spinalis between the two tubercles. Pitfall: bony spurs from the uncovertebral joint narrow the foramen and can be mistaken for a foraminal disc herniation.
landmarks: lm:Anterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4
lm:Posterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4

Vertebra C5.note: C5 lies between the C4-C5 and C5-C6 discs. Its transverse process separates Musculus scalenus anterior from scalenus medius, and the brachial plexus roots emerge between them. Pitfall: cervical nerves exit above their own vertebra, so the C6 root leaves at C5-C6; name both level and root when reporting foraminal stenosis.

Vertebra C6.note: C6 lies between discs C5-C6 and C6-C7, with Musculus longus colli and the oesophagus in front. Its large anterior tubercle (carotid tubercle) is the guide for the vertebral artery, which usually enters the foramen transversarium at C6. Pitfall: the artery may enter at C5, C4 or C7, so check for this variant before surgery.

Vertebra C7.note: C7 (vertebra prominens) sits between discs C6-C7 and C7-T1 and has a long spinous process that is not split in two. Its foramen transversarium usually carries only the vertebral vein. Pitfall: a cervical rib or long C7 transverse process can pass for the first rib. C7 transverse processes slope down, T1 processes slope up; count levels from C2.
landmarks: lm:Uncinate process of first thoracic vertebra|Vertebra T1

Vertebra L1.note: L1 lies between discs T12-L1 and L1-L2. The diaphragmatic crura lie against it from the front and side, and Musculus psoas major starts here. The conus medullaris usually ends at L1-L2. Pitfall: a small 12th rib or a lumbosacral transitional vertebra leads to wrong level numbering; count from C2 or use the lowest rib-bearing vertebra.

Vertebra L2.note: L2 lies between discs L1-L2 and L2-L3. The aorta is in front and to the left, the IVC in front and to the right, and Musculus psoas major on each side. The right crus reaches down to L2/L3. Pitfall: a thick diaphragmatic crus can look like retrocrural or retrocaval lymphadenopathy; follow it on consecutive slices.
landmarks: lm:Superior articular process of vertebra|Vertebra L3

Vertebra L3.note: L3 lies between discs L2-L3 and L3-L4, with Musculus psoas major on each side and the cauda equina in the canal. It has the longest transverse processes. Pitfall: transverse process fractures are easy to miss on axial images, so check coronal reformats. Do not confuse a fracture with an unfused apophysis, which has smooth, corticated edges.
landmarks: lm:Costal part of transverse process|Vertebra L3
lm:Superior articular process of vertebra|Vertebra L3

Vertebra L4.note: L4 lies between discs L3-L4 and L4-L5. The aortic bifurcation and the start of the common iliac veins lie in front of it. The L3-L4 facet joints are behind. Pitfall: the line joining the iliac crests (supracristal line) is not a reliable way to number levels, and the iliolumbar ligament may arise from L4 when L5 is transitional.
landmarks: lm:Inferior articular facet of vertebra|Vertebra L3

Vertebra L5.note: L5 lies between disc L4-L5 and the lumbosacral disc L5-S1, and its inferior articular processes meet the Processus articularis superior ossis sacri. The iliolumbar ligament attaches to its transverse processes. Pitfall: a transitional vertebra (sacralization of L5 or lumbarization of S1) shifts the numbering; check against whole-spine imaging before naming a level.

Vertebra T1.note: T1 carries the first rib on a full costal facet, has small uncinate processes and sits above disc T1-T2. The cervicothoracic (stellate) ganglion lies in front of its transverse process. Pitfall: mistaking a cervical rib for the first rib leads to wrong numbering; follow the rib back to a transverse process that points upward.
landmarks: lm:Uncinate process of first thoracic vertebra|Vertebra T1
neighbours: Radiate ligament of head of rib

Vertebra T10.note: T10 lies between discs T9-T10 and T10-T11 and usually carries the tenth rib on a single costal facet. The oesophageal hiatus is at about this level. Pitfall: a paravertebral line bulging from aortic tortuosity or osteophytes can look like a paravertebral mass; correlate on soft-tissue window.

Vertebra T11.note: T11 lies between discs T10-T11 and T11-T12 and carries a single facet for the 11th rib, usually without a transverse costal facet. The diaphragmatic crura are in front. Pitfall: fractures cluster at the thoracolumbar junction, and the ribs here are short and easily miscounted; number the levels from C2.

Vertebra T12.note: T12 lies between discs T11-T12 and T12-L1, with the aortic hiatus between the crura in front of it. Pitfall: a small 12th rib, or a rib on L1, makes it easy to number the levels wrongly. Confirm by counting from C2 and state the convention used in the report.

Vertebra T2.note: T2 lies above disc T2-T3 and shares its costovertebral joints with the second and third ribs. Musculus longus colli lies in front. Pitfall: at the cervicothoracic junction, shoulder streak artefact and partial volume hide fractures and lytic lesions; use thin-slice sagittal reformats and count from C2.
neighbours: Radiate ligament of head of rib

Vertebra T3.note: T3 lies above disc T3-T4, with costovertebral joints on each side and the paravertebral sympathetic trunk next to the rib heads. Pitfall: a contrast-filled Vena intercostalis superior sinistra beside the vertebra can look like a paravertebral node; follow it toward the aortic arch.
neighbours: Radiate ligament of head of rib

Vertebra T4.note: T4 lies between discs T3-T4 and T4-T5. The aortic arch is to its left and in front, and the plane of the sternal angle and carina runs through T4-T5. Pitfall: the azygos arch and the superior intercostal veins can look like right or left paravertebral nodes; trace them on contrast-enhanced images.
neighbours: Radiate ligament of head of rib

Vertebra T5.note: T5 lies between discs T4-T5 and T5-T6. The descending aorta is to its left and in front, and the azygos vein is to its right. Rib heads join its upper and lower costal facets. Pitfall: an osteophyte at a rib head or costovertebral joint can look like a paravertebral mass or bone lesion; check on bone window.
landmarks: lm:Crest of head of rib|Sixth rib

Vertebra T6.note: T6 lies between discs T5-T6 and T6-T7. The oesophagus and descending aorta are in front, and the azygos vein is in front and to the right. Pitfall: in mid-thoracic osteoporotic wedge fractures, a mild anterior height loss is easily missed on axial images; judge vertebral body height on sagittal reformats.
landmarks: lm:Crest of head of rib|Sixth rib

Vertebra T7.note: T7 lies between discs T6-T7 and T7-T8. The posterior pleura and Lobus inferior pulmonis lie on each side, the aorta is in front and to the left, and the azygos vein is to the right. Pitfall: in trauma, paravertebral haematoma can look like atelectasis or effusion, and its presence should prompt a search for a vertebral fracture.

Vertebra T8.note: T8 is a typical thoracic vertebra with upper, lower and transverse costal facets, lying between discs T7-T8 and T8-T9. The hemiazygos crosses to the azygos behind the aorta at about T8-T9. Pitfall: this crossing vein can look like a retrocrural or prevertebral node.

Vertebra T9.note: T9 lies between discs T8-T9 and T9-T10. The aorta is in front and to the left, with the azygos vein to the right and the hemiazygos to the left. The posterior lower lobes lie on each side. Pitfall: Schmorl nodes and vascular channels of the vertebral body can look like lytic metastases; look for a sclerotic rim and connection to the endplate.

Vertebral artery.note: Segments: V1 from the subclavian artery to the C6 foramen transversarium; V2 from C6 to C1; V3 over the sulcus arteriae vertebralis of the atlas; V4 intradural through the foramen magnum, joining the other side at the pontomedullary junction. Pitfall: a small foramen transversarium usually means a hypoplastic, non-dominant artery, not occlusion. Fractures through the foramen need CT angiography.
landmarks: lm:Anterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4
lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipital bone

Vertebral vein.note: A venous plexus surrounds the arteria vertebralis in the foramina transversaria from C1 to C6. It leaves through the C6 foramen and drains into the vena brachiocephalica. Pitfall: asymmetric foramina transversaria, or a small C7 foramen that carries only the vein, are normal variants. Do not report them as stenosis or a fracture line.
landmarks: lm:Anterior tubercle of transverse process|Vertebra C4

Vestibular nerve.note: Its superior and inferior parts fill the posterior half of the meatus acusticus internus, separated by the crista transversa. Bill's bar separates the superior vestibular nerve from the facial nerve at the fundus. Pitfall: the porus is often asymmetric in healthy people. Unilateral widening or erosion suggests a vestibular schwannoma, which needs MRI.
passing: Lateral pontine branches of basilar artery
landmarks: lm:Fundus of internal acoustic meatus (approx.)|Temporal bone
lm:Internal acoustic opening (porus of internal acoustic meatus)|Temporal bone

Vestibular nuclei.note: Lie under the lateral floor of the Ventriculus quartus (area vestibularis), spanning the pontomedullary junction near the lateral recess. Pitfall: posterior circulation stroke presenting with vertigo is often CT-negative, and petrous streak artefact limits the view. A normal CT does not exclude infarction.

Vestibule.note: The central chamber of the labyrinth. The oval window and Basis stapedis lie laterally, the cochlea anteriorly, the semicircular canals posterosuperiorly and the fundus of the internal acoustic meatus medially. Pitfall: a vestibule fused with the lateral semicircular canal into one cavity is a dysplasia. Compare it with the other side.
landmarks: lm:Fundus of internal acoustic meatus (approx.)|Temporal bone
lm:Petrous part of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII).note: It crosses the CPA cistern from the pontomedullary junction through the porus into the Meatus acusticus internus. At the fundus the cochlear nerve is anteroinferior, VII anterosuperior and the vestibular nerves posterior. Pitfall: the flocculus can mimic a CPA mass. Asymmetric flaring of the meatus suggests vestibular schwannoma; check the cochlear nerve canal for stenosis.
passing: Lateral pontine branches of basilar artery
landmarks: lm:Internal acoustic opening (porus of internal acoustic meatus)|Temporal bone

Vitreous body.note: The Corpus vitreum is homogeneous water-density gel behind the Lens, bounded by the Retina. Pitfall: diffuse hyperdensity after vitreoretinal surgery may be silicone oil, which is markedly hyperdense, or gas tamponade. Do not report these as vitreous haemorrhage or a foreign body.

Vomer.note: It forms the posteroinferior bony nasal septum. It sits on the nasal crests of the maxilla and palatine bone, its alae wrap the sphenoid rostrum, and its anterosuperior edge meets the ethmoid perpendicular plate and septal cartilage. Its free posterior edge divides the choanae. Pitfall: a septal spur at the vomer–cartilage junction is not a fracture.
passing: Posterior septal branches of sphenopalatine artery
Septal branches of posterior ethmoidal artery
Anterior septal branches of anterior ethmoidal artery

White matter of spinal cord.note: Peripheral mantle around the H-shaped grey matter. It is bounded by the pia mater, the subarachnoid CSF and the Dura spinalis. Plain CT shows no grey–white differentiation, and myelography outlines only the cord contour. Pitfall: cervicothoracic streak artifact and partial volume with CSF can mimic cord swelling or atrophy, so judge calibre on sagittal reformats.

White matter of telencephalon.note: White matter lies between the cortex and the ventricles and deep grey nuclei. It is judged by how well grey and white matter can be told apart. In the temporal and frontal lobes near the skull base, beam-hardening from the petrous bone and orbital roof can look like low-density white matter or early infarct. Compare both sides and the window settings.
passing: Insular branches of middle cerebral artery (M2)
landmarks: lm:Orbital plate of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Wing of central lobule.note: The Ala lobuli centralis is the lateral extension of the central lobule. It lies over the superior cerebellar peduncle, beneath the free edge of the tentorium near the incisura. Pitfall: the dense free edge of the tentorium and the ambient cistern, where the SCA and CN IV run, can mimic SAH or a small extra-axial lesion.

Xiphoid process.note: Processus xiphoideus projects caudally from the Corpus sterni between the seventh costal cartilages, in front of the diaphragm and liver, with the Linea alba attached. Pitfall: variable ossification and a bifid, perforated or forward-angled tip are normal variants and should not be reported as a fracture or mass.

Zona orbicularis.note: Circular deep capsular fibres that ring the narrowest part of the femoral neck and blend with the capsular ligaments. Pitfall: on CT arthrography this waist-like narrowing of the contrast column mimics a loose body, plica or capsular tear.

Zonular fibres.note: The Fibrae zonulares suspend the Lens from the ciliary body and are not visible on CT. Their integrity is inferred from lens position. Pitfall: lens subluxation without trauma suggests zonular weakness, for example in Marfan syndrome or homocystinuria. Compare with the contralateral lens.

Zygomatic bone.note: It articulates with the frontal, maxillary, temporal and sphenoid bones at four sutures, and a zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture disrupts all four. It forms the lateral orbital rim and floor. Pitfall: normal sutures and the zygomaticofacial foramen can look like fractures. Compare with the other side for diastasis or a step-off.
landmarks: lm:Zygomatic process of temporal bone (tip)|Temporal bone
lm:Orbital surface of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Zygomaticus major muscle.note: Runs from the lateral surface of the Os zygomaticum to the modiolus, crossing over the masseter, buccal fat and Bucinator. Pitfall: the Vena facialis passes deep to it and can look like a nodule in the buccal space. A bifid zygomaticus major is a normal variant.

Zygomaticus minor muscle.note: Runs from the Os zygomaticum, medial to zygomaticus major, to the lateral upper lip, alongside Levator labii superioris. Pitfall: it is thin and often hard to separate from zygomaticus major or Levator labii superioris on CT. Do not report its absence, and do not mistake nasolabial nodes for its muscle belly.
